AGO.name: Angola

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities may secure 'a perpetual right of useful domain' but not equivalent to private title. Right to occupy and use provided in perpetuity. 319 of 1,300+ communities communities identified for titles in 2018. San & Himba IP (26,000 of 25 million pop) struggle as their lands remote &  vulnerable to takings for cattle ranches, mining etc. Land Law 2004, Art. 37, Constitution 2010 (2021).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010 (2021) Arts  7, 15, 37, 223-225. Land Law 2004, Arts. 3, 4, 20, 22, 23, 27. Land Regulations 2007, Art. 20. Presidential Order on Community Land Titling No. 4/2018.
indicators.additional_info: Protection of 'the values and norms of customary law' are constitutionally guaranteed (Art. 223), as are the status, role and functions of traditional authorities (Art 223-225).  Problematic that limitations on the scope of identifiable community domains as owned by communities.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary land titles not equal to private titles, as covering  only provenly 'useful' area determined at adjudication. Positive in that once titled protected from issue of concessions, and compensation at takings is payable for customary domains even if unregistered. Land Act, 2004. Expropriation Law, 2021.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Arts. 10, 12, 37, 45, 55. Constitution 2010, Art. 37, Expropriation Law, 2021 Art. 6
indicators.additional_info: Tenure security is  weak without title. However, Constitution 2010 Art 37 protects communities from expropriation without compensation.  Expropriation Law 2021 requires respect for local customary, ensure participation, and compensation with goods, or land of similar area, economic, social and cultural value (Art 6), and general reference to respect other laws directed to improving their lives.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Titling for issue of Certificate of Useful Customary Domain is free of charge for communities, requires consultation with traditional leaders and families, maps & document issued, but not easy without external facilitation. Most rural communities remain without titles in 2024, despite Presidential Order No. 4/2018 promoting titling. Land Act, 2004
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 23, 24, 34, 37, 51, 53. Presidential Order No 4/18 promoting community titling.
indicators.additional_info: The title for communities is a Right of Useful Customary Domain or Direito de Dominio Util Consuedtuianario. (Land Law, 2004 Art. 34). Formalization procedure detailed in Regulations of Land Concession (August 2007), and in manual prepared by USAID (low uptake of rural community formalization), but accelerating slowly since 2018

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Judicial personhood of rural communities accepted with standing to represent themselves and may hold registered title but only to provenly used areas as determined at adjudication. Right to defend rights directly recognized in law. Land Act 2004 Art. 70.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 70
indicators.additional_info: Only legal entities or persons may obtain Right of Civil Domain (a title on public land) or a Property Right (applies to lands outside public domain).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities have legal right to self-administer lands Constitution recognizes Traditional Authorities and customary values and norms. Risk of elite capture due to lack of obligation to involve all community members in key decision-making. Once the community land is titled, state also has right to dictate rules. Land Act, 2004 Art.1. Constitution Arts. 223-225.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 1 [c], 82. Constitution 2010 Arts. 223-225.
indicators.additional_info: Notable lack of legal stipulation for inclusive  customary institutions; this can enable traditional authorities and elites to exert more than customary authority to inclusion of poorer families. Also note overriding jurisdiction of state and local governments.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: An issued 'right of customary useful domain' cannot be extinguished unless the land fails to be used or is voluntarily vacated. This right is not ownership but an exclusive right to occupy, use, and in perpetuity. Land Law 2004, Arts, 37 & 55.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 37, 55
indicators.additional_info: As with many African states where radical title remains with the State (in practice, Government), allocatees face more uncertainty of security than states where the soil and rights to the soil are directly and exclusive vested in the titled owner. This is visibly in plethora of losses to communities for diamond mining, commercial ranches, commercial ranching,  earmarking of reserves for new settlements. Refer Land Portal Country Profile on Angola, 2022.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No FPIC applied. Limited if any protection on untitled customary lands (most are untitled in 2024). Consultation, not permission is required at compulsory acquisition. Land Act,2004. Expropriation Law 2021.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 9, 12, 28. 37. Expropriation for Public Utility Act, 2021, Article 6.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Constitution 2010 defines State Property as excluding natural forests outside gazetted State Forests. Planted trees on farms belong to holder, including rural families and communities.  Forest and Wildlife Conservation Act, No. 6 of 2017.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2010, Art.. 16. Land Law, 2004, Art. 5 (f), 10.  Forest and Wildlife Conservation Act, No. 6 of 2017.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: State owns all waters, bound to assure access & use to citizens & legal entities for rational needs and uses. Constitution 2010 (2021) Art. 16. Law on Water Use, 2002.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 6 of 2002 on Water Use, Art. 5, 10 (2)
indicators.additional_info: Weaknesses in land law in respect of communal rights may impact negatively on customary rights as affecting waters beyond their farmed lands but access to water a guaranteed right for subsistence use.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest and Wildlife Law No. 6 of 2017 provides for free community use of forest resources outside State Forests for subsistence use. The law encourages community participation in conservation planning and protection.  No provision for communities to declare Community Protected Forests or Wildlife Areas on their titled or untitled domains.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, 2004, Art. 4, 10, 27, 33. Regulations 2007, Art. 30. Basic Law on Forests and Wildlife, 2017. Conservation Act, 2020, Arts. 26, 35, 37.
indicators.additional_info: While natural forests and wildlife belong to the State (2017, Art. 5), law reiterates the right of communities, with or without community land titles, to use forest and wildlife on their customary lands, so long as sustainable for solely for subsistence use of food, clothing, medicine, building, handicrafts, culture etc. (Arts. 5,  65, 66. 67). Communities also have obligations to protect forest on their lands, including forest patches, (Art. 20), and provide Observers to report unlawful use ( Art.156-158) as employees.  They may apply for exploitation rights (commercial use) (Art. 68). However, there is no provision for Communities to own Protected Areas of their own or to see restitution of such in Angola's laws. Conservation Act, 2020 reiterates rights, duties of communities, with Observers.

ARG.name: Argentina

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution "empowers Congress to" respect and protect indigenous community land rights, but this provision has not been implemented by federal legislation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011); Civil Code http://www.iwgia.org/images/stories/sections/regions/latin-america/documents/IW2013/Argentina.pdf
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution empowers Congress to guarantee respect for the community possession and ownership of lands [indigenous communities] traditionally occupy, but this is only a legislative directive (not a right) (Sec. 75(17), Constitution, 1994). Ley de Tierras Rurales is silent on whether indigenous/community lands are protected by law. NOTE: After ratifying the Convention 169, the Argentinian Government passed Law 26.160 to comply with Art.14.2 of ILO Convention 169 to prevent forcible eviction of indigenous groups on ancestral lands, but this law was only temporarily in effect until 2013. In 2006, the government launched the Agenda of Indigenous Community Land Survey by the National Institute for Indigenous Affairs, but this program was weakly implemented in Argentina. Since 2012, legal reformers have proposed including indigenous land rights as form of property right granted protection by Argentina's Civil Code, but the Code has not yet been amended.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While the Constitution calls for Congress to respect indigenous/ community land rights, federal legislation, which implements this legislative directive, has not been enacted.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina
indicators.additional_info: Article 7 of Law No. 23.302 recognizes that indigenous communities duly registered must be allocated land and awarded ownership, Argentina ratified Convention 169- Indigenous and Tribal People's Convention in 2000. Article 7 of Convention 169 calls for states to respect the land rights of indigenous populations (Art. 7, Convention 169), but Convention 169 has not been implemented through federal legislation. See recent news article on controversy over indigenous battle to reclaim ancestral lands: http://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/jul/05/argentina-fight-reclaim-ancestral-land-indigenous-leader.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Law No 23.302 (1985) provides a registration process for indigenous communities to register their lands, but the law does not establish clear, accessible, affordable procedures.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Law No. 23.302 of idngienosu policy and support to aboriginal communities; C Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011)
indicators.additional_info: Article 3 of Law No. 23.302 (1985) provides that the registration must include the name and address of community members, data and background information. However, there is no provision ensuring that detailed maps and other information will be provided.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 2 of Law No. 23.302 (1985) provides that the legal personality of indigenous communities is recognized.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation, which grants indigenous communities legal authority over their land, has not been passed.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on whether indigenous/ community lands can be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The State can expropriate collectively-owned land for a public purpose, and does not need to consult or obtain consent from indigenous communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 17, Art. 75(17) Constitution of Argentina; Ley 26.737, Tierras Rurals (2011)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on whether indigenous groups/communities have rights to trees located on or near their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley de Promocion Forestal 13273

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Civil Code grants all citizens the right to use and enjoy water resources within the country. This means that communities are granted the right to use water. Private land owners are granted ownership rights to water located on their land. However, since national laws do not granted communities ownership rights to their lands land, communities presumably do not have ownership rights (only use rights) to water located on their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Argentina; Civil Code; Ley 25668 que Regula el Régimen de Gestión Ambiental de Aguas
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 2341 of the Civil Code, "individuals have the right to use and enjoy water pursuant to the present regulation; and 3) navigable lakes and their beds." Furthemore, article 2350 states "Streams that are born and die within a particularly property belong to the owner of it.  Article 2349 state tat the use and enjoyment of the lakes that are not navigable, belongs to the riparian owners. Article 2340 provides for public ownership of surface and groundwater not located on private property. Article 6 of Ley 25668 stipulates that the use of water requires the approval of the competent government authority.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on whether indigenous groups/communities have rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley No. 22.351 de los Parques Nacionales Monumentos Naturales y Reservas nacionales

AUS.name: Australia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples (Aboriginals)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The High Court of Australia recognized indigenous communities  have rights to their land. Native is a bundle of rights and not akin to freehold title. Exactly what rights native title amounts to depends on the nature of the indigenous group’s customary use of the land. The fact that native title can be extinguished or suppressed through certain acts further weakens the legal status. But Government retains right to extinguish native titles under the Native Title Act 1993.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 10-11 Native Title Act 1993; High Court Decisions- Western Australia v. Common Wealth (1995) and Mabo v. Queensland (1992).
indicators.additional_info: High Court of Australia held that, according to common law, native title gives rise to the right  of indigenous communities to their land.  The Native Title Act 1993  formalized this recognition at common law and provides the rules for when and how native title can be recognized and “claimed” by indigenous groups through native title determinations and what acts of extinguishment give rise to compensation. The Indigenous Land Corporation assists indigenous Australians in purchasing land. NOTE: There are also land rights that are granted through specific state statutes and which are separate to native title (and also predate the recognition of native title). These are the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1978 (NT) and  Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara Land Rights Act 1981 (SA) and these do amount to freehold title – although also inalienable and subject to the terms of the act itself.  NOTE: There are several tenure types which this legal assessment does not cover, such as Northern Territory Aboriginal Lands Trust, land purchased by the Indigenous Land Corporation, and other state trusts. Legislation that protects and respects indigenous community lands was enacted at the state-level (Aboriginal Land Act 1991 (Queensland), Land Act 1995 (Queens Land), Aboriginal Lands Act 1970 (Victoria),  Aboriginal Land Act 1978 (Northern Territory), Aboriginal Communities Act 1979 (Western Territories 1979), Aboriginal Lands Act 1991 (Victoria); Aboriginal Lands Act 1995 (Tasmania), Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (New South Wales). However, the assessment of the LandMark indicators is limited to federal legislation (Native Title Act 1993). Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Native title is not given equal statutory protection as freehold tenure, and native titles must be registered to take effect and can be extinguished by the gov't under a wide range of circumstances.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 10-11, Native Title Act 1993; High Court Decisions- Mabo v. Queensland (1992), Yorta Yorta Aboriginal Community v. Victoria (Yorta Yorta) (2002)
indicators.additional_info: The High Court of Australia held in Mabo v. Queensland native title survived the Crown's acquisition of sovereignty, and so the indigenous populations of Australia continue to have rights and interests in the land they possess (paragraph 62 of Decision). The High Court also held that the law precludes any discrimination against the holders of native title which adversely affects their enjoyment of their title in comparison with the enjoyment by other title holders. Native title may be extinguished under certain circumstances as long as indigenous communities are compensated (Sec. 23, Native Title Act 1993). NOTE: 1)  In the decision of Yorta Yorta, the High Court held that, in order to prove native title, claimants must establish there has been an acknowledgment and observance of laws and customs on a substantially uninterrupted basis since sovereignty. 2) Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law requires the Register of Native Title Claims to include detailed information and a map of the land covered by a claim. Federal law established the Indigenous Land Corporation, which provides financial assistance to indigenous communities to claim native lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 62, 184- Native Title Act 1993; Land Fund and Indigenous Land Corporation (ATSIC Amendment) Act 1995
indicators.additional_info: Applications for Native Titles must include information on the boundaries of the area covered by the application and a map showing the boundaries of the area mentioned. The Federal Court of Australia is charged with deciding on claims to native titled lands. In addition to assisting ICs in acquiring their land, the functions of Indigenous Land Corporation are to "make grants of money to Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander corporations for the acquisition of interests in land." The Indigenous Land Corporation assists indigenous Australians in purchasing land. NOTE: Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court granted indigenous populations legal personality in several constitutional court cases, but must first register to obtain legal personality for the purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: High Court Decisions- Mabo v. Queensland (1992), Yorta Yorta Aboriginal Community v. Victoria (Yorta Yorta) (2002)
indicators.additional_info: To receive legal personality, indigenous groups must first register as “native title claimants” through a Native Title Prescribed Body Corporate, which is a legal entity that holds native title either on trust or as an agent for the community. NOTE: Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The High Court of Australia held that native title entitles indigenous inhabitants, in accordance with their laws or customs, to their traditional lands. Traditional customs must be observed on "substantially uninterrupted basis" to claim title. However, native title rights must generally give way to other rights and are inalienable except to the crown. Furthermore, the Native Title Act provides native title holders with a right to negotiate what can and cannot occur on their land, but these holders do not have veto power.
indicators.law_and_provision: High Court Decision- Mabo v. Queensland (No. 2) (1992); Yorta Yorta Aboriginal Community v. Victoria (Yorta Yorta)
indicators.additional_info: The High Court in Mabo held that "native title has its origin in traditional laws acknowledged by and the traditional customs observed by the indigenous inhabitants of a territory. The nature...of native title must be ascertained as a matter of fact by reference to those laws and customs" (paragraph 64 of Mabo decision). This provision indicates that indigenous populations have legal authority over their lands. NOTE: 1) In the decision of Yorta Yorta, the High Court held that, in order to prove native title, claimants must establish there has been an acknowledgment and observance of laws and customs on a substantially uninterrupted basis since sovereignty. 2) Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Formal entitlements to native title (NT) land may be held in perpetuity, and the law grants compensation when native titles are extinguished in accordance with the Native Title Act. There are no explicit durational limits on NTs established by law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 23J, 24BB-24BE Native Title Act 1993
indicators.additional_info: Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Native Title (Prescribed Bodies Corporate) Regulations 1999 provides that body corporates holding native title rights must consult and obtain consent with holders of native title holders prior to making a decision affecting their livelihood. Furthermore, the Native Title Act provides native title holders with a right to negotiate what can and cannot occur on their land, but these holders do not have veto power.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 8, 8A Native Title (Prescribed Bodies Corporate) Regulations 1999; Sec. 22H, 24JAA(13), 36B) Native Title Act 1993
indicators.additional_info: Section 25 of the Native Title Act provides a right to negotiate. In other words, native title holders have the legal right to negotiate what can occur on land for which they hold native title, and compensation is payable for any extinguishment of their rights. While native title holders do not have the right to veto activities occurring on their land, the Native Title Act sets out a process that must be followed in good faith. NOTE: 1) State-level legislation established free, prior, informed consent of indigenous communities as requisite to acquiring indigenous-held land. The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976, for example, states that the Land Council must consult with traditional Aboriginal owners of, and other Aboriginals interested in, Aboriginal land." The Land Council cannot transfer or surrender an estate or interest in land unless it is satisfied "the traditional Aboriginal owners (if any) of that land understand the nature and purpose of the proposed grant, transfer or surrender and, as a group, consent to it..." 2) Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Native Title Act does not explicitly establish indigenous community rights to trees located on indigenous-held land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Native Title Act 1993
indicators.additional_info: Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Native Title Act 1993 indicates that indigenous populations can file claims for native title to water resources, but the law does not specify the extent of indigenous water rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 184, 211 Native Title Act 1993; Water Act 2007; Water Management Act 2000
indicators.additional_info: Applications may include assertions that a person holds native title in relation to a "specified area of land or waters" (Art. 184, Native Title Act 1993). Australia's Water Act 2007 provides that "nothing in this [Water] Act affects the operation of the Native Title Act 1993." NOTE: Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No explicit ownership rights, but the law allows indigenous communities to apply for native in PAs and continue traditional use of areas within Commonwealth reserves for hunting, fishing or food-gathering or ceremonial and religious purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 8, 359A, 528, The Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999; Sec. 211, Native Title Act 1993
indicators.additional_info: The law also protects areas with evident "indigenous heritage value", defined as a place of significance to indigenous persons based on their customs, traditions, etc., by making it offense to commit acts which violate these areas (Sec. 15C, The Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999). NOTE: 1) The Native Title Act allows the government to extinguish Native Titles for the purpose of creating a protected area. The High Court of Australia, in Western Australia v. Ward, held that native title consists of a bundle of rights, which can be individually extinguished. 2) Peer reviewed by Eliza Northrop, Associate, International Climate Initiative, WRI.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Austria's federal skeletal law (corridor constitutional principle 1951) establishes rights to common property, but the details of these rights are established through state-level legislation (LandMark's legal assessment, however, is limited to federal legislation). Communities with rights over common pasture land are organized as corporations.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016
indicators.additional_info: Pasture communities in the Austrian Alps are granted communal grazing and other use rights to common pastures and through state-level legislation. For example, Law on Community Land (Vorarlberg), 2012 and Vorarlberg Agricultural Land Planning Act provides these rights. According to a secondary source, "In the mountain valleys of Austria's South-Eastern Alps (province of Kärnten), common property is one of the prevalent categories of rural land ownership and therefore a major factor in land use planning and policy. Administration of these joint ownership structures has been institutionalised in 1853 already, and since 1950 their legal status has been that of corporations under public law ("Agrargemeinschaften", rural common property). A special supervising authority ("Agrarbehörde") has been installed as early as 1883, to safeguard sustainable management of the commons...All regulations related to Agrargemeinschaften are found in the respective Austrian federal skeletal law and detailed legislation of the provinces (Federal states) based on the framework established there. Regulations comprise the appropriate and orderly management and use of commons by a majority of owners, and also the procedure of dissolution of Agrargemeinschaften. Agrargemeinschaftenare legal persons under public law. The law defines a “Agrargemeinschaft” as group of all owners of estates where ownership of the estates as such is directly connected to and results in ownership of fractional shares of the commonly owned land (tenancy in common...)". Citation: Herbst, P. Rural Common Property in Austria. ASCP Oaxaca Aug 04, Ref.Nr.: 439. Available at: https://dlc.dlib.indiana.edu/dlc/bitstream/handle/10535/1990/Herbst_Rural_040602_Paper439.pdf?sequence=1. Through state and provincial legislation, communities are also granted rights to forests. See secondary source: Weiss, G. et al. 2015. Forest Land Ownership Change in Austria. COST Action FP1201 FACESMAP Country Report. Available at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/278671932_Forest_Land_Ownership_Change_in_Austria_COST_Action_FP1201_-_FACESMAP_Country_Report

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The agricultural authorities are legally empowered to determine which properties are agricultural community property (Sec. 17, federal skeletal law). The government can expropriate commonly held agricultural land for a public purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016
indicators.additional_info: Section 15 of the federal skeletal laws recognizes the rights of common property held by agrarian communities. According to Section 17 of the federal skeletal laws, the agricultural authorities have discretion to determine which properties are agricultural community property. These properties are to be designated at the request of the agricultural authority in public books as such. If the membership of the ownership of certain properties (headquarters property) bound, this fact must be seen at the headquarters buildings. Under section 18 of the law, the sale and division of agricultural land  must be approved by the agricultural authority and provincial legislation describes the details regarding when a permit may be denied.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The federal legislation does not establish registration processes for demarcating or formalizing community pasture rights. Presumably, these processes are laid out in provincial legislation (However, LandMark's assessment is limited to national level legislation). In the federal skeletal law, there are no clear provisions ensuring agrarian communities are able to easily access and afford registration processes.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The federal skeletal act recognizes the legal personality of agricultural communities.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Agricultural communities function like decentralized corporations under public law and are therefore self-governing. The federal skeletal law grants agricultural authorities broad legal authority over agricultural community land. Not only can authorities determine which properties can be designated as community land, but Section 18 of the federal skeletal law states that agricultural authorities have discretion to approve sales and divisions of agricultural land.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016
indicators.additional_info: According to a secondary source, community pastures ("Agrargemeinschaften") are self governing as corporations under public law. The source states "It is their legal obligation to sustainably manage their commonly owned lands. Administration and management of Agrargemeinschaften is performed through their executive bodies which are the Plenary Assembly, Management Committee, Headman...Agrargemeinschaften are self-governing bodies; basically they are entitled to decide all their internal matters autonomously and self-responsibly. Still, they are subject to supervision by a special supervising authority, the Agrarbehörde, to safeguard sustainable management of the commons." Herbst, P. Rural Common Property in Austria. ASCP Oaxaca Aug 04, Ref.Nr.: 439. Available at: https://dlc.dlib.indiana.edu/dlc/bitstream/handle/10535/1990/Herbst_Rural_040602_Paper439.pdf?sequence=1

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Federal Water Act, 1959 grants all citizens the right to use water for domestic purposes. Futhermore private property owners have a right to dispose water on their property for domestic purposes, so community landowners are granted this right.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Water Act, 1959; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016
indicators.additional_info: Private waters, such as springs, small rivers, and ground waters are privately owned by the owner of the property where it is located. Private owners have a right of diposal (for domestic and household economic needs) of the water on his or her property.  Surface water is mainly publicly owned; the Austrain Water Act defines all rivers and lakes within Austria as public waters. Government permission to use water is required for any use of public waters exceeding "public use", any use of private waters touching interest or the rights of a third party, and development or use of groundwater exceeding the necessary domestic economic need of the landowner. See F. Oblerteiner. Legal Basis of Water Management in Austria. Available at: http://www.hydro.tuwien.ac.at/fileadmin/mediapool-hydro/Diverse/Lehre/Wasserrecht/Legal_Basis_of_Water_Management_in_Austria.pdf; See also OECD profile on Austrian Water Resource Allocation: https://www.oecd.org/austria/Water-Resources-Allocation-Austria.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly recognize community rights to land in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016

AUT.Communities Q1: Does the law recognize a:
Partial, significant progress — Austria's federal skeletal law (corridor constitutional principle 1951) establishes rights to common property, but the details of these rights are established through state-level legislation (LandMark's legal assessment, however, is limited to federal legislation). Communities with rights over common pasture land are organized as corporations. (Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016)
AUT.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige:
Partial, significant progress — The agricultural authorities are legally empowered to determine which properties are agricultural community property (Sec. 17, federal skeletal law). The government can expropriate commonly held agricultural land for a public purpose. (Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016)
AUT.Communities Q3: Does the law require the:
No, the law does not address the issue — The federal legislation does not establish registration processes for demarcating or formalizing community pasture rights. Presumably, these processes are laid out in provincial legislation (However, LandMark's assessment is limited to national level legislation). In the federal skeletal law, there are no clear provisions ensuring agrarian communities are able to easily access and afford registration processes. (Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016)
AUT.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t:
Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The federal skeletal act recognizes the legal personality of agricultural communities. (Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016)
AUT.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t:
Partial, significant progress — Agricultural communities function like decentralized corporations under public law and are therefore self-governing. The federal skeletal law grants agricultural authorities broad legal authority over agricultural community land. Not only can authorities determine which properties can be designated as community land, but Section 18 of the federal skeletal law states that agricultural authorities have discretion to approve sales and divisions of agricultural land. (Constitution of Austria; Forestry Act, 1975; Property Valuation Act, 1955; Gesamte Rechtsvorschrift für Flurverfassungs-Grundsatzgesetz 1951, Fassung vom
29.06.2016)
AUT.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti:
Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The federal skeletal law does not establish durational limits on the ownership rights of agricultural communities, which implies that such rights may be held in perpetuity. 29.06.2016)

BDI.name: Burundi

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land Code 2011 recognizes customary farming homesteads as property but excludes communal marshes or 'unoccupied' grazing lands or forests. Only individuals or legal entities can secure Certificates and  convertible into private title deeds (titres foncier), conversion now required if transferred (2020). Land Code 2011, Registration Law 2020.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2018 Art. 36. The Land Code, No. 1/13 of 2011. Decree  No. 100/129 of 2016, applying  the Land Code. Decree No. 100/0114 of 2016 on registration procedure. Decree No. 100/15 of 2017 on Reorganization of National Land Commission. Law No. 1/05 of 2020 Establishing The Registration Fees in Land Matters.
indicators.additional_info: Rights of Batwa forest people minority  (c. 100,000 citizens, 1% of population) lost due to nationalization of forests.. Art. 380 of Land Code, 2011: "All real rights exercised by any natural or legal person under private law by virtue of custom or title of occupation as  issued by the competent authority on non-State owned land, resulting in a personal or collective, permanent and lasting holding according to the customs of the time and of the place and accordance to the vocation of the land...".  In reality eldes play minor role with a local government 'hill council' holding authority.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition required customary titles for homes & farms only, and unequal to Titre Foncier titles. Loss of village commons would be worse if not for massive expansion of farming. IP Batwa forest people (1% pop) forced to live in allocated lands next to ancestral forests, subject to new removals to expand Protected Forests. Land Code 2011.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Land Code, No. 1/13 of 2011. Decree  No. 100/129 of 2016, applying  the Land Code. Decree No. 100/0114 of 2016 on registration procedure. Decree No. 100/15 of 2017 on Reorganization of National Land Commission.
indicators.additional_info: Legal claim of security of Land Certificates is undermined by providing opportunity to convert Certificate into Land Titles, only affordable by the wealthy and now compulsory to make transaction. The Land Code, 2011 established the National Land Commission (CFN) in Articles 452-453 and Decree No. 100/15 of 2017 to lead land reform. No provision for restitution of lands allocated to private investors and persons, and conflict continues between original customary owners who fled the civil war and those allocated or taking those lands, now for long periods.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land Code 2011 & Decree 2016 elaborate decentralized land administration regime as 'Communal Land Services'. To cut costs individual customary holders may secure Land Certificates rather than absolute statutory titles (available). Commons not included. Land Code 2011 & Reg. 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Land Code, No. 1/13 of 2011, and Code 2011 Arts 380-410. Decree  No. 100/129 of 2016, applying  the Land Code. Decree No. 100/0114 of 2016 on registration procedure. Arts. 2-3). Decree No. 100/15 of 2017 on Reorganization of National Land Commission. Law No. 1/05 of 2020 Establishing The Registration Fees in Land Matters.
indicators.additional_info: The procedure for reconnaissance of occupants, communal land plan in each area (collines, or hill commissions), identification, adjudication and demarcation of each plot is sound but only applied in half of communes (76 of 119) by 2021. Research  show that resolving disputes between original holders who fled, and those who took over occupation during the civil war, is proving beyond the capacity of the committees to resolve. Customary Certificates' comply with customary law as recognized at the time by the local hill commission' (Land Decree 2016, Art. 2-3). Only individuals can apply (often spouses apply for own plot) . Certificate not equivalent to Titre Foncier (statutory title). Conversion possible at high cost (Code, Art. 410, and Decree, Art. 52).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision in 2011 law for communities to be legal persons and cannot secure lands as communities. Registered entities such as for a large family consolidating parcels. Legal requirement in 2020 that no transactions without conversion of Customary Deed into absolute title inhibits lawful or recorded sales or transfers.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Land Code, No. 1/13 of 2011. Decree  No. 100/129 of 2016, Regulatory Application of  Land Code. Decree No. 100/0114 of 2016 on Registration. Law No. 1/05 of 2020 Establishing The Registration Fees in Land Matters.
indicators.additional_info: Most Burundians operate today as individual families, not as communities. Many lease, rent or buy land, due to dwindling land per capita in family and effects of civil war which saw many flee and their lands taken up by others,  those returning often forced to find land elsewhere.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities, as defined by hills (collines) are de facto managers; customary law the regulator, but elders councils (Bashingantahe) replaced with hill councils, reducing elders to advisers. Community Land Register opened for the colline. Supervised by CFS (Community Tenure Service) at commune level.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Code Arts. Arts. 6-45, 380-410 & Regulatory Decree No 100/129, 2016 Art. 5). Law No. 1/16 of 2015 On the Transfer of Powers from the State to Communes.
indicators.additional_info: Hill chiefs traditionally the administrators but "many disappeared in the 1960s (killed or in exile" (IS Academy, 2012). Also came into disrepute due to favouritism and corruption. "Land transactions and succession are now regulated within families, possibly accompanied by an (informal) deed outlining the transaction, which may have been witnessed by Bashingantahe (traditional institution) or the local administration (hill or commune)" (ibid). The CFS (Service  Foncier Communal) responsible for land administration. The Administrator appoints a reconnaissance hill commission to identify plots. Following resolve of objections or when deadline passes, a Communal Land Register is opened &  land certificates issued to individual parcel holders.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Ownership in perpetuity is normal under customary law,  inheritance accepted as a principle mode of transfer on death of the parcel owner. However, the incidents of the Certificate to be used for customary holdings are not specified  under Article 38-45 on Registration of Certificate (Decree No.100/129 of 2016).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Code No 1/13 of 2011. Decree No. 100/129 of 2016, Regulatory Application of  Land Code.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: FPIC is not specified. Compensation for trees, crops and buildings is to be paid prior to removal at compulsory acquisition. Arti 244 of 2011 Code obliges Government to guarantee against eviction. Decree 2002 supports relocation by returnees finding their lands occupied by others after 30 years. Land Code 2011 and its Regulatory Decree 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2018 Art. 36.Land Code No 1/13 of 2011. Decree No. 100/129 of 2016, Regulatory Application of  Land Code.
indicators.additional_info: Procedure for expropriation for public purpose is provided in Land Code 2011 at Arts. 417-419.  Crops, trees, and buildings are to be compensated (Ordinance  710/540 of 2022). Removal of longstanding holders and users of marshes and grazing lands by State which  claimed these lands as wastelands under Land Code 2011, prompted bitter complaints.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Under revised Forest Code 2016 a distinction between the State and Communal Forest Estates drawn. Villages retain all trees on their household lands. Although ownership vested in Commune, they manage forests in the area. Protected Landscapes may be declared. Forest Code 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 1/07 of 2016 Revising the Forestry Code.
indicators.additional_info: Under Forest Code 2016 village communities retain rights to forests and trees. They may create Protected Landscapes (Art. 4). Participation of communities, recognition of social and cultural values & their services are made principles (Art. 5). The Communal Forest Estate is distinct from the State Forest Estate and made the private property of communes as classified forests (Art 39). Use rights are exercised exclusively by villages in return responsibility for conservation or reafforestation (Art.55).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water falls within the public domain, and rights constitute use rights to this public resource. The Water Code 2012 establishes participation of women as a principle along with special water access for vulnerable groups. Water User Associations to govern village/colline waters may be  established.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on the Water Code, No. 1 of 2012.
indicators.additional_info: "Legally-recognized user associations can organize themselves to contribute to rational water use, in line with the principle of participatory management" (Art. 32).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rural communities cannot own State Protected Areas (PA) but may co-manage these under an MoU. Consultation & community participation is obligatory for all PA (Art. 17). A community representative is elected to the Board (Art. 178). Protected Landscapes may cover community lands outside PA but not classified as PA. Environmental Code, 2000 & Amendment 2021, Law 2011 on Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 1/09 of 2021 Amending the Environmental Code of 2000. Law No. 1 2011 on Establishment and Management of Protected Areas.
indicators.additional_info: Law of 2011 on Creation of Protected Areas, Art. 9, 12 -14).  A MoU structures roles, rights and responsibilities (Art. 15). Buffer zones are set up within national parks and other state protected areas for local use. Local use of the State Forest Estate is permitted, including specified beekeeping in buffer zones, grazing, harvesting fruit, food, medicinal plants and fuelwood collection (Art 54) exercised exclusively by local populations (Art 55).

BEN.name: Benin

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Individual/family rights for homesteads eligible for Rural Land Certificates (Customary), or more costly and with more security, statutory Land Titles of absolute ownership. Unequal. No provision for commons to be vested in community, retained by communes although village use rights identified in Rural Land Plan must be upheld by communes. Land and Property Code 2013 (2017).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.
indicators.additional_info: A rural land certificate is defined as: "A document recording and confirming land rights established or acquired in accordance with custom or local practices and standards, as extracted from the rural land plan. It carries with it a presumption of acquired rights, which is valid until proven otherwise before a judge" (Art. 7). Land title: "Only the land title confers full ownership in the Republic of Benin. All the attributes of the right of ownership are attached to it" (Art 112).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Presumption that villagers would convert weaker Customary Certificates (Arts. 112, 376) into Land Titles has not occurred. Basis of prior of rights for conversion widened  in 2017 (Art. 375). Although unequal in market value the law enables Certificates to be security for loans (Art. 35). Use rights & other derivative rights are also identified in the local Rural Land Plan & Register (Art. 359).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.
indicators.additional_info: The 2013 law assumed customary certificates would be converted into land titles. 2017 amendments centralized the procedure due to municipal corruption but as of 2021 only 60,000 of 5+ million needed titles registered. The deadline for conversion was extended by the 2017 law to 2023, subject to further extension. Cost is indicated as the main constraint. Amended art. 520 in 2017: "Rural land certificate prior ... shall, on simple presentation by the holder, be converted into a land title in accordance with Article 116". Art. 116 requires simple forms, plan of property and document of ownership with birth certificate and ID if within the Rural Plan area. Donor-funded acceleration project underway.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Titling for Customary Certificates following preparation of Rural Land Plans is inexpensive, but relies on external support. c. 500 of c.3,000 villages completed Plans by 2024 and issued Certificates. Cost of their conversion into absolute ownership Titles remains high and largely undertaken only by elites. Land & Property Code 2013 (2017).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.
indicators.additional_info: Village chiefs and councils remain key to the adjudication and mapping process including installing boundary markers between homesteads at village level and issue of Customary Land Certificates, as supervised by Commune authorities. The Plan comprises a graphic illustration of all parcels within the village and register of landholders, attached to each unit and the nature of his/her/their rights (Arts. 192-197). Register may contain individuals, producer groups, family associations or legal entities (Art. 198, Art. 348). Communes are responsible for approval of the Plans and issue of Certificates (Art. 203). Commune and national forests are excluded, only sacred forests of families/clans may be registered.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not recognize rural villages as legal persons (Art. 44, Territorial Administration Law 1999) nor provide for collective titles over all village or just its commons vested in the community. Commons retained by local governments (communes) but village rights of access & use upheld by Village Chiefs under Commune direction. Land & Property Code 2013 (2017).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15. Law Organizing the Territorial Administration of the Republic of Benin No. 97-028 of January 15 1999.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Village Chiefs & Councils key to the adjudication and mapping process & installing boundary markers between homesteads. Plan comprises map of plots and Register of rights. Commune authorities approve Plan and issue Certificates to family parcels. Commune and national forests are excluded, only sacred forests of families/clans may be registered. Land & Property Code 2013 (2017).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.
indicators.additional_info: Village chiefs and councils remain key to the adjudication and mapping process including installing boundary markers between homesteads at village level and issue of Customary Land Certificates, as supervised by Commune authorities. The Plan comprises a graphic illustration of all parcels within the village and register of landholders, attached to each unit and the nature of his/her/their rights (Arts. 192-197). Register may contain individuals, producer groups, family associations or legal entities (Art. 198, Art. 348). Communes are responsible for approval of the Plans and issue of Certificates (Art. 203). Commune and national forests are excluded, only sacred forests of families/clans may be registered.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: A customary right as documented in a Rural Land Certificate is of no fixed term, and may be acquired and transferred by inheritance, testamentary succession, inter vivos gift, etc as per local customary law (Art. 360). Legal limitations upon transfers or sales to inhibit loss of family and village lands to outsiders. Land and Property Code 2013 (2017).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.
indicators.additional_info: The supervising Commune must approve transfers/sale of land between 2-20 ha,within any village. The Agency National Domaine et du Foncier must approve transfers/sale for 20-100ha, with addition of Minister's approval for 100-500 ha. Approval of transfer/sale of village land above 500 ha requires a Decree (Art. 361).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for village community consent at expropriation. This requires requires payment of fair and prior compensation, and scope for amicable agreement through consultation (Art.. 211). A representative of affected communities is part of the enquiry commission (Art. 218). Affected persons have right to appeal decision on compensation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2013-01 as amended by Law No. 2017-15.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Planted & natural trees are attached to holdings under customary tenure effective for homesteads/farms. The State is the owner of all classified, protected and reforestation forests, management usually devolved to local communes (Forest law l1993, Art. 10).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 97-028 of January 15 1999 Organizing the Territorial Administration, Art. 33, 44. Forestry Law No. 93-009 of 2 July 1993.  Order NO.MEHU/DGLAA/PC/S  of 2012 on Conditions for Sustainable Management of Sacred Forests.
indicators.additional_info: Note that according to the 1999 law, sacred forests belonging to the whole community as compared to a family are vested in the commune due to lack of provision for collective tenure. Management is vested in the  local Community Local Forest Committees.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the State but landholders may use most waters on their lands without licences for domestic purposes. Commune local governments are responsible for overseeing management.  Water Law 2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Law, No. 2010-44 of 24 November 2010.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Tiny sacred forests abound (est. >3,000) but subject to registration and & rules since 2012. Even customarily owned larger forests are State owned and Commune manages. Villages actively involved in their management. Local use rights respected, with restrictions on felling. No  provision for community-owned protected forests. Forest Code 1993, Forest Order 0121/2012.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Code, No. 93-009 of 2 July 1993. Interministerial Order No. 0121 of 2012 On Conditions for Sustainable Management of Sacred Forests
indicators.additional_info: While customarily defined and managed sacred forest abound in Benin (estimated >3,000) these are very small, and subject to formal registration by forestry ministry, subject to restricted use rights (Order No. 0121/2012). Individuals and families remain owners of the land, distinct from status as sacred forests. Larger forests within the c. 500 communes fall under communes. Many villages are engaged in participatory management of these Commune Forests but no tenure rights over these customary domains. Most forest is State property as classified forests, national parks and other protected areas, and reforestation zones. Local rights of use are respected in State and Commune Forests, with restrictions, such as no felling or clearing (Art. 25-32, Forest Code, 1993). No legal provision exists for community-owned  forest protected forests, as no scope for collective property of villages, although may form a Cooperative for such purpose.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Tiny sacred forests abound (est. >3,000) but subject to registration and & rules since 2012. Even customarily owned larger forests are State owned and Commune manages. Villages actively involved in their management. Local use rights respected, with restrictions on felling. No  provision for community-owned protected forests. Forest Code 1993, Forest Order 0121/2012.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Code, No. 93-009 of 2 July 1993. Interministerial Order No. 0121 of 2012 On Conditions for Sustainable Management of Sacred Forests
indicators.additional_info: While customarily defined and managed sacred forest abound in Benin (estimated >3,000) these are very small, and subject to formal registration by forestry ministry, subject to restricted use rights (Order No. 0121/2012). Individuals and families remain owners of the land, distinct from status as sacred forests. Larger forests within the c. 500 communes fall under communes. Many villages are engaged in participatory management of these Commune Forests but no tenure rights over these customary domains. Most forest is State property as classified forests, national parks and other protected areas, and reforestation zones. Local rights of use are respected in State and Commune Forests, with restrictions, such as no felling or clearing (Art. 25-32, Forest Code, 1993). No legal provision exists for community-owned  forest protected forests, as no scope for collective property of villages, although may form a Cooperative for such purpose.

Unequal. No provision for commons to be vested in community, retained by communes although village use rights identified in Rural Land Plan must be upheld by communes. BEN.Indigenous Q2: Does the law give indigen: Partial, limited progress — Presumption that villagers would convert weaker Customary Certificates (Arts. 112, 376) into Land Titles has not occurred.
