BFA.name: Burkina Faso

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law since 2009 recognises customary rights as legal possession governed by customary rules - with or without issue of Certificates of Possession. These available to individuals, families or to the village if a single clan. Larger commons vested in Communes but managed by villages. Pastoral Act prioritized pastoralism in 27 zones. Land Laws 2009 & 2012. Pastoral Act 2003.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law Reorganizing Rural Tenure , 1984. Law No. 034-2009/AN  Rural Land Tenure, s. 2, 4, 6, 7,13. Law No. 034-2012  Agrarian and Land Reform. Pastoral Act 2003. National Rural Land Security Policy. Decree No. 2007-610.
indicators.additional_info: All land belongs to the nation in common; Constitution, 1991 (2015) Art. 14, Law 034-2009/AN Art. 2. Rights to land by State, local governments (Communes) and private holdings (customary or statutory) put on an equal footing. Legal provision &  guidance for  communities to define and operate customary rules under the aegis of Local Land Charters (Chartres foncières rurales) (Law No. 34-2009/AN On Rural Land Tenure, Art. 11-18). Each  community is to identify commons for local management but these forest or rangeland commons vested in Commune (Law 034-2009, Art 13 & 34).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Laws state equity of customary rights including unregistered lands as 'property assets'. Rise in status also supported by (a) devolutionary empowerment through Local Land Charters, elected village councils & committees, and (b) support for customary rules. Main legal shortfall is that larger commons vested in Communes, not villages. Land Laws 2009, 2012.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 034-2009/AN On Rural Land Tenure, s. 2, 4, 6, 7,13. Law No. 034-2012 On Agrarian Land Reform, Decree No. 2007-610, National Rural Land Security Policy.
indicators.additional_info: The 2009 & 2012 laws protect and encourage customary law and rights, instructs villages to develop Local Land Charters for regulation and management including of shared resources, like forests, sacred groves, ponds, pasture, cattle tracks. However, larger forests and grazing zones are registered under Commune. Certification of Possession over individual and family land (collective) is not compulsory. Art 44 of 2009 declares certificates of ownership have same legal force as possession, reinforced by Arts. 30, 194 and 196 in 2012 law. Not borne out in practice. Compulsory acquisition is subject to prior payment of compensation (Constit. Art 15, Law 2012 Art. 325). 2012 law also includes amicable negotiation (Art. 326). Public purpose includes nature conservation and pastoral land needs. Application of the law is slow and partial, civil conflict contributing to delays and unlawful taking of lands. Rise in gold mining boom problematic for communities.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Certificate of Possession of Rural Land (APFR) available cheaply to individuals, families, or groups for homesteads/farms. Securer statutory Land Titles are 6 x more expensive. Most of 8,000 villages have elected Land Councils.  Limited uptake of Possession Certificates outside the 60 Communes supported by donors out of 302 communes, mainly due to civil conflict.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009/AN on Rural Land Tenure; Law 034-2012, arts. Art. 13ff,. Art. 25, 34ff. Also refer  Law 034-2012/AN (Agrarian Reform Law) &  Decree No. 2007-610 on National Rural Land Security Policy. Code de Général des Collectivitiés Territoriales, No.55-2004/AN.
indicators.additional_info: Fees for issuing rural land certificates (APFRs) low as laid out in Decree no. 2012-1042, with individual titles reported in 2015 as six times more expensive that collective APFR, designed to support collectively owned family farms and discourage transactions and subdivision (Land Tenure & Development Technical Committee, 2015, Paris, Ministère des Affaires étrangères et du Développement international). Difficulty reported with Art 36 of Law 034-2009 which provides for prescriptive rights after 30 years of peaceable occupation and use, in relation to long-term tenants (P. Hochet, 2014, Burkina Faso: Vers La Reconnaissance des Droits Fonciers Locaux, Laboratoire  Citoyennetes).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Clans and lineages can be legal persons but not  village communities as a whole. While villagers retains access and use rights over commons, and Committees regularly designated as managers, ownership usually vested in the State or Commune. Rural Land Law 2009. Pastoral Act 2003. Forest Code 2011.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009/AN on Rural Land Tenure, Art. 39. Pastoral Act, 2003. Forest Code
indicators.additional_info: Art. 39: 'All rural land owners may individually or collectively seek recognition of possession' but does not normally mean the whole village or whole village area. Wildlife or forest-rich commons are registrable in name of Commune. Grazing rights (Art 13-23 of Pastoral Act 2003 and forest rights (Art 52 Forest Code) may be obtained. In short, provision for commons to be registered as collective property exists but rare given dominance of family tenure and farmers resistance to herders having rights and reluctance in  turn of indigenes to share rights with tenants.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Villages are primary authorities for land administration, including of communal lands, but which are vested in Communes. Decentralization to 302 Communes by Law No. 55-2004/AN supported by Law 034-2009 promoting Village Land Commissions (Committees). Local Land Charters enhance village authority and customary law. Facilitated adoption slow among  c. 8,000 villages.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No.55-2004/AN for decentralization. Law 034-2009  Rural Land Tenure, Art. 81ff.Village Land Commissions; Art. 11 ff for Local Land Charters.
indicators.additional_info: Reports that farmers are favoured over herders and owners over tenants in registration of Certificates of Possession (Land Tenure and Development Technical Committee, 2015, Formalising Land rights in developing countries: moving from past controversies to future strategies, Agence française de développement/; P. Hochet, 2014 Burkina Faso: Vers La Reconnaissance des Droits Fonciers Locaux, Laboratoire Citoyennetes).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights including as registered under Certificates owned in perpetuity according to rules in Local Land Charters. Certificates are transferable by succession and inter vivos. Law on Rural Land 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009 On Rural Land Tenure, Art. 4, 13, 47.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal provision for Free, Prior and Informed Consent. However, under compulsory acquisition, amicable agreement on compensation is to be sought (Art. 326 of No. 034-2013/AN) and if cannot be reached, community has right of appeal (Art. 327). Public purposes Art. 297 include urban, agricultural, pastoral, land, mining, conservation development for takings by either Commune or State.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 034-2012/AN Land and Agrarian Reorganization in Burkina Faso.
indicators.additional_info: Compensation equitable for all rights and payable prior to expropriation at compulsory acquisition (Constitution, 1991 (2012) Art. 15. Law No. 034-2012 states that compulsory acquisition applies only to real estate and real rights (Art.. 315) and definition of this uncertainly includes unregistered customary rights, which constitute the majority of rural land rights in 2024.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights include ownership of 'useful trees' and Local Land Charters provide for preservation of flora & fauna including small village forests & sacred groves. Significant forests are vested in the State as classified forests or Communes. Communes may transfer management to village or inter-village bodies under contracts. Land Codes 2009, 2012. Forest Code, 2011.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009, Arts. 6, 7 & 13. Forest Code Law No. 003-2011/AN, Arts.15
indicators.additional_info: Forest Code No.003-2011/AN vests forests in either the national state or local authorities (302 rural communes) (Art.15). Private landowners with titles may manage forests (Art. 31). 'Useful trees' may be owned, implies  protected trees may not. Local Land Charters regulate use of commons implying de facto ownership but significant commons vested in Communes.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a national resource belonging to society. Domestic use rights guaranteed. Pastoralists guaranteed water access. Local land charters allow communities to regulate ponds and local waters.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 002-2001/AN On the Water Management, Art. 2 & 5; Pastoral Code Law No. 034-2003/AN, ART. 28; Law 034-2009/AN, Art. 6, 7, 13.
indicators.additional_info: Legal provision for village communities to  define and operate customary rules including affecting natural water sources under local land charters (Chartres foncières rurales) (Law No. 34-2009/AN On Rural Land Tenure, Art. 11-18).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Code 2011 permits villages to manage Commune Forests under contract, use and delimit village use and hunting zones, managed by associations, under oversight of Wildlife Authority. Use is mostly banned in classified forests. No provision for village to retain, declare and manage their own Protected Forests. No legal provision for restitution of taken forests for Commune or National PA.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 003-2011 Forestry Code. Arts. 55-56, 65-67, 91-92, 104-105). Law No. 034-2009 On Rural Tenure, Arts. 3.6.7., 13.
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Code 2011 addresses forest and wildlife resources in distinct Books. Non-private forests include classified and protected forests. Classified include national parks, biosphere reserves, integral nature reserves, wildlife reserves, corridors and sanctuaries (Art. 19) under the State public domain. Communities have l rights to dead wood collection, fruit gathering and medicinal plant collection only (Art 54). In Commune Protected Forests they may graze animals, harvest forest products and cultivate if appropriate to the PA  (Art. 55). In all cases traditional use rights are authorized only as per the management plan specific to the forest (Art. 56).

indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Villages are primary authorities for land administration, including of communal lands, but which are vested in Communes. Decentralization to 302 Communes by Law No. 55-2004/AN supported by Law 034-2009 promoting Village Land Commissions (Committees). Local Land Charters enhance village authority and customary law. Facilitated adoption slow among  c. 8,000 villages.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No.55-2004/AN for decentralization. Law 034-2009  Rural Land Tenure, Art. 81ff.Village Land Commissions; Art. 11 ff for Local Land Charters.
indicators.additional_info: Reports that farmers are favoured over herders and owners over tenants in registration of Certificates of Possession (Land Tenure and Development Technical Committee, 2015, Formalising Land rights in developing countries: moving from past controversies to future strategies, Agence française de développement/; P. Hochet, 2014 Burkina Faso: Vers La Reconnaissance des Droits Fonciers Locaux, Laboratoire Citoyennetes).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights including as registered under Certificates owned in perpetuity according to rules in Local Land Charters. Certificates are transferable by succession and inter vivos. Law on Rural Land 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009 On Rural Land Tenure, Art. 4, 13, 47.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal provision for Free, Prior and Informed Consent. However, under compulsory acquisition, amicable agreement on compensation is to be sought (Art. 326 of No. 034-2013/AN) and if cannot be reached, community has right of appeal (Art. 327). Public purposes Art. 297 include urban, agricultural, pastoral, land, mining, conservation development for takings by either Commune or State.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 034-2012/AN Land and Agrarian Reorganization in Burkina Faso.
indicators.additional_info: Compensation equitable for all rights and payable prior to expropriation at compulsory acquisition (Constitution, 1991 (2012) Art. 15. Law No. 034-2012 states that compulsory acquisition applies only to real estate and real rights (Art.. 315) and definition of this uncertainly includes unregistered customary rights, which constitute the majority of rural land rights in 2024.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights include ownership of 'useful trees' and Local Land Charters provide for preservation of flora & fauna including small village forests & sacred groves. Significant forests are vested in the State as classified forests or Communes. Communes may transfer management to village or inter-village bodies under contracts. Land Codes 2009, 2012. Forest Code, 2011.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 034-2009, Arts. 6, 7 & 13. Forest Code Law No. 003-2011/AN, Arts.15
indicators.additional_info: Forest Code No.003-2011/AN vests forests in either the national state or local authorities (302 rural communes) (Art.15). Private landowners with titles may manage forests (Art. 31). 'Useful trees' may be owned, implies  protected trees may not. Local Land Charters regulate use of commons implying de facto ownership but significant commons vested in Communes.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a national resource belonging to society. Domestic use rights guaranteed. Pastoralists guaranteed water access. Local land charters allow communities to regulate ponds and local waters.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 002-2001/AN On the Water Management, Art. 2 & 5; Pastoral Code Law No. 034-2003/AN, ART. 28; Law 034-2009/AN, Art. 6, 7, 13.
indicators.additional_info: Legal provision for village communities to  define and operate customary rules including affecting natural water sources under local land charters (Chartres foncières rurales) (Law No. 34-2009/AN On Rural Land Tenure, Art. 11-18).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Code 2011 permits villages to manage Commune Forests under contract, use and delimit village use and hunting zones, managed by associations, under oversight of Wildlife Authority. Use is mostly banned in classified forests. No provision for village to retain, declare and manage their own Protected Forests. No legal provision for restitution of taken forests for Commune or National PA.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 003-2011 Forestry Code. Arts. 55-56, 65-67, 91-92, 104-105). Law No. 034-2009 On Rural Tenure, Arts. 3.6.7., 13.
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Code 2011 addresses forest and wildlife resources in distinct Books. Non-private forests include classified and protected forests. Classified include national parks, biosphere reserves, integral nature reserves, wildlife reserves, corridors and sanctuaries (Art. 19) under the State public domain. Communities have l rights to dead wood collection, fruit gathering and medicinal plant collection only (Art 54). In Commune Protected Forests they may graze animals, harvest forest products and cultivate if appropriate to the PA  (Art. 55). In all cases traditional use rights are authorized only as per the management plan specific to the forest (Art. 56).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Statutory laws are silent on whether communities have legal rights to land.
indicators.law_and_provision: State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950; Transfer of Property Act 1882; Registration Act 1908; Land Reform Law 1984; Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982; Land Reforms Ordinance 1984.
indicators.additional_info: Under statutory law, land in Bangladesh is either owned by private individuals and entities or the state. There are no explicit community land rights granted under statutory law, although customary law in Bangladesh recognizes community land rights in the Chittagong Hill Tracts region (http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/country-profiles/full-reports/USAID_Land_Tenure_Bangladesh_Profile.pdf)

local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The national level law does not explicitly grant rural communities rights to community forests in Bulgaria. Control and management of community forests is vested in municipalities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Bulgaria; Law for restoration of ownership of forests and forest land entirety; Ownership Act 1951; Ownership and use of farmland Act, 1991; Law for the Preservation of Agricultural Lands, 1996
indicators.additional_info: Article 3 of the Ownership and Use of Farmland Act provides "Farmland may be individual citizen's, state, municipal, or legal persons' property." NOTE: "Community Forests" in Bulgaria is owned by the municipalities, which are governed by democratically elected bodies. Management of Community Forests is done either by a special established by a specially established Community Forest Management Department within the structure of the municipality, or by the Forest Management Enterprise. See FORZA, the Swiss-Ukrainian Forest Development Project. How communities manage forests. In Bulgaria, common lands are areas on which common rights are exercised by the holdings, without having ownership over the land itself. These lands are managed by different administrations: municipalities, the State, and the forestry agency . See the Eurostats study on common lands in Bulgaria (2010). http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/749240/749313/BG_NMR_FSS_2010.pdf/29fde8a8-4751-4217-a1cf-b2f4bb2aefd5

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Federal Water Act, 1999 recognizes the right of all citizens to use water for domestic purposes, and protects private ownership of water located within the boundaries of landowner. However, since communities in Bulgaria are not granted ownership rights to their lands, they are also not granted ownership rights to water located within their land. Under federal law, communities only have rights as citizens to use water for domestic purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Bulgaria; Water Act, 1999 (amended 2011)
indicators.additional_info: Article 3 of the Water Act provides that "freshwaters within the territory of the Republic of Bulgaria shall be national strategic resources." Article 7 provides protection of private ownership rights to water "insofar as the exercise of such right does not interfere with the integriy and unity of the hydrological cycle and of the natural aquatic system." Article 8 recognizes a right to common water abstraction and use of water sites and water abstratction to satisfy domestic needs, but using water for commercial/economic purposes requires payment of a fee.

Under federal law, communities only have rights as citizens to use water for domestic purposes. (Constitution of Bulgaria; Water Act, 1999 (amended 2011))
BGR.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: No, the law does not address the issue — The national level law does not explicitly grant rural communities rights to community forests in Bulgaria. Control and management of community forests is vested in municipalities. (Constitution of Bulgaria; Law for restoration of ownership of forests and forest land entirety; Ownership Act 1951; Ownership and use of farmland Act, 1991; Law for the Preservation of Agricultural Lands, 1996)

local_communities_entries.framework: Rural communities
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize the land rights of rural communities in Belarus.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Belarus; Land Code (Law No. 425-Z) (amended 2011); Presidential Decree No. 622 “On improvement of regulation of land relations and state control over land management and protection”; Law No. 66-Z amending Forest Code (Law No. 420-Z); Presidential Decree No. 64 amending Presidential Decree No. 667 regarding expropriation and allotment of land plots; Law No.2417-XII of 1993 regarding the right to land property; Law on Protected Areas (1994)
indicators.additional_info: According to a secondary source, rural communities exist in Belarus in forest areas, but the Forest Code and other applicable laws do not explicitly grant these communities ownership or use rights to forests. Forests in Belarus are owned by the State under the Forest Code. 2014. Lazarav, M. Forest Dependence of Rural Communities in the Republic of Belarus. Available at: http://www.enpi-fleg.org/site/assets/files/1911/forest_dependency_belarus.pdf. The Land Code establishes the following tenure types: the following types of ownership are envisaged: (a) public property; (b) private property; (c) foreign property, including property of international organizations; (d) lifelong hereditary ownership; (e) open-ended (permanent) ownership; (f) provisional ownership; and (g) lease (sublease). However, community ownership or use rights are not explicitly established in the Land Code. Article 13 of the Constitution and Article 7 of the Forest Code of Belarus provide that the forests of the country are under conditions of exclusive state ownership. Under Article 13 of Land Code, parcels of land included, in particular, in the land of the forest fund are not to be provided as private property or property of foreign states or property of foreign states and international organizations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Belize's statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize community rights to land.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Lands Act, 1992; Land Development Authority Act, 2000; Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Act; Land Reform (Security of Tenure) Act, 1962; Forest Code (Law No. 420-Z).
indicators.additional_info: NOTE: In April 2015, the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled in favor of the Mayan communities and reaffirmed that the 38 Q’eqchi and Mopan Maya Indigenous communities of southern Belize have rights to the lands they have customarily used and occupied. The judgment requires the government to demarcate ?and register Maya village lands, and to cease and desist from any further interference, destruction, or use of the lands that would interfere with the Maya peoples’ enjoyment of their lands. The court also awarded damages to the Maya people?in compensation for the moral and physical harm wrought?by the bulldozing of crops and destruction of rainforests and watersheds caused by outside concessions granted by the State for logging, oil exploration, and other development without the Free, Prior and Informed Consent of Maya communities. The court retained supervision of the implementation of the ruling to ensure that the government complies, and could enforce fines if they do not. In 12 months, both parties are required to report on the implementation process. However, researcher could not find information on whether this Caribbean Court of Justice decision has been implemented. For more info, see https://www.culturalsurvival.org/publications/cultural-survival-quarterly/maya-win-unprecedented-land-rights-belize-international

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Water Industry Act, 2001 implies that the government owns all water resources in Belize. Use of water requires a license under the Water Industry Act (sec. 61). The Water and Sewage Authority is in charge of issuing licenses and administration of water use.  The Carribean Court of Justice held that Mayan communities in Belize have rights to lands they have customarily use and occupied. It can be implied that this judgement also recognized that Mayans have rights to use water located on such lands. However, the Carribean Court of Justice judgment has not been implemented through national legislation or regulation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Industry Act (No. 1 of 2001); Supreme Court of Belize (Claim No. 540 of 2006) National Fisherman Producers Co-Operative Society and Brown Surgar Market Place Limited. National Lands Act, 1992; Land Development Authority Act, 2000; Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Act; Land Reform (Security of Tenure) Act, 1962; Forest Code (Law No. 420-Z).
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court of Belize (Claim No. 540 of 2006) held that riparian owners have a right to ordinary and primary use of water located near their property. However, since Belize's national level laws do not recognize the ownership rights of communities, communities may not be entitled to the riparian rights protected by the Supreme Court. The court retained supervision of the implementation of the ruling to ensure that the government complies, and could enforce fines if they do not. The judgment requires the government to demarcate ?and register Maya village lands, and to cease and desist from any further interference, destruction, or use of the lands that would interfere with the Maya peoples’ enjoyment of their lands. The court also awarded damages to the Maya people?in compensation for the moral and physical harm wrought?by the bulldozing of crops and destruction of rainforests and watersheds caused by outside concessions granted by the State for logging, oil exploration, and other development without the Free, Prior and Informed Consent of Maya communities. The court retained supervision of the implementation of the ruling to ensure that the government complies, and could enforce fines if they do not. In 12 months, both parties are required to report on the implementation process. However, researcher could not find information on whether this Caribbean Court of Justice decision has been implemented. For more info, see https://www.culturalsurvival.org/publications/cultural-survival-quarterly/maya-win-unprecedented-land-rights-belize-international

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Water Industry Act, 2001 implies that the government owns all water resources in Belize. Use of water requires a license under the Water Industry Act (sec. 61). The Water and Sewage Authority is in charge of issuing licenses and administration of water use.  The Carribean Court of Justice held that Mayan communities in Belize have rights to lands they have customarily use and occupied. It can be implied that this judgement also recognized that Mayans have rights to use water located on such lands. However, the Carribean Court of Justice judgment has not been implemented through national legislation or regulation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Industry Act (No. 1 of 2001); Supreme Court of Belize (Claim No. 540 of 2006) National Fisherman Producers Co-Operative Society and Brown Surgar Market Place Limited. National Lands Act, 1992; Land Development Authority Act, 2000; Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Act; Land Reform (Security of Tenure) Act, 1962; Forest Code (Law No. 420-Z).
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court of Belize (Claim No. 540 of 2006) held that riparian owners have a right to ordinary and primary use of water located near their property. However, since Belize's national level laws do not recognize the ownership rights of communities, communities may not be entitled to the riparian rights protected by the Supreme Court. NOTE: In April 2015, the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled in favor of the Mayan communities and reaffirmed that the 38 Q’eqchi and Mopan Maya Indigenous communities of southern Belize have rights to the lands they have customarily used and occupied. The judgment requires the government to demarcate ?and register Maya village lands, and to cease and desist from any further interference, destruction, or use of the lands that would interfere with the Maya peoples’ enjoyment of their lands. The court also awarded damages to the Maya people?in compensation for the moral and physical harm wrought?by the bulldozing of crops and destruction of rainforests and watersheds caused by outside concessions granted by the State for logging, oil exploration, and other development without the Free, Prior and Informed Consent of Maya communities. The court retained supervision of the implementation of the ruling to ensure that the government complies, and could enforce fines if they do not. In 12 months, both parties are required to report on the implementation process. However, researcher could not find information on whether this Caribbean Court of Justice decision has been implemented. BOL.name: Bolivia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Adriana Vidal, Independent Land Tenure and Natural Resource Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: PIOC, ICO, and PC are recognized by the Constitution. Their customary rights on the land are recognized, protected, and guaranteed. Recognition of legal standing exists but in practice there are certain limitations for the exercise of their rights
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 2, Art 30, Art.290, 291, 403, 393; Law 1715, Art. 3; Supreme Decree 29215, Art. 355 - 373; Law 1551, Art. 2, 4, 5.
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original peasant indigenous people, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. PIOC, ICO, and PC have the right to receive the legal title over their lands (Constitution Art 30.II.6). Communities have the duty to respect the social and economic purposes of the land while exercising their rights. These purposes are maintained when communities use their land to fulfill their identity, traditions, and other needs as a group.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: IP and LC's lands receive the same level of protection as forms of private agricultural property (recognition, protection and guarantee over rights). Customary land rights are recognized but formalization is promoted and needed.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 393, Art. 394; Law 1715, Art. 3.
indicators.additional_info: IP = Indigenous Peoples, PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities, LC = Local Communities. It is necessary that IP, ICO, and LC establish a legal entity in order to receive formal title over their lands. The mandate of Law 3545 is to regularize and issue land title for all types of agricultural property including IP, ICO, and LC. It is possible for PIOC, ICO, and PC to receive the legal title over their lands simultaneously with other private owners (community members). In that case both regimes would coexist.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Formalization is promoted and applied ex-officio by the state the same as by request of the communities. Procedure free of cost to grant lands to PIOC, ICO, and PC as community lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 192; Law 1715 Art. 42.II, Art. 72.
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Although IP, ICO and PC have Constitutional recognition, in order to have a legal title of their lands they need to establish a legal entity (register as a PIOC or ICO) in order to receive such a title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Supreme Decree 29215 Art. 99 Art. 378
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: PIOC, ICO, and PC have the authority to determine the distribution of their lands according to their own customary rules (so long as it is compatible with public law). They also have autonomy to govern themselves in every level of their organization.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 403
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: PIOC, ICO, and PC land's rights are vested in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley 1715 Art 3, Art 41.I, 59.III
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. In addition, PIOC, ICO, and PC lands are inalienable, indivisible, unseizable, collective, and non-reversible.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Consultation regarding exploitation of non-renewable natural resources is mandatory. Expropriation based on precedence of biodiversity conservation or public interest in which case proper compensation is due.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 352, 403, 30.II; Supreme Decree 29033 - Regulates FPIC for hydrocarbon resources utilization
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. FPIC in PIOCs' territories will develop according to their own rules and traditions (Constitution Art 352). PIOC, ICO, and PC decisions, views and concerns represented in the "Act of Understanding" should be incorporated in the decision regarding the feasibility of the project or legislative measure, together with an environmental impact assessment.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: IP, ICO, and PC have exclusive rights over forest resources. Commercial use is subject to the approval of a management plan. Limitation regarding previous rights over forests acquired by third parties.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art 386, 388, 403, 30.17; Forest Law Article 3, 27, 32; Supreme Decree 29215
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. The ownership of natural resources from forests rests under the State however PIOCs have the right to use forest resources for traditional practices and sustenance. Commercial use is dependent upon the approval of a management plan. Forest concessions granted on indigenous lands previously to the recognition of IP rights are protected by Constitution.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Rights and the sustainable management of water resources are recognized, respected and protected, including PIOC's, ICO's and PC's customary practices of managements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art 374
indicators.additional_info: PIOC, ICO, and PC are recognized by the Constitution. Their customary rights on the land are recognized, protected, and guaranteed. Recognition of legal standing exists but in practice there are certain limitations for the exercise of their rightsPIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: PIOC's land titling is possible on areas previously recognized as natural protected areas. Management is shared with the government and subject to the IP's customary rules.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 385.II, Art. 403; Law 1333, Art. 62, Art. 64. Art 78; Supreme Decree 24781 Art. 9, Art. 47. Art. 79
indicators.additional_info: PIOC=Original Peasant Indigenous People, ICO=Intercultural Communities of Origin, PC= Peasant Communities. Management of natural protected areas coexisting with PIOC's territories will be developed following traditions and customs from these groups, while at the same time respecting the objective of the protected area. Regulation on protected area incentivizes the participation of PIOCs or ICOs in the management of the area.

BRA.name: Brazil

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Adriana Vidal, Independent Land Tenure and Natural Resource Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution recognizes possession rights to the lands traditionally occupied. This includes lands where communities live on a permanent basis, those used for productive activities, and those necessary to protect communities' well being.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 231
indicators.additional_info: Ownership of indigenous territories remains with the Federal government. Permanent possession and the exclusive right to usufruct natural resources is guaranteed. Legal transactions that restricts IP's rights over the land are prohibited (Law 6001, Art. 18).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The land rights granted to indigenous people is that of permanent possession with the exclusive right to natural resources of the soil, rivers, and lakes. This is the same level of protection of land rights as other nationals.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art 20 No XI, Article 231 paragraph 2 and 6; Law 4504, Art 2.4; Law 6001, Art 1, Art. 2.IX, Art. 20
indicators.additional_info: Expropriation is possible only in cases of relevant public interest of the Republic, exploitation of subsoil resources of national interest, disease control, national security, or for peace keeping purposes. Indigenous people receive proper compensation. Only Congress can authorize the exploitation and use of hydric resources and the prospecting and mining of mineral resources (Constitution Art. 49.XVI).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition of the rights of indigenous and tribal groups to the possession of their lands is not subject to demarcation. However it is necessary to formalize the land title to reinforce the rights over the area.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 67; Law 6001 Art. 1, Art. 19, Art. 25; Decree 1775, Art. 1
indicators.additional_info: The federal government has the duty to recognize, identify and protect indigenous lands. These lands, although belonging to the nation, can only be used by indigenous people as ancestral owners, who enjoy exclusive usufruct rights to the wealth of the soil, rivers, and lakes existing on their lands. Administrative procedure is well defined and participatory with indigenous communities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous people (IP) are recognized as a legal entity for the purpose of ownership. They have standing under the law to sue in order to defend their rights and interests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 231, Art. 232
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous people recognized are 'isolated native communities', 'in integration', and 'integrated communities' (Law 6001, Art. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution recognizes IPs social organization, customs, languages, creeds, and traditions. Free choice of livelihood and subsistence. Respect for the rules applied to ownership of land
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art 231; Law 6001, Art. 2, Art. 6

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous land rights are inalienable and granted in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 231.4; Law 6001, Art. 22

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Congress authorizes exploitation of water and mineral resources in IP's lands. Communities will participate in hearings during the decision process. Compensation is due if displacement occurs. Agreements with outside actors are regulated.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art 231.3; Law 6001, Art. 8
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution allows the National Congress to grant authorization to third parties to explore resources such as water (rivers and lakes), including for energy generation, and subsoil minerals on an exceptional basis, following consultation with affected communities. Communities have the right to receive part of the revenues from mining activities in their lands. Agreements between IPs and third parties will be void unless the competent authority intervenes to provide guidance and clarity on the matter to the community.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities have the exclusive rights over forest resources, but limited by sustainable agroforestry exploitation. Communities should maintain a minimum percentage of forest cover within their amazon lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 11284, Art. 3.VI, Art 2.IX.b, Art. 6; Law 6001, Art. 22, Art. 24; Law 12651, Art. 11, 12
indicators.additional_info: Forest concessions exclude areas occupied by Indigenous peoples. Law 11284 refers to several forms of forest tenure in favor of Indigenous peoples: forest settlement projects, sustainable development, agro-extractive. This is in addition to the categories within conservation units exclusively created for lands occupied by Indigenous peoples.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Indigenous peoples are entitled to the exclusive use of the rivers and lakes within their territory. Since the right is to exclusive use, but not ownership, a score of 2 is justified.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Article 231.2; Law 6001, Art. 22, Art. 24

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Extractive Reserves and Sustainable Development Reserves are categories where IPs can inhabit. Forest resource extraction for sustenance purposes is allowed. Relocation is needed if communities are located in other conservation categories.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4340, Art. 39; Law 9985, Art. 14, Art. 18, Art. 20, Art. 42
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous peoples (IPs) legal title over the land can coexist with certain conservation units indicated by law. IPs have the obligation to preserve, regenerate and defend the purpose of the area in accordance with the Management Plan approved for the area. If relocation is due to incompatibility of IP activities and the purpose of the conservation unit, the State will compensate in terms agreed by the community.

local_communities_entries.framework: Quilombo Communities
local_communities_entries.source: Adriana Vidal, Independent Land Tenure and Natural Resource Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Areas occupied by the remnants of the Quilombo communities are recognized. Definitive ownership, demarcation, and titling are stated as the government's duty.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act of Transitory; Constitutional Provisions (Art. 68); Decree 4887, Art. 1, Art. 2, Art. 5
indicators.additional_info: The characterization of the remnants of Quilombo communities will be attested by auto definition by the community.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Quilombo communities receive the same level of protection as other types of private property, including compensation for expropriation. In instances of overlapping rights with regard to third parties laws favor the rights of the Quilombo communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 13

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment:
It is not mandatory but is promoted to reinforce Quilombo communities' land rights. Demarcation following self-assessment of Quilombo communities.
The procedure is done at no cost to the community and provides  legal title over the land
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 1, Art. 2, Art. 22
indicators.additional_info: Delimitation and titling of Quilombo communities' lands is a constitutional mandate. The purpose of the land titling process is to clear overlaps between customary lands and other types of property, as well as recognize Quilombo communities' rights on their lands rather than to impose a legal burden on the communities. Procedure with clear rules and guidance to communities through the process.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Certification and registration as a Quilombo community is not mandatory but necessary to receive legal rights over their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: 231 Constitution; Decree 4887, Art. 7
indicators.additional_info: The Palmares Foundation is the entity assigned by law to provide support to the Quilombo communities with the registration process (Decree 4887, Art 3).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Quilombos communities have the right to use their lands to fulfill their physical, social, economic and cultural needs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 2

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Quilombo communities land title is granted in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 17
indicators.additional_info: These land rights are also inalienable and unseizable.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: ILO 169 rules are applied to Quilombo communities for administrative and legislative measures applied by the government within community lands. Land rights are inalienable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Legislative Decree 143; Case 027/2007/JCM/JF/MA

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Quilombo communities have the exclusive right over forest resources being of social interest, but limited by sustainable agroforestry exploitation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 10; Law 12651, Art. 3.X.e, Art. 11, Art. 12

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Quilombo communities have rights to water and the government has the duty to issue a legal title that allows the community to exercise their right.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 4887, Art. 10

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: When the lands occupied by Quilombo communities overlap conservation units, the government has the duty to take necessary measures to ensure the livelihoods and sustainability of the community while preserving the objective of the conservation unit.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 9985, Art. 42; Decree 4340 Art. 39; Decree 4887, Art. 11.
indicators.additional_info: If relocation is due to incompatibility of IP activities and the purpose of the conservation unit, the State will compensate in terms agreed by the community.

BWA.name: Botswana

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Post-colonial recognition of customary ownership (1968) has given way to compulsory conversion of private customary deeds into statutory grants (2018). Sustained absence of legal provision for collective tenure, most negative for San hunter-gatherers and poorest farming villages with limited access to commercializing 'tribal' grazing lands. Tribal Land Act 2018.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Act No 1 of 2018, which came into force in 2022. Acquisition of Property Act (CAP 32:10) sec. 2. Botswana Land Policy, 2015, as revised up to 2019.
indicators.additional_info: 1968 and 2007 laws on tribal lands did not stipulate that existing unregistered customary rights are lawful interests but this was upheld by courts as the case (e.g. AHRLR 183 (BwHC) 2006, Sesana, Sethobogwa and Others v. Attorney General). This is not the case with customary communal lands. eg. in  Ghanzi and Kgalagadi Districts (2 of 12 Districts) only one third of tribal land is available today for  mixed farming, grazing, hunting and gathering, the rest under leaseholds (and  freeholds) allocated for private ranches and to private tourism and hunting companies. Ability to pay for survey also  divides those holding Customary Grants and Common Law Grants making the former more vulnerable. 2018 law requires  customary certificates to be converted to statutory deeds.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protection since 1968 of unregistered customary homestead rights removed in 2018. No legal provision for collective entitlements for village grazing areas nor  hunter-gatherer domains. Pro-elite bias to conversion of commons into commercial ranches, tourism & hunting enterprise, now open to foreign enterprise. Compensation prior to eviction only for 'improvements' to land. Tribal Land Act 2018.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Act No 1 of 2018. Acquisition of Property Act CAP 32:10 sec. 2. Tribal Land Regulations, Regs. 14A, 15.
indicators.additional_info: Examples of shortfalls (a):District Land Boards are now de facto state agency, not a community or customary body; (b) compensation paid only for improvements to land; (c) Tribal territories (vested in Boards) not held to be real property; (d) amendment to  the Tribal Land Act in 1993 to convert 'tribesmen' to 'citizens'  removed customary ownership of tribal territories even at trustee level (Boards) & increased vulnerability of commons being allocated to wealthy outsiders; (e) consultation rather than consent of local leaders & families is required; (e) law can register only an individual as use right owner; no provision for family, village or village cluster (ward) tenure (the latter important for grazing); (g) grounds for cancellation of grants of customary use rights wide; (h) common law leases to individuals take grazing land out of community reach or rights. No new policies address San or other rural community land rights including the weak Revised Remote Area Development Programme, 2009; Affirmative Action Framework for Remote Area Communities, 2014, National Land Policy, 2015 (revised in 2019). 2025 formation of Commission to investigate Barsarwa (San) right.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Procedures cheap and easy but limited to private lands. Certificate of Customary Rights must now be converted into more costly Statutory Deeds. Common law leases taken up by elites require survey. Still no openings for village, group or community to secure collective title. Hunting and gathering continues to be denied status as a viable land use as basis for ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: For Certificate of Customary Grant; Tribal Land Act 2018Part IV (secs. 2225). Grant of Land Rights under Common Law, Tribal Land Act, 2018 Part V (sec 26-28).
indicators.additional_info: No charges to citizens for Certificates of Customary Rights (only available for inheritable use rights for residence, ploughing & grazing). Simple, accessible procedure. No requirement that rights granted before 1970 (when Tribal Land Act came into force) be registered but certificates obligatory for new customary rights. Procedure for acquiring common law leases on tribal land  complex, not free & requires formal survey and registration in Deeds Registry and title is subject to rent. No means for communities or groups to apply for titles, either customary or statutory.  Only 2 San communities own lands, via a church and private game ranch making this possible in form of a Trust: D'Kar, Dquae Qare Game Farm Trust. No other cases of communities holding title to community lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Neither families, communities, nor even tribes have legal personality, hence vesting of ownership in Boards (de facto state institutions). To secure customary use right or common law lease, family or group must form legal entity and for commercial purpose (e.g. Community Trust, Syndicate).
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Act, 2018. Tribal Land Regulations 2022 Reg. 6
indicators.additional_info: Law is contrary to customary law as most rights were traditionally devolved to sub-chiefdoms, villages, including administration to village headmen,  now disempowered by centralized Land Boards, only need to be consulted prior to allocations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No recognition of community as lawful administration although until 2022, Village Headmen handled allocations & transfers including where plots not registered. Now Headmen & Committees, District Councils, Tribal Administration are only consulted by central government staffed Boards in each District. Tribal Land Act 2018 & Regs. 2022.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Regulations, 2022, eg. 7
indicators.additional_info: Legal administrator of customary (tribal) land is not the tribe but an administrative Board,of  mainly appointed members by Ministry. The  election of the minority representation is undemocratic in that through choice of Board's shortlist. Local ward head must give opinion and public can make representations re applications, but Board decides.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Board owns tribal land in perpetuity in trust for citizens, citizens with titles hold exclusive rights to occupy, use parcel in perpetuity and may transfer/sell. No mechanism for villages or hunter-gatherer bands to secure collective titles endowing rights in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Act 2018 (CAP 32:02), s. 10,  13.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No FPIC in law. Opinions must be sought including in public and recorded but formal consent of villages, village clusters (wards) or traditional leaders is not required. Aggrieved persons may appeal against decision. Rapid rise in commercial allocations of community commons, and appeals with little remedy.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Regulations Reg.6-14.
indicators.additional_info: As fast rising percentage of tribal lands under commercial lease to ranchers, tourism bodies, and other individuals including foreigners, curtailment of traditionally occupied and used lands is common. Supported by  Settlement Policy(1980) and CBNRM Policy (2007) in respect of vast areas of tribal lands set aside as Wildlife Management Areas (WMA), increasingly allocated to private tourism enterprises. Assistance of District Commissioner to be provided to aggrieved. Appeal is to Minister; many appeals reported.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No provision in Tribal Land Act 2018 as to incidents of either a Deed of Customary Land Grant or a Grant of Land Rights under a Common Law Lease, but if assumed that rights continue as per the 1968 TLA, likely that the holder controls all uses including rights to trees. Tribal Land Act 2018. Forest Act 1968 (2008).
indicators.law_and_provision: Tribal Land Act (CAP 32:02, now repealed but many of its provisions retained in new law in force since 2022, s. 13. Forest Act (CAP 38:03) (1968, amended 2008) s. 11 .
indicators.additional_info: Forest Act 1968 (2008) provides for declaration of protected trees but cannot do this 'without the consent of the owner thereof' (s. 11).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water made appurtenant to land right, therefore owned for domestic purposes including watering stock. Free use of  'public water' which comprises, streams, rivers, lakes, pans, swamps & underground water not lawfully appropriated for use. Most communities access 'public water'. Water Act 1968 (2008).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act (CAP 34:01, 1968, last amended 2008), s.2, 4-16.
indicators.additional_info: Syndicate Ranches, Private Ranches, Lessors often sink boreholes and this water is deemed to be private water for domestic or legal commercial uses. Public water cannot be owned (Water Act, s. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: State holds National Parks & Wildlife Reserves with no legal obligation to respect customary rights of occupancy or use. Main activity in Wildlife Management Areas is commercial hunting and tourism. >50 Community Trusts operate (these hold rights only to manage tribal lands for wildlife) as many cancelled and located to commercial operators. Wildlife Conservation Act (1992 (2023).
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife Conservation and National Parks Act (CAP 38:01) (1992, 2023), s. 6, 20, 24-25, 53. Amendment No 15 of Nov 2023 on subsistence hunting.  Rep. of Botswana (2007) Government Paper, Community Based Natural Resources Management Policy.  Forests (CAP38:03 (1968, last amended in 2008).
indicators.additional_info: Creation of millions of ha of Wildlife Management Areas on communal lands including sub-areas for commercial hunting concessions (Controlled Hunting Areas, CHA)) launched in 2002 as Community Based Natural Resource Management with a White Paper Policy No 2 of 2007. Up to 160 Community Trusts formed, less than 70 registered. Research in 2016, 2020, 2023 all concludes that WMA and CHA largely under control of elites in hunting and tourism sector, minimal return to communities; 65% revenue goes to Government Fund, 35% to community. Local rights even to use historically communal lands is limited to issue of 15 year Community Natural Resource Management Lease. Many communities including San have lost leases peremptorily by Government order and passed directly to commercial operators.  Court Order in 2006 to permit San to reside if not own the 52,730 sq. km Central Kalahari Game Reserve not implemented. Licences required for any use of WMA including hunting, recently softened to enable hunting for consumption in local areas (Amt of sec. 19 of Wildlife law). No provision for Community owned Forest or Wildlife Reserves. Even use rights illegal without licences or exemptions (Forest Act 1968 (2005) secs. 12 & 13, and sec. 17).
