CAF.name: Central African Republic

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Yves Delor Moussa, Bangui University & Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Despite majority customary possession of national area by IP & LC, 1964 law remains in force; deems their lands to be vacant & hence alienable State land. Security only via individualized statutory titles with extinction of customary law & governance. Reformed law since 2011 has failed due to civil war & conflicts until present.  Law No 63/144 1964.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 63/441 of 9 January 1964 Law on the National Domain.
indicators.additional_info: Most of CAR is historically and presently subject to customary possession by Indigenous Peoples and other customary  communities. The colonial regime is sustained until the present (2025)  by which unregistered lands are deemed without owners and thereby within the alienable private domain of the State. Nor are there legal measures setting aside community lands as protected occupation and use. Tenure security is obtainable only through extinction of customary rights & subdivision & conversion of land into individual statutory parcels, requiring development (houses, clearing for farms etc). No legal provision for family or collective tenure. Customary tenure remains a  land occupation and use regime only in law. The few new laws (wildlife and forest) sustain this position. Attempts from 2011 to develop new tenure and agropastoral law have failed due to civil war, fall of governments and sustained conflict.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary rights only lawful occupation & use rights on alienable State domain. Therefore minimal protection for rural communities, including vulnerable Mboro Peulh pastoralists & BaAka forest peoples. Even compensation is not payable when evicted, although concession holders are compensated. Constitution 2016, Law on Expropriation, 1961.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2016, Art. 18. Law on Expropriation for Public Purpose, No. 61.262 of 21 November 1961.
indicators.additional_info: The private domain of the State is managed in two ways: (a)  allocation for civil service or other government purposes; and (b) issue of concessions to benefit of natural persons or legal entities (Art. 46). It includes vacant lands (unregistered land).  Recognition of customary occupation and use exists. This is despite ratification of ILO 169 without reservation in respect of IP, meaningless until the present.  Constitutional protection of private property extends only to natural & coporate persons (Art 18). Customary owners are ineligible for 'fair and prior' indemnification' (2016 Art. 18). Elaborated in Law No. 61.262 of 21 November 961 which limits expropriation with compensation to statutory holders of registered parcels or concessions (Art 1).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for family or community land and no cheap and accessible mechanism even for individual statutory titles. Titles rare in rural areas. Law on Public Domain 1964.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 63/441 of 1964 On Public Domain.
indicators.additional_info: No. 63/441 Law of  9 Jan 1964 on national domain grants private property to private individuals in the private domain of the State (Art 29 (1)).  Art. 38 makes state ownership clear: "... the State, by virtue of its right of sovereignty, is presumed to own land which ... is not owned by third parties in accordance with the law on land tenure under the regular concession titles". No provision for collection titles or recognition of any form of customary ownership other than rights of use and occupation on unowned/State land exist.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no recognition of customary communities as natural persons or means whereby they could register even  statutory titles as a community for all or part of the customary domain. Land Law 1964, Constitution 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2016, Arts. 2 (2) and 38.
indicators.additional_info: Ratification of ILO 169 has not delivered implementation  including the duty to acknowledge IP as communities with legal personality. The Constitution (2016) declaims "Resolved to build a State of Law founded on a pluralistic democracy, the respect for the separation and the equilibrium of the powers to guarantee the security of persons and of property the protection of the most weak, notably vulnerable persons, the minorities, and the full exercise of the fundamental freedoms and rights" ( Preamble).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary norms of leadership and decision-making operate without legal backing. However, communities to partner departments in regulating  access & use of their resources entered into new laws for defined community forest areas, but unlikely to be effective in current conflicted environment, wherein mass logging by outsiders persists. Forest Code 2008 & Decree 2015.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2016, Art. 128. Law No. 09-003 on Territorial Land Use Planning. Forest Code, Law No. 08-022 of October 17, 2008. Decree Stipulating the Conditions for the Management of Community Forests, No. 15-463 of 3 December 2015. Code for Management of Wildlife and Protected Areas No 20-026 of 30 November 2020.
indicators.additional_info: Colonial law dating to 1899 establishes present-day legal norms that customary law does not deliver lawful property rights, the State consecrated as owner of all lands and alone able to dispose of lands or admit ownership, using French civil code. No recognition of community-based regulation of customarily-held lands, although this is the de facto case. However, the Forest Code 2008 and subsequent Decree 2015 provide for local regulation within the framework of participatory forest and wildlife management; a portion of forest may be set aside as community forest, and which they manage according to own rules with State as adviser.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: As there is no recognition of customary tenure as ownership there is no legal backing for communities or members to hold land in perpetuity. However this is the de facto customary system, rights of occupancy & use being inherited. Land Law 1964.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 46 of the No. 63-441 Law of 9 January 1964
indicators.additional_info: Article 46 of the No. 63-441 Law of 9 January 1964 only stipulates that urban and rural lands may be granted to legal entities or natural persons, no provision for communities as legal persons.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Despite ratifying ILO 169, law does not require consent of takings of customary lands. While the Environmental Code 2007 provides for public hearings for consultation, only 'a natural person or legal entity' may refer matter to Minister along with a file justifying a call for public hearing. Communities are not legal persons or registered legal entities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Environmental Code, No. 01-07 of 28 December 2007.
indicators.additional_info: n recent years, the issue of indigenous peoples' consent has been raised, especially as CAR has ratified ILO 169.  The Forest Governance Process (APV-FLEGT) requires transparency and consent of indigenous peoples for logging activities. So far no support for Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) within CAR statutes. However laws still do not require consent of even IP communities for taking of their customary lands, as deemed vacant State property (terres sans maître). Consultation and participation is obligatory for large projects as per Arts. 87, 94-97 of the  Environment Code, via public hearings. However, only 'a natural person or legal entity' may refer matter to Minister i/c Environment, along with a file justifying a call for public hearing.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No legal statement on ownership on planted trees by customary occupants but may be assumed as customarily practised. New forest law permits use of natural forests under customary rules, free of charge. Community Forests incl. for harvesting may be managed under agreed Plans. Forest Code 2008 & Decree 2015.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, 17 Oct. 2007. Decree No 15-463 of 03 December 2015 Laying Down the Terms and Conditions For the Allocation and Management of Forests.
indicators.additional_info: Community Forests may be designated, subject to agreement between a Village and/or an Indigenous Community & the Forest Admin. (Art. 133). The CF must be used in accordance with agreed management plan for sustainable harvesting (Art. 166). The Decree 2015 defines a Village and/or Indigenous Community as a population organized 'on the basis of custom and united by ties of ethnic, clan or extended family cohesion, length of occupation, attachment and its strong economic, social and cultural dependence on the environment' (Art. 4). A Community Forest is allocated under Permit and is between 50-5,000 ha (Art. 8). Provision for forest management by the Forest Code Art. 152-168 is not echoed by the Environment Code 2007 which only mentions the Ministry as manager (Article 31). The Forest Code encourages local regulation including repression of offences and assisting the state services to investigate and record infractions (Art. 165).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the State but Indigenous peoples/communities may lawfully use waters on their lands including from small rivers. Traditional use rights are free for customary communities. Water Code 2006.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 63-441 of 1964 (Art. 2) and the Water Code No. 06.001 Law of April 12, 2006.
indicators.additional_info: CAR laws identify water as an inalienable public resource, available for use (Art 2 of Law No. 63-144 of 1964, Art. 15 of Water Code, 2006). Use for non-commercial purposes is free including domestic needs, animal watering, rites, worship, initiation of young people, spiritual recollection and traditional fishing.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community managed & used Forests are provided for under 2008 & 2015 laws (see Indic. 8). Wildlife law 2020 also allows villages & IP to hunt &  fish for subsistence, and to reach agreement with concessionaires to delimit own Hunting and Wildlife Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, 2008, Forest Decree, 2015. Code for Management of Wildlife and Protected Areas, 2020.
indicators.additional_info: Community Forests are provided for under 2008  & 2015 forest laws. Few established due to armed factions & commercial operations. The Wildlife Law 2020 also recognizes village and indigenous communities as entitled to use traditional practices to hunt and fish for subsistence (Art. 110). Hunting requires issue of Customary Hunting Rights (Art. 105). No sale of animals or products permitted (Art. 107). Communities may also make MoU with concessionaires to identify Village Hunting Areas, Community Wildlife Areas (Arts. 46-54), managed by community associations. Communities may participate in management of Wildlife Protected Areas, the State  obliged to collaborate with the local population to sustain protection 'without prejudice to the exercise of customary rights' (Art. 109). No such rights are alienable (Art . 111).

Communities may also make MoU with concessionaires to identify Village Hunting Areas, Community Wildlife Areas (Arts. 46-54), managed by community associations. Communities may participate in management of Wildlife Protected Areas, the State  obliged to collaborate with the local population to sustain protection 'without prejudice to the exercise of customary rights' (Art. 109). No such rights are alienable (Art . 111).

CAN.name: Canada

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court, the Constitution Act, 1982, and the Indian Act recognize aboriginal land rights (aboriginal title). But State retains underlying ownership, aboriginal title is a right to occupy and use lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014); Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Sec. 35(1) Constitution Act, 1982; Sec. 18, Indian Act; First Nations Land Management Act
indicators.additional_info: Section 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 provides that "the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.  The Indian Act defines "reserve" as "a tract of land, the legal title to which is vested in Her Majesty, that has been set apart by Her Majesty for the use and benefit of [Indian] band" (see Section 18, the Indian Act). In the Delagamuukw Supreme Court case (1997), the Supreme Court established a three-part test for claiming aboriginal title.  The Supreme Court held that aboriginal title constitutes a right to the land itself---but this limited to the right of occupancy/use/enjoyment.  NOTE: this legal assessment focuses exclusively on Category I lands and does not account for the full range of treaty rights. Some treaties (such as the TLICHO and the Unuvialuit treaties) in Canada grant fee simple ownership to aboriginals.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities (ICs) must register to obtain land rights (or be granted treaty rights). While some treaties grant fee simple ownership to aboriginals, the Supreme Court held that (non-treaty based) aboriginal title is not equated with a fee simple ownership interest.
indicators.law_and_provision: Para. 33- Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver Town; Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Sec. 35(1) Constitution Act, 1982; Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014); Secs. 20, 35 Indian Act 1985; R. v. Sparrow (1990)
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court in Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014) held that Aboriginal title is a right to use/ possess/ occupy/ enjoy land, but State retains underlying control and title and must approve any alienation. The State may expropriate aboriginal land for a "valid legislative objective" if infringement is minimized, fair compensation is provided, and aboriginals are consulted (R. v. Sparrow (1990); Sec. 35 of the Indian Act). However, Sec. 91(24) of the Constitution Act grants the State exclusive power over Indians with native title. Section 20 of the Indian Act provides that "no Indian is lawfully in possession of land in a reserve unless, with the approval of the Minister, possession of the land is allotted to him by the council of the [Indians]." NOTE: several treaties, including the agreements made between the Canadian government and The TLICHO and the Unuvialuit tribes, grant stronger rights than those recognized by federal legislation (fee simple ownership in some case), but the federal legislation establishes a minimum.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While the Indian Act establishes a register and the Supreme Court established a three-part test for proving Aboriginal title, there are no clear, accessible, and affordable procedures for formalizing/mapping indigenous community rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014); Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Sec. 21, Indian Act; Sec. 25, First Nations Land Management Act
indicators.additional_info: Section 21 of the Indian Act provides that there shall be a Department register, to be known as the Reserve Land Register, in which shall be entered particulars relating to Certificates of Possession and Certificates of Occupation and other land transactions. However, there are no requirements ensuring procedures are affordable and accessible for aboriginal peoples. Section 25 of the First Nations Land Management Act indicates that there are fees associated with registering interest and rights.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court granted legal standing to indigenous communities in several constitutional cases, but they are not always legal persons for the purposes of land ownership and must first register or obtain treaty rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town) 2001 SCC 85; Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014)
indicators.additional_info: Sec. 14.2 of the Indian Act provides that Indian ""bands"" can contest decisions relating to their reserves and appeal such decisions in court.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: First Nations and other aboriginals have a right to self-government and may exercise management and control over their lands in native reserves, but this authority is subject to the Governor of Council's approval under Sec. 60 of the Indian Act.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 18, First Nations Land Management Act; Secs. 18, 60 Indian Act 1985; Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town) 2001 SCC 85; Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014)
indicators.additional_info: Section 18 of the Indian Act grants the Governor in Council broad power to determine the purposes for which IC reserve land is used. Section 20(4) of the Indian Act provides that "...the Minister may, in his discretion, withhold his approval [for possess] and may authorize the Indian to occupy the land temporarily and may prescribe the conditions as to use and settlement that are to be fulfilled by the Indian before the Minister approves of the allotment." Furthermore, Sec. 60 of the Indian Act provides that "the Governor in Council may be the request of a band [of Indians] grant to the band the right to exercise such control and management over lands in the reserved occupied by that band as the Governor in Council considers desirable." Sec. 18 of the First Nations Land Management Act provides that First Nations may "exercise the powers, rights and privileges of an owner in relation to that land..." This power is exercised by the council of a First Nation.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While in some cases reserve land may be held in perpetuity, the Indian Act grants the Minister discretion to issue temporary certificates of occupation and only grant temporary rights to possession.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 20(4)-(6), Indian Act 1985; Delagamuukw v. British Columbia [1997] 153 D. L. R. (4th); Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town) 2001 SCC 85; Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014)Sect
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court in Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014) held that aboriginal title confers on aboriginals: the right to decide how the land will be used. Section 20(4) of the Indian Act provides that "...the Minister may, in his discretion, withhold his approval [for possess] and may authorize the Indian to occupy the land temporarily and may prescribe the conditions as to use and settlement that are to be fulfilled by the Indian before the Minister approves of the allotment."

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court held that, when expropriating Aboriginal-titled land for a public purpose, the government has a procedural duty to consult with the indigenous populations affected.
indicators.law_and_provision: Supreme Court cases- Para. 78-79, Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014); R. v. Sparrow, 1990
indicators.additional_info: While there is no explicit consent requirement, the Supreme Court, in Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia,  held that "where the Crown has real or constructive knowledge of the potential or actual existence of Aboriginal title, and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it, the Crown is obliged to consult with the group asserting Aboriginal title...the level of consultation and accommodation required is proportionate to the strength of the claim and the seriousness of the adverse impact [of the government action]" (Para. 78-79, Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia (2014)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Forest Act and other federal legislation is silent on whether aboriginals have a right to trees.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Act 1985; Indian Act 1985
indicators.additional_info: Some First Nations treaties grant natural resource rights, such as the right to harvest plants (See TLICHO Agreement)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Federal Water Act, 1985 does not establish ownership or use rights to water for citizens; it only establishes Canada's water governance structure. Water rights are governed at the provincial level in Canada, and most provinces require a permits or licenses to use water. Communities, as citizens, have rights to safe drinking water under the Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act
indicators.law_and_provision: Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act, 2013; Water Act  1985; Indian Act 1985
indicators.additional_info: Section 3 of the Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act, 2013 provides "For greater certainty, nothing in this Act or the regulations is to be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from any existing Aboriginal or treaty rights of the Aboriginal peoples of Canada under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982, except to the extent necessary to ensure the safety of drinking water on First Nation lands." Some treaties granted to First Nations grant natural resource rights, but require that the Canadian government retains the right to manage and control waters (see Inuvialuit Final Agreement). Furthermore, it has been argued that aboriginal title principle (recognized as applying to land) could equally apply to water as long as there is no express extinguishment of this right by the government. However, Canadian Supreme Court has not explicitly addressed this issue. For more info, see Nowlan. L. Customary Water Laws and Practices in Canada. Available at: http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/templates/legal/docs/CaseStudy_Canada.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on whether indigenous communities have rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Canada National Parks Act, 2000; Indian Act 1985
indicators.additional_info: Section 4 of Canada's National Parks Act provides  that "the national parks of Canada are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment, subject to this Act and the regulations, and the parks shall be maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations." However, the law is silent on whether aboriginal title includes the rights to resources within protected areas.

indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: State-level (cantonal) laws recognize community rights to "Group inherited” forests and common pastures (e.g. Canton Graubünden). However, since LandMark's assessment is limited to national level laws, state-level laws are not assessed. There are no explicit provisions recognizing and protecting community land rights in federal laws.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Switzerland; Loi fédérale sur l'aménagement du territoire (Loi sur l'aménagement du territoire, LAT), 1979; ordinance on summer pasturing payments (Sömmerungsbeitragsverordnung, SöBV) in 1999; Loi fédérale sur les forêts (Loi sur les forêts, LFO); law on the communes (Gemeindegesetz, GG- cantonal-level law)
indicators.additional_info: For information on community forests in Switzerland, secondary source entitled: Forza (the Swiss-Ukrainian Forest Development Project). 2010. How Communities Manage  Forests: Selected Examples from Around the World. indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Publicly-owned water bodies include surface waters (rivers, streams, lakes) (Article 664 of the Civil Code). The Civil Code also provides that landowners have ownership rights to the springs and groundwater located on their property (Art. 704, Civil Code). Therefore community landowners of forest areas and common pastures have ownership rights to the forests and common pastures. State-level (cantonal) laws recognize community rights to "Group inherited” forests and common pastures (e.g. Canton Graubünden). However, LandMark's assessment is limited to national level laws, state-level laws are not assessed. Nevetheless, the Civil Code demsontrates that federal laws recogniz ownership rights to water.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Code (1912); Water Protection Law, 1991; The Ordinance on Water Protection, 1998; Constitution of Switzerland; Loi fédérale sur l'aménagement du territoire (Loi sur l'aménagement du territoire, LAT), 1979; ordinance on summer pasturing payments (Sömmerungsbeitragsverordnung, SöBV) in 1999; Loi fédérale sur les forêts (Loi sur les forêts, LFO); law on the communes (Gemeindegesetz, GG- cantonal-level law)
indicators.additional_info: Article 704 of the Civil Code staets that "Springs are an integral part of the land and their ownership ay be acquired only through ownership of the land from which they rise...Groundwater is deemed equivalent to springs." Therfore, community forest owners in Switzerland are granted ownership rights to springs and groundwater located on their property. Furthermore, article 689 provides that "every landowner is obliged to receive the waters flowing naturally from a high-lying parcel of land, such as rain water, melting snow and water from unchannelled springs." Every citizen also has a right to use public waters for bathing and domestic purposes. CHL.name: Chile

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Communities
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities are recognized by Law 19253 as the legal owners of their land (art. 12). However, these rights are subject to certain limitations, such as approval by the National Indigenous Development Corporation on matters relating to registration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Chile; Government of Chile. 1993. Ley Indigena No. 19.253 Articulo 20-A,B.. Available at: http://www. conadi.gob.cl/documentos/LeyIndigena2010t.pdf; Government of Chile. 1979. Decreto Ley No. 2.695, Fija Normas para Regularizar la posesión de la pequeña propiedad Raíz y para la Constitución del Dominio Sobre Ella. May 30. Available at: http://www.leychile.cl/ Navegar?idNorma=6982;
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution of Chile, 1980 does not explicitly grant land rights to indigenous peoples. However, Article 1 of Law No. 19253 provides "the State recognizes that Chile's indigenous inhabitants are the descendants of human groups that exist in the national territory since pre - Columbian times, which preserve ethnic and cultural manifestations own the land being for them the principal foundation of their existence and culture." Article 12 of Law No. 19253 indicates that communities hold ownership and possession rights when they obtain land titles following the procedures established by said Law. Article 9 provides a definition of indigenous community and states "indigenous community means any group of people belonging to the same indigenos ethnic group and that have one of the following characteristics...recognized traditional leadership...holdings or having held indigenous land in common." ILO Convention 169 (Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention) was ratified by Chile in 2008. However, according to some secondary sources, implementation has been slow and the indigenous right to consultation prior to acquisition has not been fully implemented.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 13 of Law No. 19253 provides that indigenous lands may not be sold, seized, taxed or acquired by prescription, except between communities or indigenous people of the same ethnic group. All land owned by communities may not be leased, given on loan, or assigned to third parties in use, enjoyment or administration. Article 3 and Article 12 of Law No. 12253 indicates that indigenous land must be registered to receive the legal protection under Law No. 19253.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Chile; Government of Chile. 1993. Ley Indigena No. 19.253 Articulo 20-A,B.. Available at: http://www. conadi.gob.cl/documentos/LeyIndigena2010t.pdf; Government of Chile. 1979. Decreto Ley No. 2.695, Fija Normas para Regularizar la posesión de la pequeña propiedad Raíz y para la Constitución del Dominio Sobre Ella. May 30. Available at: http://www.leychile.cl/ Navegar?idNorma=6982;
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of Law. No. 19253 provides "It is the duty of society in general and the State in particular, through its institutions respect, protect and promote the development of indigenous people, their cultures, families and communities, adopting appropriate for such purposes and protect indigenous lands mediated, ensure for its proper operation, for its ecological and foster its expansion balance." In Chile, the following communal tenure types are recognized: Títulos de Merced Antiguos Indivisos, pueblo Mapuche (Antique Indivisible Gifted Titles, Mapuche Communities), Subsidios Comunitarios (Community Subsidies), Compras de Tierras Comunitario (Community Land Purchases), Transferencias Fiscales (Fiscal Transfers), Regularización propiedad comunitaria (Regularized Community Property), Comunidad Agrícola Diaguita Huasco Alto (Diaguita Agricultural Community of Huasco Alto), and Comunidades Agrícolas Región de Coquimbo (Agricultural Communities in the Coquimbo Region). See Rights and Resources Initiative. 2015. Who Owns the World’s Land? A global baseline of formally recognized indigenous and community land rights. Washington, DC: RRI.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 10 of Law 19253 establishes procedures by which community may be registered in Chile. Indigenous people must present an authorized copy of the community's constitution to the respective national or regional government office or to the Bureau of India Affairs Corporation. However, there are no explicit provisions ensuring that procedures will be accessible and affordable for indigenous communities. Under Law 19253, there are no provisions for mapping indigenous land or otherwise collecting documentary evidence.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 10 of Law 19253 recognizes the legal personality of indigenous communities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 7 of Law 19253 provides "The State recognizes the right of indigenous peoples to maintain and develop their own cultural manifestations, in all that is not contrary to the morals, good customs and public order. The State has the duty to promote cultures Indians, which are part of the heritage of Chilean nation" (unofficial translation). However, the law grants the National Indigenous Development Corporation authority over indigenous land (Arts. 11, 13, 15 Law No. 19253).

indicators.additional_info:
Article 19 of Law No. 19253 provides that Indigenous shall have the right to communally pursue activities in holy sites, ceremonial cemeteries... However, the National Indigenous Land Corporation has discretion to deny applications for indigenous land registration. Article 11 states "within thirty days from the date of deposit documents, may object to the establishment of the Indigenous Community if it has not complied with the
requirements of law and regulations state for training and for approval of its statutes." Article 16 states "the division of indigenous lands from titles of mercy must be formally requested the competent judge by the absolute majority of holders resident in her inheritance rights. The judge, without trial / and the report of the Corporation shall divide the common title, giving each indigenous as appropriate applying there customary law in accordance with Article 54 of this law and, in lieu thereof , the common law."  Article 54 recognizes the right of communities to assert customary laws in indigenous cases as long as such laws do not conflict with the Constitution.

indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: There are no durational limits established by Law No. 19253, which suggests that indigenous land rights may be held in perpetuity.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: There are limited rights to give to consent prior to acquisition, but it is clear that FPIC has not been fully recognized by Chile's national laws.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Chile; Government of Chile. 1993. Ley Indigena No. 19.253 Articulo 20-A,B.. Available at: http://www. conadi.gob.cl/documentos/LeyIndigena2010t.pdf; Government of Chile. 1979. Decreto Ley No. 2.695, Fija Normas para Regularizar la posesión de la pequeña propiedad Raíz y para la Constitución del Dominio Sobre Ella. May 30. Available at: http://www.leychile.cl/ Navegar?idNorma=6982;
indicators.additional_info: A regulation governing the environmental impact assessment system (S.D. No. 40) was enacted in 2012, which contains rules governing the "consultation" indigenous peoples with regard to investment projects that are subject to an EIA. However, this Regulation has been criticized as failing to meet the standards established in ILO Convention 169. Specifically, the Regulations has been criticized for "limiting the requirement for prior consultation to high-impact projects; b) restricting consultation to cases that directly affect indigenous peoples, this being determined in advance by the authority (Articles 27 and 86); c) handing over sole responsibility for the design and implementation of consultation processes to the Environmental Assessment Department, without including the interested peoples (Article 85)." See link to secondary source: http://www.iwgia.org/images/stories/sections/regions/latin-america/documents/IW2014/ChileIW2014.pdf. Article 29 of Law No. 19253 provides that "in order to protect the heritage of historical Indian cultures, excavators of indigenous historic cemeteries for scientific purpose must obtain the consent of the affected indigenous community. " NOTE: Although ILO Convention 169 was ratified by Chile in 2008, implementation of the consent provision has been riddled with delays and temporary measures that failed to fully meet the Convention 169 standards. For more information, see: http://www.dplf.org/sites/default/files/executive_summary_consultation_2015_web_02-17-2016_c.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Law No. 5 on Agricultural Communities 1968 (Amended 1993) provides communities with rights to own, use and enjoy lands held in common. However, the law establishes limitations on these ownership rights and it is unclear whether communities can use these lands for non-agricultural purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Chile; Government of Chile. 1993. Ley 19.233, Modifica Decreto con Fuerza de Ley No. 5, de 1968, del Ministerio de Agricultura, que contiene la normativa legal sobre las Comunidades Agrícolas. August 5. Available at: http://chile.justia.com/nacionales/leyes/ley-n-19-233/gdoc; Decreto con fuerza de Ley Nº 5 - Comunidades Agrícolas, Decreto con fuerza de Ley Nº 19. Texto refundido.
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of the Law on Agricultural Communities defines agricultural communities a "grouping of rural land owners that occupy, exploit, and cultivate land in common and are organized in accordance with this law." Law No. 5 recognizes community property rights and states "the villagers are owners of a right or share on common property, which allows access to the use and enjoyment of community property." NOTE: "In Chile, the following communal tenure types are recognized: Títulos de Merced Antiguos Indivisos, pueblo Mapuche (Antique Indivisible Gifted Titles, Mapuche Communities), Subsidios Comunitarios (Community Subsidies), Compras de Tierras Comunitario (Community Land Purchases), Transferencias Fiscales (Fiscal Transfers), Regularización propiedad comunitaria (Regularized Community Property), Comunidad Agrícola Diaguita Huasco Alto (Diaguita Agricultural Community of Huasco Alto), and Comunidades Agrícolas Región de Coquimbo (Agricultural Communities in the Coquimbo Region)" See Rights and Resources Initiative. 2015. Who Owns the World’s Land? A global baseline of formally recognized indigenous and community land rights. Washington, DC: RRI.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The state retains authority to expropriate agricultural community property upon paying just compensation (Art. 31, 40, Law No. 5 on Agricultural Communities). The Agrarian Reform Corporation retains overarching authority over agricultural land owned by communities. Voluntary transfers of rights held by agricultural communities may be authorized by the Head of the Land Office (Art. 39, Law on Agricultural Communities).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community members retain authority to use and enjoy the land and water for agricultural purposes; however, their authority is subject to overarching limitations established by the state. Authority over the agricultural community is also vested in Board of Directors and President of the Agricultural community (Art. 17-22, Law on Agricultural Communities) as opposed to the community members themselves.

indicators.additional_info: Article 20 of the 1968 Law on Agricultural Communities provides that the powers of the Board of Directors are: administration of assets, ensuring compliance with agreements made at the general meeting of the agricultural community, and other responsibilities.

CHN.name: China

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities (indigenous and non-indigenous)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI; Harvard LIDS

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law grants ownership of collectively-owned lands, forests, mountains, grasslands, unclaimed land, beaches to all members of the village collectives.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 58, Property Rights Law 2007; Art. 10, PRC Constitution; Law on Land Administration
indicators.additional_info: Article 10 of the Chinese Constitution establishes that "land in the rural and suburban areas is owned by collectives except for those portions which belong to the State...house sites and privately farmed plots of cropland and hilly land are also owned by collectives." Article 58 of the 2007 Property Law provides that the "immovables and movables owned by the collective include the following: (1) the land, forests, mountains, grasslands, wasteland and tidal flats belong to the collective..."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Collectively-owned properties are protected by law, but the right only takes effect upon registration. The State retains broad power to expropriate or requisition collectively-owned property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 58, 59, 60, Property Rights Law 2007; Art. 10, PRC Constitution; Art. 8-10, Law on Land Administration
indicators.additional_info: Article 9 of the Property Law states that "the creation, alteration, transfer or extinction of the property right shall become valid upon registration according to law..." Article 61 of the 2007 Property Law provides that the collective shall "enjoy the right to possess, utilize, dispose of and obtain benefit of such properties." Art. 63 provides that "the collectively-owned properties shall be protected by law and shall not be occupied, privately divided, withheld, damaged by any institution and individual." Art. 10 of the Constitution and Art. 42 of the 2007 Property Law provide that "collectively owned land can be expropriated to meet the needs of public interests (Property Law/2007, Art. 42).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While the law is silent on whether registration must be affordable, there are clearly defined procedures and collectives can obtain government assistance in registering their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 11, Law on Land Administration; Arts. 9-22, 2007 Property Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 11 of the Law on Land Administration states the ""People's government at the county level shall register and put on record lands collectively owned by peasants and issue certificates for the ownership concerned."" Arts. 9-22 of the 2007 Property Law establish registration procedures which collectives must follow to obtain ownership certificates. Art. 18 of the 2007 Property Law states that ""the registration department shall provide assistance to the obligee and interested party to review and make a copy of the registration information.""

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law establishes legal personality for members of the collective where decisions of the collective organizations infringe on their legal rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 63, 2007 Property Rights Law
indicators.additional_info: The current law does not require the establishment of a legal entity first for the acquirement of the collective land ownership by collective farmers. Although according to the Organic Law of the Villagers Committees of the PRC (2010 Revision, Art.7), the establishment of the Villagers Committee has to be approved by county governments, it is not a precondition for acquiring the collective land ownership for collective farmers. Art. 63 states "Where the decisions made by the collective economic organizations, villagers’ committee or other principals infringe upon the legal rights and interests of members of the  collective, the infringed members may claim revocation of such decisions with the people’s court. (Personal communication with Dr. Linlin Li, PhD, University of Groningen)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Members of the collective retain legal authority over the collectively-owned land. Decisions on land contract schemes, utilization of land, etc. are subject to members of the collective. But collective authority is subject to overarching government approval.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 59, 2007 Property Law; Art. 10 of the Land Administrative Law; Article 12 of the Rural Land Contracting Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 59 of the 2007 Property Law states "The real and movable properties which are collectively-owned by the urban collective shall be collectively owned by members of such collective. Things stated below shall be decided collectively by the members of the respective collective in accordance with relevant legal procedure: (i) The land contract scheme and subcontracting of the lands to institutions; (ii) The adjustment of the contracted lands among contractor of the right to; (iii) The utilization and distribution ways in respect of such fees as land; (iv) Such matters as changes of ownership of the enterprises whose capital is contributed by the collective; (v) Other matters required by law. the legal authority is granted to representative bodies such as Villagers Committee or Villagers Groups, instead of collective members themselves. See Art. 10 of the Land Administrative Law and Art. 12 of the Rural Land Contracting Law (Personal Communication with Dr. Linlin Li, PhD)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Under Art. 14 of the Land Administrative Law and Art. 126 of the Property Law, there is a time limit on the use rights to farmland, forest land, and grassland. Although these rights can be renewed, it is not an automatic renew.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2007 Property Rights Law; Law on Land Administration; Land Administrative Law

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The State can expropriate collectively-owned land for a public purpose, and does not need to consult or obtain consent from collective.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 42, Property Rights Law; Art. 2, Law on Land Administration
indicators.additional_info: Art. 42, Property Rights Law provides compensation to the collectives when their land is expropriated for a public purpose.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Forest Law recognizes the right of collectives to own forests resources, including trees. Collectives can utilize, dispose and obtain benefit from movable properties collectively owned.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 58, 61 Property Rights Law 2007; Art. 3, the Forest Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 3 of the Forest Law states that forest resources shall belong to the state, unless the law states they shall be owned by the collective"; Art. 27 of the Forest Law states that "the trees planted by a collectively owned organization shall be owned by the organization."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Chinese government owns all water resources. Collectives are only granted use rights. The Ministry of Water Resources is charged with allocating water entitlements on an annual basis.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 3, 2002 Water Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 3 of China's 2002 Water Law provides that "water resources are owned by the State. The State Council, on behalf of the State, exercises the right of ownership of water resources. The water of ponds belonging to rural economic collectives and the water of reservoirs built and managed by such collectives shall be used by the collectives respectively."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Chinese legislation does not explicitly grant indigenous/community land rights in protected areas.
indicators.additional_info: The Regulations of the People's Republic of China on Nature Reserves (Art. 27) requires that "residents in nature reserves must comply with administrative regulations and subject themselves to management authority." This implies that collectives are allowed to reside within protected areas, even though they may not have legal rights within such areas.

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary tenure under laws have recognition only at will of state. Law (1998 amended 2004) recognizes commons as well as individual parcels may be certificated but sustains compulsory conversion of all Certificates into statutory private titles. Legal implication is of forced subdivision of collective Certificates at conversion  (Decree 2019 Art. 24).
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law No. 98-750 as amended in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: Community/ customarily held lands recognized but denied status as property until certificated and Certificates converted into absolute titles, compulsory with time limit currently set at 2023, likely to be re-extended. Collective ownership permitted but also temporary pending final titling (Decree No. 2019-266, Art. 24).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary Rights remain inferior to statutory private title under 2004 amendment of 1998 law - and face total extinction. Certificates, including for commons owned by groups or communities must be converted into individual statutory titles by cut-off date, or become unowned public land; can avoid this only via registration of corporate entity in which to vest title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) as amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law, No. 98-750 as amended in 2004. Law of 2013 extended time to 2023, to be re-extended as most of pop. do not yet hold  Certificates.
indicators.additional_info: A positive provision of land law is that 2004 amendment provides for commons to be certificated as well as individual parcels. Compulsory conversion of certificated rights into individual or corporate statutory titles signals extinction of customary tenure & governance. No compensation at compulsory acquisition unless the land is developed (i.e. settled, farmed). Customary lands also have no protection from already reallocated land taken for lease or concessions, although a procedure of 'amicable resolution' exists when communities protest (Rural Land Law, 1998 (2004) Arts.11-14).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Amendment 2004 mplified procedure for issue of Customary Certificates by state-assisted village survey, parcel identification, mapping & devolved registration & issue of Certificates. Also enabled groups to secure collective certificates without forming legal entities by vesting land in name of appointed Manager - but temporary until final titling unless form corporation in which to vest title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) as amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law, No. 98-750 as amended in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: Certification of customary land rights is temporary under current law (1998 as amended in 2004). Their compulsory conversion into statutory individual titles signals end of community jurisdiction and customary norms. High costs and multiple land losses anticipated. Presently limited number of rural persons have Certificates.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal provision for groups or communities to be legal persons. Since 2004 they may acquire Customary Certificates in the name of an appointed manager. This cannot be sustained at compulsory conversion into individual statutory titles, unless group registers a corporate entity to own the land. Unless legal changes most commons likely to become public land vested in local governments.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No.98-750 of 1998 (2004), Art.1. Implementation Decree No. 2019-266.
indicators.additional_info: The 1998 (2004) law retained colonial provision in Decree 55-580 of May 1955 permitting recordation of customary rights by groups/ communities, but required formation of legal entities in order for certification to be transformed into property titles by groups now requiring communal Certificates to be vested in the name of a designated Manager' (2004, Arts. 1,9,17,19). Should law remain unamended unregistered commons and Certificates not converted into titles held by registered legal entity will become public land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Village roles are limited to committees to identify and record rights, with assistance of surveyors & officials, but not elected and vested with general land administration powers. Customary norms continue.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree Establishing Rural Land Management Committees, Decree No. 99-593 of 1999 and Order of 12 June 2001 elaborating Decree. Law on General Organization of the Territorial Administration, No. 2014-451 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Villages are administrative units and Village Councils (not elected bodies) are created under Law No.2014-451 on General Territorial Organization. Village Land Management Committees (VLMC) is alsounelected, are created by the Rural Land Law 1998 and responsible only for delimitation of village territories (Decree 2013-296 Stipulating Procedure for Delimitation of Village Territories) and individual & collective holdings within village domains (Rural Land Law 1998 (2004) Art.8-10). The laws are silent  on routine land management, presumed to be a state function once all lands titled, but potential for community-based management institutionally exists in these laws.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: May be assumed that customary rights are owned in perpetuity and will be upheld when Certificates converted into statutory Land Titles, but under State authority and administration. Majority certification far from achieved.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (2004).
indicators.additional_info: Nor has there been policy and legal change vesting more powers in community to administer lands or removal of compulsory Certification and conversion into statutory Titles.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: State may allocate leases or concessions on unregistered community land without consent, but objections may be submitted within three months, heard, and decision made.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law, 1998 (2004), , Arts. 11-13). Decree No. 99-595 on Provisional Concession Subject to Third Party Rights, Art. 8 -9.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Forest law in 2014 transferred tree ownership from state to individual or collective land owner, retained in the new forest code of 2019.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, Law No. 2019-675 of July 23 2019, Arts. 26 & 27.
indicators.additional_info: Forest Code 2019 Art. 26: "Ownership  of a natural forest or tree belongs to the owner of the land on which it is located". Art. 27:  "Ownership of a created forest or planted tree is vested in the landowner or to the person who created or planted it under an agreement with the landowner".

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water has been the common property of the nation since 1928. The Water Law 2023 confirm use rights for all, including right of communities to protect and use waters for sacred purposes. Privately titled owners have rights to freely use water on their lands but must allow for easements for agro-pastoral, industrial, fishing, recreation and transportation access.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law of Public Domain 1928. Water Law No. 2023-902.
indicators.additional_info: Law of Public Domain, 1928 amended to include all waters as state property. The Water Code (2023) admits sacred waters as controlled by communities (Art. 28) & and permits free use for listed domestic purposes (Arts.18, 27-28).  (Art.89).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The 2019 forest code recognizes natural & planted forests on customary land as customary property (Art. 25).  Limited use rights are available to communities in State or Local Authority Protected Forests; ie. collecting dead wood, picking fruit, food, medicinal plants, harvesting honey, gums, resins, mushrooms, etc. (Art. 39).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code,  No. 2019-675 of July 23 2019.
indicators.additional_info: Sacred forests are protected by the Administration, whilst respecting the rights, habits, and customs of rural communities, under conditions determined by decree (Art. 26). No provision for communities to have other forests recognized as their own property.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary tenure under laws have recognition only at will of state. Law (1998 amended 2004) recognizes commons as well as individual parcels may be certificated but sustains compulsory conversion of all Certificates into statutory private titles. Legal implication is of forced subdivision of collective Certificates at conversion  (Decree 2019 Art. 24).
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law No. 98-750 as amended in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: Community/ customarily held lands recognized but denied status as property until certificated and Certificates converted into absolute titles, compulsory with time limit currently set at 2023, likely to be re-extended. Collective ownership permitted but also temporary pending final titling (Decree No. 2019-266, Art. 24).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary Rights remain inferior to statutory private title under 2004 amendment of 1998 law - and face total extinction. Certificates, including for commons owned by groups or communities must be converted into individual statutory titles by cut-off date, or become unowned public land; can avoid this only via registration of corporate entity in which to vest title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) as amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law, No. 98-750 as amended in 2004. Law of 2013 extended time to 2023, to be re-extended as most of pop. do not yet hold  Certificates.
indicators.additional_info: A positive provision of land law is that 2004 amendment provides for commons to be certificated as well as individual parcels. Compulsory conversion of certificated rights into individual or corporate statutory titles signals extinction of customary tenure & governance. No compensation at compulsory acquisition unless the land is developed (i.e. settled, farmed). Customary lands also have no protection from already reallocated land taken for lease or concessions, although a procedure of 'amicable resolution' exists when communities protest (Rural Land Law, 1998 (2004) Arts.11-14).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Amendment 2004 mplified procedure for issue of Customary Certificates by state-assisted village survey, parcel identification, mapping & devolved registration & issue of Certificates. Also enabled groups to secure collective certificates without forming legal entities by vesting land in name of appointed Manager - but temporary until final titling unless form corporation in which to vest title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No 98-750 of 1998 (Cht 1 & 2) as amended by 2004-412 of 2004. Decree No. 2019-266 fixing application mode of rural land law, No. 98-750 as amended in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: Certification of customary land rights is temporary under current law (1998 as amended in 2004). Their compulsory conversion into statutory individual titles signals end of community jurisdiction and customary norms. High costs and multiple land losses anticipated. Presently limited number of rural persons have Certificates.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal provision for groups or communities to be legal persons. Since 2004 they may acquire Customary Certificates in the name of an appointed manager. This cannot be sustained at compulsory conversion into individual statutory titles, unless group registers a corporate entity to own the land. Unless legal changes most commons likely to become public land vested in local governments.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Law No.98-750 of 1998 (2004), Art.1. Implementation Decree No. 2019-266.
indicators.additional_info: The 1998 (2004) law retained colonial provision in Decree 55-580 of May 1955 permitting recordation of customary rights by groups/ communities, but required formation of legal entities in order for certification to be transformed into property titles by groups now requiring communal Certificates to be vested in the name of a designated Manager' (2004, Arts. 1,9,17,19). Should law remain unamended unregistered commons and Certificates not converted into titles held by registered legal entity will become public land.
