CMR.name: Cameroon

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rights limited to peaceful customary occupancy and use of national/public lands, not ownership' (1974 law). Certificates introduced in 2024. Individuals may secure statutory titles for houses, farms etc but survey high cost. No provision for collective title for other than developed or to-be-developed lands (1976 Law). New forest law 2024 is prompting tenure change.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 (2008). Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure. Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Decree No. 76-165 1976 as revised by Decree No. 2005/481 on Procedure for Securing Title. Decree 2016 on Advisory Commission on Land and Property Matters (May 27 2016). Law 2024/008 of 24 July 2024 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Cameroon's law sustains the customary right to peacefully occupy and use national land, but does not protect this right from reallocation to investors  without compensation. New regulation which gives communities a pre-emptive right to dispose of products on their forest land (2024). Land law  recognizes land may be held individually or collectively as occupation and use on unowned public or national lands. Despite reference to 'clan property' and 'the properties of traditional chiefdoms'. Communities may improve their security by applying for a Land Certificate for National Lands (Decree 76-165, s. 4) a formal right to occupy, not own, and excludes unfarmed lands (eg forests). No legal provision for IP to secure traditional territories other than under the new forest & wildlife  law, but which require land tenure regulations to be activated.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: There is no equivalency in the legal force of a statutory private title to land and customary occupancy on national lands. Security limited to developed lands (houses, farms, plantations, etc). New Forest Law in 2024 challenges the absence of collective title by providing for communities to own forests; needs new land law to be implemented.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Law No. 85-09 of 1985 to Lay Down the Procedures Governing Expropriation for Public Purposes. Valuation, Law No. 85/09 (s. 7). Law 2024/008 of 24 July 2024 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Section 7 of Ordinance 1974-2 declares that "bone fide owners and occupants of public property may not be dispossessed thereof unless the public interest so requires, and subject to compensation". Only refers to developed land. Appeal is limited to amount of compensation.  This does not protect traditional community-based rights to forestlands  or most grazing land by pastoralists. Pygmy IP have no legal protection as their traditional lands are collectively held and used forests with few permanent houses or farms.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No affordable titling under 1974 land law for registration but 1976 and 2004 circulars simplify Certification. Extinction of customary rights in favour of statutory title is unaffordable  limited to homesteads. A clan, chiefdom, community or developer may secure a certificate of occupancy for developed/developing lands under 1976 decree & 2024 circular.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Regulations Governing Cadastral Surveys and Records. Decree No. 76-165 of 1976 (2005) to Establish the Conditions for Obtaining Land Certificates. Circular 0002 of Feb 2024 Procedure for Issue of Certificates of Possession of Customary Rights.
indicators.additional_info: Despite state willingness for communities to identify their collective areas, no provision for collective ownership, although possibilities to secure lawful occupancy exist under Category 1 National Lands (lands occupied with houses, farms, plantations and grazing lands' )(Ord. 1974-1, s. 15). Registration of rights refers only to developed lands "where human presence and development is evident" (s. 17), or for development by a commercial land developer. Undeveloped lands held by communities by tradition are deemed to be  "free of any effective occupation" (s. 15).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are not recognized as legal persons for purposes of owning lands. While the new forest law July 2024 provides for Community Protected Areas,  mechanisms lack clarity; require new tenure law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure. Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Constitution, Law No. 96-6 of 1996 amending Constitution of 1972.  Law 2024/008 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Legal acknowledgement that  customary communities exist in provisions for traditional chiefdoms to be allocated tracts of public land, as lawful occupants. Section 4(1) of Ord. 74-1 refers to this as "...more especially in the provinces where the concession of chiefdoms is considered the joint property of the community, the chief having only the enjoyment thereof". These lands are included as Artificial Property, a sub-category of inalienable Public Property, along with ports, roads, railways, etc. These enables a community to secure lawful recognition of its occupancy on National Lands - but confined to development/ 'to be developed' lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary norms and governance apply in communities, led by Traditional Authorities. No elected community councils or land committees. Force & effect may fail given overriding decision-making powers by local councils and national land bodies. Land law 1974.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure.
indicators.additional_info: Communities may regulate lands by custom, but without explicit force and effect should decisions not concur with  national or local council decisions. Local councils number c.  400, comprise numerous villages; no official village level government system. Traditional authorities may be members of consultative land boards deciding allocation of National Lands.  The customary courts constitute the first level in the judiciary system, superseded by modern courts.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: By custom, rights are continuous and inheritable. The land law 1974 makes no mention of occupancy and use on national lands as limited in term. But neither does it acknowledge customary occupation rights as property rights. Statutory titles and Certificates issued for developed lands are also of unspecified term.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure. Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands.  Law 2024/008 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Note that the new forest enactment (July 2024) provides for Community Protected Areas distinct from forests allocated on short term (now up to 25 years) for extractive harvesting. New law specific to  local and/or indigenous communities (sec. 3).  Section 5 declares that "The State, regional and local authorities, local communities and individuals shall exercise all their ownership rights on their forest and in agroforestry zones subject to the restrictions provided for by laws in force and this law".  It is unclear how this ownership will be recognized although tenure regulations promised.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no legal requirement for consent of occupants of public land prior to disposal of their lands by the State although compensation for lost structures and crops may be paid. Law provides for local advisory committees prior to issuing large-scale lands, but with limited powers.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2001-1 to Establish the Mining Code. The Pipeline Law, Decree No. 97-116 of 1997. Gas Code, Law 2002-13 of 2002. Forest Decree 95/531/PM of 1995. Decree on Advisory Commissions of 27 May 2016. Law 2024/008 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Decision No. 1354 of 26 Nov 1999 under the Forest Law, No. 94-1 of 1994 repealed by new law but retains participatory procedure for classification of forest;   only requires prior information be given, not consent from communities. Expropriation requires compensation but does not include unregistered landholders. The decentralized advisory land commission is chaired by the sub-division officer and comprises among others the Chief & two notables from the community. Representation of IP communities with no recognized chiefs is not provided for. Reccs are just reccs. Decision-making process is not laid out.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: State owns all natural trees, only planted trees belong to landowner including to customary occupants.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 94-1 of 1994 to Lay Down Forestry, Wildlife and Fisheries Regulations. Framework Law No. 96/12 of 1996 Relating to Environmental Management. Decree No. 76-167 to Establish the Terms and Conditions of Management of the Private Property of the State. Law No. 85/09 of 1985 on Expropriation. Law 2024/008 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Use rights are provided to communities neighbouring forest concessions. Communities may participate in decision-making for forest concession, but little influence. Local management rights may be  granted on forest not exceeding 5000 ha so long as the area is outside prohibited or protected forests. Communities are provided pre-emption rights by which they can withdraw a surface area from a forest concession in order to create their community forest areas, in accordance with specific regulations. 2024 Law extends this to pre-emptive right to dispose of forest products but unclear how the land will be certified (tenure regulations still to come Mar 2025). Community forests may be used for logging or protection. However, State not prevented from reallocating these to large-scale land-based investments (agri-business, mining, etc.). No indication of compensation and/or benefit-sharing in this event.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a national resource, with devolved management to local governments, and further devolved roles of traditional or village authorities including dispute resolution using customary procedures. Domestic access free for villagers. Water Law 1998.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 98-5 of 1998 Governing Water Resources. Law No. 2004-18 to Establish Rules Applicable to Communes. Decree No. 2010/0239/PM Transferring Well & Borehole Development to Communes. Draft Water Law, 2013.
indicators.additional_info: The main thrust of water law is that management is to be increasingly devolved to local governments. No provision for recognition that waters on community lands belong customarily to communities or may be formally regulated by communities. Nevertheless, community leaders have de facto authority over immediately local water matters in that: "Traditional authorities shall be empowered to settle disputes relating to the use of water resources on the basis of local customs and practices, without prejudice to the rights of the parties concerned to refer the matter to the competent court" s.24 of Law No. 98-5 of 14 April 1998 To Lay Down Regulations Governing Water Resources.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community rights to State Protected Areas are limited to access and use as per management plans. Buffer zones allocated to communities to use. Under laws of 1994 Community Forests were limited to short-term concessions to harvest. New 2024 law provides for Community Protected Forests, yet to backed up by tenure and other regulations.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 94-1 of 1994 to Lay Down Forestry, Wildlife and Fisheries Regulations. Framework Law No. 96/12 of 1996 Relating to Environmental Management. Decree No. 76-167 to Establish the Terms and Conditions of Management of the Private Property of the State. Law No. 85/09 of 1985 on Expropriation. Law No. 2024/008 of July 2024 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Forests and wildlife are national assets and State Forests are the private property of the State. Community Protected Areas defined as outside State lands. Compensation for loss of local lands is limited to evidence of effective occupation, and obligatory only in case of registered landowners. Buffer zones around Protected Areas available for local use. Customary rights  extinguished in State Forests. Hunting is normally banned. Some Park management plans permit customary access for specific uses & include community reps in some decision making.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rights limited to peaceful customary occupancy and use of national/public lands, not ownership' (1974 law). Certificates introduced in 2024. Individuals may secure statutory titles for houses, farms etc but survey high cost. No provision for collective title for other than developed or to-be-developed lands (1976 Law). New forest law 2024 is prompting tenure change.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 (2008). Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure. Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Decree No. 76-165 1976 as revised by Decree No. 2005/481 on Procedure for Securing Title. Decree 2016 on Advisory Commission on Land and Property Matters (May 27 2016). Law 2024/008 of 24 July 2024 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Cameroon's law sustains the customary right to peacefully occupy and use national land, but does not protect this right from reallocation to investors  without compensation. New regulation which gives communities a pre-emptive right to dispose of products on their forest land (2024). Land law  recognizes land may be held individually or collectively as occupation and use on unowned public or national lands. Despite reference to 'clan property' and 'the properties of traditional chiefdoms'. Communities may improve their security by applying for a Land Certificate for National Lands (Decree 76-165, s. 4) a formal right to occupy, not own, and excludes unfarmed lands (eg forests). No legal provision for IP to secure traditional territories other than under the new forest & wildlife  law, but which require land tenure regulations to be activated.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: There is no equivalency in the legal force of a statutory private title to land and customary occupancy on national lands. Security limited to developed lands (houses, farms, plantations, etc). New Forest Law in 2024 challenges the absence of collective title by providing for communities to own forests; needs new land law to be implemented.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Law No. 85-09 of 1985 to Lay Down the Procedures Governing Expropriation for Public Purposes. Valuation, Law No. 85/09 (s. 7). Law 2024/008 of 24 July 2024 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Section 7 of Ordinance 1974-2 declares that "bone fide owners and occupants of public property may not be dispossessed thereof unless the public interest so requires, and subject to compensation". Only refers to developed land. Appeal is limited to amount of compensation.  This does not protect traditional community-based rights to forestlands  or most grazing land by pastoralists. Pygmy IP have no legal protection as their traditional lands are collectively held and used forests with few permanent houses or farms.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No affordable titling under 1974 land law for registration but 1976 and 2004 circulars simplify Certification. Extinction of customary rights in favour of statutory title is unaffordable  limited to homesteads. A clan, chiefdom, community or developer may secure a certificate of occupancy for developed/developing lands under 1976 decree & 2024 circular.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Regulations Governing Cadastral Surveys and Records. Decree No. 76-165 of 1976 (2005) to Establish the Conditions for Obtaining Land Certificates. Circular 0002 of Feb 2024 Procedure for Issue of Certificates of Possession of Customary Rights.
indicators.additional_info: Despite state willingness for communities to identify their collective areas, no provision for collective ownership, although possibilities to secure lawful occupancy exist under Category 1 National Lands (lands occupied with houses, farms, plantations and grazing lands' )(Ord. 1974-1, s. 15). Registration of rights refers only to developed lands "where human presence and development is evident" (s. 17), or for development by a commercial land developer. Undeveloped lands held by communities by tradition are deemed to be  "free of any effective occupation" (s. 15).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are not recognized as legal persons for purposes of owning lands. While the new forest law July 2024 provides for Community Protected Areas,  mechanisms lack clarity; require new tenure law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 74-1 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing Land Tenure. Ordinance No. 74-2 of 1974 to Establish Rules Governing State Lands. Constitution, Law No. 96-6 of 1996 amending Constitution of 1972.  Law 2024/008 To Lay Down Forestry and Wildlife Regulations.
indicators.additional_info: Legal acknowledgement that  customary communities exist in provisions for traditional chiefdoms to be allocated tracts of public land, as lawful occupants. Section 4(1) of Ord. 74-1 refers to this as "...more especially in the provinces where the concession of chiefdoms is considered the joint property of the community, the chief having only the enjoyment thereof". These lands are included as Artificial Property, a sub-category of inalienable Public Property, along with ports, roads, railways, etc. These enables a community to secure lawful recognition of its occupancy on National Lands - but confined to development/ 'to be developed' lands.

COD.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Pygmy Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Under law applying to all customary communities, IP rights are based on (i) all land belongs to the State; (ii) customary tenure is accorded strong place as a form of rights to land; (iii) statutes do not yet exist through which any community can secure a land title, without extinguishing customary rights (the Bill for a new land law is in draft as of April 2024). Under Law No. 22/030 of 2022 in force since 2023, IP are guaranteed  "their right to the land and natural resources they own, occupy or use ..." ( Art. 42).  Law No. 22/030 is premised on articles 51 & 123 of the Constitution protecting vulnerable groups.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2006 (2011) Art. 9, 34, 51, 123. General Law on Property,  No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980. Law No. 22/030 On Protection & Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples
indicators.additional_info: Art.9 of Constitution: "The State exercises a permanent sovereignty notably over the soil, the subsoil, the waters and the forests, over the air, river, lakes and maritime spaces of the Congo as well as over the Congolese territorial sea and over the continental shelf". Art 34 states that "The State guarantees the right  individual or collective property acquired in conformity to the law or to custom". Law No. 80-008 of July 18 1980 amended Law 73-021 to assure Zairians with titles prior to 1973 continuity of rights through their conversion into concessions (contracts). Not practically relevant to customary landowners.  National Land Policy 2022 (not available as of April 2024) supports registration of customary rights.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: On paper, IP and other customary rights are equally protected as for statutory titles via issue of 25 year or permanent concessions to applicants for development purposes, an with parcel size limitations. IP  have the added advantage of protection from land takings without their free, prior and informed consent, but failure of which can still result in which is still phrased in such a way that compulsory acquisition, with relocation to equivalent area and land type (Art. 42-43 of Law No. 22/030). The 1973 law and Constitution Art. 34 imply equal force and effect between a right secured under customary law and a right secured under statutory provision - via application for a certificate ('concession') issued for 25 years, limited to proposed  development of the land (building etc), ot issue of a permanent concession to citizens. Survey and other costs are prohibitive and rarely adopted by the 70% of Zairians who hold land under customary tenure, including IP.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2006 (2011). General Law on Property, No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980. Law No. 22/030 of July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of  IP.
indicators.additional_info: Legal declamation or equity is not echoed in practice for as long as there is no mechanism for a customary owner to secure registrable customary ownership; not yet provided as of April 2024. The Expropriation  Law 2006 does not protect customary lands from takings and specifically includes areas under collective rights (Art. 8). A survey is required to determine compensation (Art. 12), and which must be based on the value of the property, to be paid prior to transfer (Art. 18). IP are in better position than other customary communities in that their FPIC must be initially sought (Art. 42 Law No. 22/030).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary rights to occupy and use land have long been recognized and embedded in Arts 387-388 of the 1973 land laws. The Constitution 2006 establishes customary ownership as lawful property. However there remains no procedure to activate this in terms of registration. Securing a concession is possible but extinguishes the customary form and jurisdiction. It is anticipated that the promised new land law by the end of 2024 will provide directly for formalization of customary rights when sought.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2006 (2011). General Law on Property, No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980. Law No. 22/030 of July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of  IP.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No explicit definition of a community as a legal person. This is however an implied presumption of the law; eg. Forest law 2014 recognizes a community as a legal person without registering itself as an association or other legal entity, in enabling a community to secure a forest concession. Earlier the Agricultural Act 2011 provides for customary landholders including as communities to secure agricultural concessions without requirement to form and register an association.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 22/030 of July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of  IP. Forest Code 2002. Decree No. 14/018 of 2 Aug 2014 on the Conditions for Assigning Forestry Concessions to Local Communities, Ministerial Order  No. 025/2016 of 9 Feb 2016 Establishing for Management and Logging of Local Communities' Forestry Concessions.  Agricultural Law No. 11/022
indicators.additional_info: Article 48 of Law No. 22/030 of 15 July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples states: "The State grants legal recognition and protection to the lands and resources traditionally owned, occupied or used by indigenous pygmy peoples. This recogntiion respects the habits and customs of the peoples concerned".

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Even under the colonial era customary land tenure was accepted as a regime enabling a community to govern and regulate its own land relations within customary domains. This situation has been sustained until the present. There are no statutory directions on principles which a community must apply such as inclusive decision-making. The right which communities execute are limited to the use and management of the land, as the state remains the landowner. Customary land in 1973 was defined as "land occupied by local communities that they inhabit, cultivate or use is some way, individually or collectively, in accordance with local customs and practices" Art. 388. this also applies to IP; they may make their own rules and norms as to their land uses and its regulation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2006 Arts. 9, 34, 51, 123. General Law on Property 1973, Arts. 387-388. Law No. 22/030 of 15 July 2022 on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples. Arts. 42-48.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All land in DRC belongs to the State so what is owned is a right to a specific parcel. This is a property right. Customary landowners own only the occupation and use of the land, and which is not alienable. This right is however, sustained in perpetuity as inheritable. It is not protected from compulsory acquisition. IP are offered a much stronger guarantee of customary land security than non-IP communities through statement their legal ownership of their lands as: "The State grants legal recognition and protection to the lands and resources traditionally owned, occupied or used by indigenous pygmy peoples" (Art. 48 of Law No. 22/030 of 2022).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2006 Arts. 9 and 34. General Law on Property 1973, Arts. 387-388.
indicators.additional_info: In practice, no mechanism has yet been developed to issue proof of ownership to an IP community, also the case for other customary communities; pending the enactment of a long-promised new land law in 2024.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: IP are guaranteed the right to own, occupy and use their lands, and that "No relocation an take plae without free, prior and informed consent" (Art. 42 of Law No. 22/030 of 2022. However, compulsory acquistion may be activated; with relocation to other land equivalent in quality and extent (Art. 43). Unlike other holders, IP are guaranteed priority for return of the original land if the public purpose is not fulfilled  (Art. 42). For non-IP, there is no requirements for consent when the State determines the land is needed for another public purpose. It is obliged to pay compensation including to customary owners of the rights to that land, and the amount of which is negotiated, and must be paid before change of rights to that land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Expropriation Law No. 77-001 of 1977. Law No. 22/030 of July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Forests are state property (Forest Code 2002 Art. 7). However, "Trees located in a village or its immediate surroundings, or in a collective or individual field, are the collective property of the village or of the person to whom the field belongs" (Art. 9). Provision of Community Forests (as concessions up to 50,000 ha, held in perpetuity, has been an enormously successful development in light of their forest dwelling and forest dependence as forest peoples. IP also benefit from legal provision that "Indigenous Pygmy peoples have the right to full enjoyment of all natural resources, timber and non-timber as well as the benefits derived from environmental services on the lands they traditionally own, occupy or use". Art. 44 of Law No. 22/030 of 2022.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 011/2002 of August 20 2002 Forestry Code. Law No. 22/030 of July 2022 on Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the State (Constitution 2006 Art. 9). The  State is obliges to ensure human water needs are met (Art. 48).No authorization is requires for use of water from the public domain for domestic purposes (Water Law, 2015 Art.. 24). "Domestic use is defined as any withdrawal of water intended exclusively for satisfying the needs of individuals and for family or family-type plant or animal production" (Art. 24).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2006 Arts. 9 & 48. Water Law No. 15/026 od Dec 31 2015, Art.24

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: DRC is achieving mass institution of community controlled forests, now number 222 over 4. 14 Mha as of 1 April 2024. These are in form of concessions held exclusively and in perpetuity by the community. This reform began with the Forest Code 2002, opening way for communities "to apply for a concession for some or all of the forests protected under customary law" (Art. 22), and if seek to harvest, under technical supervision (Arts. 111-113). Decree No. 14/2018 set terms and conditions, one being that the forest is owned by custom (Art. 2). The area may not exceed 50,000 ha (Art. 17). "For the purposes of exploiting the forest concession a local community may organize itself as either a non-profit association, a cooperative society, or in the form of a local development committee following the standard model of the Ministry of Rural Development" (Art. 21). These areas are defined as  Local Community Forest Concessions (CFCL). These concessions are proving to be a way through which communities may secure mapped exclusive rights to their land, pending new land law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code , Law No. 011/2002. Decree No. 14/018 of August 02 2014 on Terms and Conditions of Forest Concessions to Communities.  Ministerial Order 025/CAB/MIN/ECN-DD/CJ/00 RBM/2016 9 Feb 2016. on CFCL. National Strategy on Community Forestry, 2018.  Law No. 22/030 of July 15 2022 on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.
indicators.additional_info: Forest is categorized as Classified Forests (eg. Nature Reserves, National Parks) with restrictive conditions; Protected Forests, unclassified and with more flexible use and management regimes, and Production Forests, removed from Protected Forests for commercial harvesting (Art. 10). "The forest use rights of populations living in or near the forest estate are those resulting from local customary and traditions, insofar as they are not contrary to law and order. These allow these populations to harvest forest resources to satisfy their individual or community domestic needs" (Art. 36). "Communities may continue to exercise their traditional use rights on concessions insofar as this is compatible with logging to the exclusion of agriculture" Art. 44). The community has a committee reporting to the Community Assembly of all adults, and a monitoring committee, and chiefs may not use his title to claim personal benefit from the forest Ministerial Order 2016, Art. 21). Logging is subject to special permits (Art. 41).

COD.Indigenous Q9: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, significant progress — Water belongs to the State (Constitution 2006 Art. 9). The  State is obliges to ensure human water needs are met (Art. 48).No authorization is requires for use of water from the public domain for domestic purposes (Water Law, 2015 Art.. 24). "Domestic use is defined as any withdrawal of water intended exclusively for satisfying the needs of individuals and for family or family-type plant or animal production" (Art. 24).  (Constitution 2006 Arts. 9 & 48. Water Law No. 15/026 od Dec 31 2015, Art.24)
COD.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — DRC is achieving mass institution of community controlled forests, now number 222 over 4. 14 Mha as of 1 April 2024. These are in form of concessions held exclusively and in perpetuity by the community. This reform began with the Forest Code 2002, opening way for communities "to apply for a concession for some or all of the forests protected under customary law" (Art. 22), and if seek to harvest, under technical supervision (Arts. 111-113). Decree No. 14/2018 set terms and conditions, one being that the forest is owned by custom (Art. 2). The area may not exceed 50,000 ha (Art. 17). "For the purposes of exploiting the forest concession a local community may organize itself as either a non-profit association, a cooperative society, or in the form of a local development committee following the standard model of the Ministry of Rural Development" (Art. 21). These areas are defined as  Local Community Forest Concessions (CFCL). These concessions are proving to be a way through which communities may secure mapped exclusive rights to their land, pending new land law.  (Forest Code , Law No. 011/2002. Decree No. 14/018 of August 02 2014 on Terms and Conditions of Forest Concessions to Communities.  Ministerial Order 025/CAB/MIN/ECN-DD/CJ/00 RBM/2016 9 Feb 2016. on CFCL. National Strategy on Community Forestry, 2018.  Law No. 22/030 of July 15 2022 on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.)
COD.Communities Q1: Does the law recognize a: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — All land belongs to the State (1973, 2006). Rights to the land are lawfully secured under customary law or state allocated concessions. Law 2022 guarantees IP rights to occupy, use land & resources they customarily own (Art. 42).  National Land Policy 2022 commits to securing community & IP lands under customary collective entitlement. Land  Code promised in 1973 now in draft (2025). (Constitution, 2006 (2011) Art. 9, 34. General Law on Property,  No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (1980). Law No. 22/030 2022 on the Protection and Promotion of Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples. National Land Policy Document, January 2022. Bill for National Spatial Planning, November 2023. Draft Tenure Code 2024.)
COD.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Consistently  indicated equitable recognition of customary and statutory property rights. 70% of Zairians hold land under customary tenure. The 1973 law & 2006 Constitution indicate equivalent legal force & effect of customary rights and statutory Certificates issued for 25 years, usually limited to development or commercial purposes, and with prohibitive survey costs. (Constitution, 2006 (2011). General Law on Property, No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980. Law Protecting Indigenous Pygmy Peoples No. 22/2022 & Order Establishing Multi-Stakeholder Forum on IP, Order No. 023/2025)
COD.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — Despite embedded recognition of customary tenure, still no legal procedure to register such rights, other than through issue of concessions which, depending on the term and type may extinguish customary rights. Customary authorities regulate lawfully but without required recordation of rights or inclusive decision-making by members. (Constitution, 2006 (2011). General Law on Property, No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980.)
COD.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — While no definitive clause, it is a working assumption of the laws that communities are legal persons; eg. Enabling the Agricultural Act 2011 to allow communities to secure agricultural concessions without registering associations for this purpose. So too the Forest Law 2014 enables allocation of forest concessions to rural communities in their own name. (Agricultural Law No. 11/022 Forest Code 2002. Decree No. 14/018 of 2 Aug 2014 on the Conditions for Assigning Forestry Concessions to Local Communities, Ministerial Order  No. 025/2016 of 9 Feb 2016 Establishing for Management and Logging of Local Communities' Forestry Concessions.  )
COD.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Even under the colonial era customary tenure lawfully enabled a community to govern its own domain, sustained until today. Directions to modernize customary governance norms are lacking, eg. requiring inclusive participation of members or gender balance, or guidance for electing local land committees.  (Constitution, 2006 (2011) Art. 9, 34, 51, 123. General Law on Property,  No. 73-021 of July 20, 1973 (as amended 1980 Arts. 387-388. Law No. 22/030 of 2022 On Protection & Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.)
COD.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Partial, significant progress — Customary landowners own exclusive occupation and use rights in perpetuity as inheritable. The land itself belongs to the State. National Land Policy 2022 is adamant that the customary rights of local communities and the IP population must be secured; the latter was secured in 2022 law and in April 2022 a Multistakeholder Forum set up to mobilize and coordinate law's implementation. (Constitution 2006 Arts. 9 and 34. General Law on Property 1973, Arts. 387-388. Law No. 030/2022 On Protection & Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples. Order No. 023/2025 Establishing MultiStakeholder Forum to implement No. 030/2022.)
COD.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — The National Land Policy 2022 and the Land Use Planning Bill 2023 are adamant that FPIC is required and applicable to all communities including IP. Only IP by end 2024 are are legally assured FPIC (2022). However, commitment to FPIC does not protect them from expropriation for public purposes with compensation, should the community not grant consent.  (Expropriation Law No. 77-001 of 1977. National Land Policy 2022.)
COD.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully —  "Trees located in a village or its immediate surroundings, or in a collective or individual field, are the collective property of the village or of the person to whom the field belongs" Forest Code 2002. Art. 9. (Law No. 011/2002 of August 20 2002 Forestry Code)
COD.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water belongs to the State (Constitution 2006 Art. 9). The  State is obliges to ensure human water needs are met (Art. 48).No authorization is requires for use of water for domestic purposes (Water Law, 2015 Art. 24).  (Constitution 2006 Arts. 9 & 48. Water Law No. 15/026 od Dec 31 2015, Art.24)
COD.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Forests are state property (Forest Code 2002 Art. 7). This excludes trees/forest within village domains. Forest law made advances in allocating substantial tracts of forest to communities under concessions held in perpetuity, subject to regulations as to their governance and use. Mixed IP& IPLC communities are a main beneficiary. Forest Decree 2014 & Ministerial Order 2016. (Forest Code , Law No. 011/2002. Decree No. 14/018 of August 02 2014 on Terms and Conditions of Forest Concessions to Communities. Ministerial Order 025/CAB/MIN/ECN-DD/CJ/00 RBM/2016 9 Feb 2016. on CFCL. National Strategy on Community Forestry, 2018. Law No. 030/2022 On Protection & Promotion of the Rights of Indigenous Pygmy Peoples.)

COG.name: Republic of Congo

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Idnigenous Peoples only (Pygmies)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: A law on IP (2011) recognizes that IP exist (c. 10% of population), protects their property rights, and acknowledges that the population sustain those rights in the absence of registration. Six Decrees issued in 2019  elaborating  procedures for consultation of IP in socio-economic development; access to social and health services; access to education; issue of civil status documents; measures to protect cultural rights and sites; and establishment of a national committee to ensure promotion and protection of IP rights. However, no Decree as of 2024 elaborating the commitment of Law 5-2011 to facilitate demarcation of IP lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No 5- 2011 du 25 fevrier 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones. Title VII (Arts 31-42) on Property Rights.
indicators.additional_info: The 2011 law bans the term 'pygmy', forbids discrimination,  torture, and forced assimilation, requires consultation with IP on all matters of concern to them, guarantees their right to administer their own affairs and recognizes their villages as administrative entities, provides for rights to education, health, and other matters. Title VII addresses property rights "IP have a collective and individual right to property, to possession, to access and utilization to lands and natural resources which they traditionally occupy and use for their subsistence, medical use and work" (Art. 31, 5-2011). This right is protected "in absence of land titles" (Art. 32).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law protects IP land rights to a greater extent than provided for other customary communities who may only secure titles to developed lands. IP also do not need titles to be recognized as owners of real land rights and these rights include communal forest lands (Law 5-2011 Art. 32). However, IP are not protected from compulsory acquisition for public purposes  (Art. 32, 34, 41), only assured benefit from such projects, and requirement that all exploration, exploitation and conservation on their lands are first subject to a socio-economic and environmental impact assessment (Art. 35). Consent prior to classification of and forest is required from affected local communities and IP (Decree No 2023-118).
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts 31-42, Loi No 5- 2011 du 25 fevrier 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones. Law 21-2018 fixing rules of occupation and acquisition of lands. Decree 2023-118 on obligatory FPIC prior to classification of forests.
indicators.additional_info: Vague definition of 'public purpose' as justified for 'conservation, public facilities, and development of areas of specific interest for the satisfaction of the needs of the population' (Art. 43, Law No. 11-2004).  Law 21-2018 enables compensation by agreement for unregistered communities at compulsory acquisition (Art 43).  Note that many concessions for logging and mining overlap the lands of both IP and local communities.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Unlike for local communities which must secure titles to hold legally recognized property, there is no provision for IP to secure title, or that this be through simple, affordable and accessible means. The 2011 law says the state will facilitate the delimitation of IP land 'to guarantee their recognition'. It also provides that these rights are in law secure without titling (Art 32). No application decree by 2024 for promised demarcation (Art. 32). The law protects IP right to 'define priorities and strategies for the development, use and control of their lands and other resources within the limits of the law' ( Art. 36).
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 32, 36 , Law No. 5 -2011 on Promotion and Protection of the Rights of IP.
indicators.additional_info: Note that IP are exempt from the requirement to develop the land, obligatory for other customary landholders. No evidence that any IP community has secured title, or that beyond promised demarcation, that there is political intention to title these lands (many concessions and protected areas overlay their lands).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: An IP community may be recognized as land owner as individuals or collective. This does not necessarily mean they are accordingly held to be legal persons as there is no provision for issue of titles to IP communities, only demarcation of their lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 32, Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 9 of Loi No. 10-2004 fixant les principes generaux applicables aux regimes domanial et foncier, provides that in the case of collective property, registration may be in the name of the collective or any group it has established.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law of 2011 permits IP to exercise their customs and traditional institutions, to define their own land uses, and to exercise their right to develop their economic and social systems to secure subsistence.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 13, 32, 36, 37 of Loi No. 5-2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones.
indicators.additional_info: While there is no specific provision for IP to follow traditional leadership systems, other articles appear to take this for granted.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The rights of IP to their lands are imprescriptible and inalienable; they may not be sold. Although not stated, it is safely presumed that IP land rights are held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 32, Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: IP to be consulted before projects are formulated that will affect their lands and resources, and socio-economic assessments to be undertaken. IP and other local communities must be consulted and their consent obtained prior to forest classification of (Decree No. 2023-118). This is also more generally required 'during the preparation, implementation and monitoring of actions and decisions affecting them in terms of the exploitation and sustainable management of forest resources' (Art 5 Law No. 33-2020 on the Forestry Code). As IP are largely within forests and affected by forest policy and law, it is not significant that FPIC outside forest areas is not provided for.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 38 & 39 , Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones. Art. 5, Law 3 No 33-2020 on the Forestry Code. Decree No. 2023-118 on Classification of Forest.
indicators.additional_info: A socio-economic and environmental impact study must be carried out prior to any project for exploitation or conservation (Art. 35, Loi 5- 2011).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: IP are assured rights to own, possess, access and use natural resources as required for subsistence, medical use and for 'their work'. They also have a right to benefit from commercial exploitation of their resources.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art.31 Loi No. 5 -2011, Art. 41 Loi No. 5-2011.
indicators.additional_info: In practice, concessions may be allocated over IP lands, also implied in their requirement that before protected areas or exploitation takes place, that an impact assessment is carried out (Art. 35, Loi 5-2011).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law No. 9-2004 on the Domain of the State, defines water as part of the public domain at Art. 5. Water within domains traditionally occupied and used by IP is freely able to be used by IP (Law  No. 5-2011 Art. 31).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 5-2011, Art. 31. Law No. 9-2004 on the State Domain, Art. 5.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: IP may obtain rights of use in PA as defined by the Management Plan of each PA. Use rights  in Law No. 33-2020 are defined as 'rights resulting from local customs or traditions whereby the local community or indigenous peoples may, in a forest that does not belong to them, either harvest certain products or engage in certain activities, whether or not for sale, within the limits of satifying theri vital domestic or customary needs' (Art. 2).  In practice some IP live within PA, but with no specific legal provisions on this. Habitation is likely to determine the type of PA declared since Decree No. 2023-118 requiring FPIC prior to classification of forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: In some cases customary rights including for IP have been denied; e.g. Decret No 99-136 on Conkouati-Douli National Park extinguished all use rights.
indicators.additional_info: IP must be consulted an their consent obtained prior to creation of protected areas; Art. 39, Loi 5-2011, Decree No. 2023-118 on FPIC for Forest Classification.

local_communities_entries.framework: Local communities (separate law specifically for Indigenous Peoples)
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Titling of customary rights is compulsory and without which registration there is no security of tenure (Laws 10/2004, 21/2018). Only developed lands may be registered (Art. 53 of 21/ 2018). IP are exempt from need to register rights (No.5/2011).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2015 (2022) Arts. Loi No. 10-2004 Fixing Principles of General Application to National Lands and Tenure, Art. 31.Law No. 21-2018 Establishing the Rules for the Occupation & Acquisition of Lands. Law No. 25-2008 Concerning Agricultural Tenure, Art. 16. Law No. 5/2011 Promotion &  Protection of Indigenous Peoples. Decree No. 2018-484 fixing Functions of National Commission for Customary Lands.
indicators.additional_info: Art 33 of 2004 opened way for issue of collective titles for customary commons & Art 34 protected customary rights. Constitution 2015, & laws of 2008, 2018 removed both openings, state retains all undeveloped lands (forests, pastures etc). Law 21/2018  also makes recognition dependent upon registration. Law 484/2018 centralizes procedures. In short, access to customary tenure security has declined in RoC  since 2004 law.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Equal force and effect with land titles only with the State (Art. 10 of Law 21/2018). Exclusion of communal lands & collective titles limiting. IP are exempt from titling requirement by Law  5/2011, but as most live within Protected Areas, in practice only occupancy & use guaranteed. No provision for restitution.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 10-2004, and Law No. 25-2008. Decree No. 2006-255 & No. 2006-256 on institutions for adjudication and registration of customary rights. Law No. 25-2008. Law No 05/2011 on IP. Law No. 21-2018.  Law No. 26-2022 on Registration. Decree 2023-118 on FPIC in forest sector.
indicators.additional_info: Low uptake of customary titling. Hindered by  2018 repeal of 2006 law devolving Land Commissions to identify customary rights. Local communities are not exempt from compulsory acquisition of their lands under Law 11-2004, but since Decree No 2023-118 they must be consulted and their consent or refusal established - but only for forest developments. Decrees of 2006 confirmed by Arts 16-17 No. 25-2008 law makes only developed rural lands registrable, and Art 9 of Decree 2011-548 states that transactions are invalid without prior registration. These contradict Law 10-2004 which curiously remains in force. More remote & onerous procedure to secure title by 2018  (Art. 53).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Procedures for customary tenure security have become difficult uder laws of 2008 & 2018. Local Commissions replaced by a National Commission hindering access, costs high, customary titles only for developed lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 25-2008, concerning the Agricultural Tenure Regime, No. 21-2018 Establishing Rules for Occupation & Acquisition of Lands. Law No. 26-2022 on Rules for Registration of Real Property.
indicators.additional_info: Law No. 10-2004 provides for customary landholders to secure entitlement. Customary owners could also be allocated 'provisional concessions' after customary rights have been purged, obliged to develop the lands within five years (Art. 21). The procedures were free. The committees or commissions were revoked by No. 21-2018. Law No. 25-2008 limits rights to developed lands reiterated in Law 21-2018 (Art 53). Two pluses are that, once titled considered equivalent to private titles, and consent of a local community or Indigenous People required during the preparation, implementation and monitoring of actions and decisions affecting them in terms of the exploitation and sustainable management of forest resources (Art 53 of Law 21-2018 & Art. 5 of Law 33-2020).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal provision for local communities of IP to be recognized as legal persons. Despite legal provision in 2004 opening way for community commons to be collectively registered, and that the law is still in force, later laws 2008-2018 have removed this opportunity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 9 & 33 of Loi No. 10-2004 Fixing Principles of General Application for Tenure. Art. 53 of Law 21-2018
indicators.additional_info: Due to limit of registration of customary lands to developed lands/lands for development (2008, 2018), following opening for collective entitlement is not viable, despite still being in force: Art. 33 of Loi No. 10-2004: 'Establishment and guarantee of customary rights delivered in titles, as  held by those acting on behalf of a property collective, endows property rights'.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Traditional or elected land authorities not provided for but Decree 2013-280 on local government authorities provides for community development committees at village level with significant powers including relating to land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2015 (2022) Art. 230-231).  Decree 2013-280 on local government.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution 2015 (last amended in 2022) provides for A Consultative Council of the Wise and of Traditional Notables, responsible for giving opinions on social and cultural governance (Art. 230-231).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary use and occupation rights are not time limited. Entitlement of customary ownership over titled developed lands (houses, farms, etc.) is secure, and held with no fixed term.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 21-2018. fixing rules of occupaton and acquisition of lands.
indicators.additional_info: Law No 26-2022 Fixing Rules of Titling of Immoveable Property relate specifically issue of private titles, which if used in the customary sector extinguish all customary attributes. Resulting Land Titles have no fixed term.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Consent required - but limited to issue of forest concessions (Art 5 Law 33-2020). Compensation is  limited to registered property (Const. Art 23) but with provision that compensation is available by agreement to unregistered communities at compulsory acquisition (Law 21-2018 Art 43).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 11-2004. Constitution 2015. Law 21-2018 Fixings Rules of Occupation & Acquisition of Land.
indicators.additional_info: Definition of 'public purpose' is for 'conservation, public facilities, and development of areas of specific interest for the satisfaction of the needs of the population' (Art. 43, Law No. 11-2004). Procedure for compulsory acquisition given in Law No. 11-2004 and Law No. 21-2018. An enquiry prior to expropriation occurs only with village authorities and affected landowners (title holders) who have a casting vote (Art. 43, Law No. 11-2004). Compensation  set by agreement with the parties or if disagreement, by the court (Arts 25 & 35, Law No 11-2004). Appeal is possible (Art 95-96, Law No. 11-2004). Confirmed in Law 21-2018.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Planted trees belong to the community but felling is subject to a permit (Art. 20 Law No. 33-2020). Use of natural forests permitted including Protected Areas (Art 59, 61). Legal obligation for concessionaires to consult with communities/IP, to share benefits, and to engage in management decisions. Postive provisions for Community Forests outside Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No.33-2020 Forestry Code.
indicators.additional_info: Community Forests are part of the permanent forest estate belonging to the State domain (Art 10  Law No. 33-2020).  Community Forests include: a forest located within a commercial concession, a forest plantation belonging to or created by a community or Indigenous People, or a  forest classified for community's benefit (Art. 15). Community Forests require a simple management plan. Revenue from sale of products goes to the community or Indigenous People (Art. 19). No new classified forest may be declared without FPIC of local populations  and negotiation as to rights(Art 40-42).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law No. 9-2004 on the Domain of the State, defines water as part of the public domain at Art. 5. Art. 9 elaborates that this includes that water and natural resources on soil and seabed, river and land are owned by the State. Law on Water 2003  (No.13-2003) focused on commercial extraction but appears in Art 12 to permit free domestic use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No 9-2004 on the Domain of the State. Law 13-2003 o the Water Code.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No provision for communities to own Classified Forests but retain significant use rights (Art 59 Law 33-2020). Provision for Community Forests including classifiable as Protected Forests (Art. 10 & 15).  FPIC from IPLC required prior to 'any action affecting them in terms of exploitation and sustainable forest management' (Art. 15). Decree No. 2023-118 extends this to classification of a forest.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 33-2020 on the Forestry Code. Decree No. 2023-118 Determining the Terms and Conditions for Free, Informed and Prior Consent with Regard to the Classification of Forests.
indicators.additional_info: Participatory management is a principle of  both forest 2020 and environmental codes 2023. Environment Code lists respect for traditional knowledge and  that customary rules apply in absence of statutory rules (Art. 3). Legal distinction is drawn between Classified Forests and Protected Forests outside the permanent forest estate (No. 33-2020, Art. 2). In Protected Forests, local communities and indigenous peoples may harvest wood and non-wood products for domestic purposes, hunt and fish for local consumption, grow crops using tradition methods, graze livestock, keep beehives, use the forest for rituals, and access water (Art. 59).  Diverse types of Community Forests provided for including for protection.  FPIC of local authorities, local communities and  indigenous peoples  required prior to 'any action affecting them in terms of exploitation and sustainable forest management' (Art. 15). Decree No. 2023-118 extends this to classification of a forest.

(Art. 32, 36 , Law No. 5 -2011 on Promotion and Protection of the Rights of IP.)
COG.Indigenous Q4: Does the law recognize th: Partial, significant progress — An IP community may be recognized as land owner as individuals or collective. This does not necessarily mean they are accordingly held to be legal persons as there is no provision for issue of titles to IP communities, only demarcation of their lands. (Art. 32, Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones.)
COG.Indigenous Q5: Does the law recognize th: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The law of 2011 permits IP to exercise their customs and traditional institutions, to define their own land uses, and to exercise their right to develop their economic and social systems to secure subsistence. (Art. 13, 32, 36, 37 of Loi No. 5-2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones.)
COG.Indigenous Q6: Do the law and formal tit: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The rights of IP to their lands are imprescriptible and inalienable; they may not be sold. Although not stated, it is safely presumed that IP land rights are held in perpetuity.  (Art. 32, Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones. )
COG.Indigenous Q7: Does the law require the: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — IP to be consulted before projects are formulated that will affect their lands and resources, and socio-economic assessments to be undertaken. IP and other local communities must be consulted and their consent obtained prior to forest classification of (Decree No. 2023-118). This is also more generally required 'during the preparation, implementation and monitoring of actions and decisions affecting them in terms of the exploitation and sustainable management of forest resources' (Art 5 Law No. 33-2020 on the Forestry Code). As IP are largely within forests and affected by forest policy and law, it is not significant that FPIC outside forest areas is not provided for.  (Art. 38 & 39 , Loi No. 5 of 2011 portant promotion et protection des droits des populations autochtones. Art. 5, Law 3 No 33-2020 on the Forestry Code. Decree No. 2023-118 on Classification of Forest. )
COG.Indigenous Q8: Does the law explicitly r: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — IP are assured rights to own, possess, access and use natural resources as required for subsistence, medical use and for 'their work'. They also have a right to benefit from commercial exploitation of their resources. (Art.31 Loi No. 5 -2011, Art. 41 Loi No. 5-2011.)
COG.Indigenous Q9: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, significant progress — Law No. 9-2004 on the Domain of the State, defines water as part of the public domain at Art. 5. Water within domains traditionally occupied and used by IP is freely able to be used by IP (Law  No. 5-2011 Art. 31).  (Law No. 5-2011, Art. 31. Law No. 9-2004 on the State Domain, Art. 5. )
COG.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Partial, significant progress — IP may obtain rights of use in PA as defined by the Management Plan of each PA. Use rights  in Law No. 33-2020 are defined as 'rights resulting from local customs or traditions whereby the local community or indigenous peoples may, in a forest that does not belong to them, either harvest certain products or engage in certain activities, whether or not for sale, within the limits of satifying theri vital domestic or customary needs' (Art. 2).  In practice some IP live within PA, but with no specific legal provisions on this. Habitation is likely to determine the type of PA declared since Decree No. 2023-118 requiring FPIC prior to classification of forests. (In some cases customary rights including for IP have been denied; e.g. Decret No 99-136 on Conkouati-Douli National Park extinguished all use rights.)
COG.Communities Q1: Does the law recognize a: Partial, significant progress — Titling of customary rights is compulsory and without which registration there is no security of tenure (Laws 10/2004, 21/2018). Only developed lands may be registered (Art. 53 of 21/ 2018). IP are exempt from need to register rights (No.5/2011).  (Constitution 2015 (2022) Arts. Loi No. 10-2004 Fixing Principles of General Application to National Lands and Tenure, Art. 31.Law No. 21-2018 Establishing the Rules for the Occupation & Acquisition of Lands. Law No. 25-2008 Concerning Agricultural Tenure, Art. 16. Law No. 5/2011 Promotion &  Protection of Indigenous Peoples. Decree No. 2018-484 fixing Functions of National Commission for Customary Lands.)
COG.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: Partial, significant progress — Equal force and effect with land titles only with the State (Art. 10 of Law 21/2018). Exclusion of communal lands & collective titles limiting. IP are exempt from titling requirement by Law  5/2011, but as most live within Protected Areas, in practice only occupancy & use guaranteed. No provision for restitution. (Law No. 10-2004, and Law No. 25-2008. Decree No. 2006-255 & No. 2006-256 on institutions for adjudication and registration of customary rights. Law No. 25-2008. Law No 05/2011 on IP. Law No. 21-2018.  Law No. 26-2022 on Registration. Decree 2023-118 on FPIC in forest sector.)
COG.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, limited progress — Procedures for customary tenure security have become difficult uder laws of 2008 & 2018. Local Commissions replaced by a National Commission hindering access, costs high, customary titles only for developed lands.  ( Law No. 25-2008, concerning the Agricultural Tenure Regime, No. 21-2018 Establishing Rules for Occupation & Acquisition of Lands. Law No. 26-2022 on Rules for Registration of Real Property.)
COG.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — No legal provision for local communities of IP to be recognized as legal persons. Despite legal provision in 2004 opening way for community commons to be collectively registered, and that the law is still in force, later laws 2008-2018 have removed this opportunity. (Art. 9 & 33 of Loi No. 10-2004 Fixing Principles of General Application for Tenure. Art. 53 of Law 21-2018)
COG.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — Traditional or elected land authorities not provided for but Decree 2013-280 on local government authorities provides for community development committees at village level with significant powers including relating to land.  (Constitution 2015 (2022) Art. 230-231).  Decree 2013-280 on local government.)
COG.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Customary use and occupation rights are not time limited. Entitlement of customary ownership over titled developed lands (houses, farms, etc.) is secure, and held with no fixed term.  ( Law No. 21-2018. fixing rules of occupaton and acquisition of lands.)
COG.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — Consent required - but limited to issue of forest concessions (Art 5 Law 33-2020). Compensation is  limited to registered property (Const. Art 23) but with provision that compensation is available by agreement to unregistered communities at compulsory acquisition (Law 21-2018 Art 43).  (Law No. 11-2004. Constitution 2015. Law 21-2018 Fixings Rules of Occupation & Acquisition of Land.  )
COG.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Planted trees belong to the community but felling is subject to a permit (Art. 20 Law No. 33-2020). Use of natural forests permitted including Protected Areas (Art 59, 61). Legal obligation for concessionaires to consult with communities/IP, to share benefits, and to engage in management decisions. Postive provisions for Community Forests outside Protected Areas. (Law No.33-2020 Forestry Code. )
COG.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Law No. 9-2004 on the Domain of the State, defines water as part of the public domain at Art. 5. Art. 9 elaborates that this includes that water and natural resources on soil and seabed, river and land are owned by the State. Law on Water 2003  (No.13-2003) focused on commercial extraction but appears in Art 12 to permit free domestic use.  (Law No 9-2004 on the Domain of the State. Law 13-2003 o the Water Code. )
COG.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — No provision for communities to own Classified Forests but retain significant use rights (Art 59 Law 33-2020). Provision for Community Forests including classifiable as Protected Forests (Art. 10 & 15).  FPIC from IPLC required prior to 'any action affecting them in terms of exploitation and sustainable forest management' (Art. 15). Decree No. 2023-118 extends this to classification of a forest. (Law No. 33-2020 on the Forestry Code. Decree No. 2023-118 Determining the Terms and Conditions for Free, Informed and Prior Consent with Regard to the Classification of Forests.  )
