indicators.comment: Cooperative farming of 1990s gave way to forced privatization in 2008/2011 and preferential allocation to investors for commercial estates. Agro-pastoralism in Steppe largely sedentary. Taureg nomads occupy & use but don't own domains in Cultural Parks in Sahara. Law No. 02/2010 & Circular No. 108/2011 National Land Use Planning. Decree No.20-265 of 2020 re Industrial agriculture in Sahara.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 90-25 relative a orientation fonciere, Art. 39, 64 & 65. Loi No. 90-30 State Lands. Decree No. 459 of 1996 Agricultural Cooperatives. Decree No. 97-483 of 1997 Agricultural Concessions. Law No. 03 of 2004 Protection of Mountain Areas. Law No. 02 of 2010 National Land Use Planning. Circular No 108, February 2011. 2020 Décret exécutif n° 20-265 of 2020 Establishing Office for Industrial Agriculture in Saharan Lands.
indicators.additional_info: Lack of information as to number of Cooperatives still held by peasant groups, agro-pastoralists or indigenous Amazigh, given that only three persons can now own each parcel. Family tenure dominates in subdivisions. Local governments earmark grazing areas in steppe and near desert lands for farmers and  small numbers of semi-nomadic  pastoralists. Since repeal of Pastoral Code in 1982 there is no provision for supporting pastoralism; 95% reported as sedentary by 2006, supplementing local pasture with barley and other fodder crops. Policies follow abandonment in 1990s of redistributive reforms in favour of  commercial arable development extending into desert. Current status of collective tribal property (arch) is vague, or how rights to barren land (80.33% of country) are distributed. De facto recognition as customarily owned in that investors routinely pay tributes to traditional leaders.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No equality between titled lands & customary rights. Only occupation & use assured for transhumant Taureg in South and seasonal use of residual pastures in Steppe by  agro-pastoralists. Decrees since 2008  prioritize private titling and allocation to large scale investors including in Sahara. Exec. Decree No. 20-265/2020 lists provinces where industrial farming under concession favoured.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 24-27, 64-65 of Loi No. 90-25 relative a orientation fonciere (Art. 24-27, 64-65)  still in force. Décret exécutif n° 20-265 du 4 Safar 1442 correspondent au 22 September 2020 portant creation de office de development de agriculture  Executive Decree No 20-265 lists the districts (wilaya) where expansion of industrial farming  is to occur (by issue of industrial concessions).
indicators.additional_info: In late 1980s/early 1990s families, clans and commercial group were  assisted to form Collective Agricultural Enterprises (EAC) to develop farming and to which Certificates of Possession issued. EAC held 1% of country in 2005 (FAO, 2005, Utilisation des engrais par culture en Algerie). Policy since has been to individualize parcels, and to expand industrial agriculture. Wilaya (districts) allocate residual pasture to those in need. Tribal use rights to nomadic pastoral communities in the Sahara exist.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No procedure for community titling, most negative for indigenous Amazigh in Steppe and Taureg in Sahara. Taureg lawfully occupy and use historic domains in vast Cultural Parks. Customary communities incl. Arab communities are recognized as social forms and must be consulted in planning, but titling limited to individual & corporate entities. eg. Mountain Management Law No. 04-03 of 2004.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 90-25 relative a orientation fonciere, Art. 39, 64 & 65. Loi No. 90-30 State Lands. Decree No. 459 of 1996 Agricultural Cooperatives. Decree No. 97-483 of 1997 Agricultural Concessions. Law No. 03 of 2004 Protection of Mountain Areas. Law No. 02 of 2010 National Land Use Planning. Circular No 108, February 2011. 2020 Décret exécutif n° 20-265 of 2020 Establishing Office for Industrial Agriculture in Saharan Lands.
indicators.additional_info: Inadequate information on how agro-pastoralists and nomadic pastoralists may secure stable access to rangelands, and major loss of accessible domain through conversion into settled agriculture and exclusion of all traditional forested areas. Land policy and law since 1990 geared to settled farming and since then, although no legal statement, favours self-funded or investor large-scale industrial farming on semi-arid lands. Note that consultation with communal peoples assemblies is legally required for land use planning in rural areas including mountains and rangelands (Art 9 of Mountain  Management Law No 04-03 (2004).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal recognition of groups larger than 3 persons or communities to be registered owners of customary lands. Did exist via cooperatives from 1990 to 2008 forcibly subdivided from 2008 to 2011
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 90-25 of 1990 on Land Tenure. Law No. 459 of 1996 on Agricultural Cooperatives. Law No. 03 of 2010 on Exploitation of the Agricultural Lands of the State. National Land Use Planning. Circular No 108, 2011.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition that both Arab and Berber Amazigh IP even if not recognized owners operate collectively in rangeland use in the Steppe, even as rangeland has dramatically declined due to expansion of private farming. Taureg expected to govern own domains sustainably within vast State-owned cultural parks of Tassili `N'Ajjier and Ahaggar (5 Cultural Parks cover 44 million ha).
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi no. 90-25 relative a orientation fonciere, Art. 24, 58, 61. Decret executif no. 96-459 du 7 Chaabane 1417 correspondent au 128 decembre 1996 fixant les regles applicable aux cooperatives agricoles.
indicators.additional_info: Provisions by which to manage lands are straightforward. Commission for the Development of the Steppe supervises developments.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Without Certificates of Title, available only to individuals or registered corporate entities, communities hold use rights, some of which must be renewed annually such as access and use of Steppe State grazing lands. However in principle occupation and use rights are deemed to be held in perpetuity such as by Taureg nomads in south.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi no. 90-25 Art. 64

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal requirement for consent from communities prior to allocation of historical lands to outsiders, but must be consulted, and negotiation is possible as to rights to continue use. Constitution 2010 (2021). Expropriation Law 1991.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010. Loi no. 91-11 du 27 avril 1991, completee, fixant les regles relatives a l'expropriation pour cause d'utilite publique.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All natural forests fall within the national domain under authority of the state and local governments. Planted forests may be owned. Communities may freely use trees they have planted on their lands. Forest Law 2023.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi no 90-30 du 1er decembre 1990 portant loi domaniale, Art. 15

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Law guarantees water for domestic and agricultural needs. All water belongs to the state (national domain). Constitution 2010. Water Law No. 12 of 2005.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi no 05-12 du 28 Joumada Ethania 1426 correspondent au 4 aout 2005 relative a l'eau, Art. 2 & 3.
indicators.additional_info: Since repeal of Pastoral Code in 1982 no provision for semi-nomadic and nomadic pastoralists but 95% by 2006 reported as sedentary supplementing flocks with barley and other crops. Exception is Taureg in Saharan South. Exact status of traditional collective tribal property (arch) in 2024 unknown and no provision for community land titling, nor to whom rights to  barren land (80.33% of country) are distributed or rights to water on these state-owned lands.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rights of access & use of Protected Areas are available to communities, all under State ownership & control. However, only Strict Nature Reserves exclude habitation, and use. No legal provision for Community Protected Areas. Protected Areas Law No 11-2011. Mountain Management Law No. 03-2004 & Decree 2007. Forest Law 2023.
indicators.law_and_provision: Protected Areas Law No 11-2011. Mountain Management Law No. 04-03 (2004) & Decree 2007. Cultural Heritage Law NO. 4 of 1998) Establishing Cultural Parks. Forest Law 2023.
indicators.additional_info: Five Cultural Parks cover 44% of territory, include a mix of community, private and state lands, governed by the State. Eg. Ahggar National Park at 450,000 sq. km  & Tassli n'Ajjer National Parks at 72,000 sq. km historically inhabited for 12,000 years by pastoral communities. However, their customary rights are acknowledged, managing and regulating their own lands within the parks.

ECU.name: Ecuador

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (indigenous peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2008 Constitution establishes that Indigenous communes, communities, peoples and nations are recognized and guaranteed protection.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Article 57 of the 2008 Constitution states "indigenous communes, communities and nations are recognized and guaranteed...to keep ownership, without subject to a statute of limitations, of their community lands, which shall be unalienable, immune from seizure and indivisible...to keep ownership of ancestral lands and territories and obtain free awarding of these lands...." Article 60 of the Constitution states "Communities (comunas) that have collective land ownership are recognized as an ancestral form of territorial organization." NOTE: Ecuador ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples in 1998

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 57(4) of the Constitution provides that indigenous communes and communities can "keep ownership, without subject to a statute of limitations, of their community lands, which shall be unalienable, immune from seizure and indivisible." However, registration is required to receive protection.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Article 59 of the Constitution states "the collective rights of the coastal back-country people (montubios) are recognized to guarantee their process of integral, sustainable and durable human development, the policies and strategies for their progress and their forms of societal management, on the basis of knowledge about their reality and respect for their culture, identity, and own vision, in accordance with the law."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 60 of the Constitution provides "Ancestral, indigenous, Afro-Ecuadorian and coastal back-country (montubios) peoples can establish territorial districts for the preservation of their culture. The law shall regulate their establishment. Communities (comunas) that have collective land ownership are recognized as an ancestral form of territorial organization." Community land was registered under the Law of the Communas 1936, but is unclear whether the registration procedures are accessible and not cumbersome.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities are granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership under the Constitution of Ecuador, 2008
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 57(10) of the Constitution provides communities with the right to "create, develop and practice their own legal system or common laws, which cannot infringe constitutional rights, especially those of women, children and adolescents." However, this provision is not implemented through legislation or regulations.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Article 57(1) provides that indigenous communes and communities can "freely uphold, develop and strengthen their identity, feeling of belonging, ancestral traditions and forms of social organization."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution indicates that indigenous and community land rights have no durational limits and thus may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 57(7) of the Constitution provides communities with the right "to free prior informed consultation, within a reasonable period of time, on the plans and programs for prospecting, producing and marketing nonrenewable resources located on their lands and which could have an environmental or cultural impact on them..." Presidential Decree 1247 (2012) establishes procedures for gathering the free, prior, and informed consent of communities prior to acquisition for hydrocarbon exploitation, but it is unclear whether this Decree applies when land is acquired for exploitation of other resources.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Article 57(7) further provides that communities have the right to "participate in the profits earned from these projects and to receive compensation for social, cultural and environmental damages caused to them. The consultation that must be conducted by the competent authorities shall be mandatory and in due time. If consent of the consulted community is not obtained, steps provided for by the Constitution and the law shall be taken. "  Article 4 of the Decree 1247 provides that FPIC will take place prior to the acquisition of land for hydrocarbon exploitation/exploration.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Both the Forest Law and Environmental Management Law provide that indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian peoples will have priority in the use of community lands and forest products, and that local authorities must consult these peoples before issuing policies for the demarcation, management or administration of conservation areas and ecological reserves.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Article 39 of the Forestry Law states the indigenous, black or Afro-Ecuadorian will have exclusive right to the use of products of different forest timber and wildlife in the lands of its domain or possession. The Ministry of Environment and demarcate these lands given to technical advice communities. Article 57(6) of the 2006 Constitution provides that communities have the right to "participate in the use, usufruct, administration and conservation of natural renewable resources located on their lands."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Water Resources Act 2014 has passed in Ecuador and reportedly limits the water rights of indigenous communities by privatizing these rights (reviewer could not find a copy of this legislation online).
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247 (2012); Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous peoples in Ecuador have protested the new water law (Water Resources Act 2014), which privatizes water rights (https://fsrn.org/2014/07/indigenous-march-for-water-rights-in-ecuador-reaches-quito/). Article 57(6) provides that communities have the right to "participate in the use, usufruct, administration and conservation of natural renewable resources located on their lands.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Local authorities must consult indigenous, black and Afro-Ecuadorian peoples before issuing environmental policies and policies for demarcation, management or administration of conservation areas and ecological reserves.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 13, Environmental Management Law, 1999; Biodiversity Law; Art. 57, Constitution, 2008; Ley Nº 54 - Ley de Desarrollo Agrario; Presidential Decree 1247; Law No. 46-2006 the Collective Rights Act of Black People or Afroecuadoreans
indicators.additional_info: Although consultation rights are provided by law (Art. 13, Environmental Management Law), it is unclear whether communities have ownership rights to land within protected areas. Article 28 of the Law of Environmental Management, 1999, establishes that all persons, including Indigenous Peoples, blacks, and Afro-Ecuadorians, have the right to participate in environmental management. Article 87 of the Forest, Conservation and Natural Areas and Wildlife Law prohibits the unauthorized hunting, fishing, and use of explosives and poisonous substances within protected areas, with the exception of traditional systems of subsistence fishing by Indigenous Peoples, black, and Afro Ecuadorians

EGY.name: Egypt

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Desert customarily owned by Bedouin, now living in settlement & housing blocks in  Sinai & Red Sea due to  takings for tourism. Landless Bedouin turning to smuggling. Only statutory individual titles available. Non-Bedouin Cust. Inheritance norms keep parcels in family.  'Collective' farming coops >300ha, some allocated to Bedouin.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Code, 1948. Agrarian Reform Law, No. 178 1952, repealed by No. 96/1992.  No. 124/1958 & 1969 laws nationalized unregistered lands. Increased rents by 1969 law & eliminating inheritable rights of tenants. No 110/1975 on Cooperatives amended by  No. 204/ 2014. Desert Law amended by Investment Law 2007 to create large Investment Zones.
indicators.additional_info: 112 of 114 million Egyptians live along Nile in cities and as irrigated farm land (5% of country area). Feudalism gave way to agrarian reform in 1952 with redistribution of arable lands. Counter revolution by  1990s left 57% of arable lands (5 Mha) owned by 5% pop. 5,435 Village Cooperatives max. of 300 ha each but 2014 law encouraging conversion into shareholding companies. Cooperatives promoted for housing estates in Desert via leases under 1969 law.  Egyptian inheritance rules ensure titled lands remain in same family.  Civil Code enables families, companies & groups to claim farm & house ownership after 12 years occupation.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue

indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for titling of customary rights nor collective ownership. However, customary rights can be a basis of proof for application for individual statutory title. ERI.name: Eritrea

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A level playing field in that while state owns all land, citizens equally eligible for lifetime usufructs for houses & arable farms. No provision for communal agro-pastoral or pastoral tenure but access areas defined on village basis. Constitution 1997. Land Proclamation 1994.
indicators.additional_info: Customary rights abolished; despite (i) long customary history of family/clan tenure (enda, risti), village communal ownership (diesa or shekh'na) and (ii) high proportion of agro-pastoral & pastoralist families (est. 65% rural pop in 2001). The  1994 law does not provide for collective tenure, other than for arable farming cooperatives. State takes direct control of woodlands/shrublands (6%), barren & grazing lands (95% of country area) but enables access on village by village basis as is traditional. Emphasis on sedentisation; only those permanently resident in village get allotted parcel. Males & females allocated individually.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protection in that allocated or confirmed rights to house & farm plots equally subject to compensation at compulsory acquisition and by agreement, and common regime for all rural dwellers. However, desecured to extent that customary norms and governance is repealed & no provision for common properties, most critical for pastoralists but replaced with village based commons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1997, Art. 23. Proclamation No. 58/1994, Art. 50-53, 39, 4.
indicators.additional_info: Uncertain  and customarily insecure: right to house in home village dependent on fulfilment military duties. Registration of usufructs is compulsory but not activated in most rural areas. Every citizen obtains an agricultural usufruct for house or farm or both (Art. 4 Law 58/1994) provided by elected village councils. While the State  controls rangeland & forests (woodland, shrublands), law does prescribes this for 'all villages in Eritrea, according to local custom use their own pasture and wood' subject to regulations (Law 1994 Art. 48). This (customary) opportunity actively adopted.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Procl. 86/1996 confirms each village/area has a general assembly of all adults ('megaba'aya') with elected  decision making council (baito). Many issue heritable family plots in accordance with customary diesa where remote titling offices fail to reach villages. Village based procedure and legal provisions similar.
indicators.law_and_provision: Regional Administration Proclamation No. 86/1996. Legal Notice No. 31/1997.  Proclamation No. 95/1997.
indicators.additional_info: Devolution of authority is a partly unmet Constitution pledge. Law 37/1993 recognized 2,580 villages and 699 'village area administrations' in remoter areas. 'Lifetime' usufructs in practice heritable in similar ways to customary  diesa (village-based family titles taken up in absence of official allotment, certification & registration. Land Administration Bodies remote from villages. No registration of collective customary rights although the law commits to 'All villages in Eritrea, shall, according to local custom, use their own pasture and woods' (Art. 48 of Law No. 58/1994) and do so, almost only official opening for customary norms.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for villages as legal persons. No collective titles in the law. However (a) Art. 48 of No 58/1994 permits villages to use their own pasture and woodlands in accordance with local custom.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1997, Art. 23, Proclamation 58/1994, Art. 11 (5), 40, 48.
indicators.additional_info: Issue of rights is to individuals, male & female made distinctly. No provision for collective rights to be titled.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: 1994 land law implies village assemblies will be members of Land Administrative Bodies (under Land Commission in Ministry of Lands & ) but devolution abandoned for lack of funds & staff. Traditional village assemblies (Megaba'aya) and customary councils of elected elders (baito adi) issue customary rights in default of remote Provincial Land Commissions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 10; Land Proclamation No. 58/1994, Art. 10; Proclamations No. 37/1993 &  86/96 on Regional Governments.
indicators.additional_info: Legal land authority vested in Land Administration Bodies at provincial level, assemblies of 699 village clusters were supposed to be part of the Land Administration Bodies. No information on how many LAB established. Elected  village council exercise authority although not specified as one of their functions.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Rights may be  held in perpetuity despite definition as lifetime usufructs (1994 Art 12.1). Legitimized by  enabling surviving spouses & minors to retain the land Arts 12.3, 12.4. Registered usufructs described as 'private' and convertible to lease but cannot be sold Art 18, 24.1.  However, the house itself may be sold, leased, mortgaged  - and inherited Art 31-34.
indicators.additional_info: The law has found ways to sustain many norms of village-based customary tenure, most applicable to majority tribes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for consent or consultation at compulsory acquisition. However, compensation is payable. The right to negotiate compensation is also  provided Art.51.2, 51.3. Permits petition to High Court Art. 51.4. Compensation must be paid prior to owner vacating the land Art. 52.1. Level playing field for titled and untitled usufructs. No clarity on village communal lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Proclamation 58/1994, Art. 51-52.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Forestry and Wildlife Conservation Act No. 155/2006 stipulates that 'Any persons who plants trees on land shall be the owner of such trees and may dispose of them' (Art 23). Art 24.3 encourages community/several communities to create community and private woodlots incl. owning trees, and no requirement for permits to fell, use or sell.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A level playing field in that while state owns all land, citizens equally eligible for lifetime usufructs for houses & arable farms. No provision for communal agro-pastoral or pastoral tenure but access areas defined on village basis. Constitution 1997. Land Proclamation 1994.
indicators.additional_info: Customary rights abolished; despite (i) long customary history of family/clan tenure (enda, risti), village communal ownership (diesa or shekh'na) and (ii) high proportion of agro-pastoral & pastoralist families (est. 65% rural pop in 2001). The  1994 law does not provide for collective tenure, other than for arable farming cooperatives. State takes direct control of woodlands/shrublands (6%), barren & grazing lands (95% of country area) but enables access on village by village basis as is traditional. Emphasis on sedentisation; only those permanently resident in village get allotted parcel. Males & females allocated individually.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protection in that allocated or confirmed rights to house & farm plots equally subject to compensation at compulsory acquisition and by agreement, and common regime for all rural dwellers. However, desecured to extent that customary norms and governance is repealed & no provision for common properties, most critical for pastoralists but replaced with village based commons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1997, Art. 23. Proclamation No. 58/1994, Art. 50-53, 39, 4.
indicators.additional_info: Uncertain  and customarily insecure: right to house in home village dependent on fulfilment military duties. Registration of usufructs is compulsory but not activated in most rural areas. Every citizen obtains an agricultural usufruct for house or farm or both (Art. 4 Law 58/1994) provided by elected village councils. While the State  controls rangeland & forests (woodland, shrublands), law does prescribes this for 'all villages in Eritrea, according to local custom use their own pasture and wood' subject to regulations (Law 1994 Art. 48). This (customary) opportunity actively adopted.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Procl. 86/1996 confirms each village/area has a general assembly of all adults ('megaba'aya') with elected  decision making council (baito). Many issue heritable family plots in accordance with customary diesa where remote titling offices fail to reach villages. Village based procedure and legal provisions similar.
indicators.law_and_provision: Regional Administration Proclamation No. 86/1996. Legal Notice No. 31/1997.  Proclamation No. 95/1997.
indicators.additional_info: Devolution of authority is a partly unmet Constitution pledge. Law 37/1993 recognized 2,580 villages and 699 'village area administrations' in remoter areas. 'Lifetime' usufructs in practice heritable in similar ways to customary  diesa (village-based family titles taken up in absence of official allotment, certification & registration. Land Administration Bodies remote from villages. No registration of collective customary rights although the law commits to 'All villages in Eritrea, shall, according to local custom, use their own pasture and woods' (Art. 48 of Law No. 58/1994) and do so, almost only official opening for customary norms.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for villages as legal persons. No collective titles in the law. However (a) Art. 48 of No 58/1994 permits villages to use their own pasture and woodlands in accordance with local custom.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1997, Art. 23, Proclamation 58/1994, Art. 11 (5), 40, 48.
indicators.additional_info: Issue of rights is to individuals, male & female made distinctly. No provision for collective rights to be titled.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: 1994 land law implies village assemblies will be members of Land Administrative Bodies (under Land Commission in Ministry of Lands & ) but devolution abandoned for lack of funds & staff. Traditional village assemblies (Megaba'aya) and customary councils of elected elders (baito adi) issue customary rights in default of remote Provincial Land Commissions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 10; Land Proclamation No. 58/1994, Art. 10; Proclamations No. 37/1993 &  86/96 on Regional Governments.
indicators.additional_info: Legal land authority vested in Land Administration Bodies at provincial level, assemblies of 699 village clusters were supposed to be part of the Land Administration Bodies. No information on how many LAB established. Elected  village council exercise authority although not specified as one of their functions.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Rights may be  held in perpetuity despite definition as lifetime usufructs (1994 Art 12.1). Legitimized by  enabling surviving spouses & minors to retain the land Arts 12.3, 12.4. Registered usufructs described as 'private' and convertible to lease but cannot be sold Art 18, 24.1.  However, the house itself may be sold, leased, mortgaged  - and inherited Art 31-34.
indicators.additional_info: The law has found ways to sustain many norms of village-based customary tenure, most applicable to majority tribes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for consent or consultation at compulsory acquisition. However, compensation is payable. The right to negotiate compensation is also  provided Art.51.2, 51.3. Permits petition to High Court Art. 51.4. Compensation must be paid prior to owner vacating the land Art. 52.1. Level playing field for titled and untitled usufructs. No clarity on village communal lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Proclamation 58/1994, Art. 51-52.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: According to a secondary source (see comments box), some privately owned forests in Spain are held and managed collectively in practice. However, the national law on Forests (Law No. 43/2004) does not explicitly grant communities rights to forest lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 43/2003 on Forests (http://forestportal.efi.int/view.php?id=1635&c=ES); Constitution of Spain, 1978
indicators.additional_info:
Ley 43/2003 (the Forest Act) establishes legal regimes for public forests, private forests, and protected forests. However, reviewer could not find any legal provisions that explicitly granted to communal rights to forests. According to a secondary source, private collective ownership in Spain is essentially a private use right for community ownership. NOTE: Some subnational forest laws may grant collective rights to forests, but LandMark only basis its indicator assessment on national level laws. For more info, see: Quiroga, S., Domínguez, G., Suárez, C., Gorriz, E., Barrio, M., Marey, M., Martínez de Arano, I., Ojea, E., Solís, J. D. (2015) Forest Land Ownership Change in Spain. COST Action FP1201 FACESMAP Country Report, European Forest Institute Central-East and South-East European
Regional Office, Vienna. Available at: http://facesmap.boku.ac.at/index.php/library2/doc_download/450-fp1201-country-report-spain

ETH.name: Ethiopia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All land is owned by the State. Exclusive rights issued as Holding Rights to individuals at scale since 2004. New Federal Proclamation 2024 clearer that Holding Rights may also be issued to communities, including rangelands to pastoral communities. New forest law 2018 & Regs 2024 encourage issue of Holding Rights to communities to protect & reforest.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1995 Art. 40. Federal Rural Lands Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 1324/2024. Federal Forest Law 2018, Forest Regulation No. 544/2024.
indicators.additional_info: Land and resources are the common property of all Ethiopians and inalienable ;Const. 1995 Art. 40.3. Property rights refer to exclusive rights to parcels. Every private person, community, religious institution and the state is equally entitled to a free Holding Right as a legal person; Fed. Rural Lands Law 2024 Art. 7 & 8.  Support for pastoral communal holdings defined with equal rights to own, lease, collateralize, but not to partition or privatize (Art. 35).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: New  protection of communal lands, may no longer be partitioned or privatized, but community may lease if 3/4 members agree: Arts. 36, 38. Customary institutions & rules to be respected; Art. 37. Echoed in equal & improved treatment of rights in Federal Expropriation Proclamation 2019 Art. 8-13.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Rural Lands Administration and Use Proclamation No. 1324/2024. Expropriation of Landholdings for Public Purpose and Payment of Compensation Proclamation No 1161/2019.
indicators.additional_info: Since 1970s reforms minimal protection of rural holdings undermined by redistribution, weak protection of communal land from reallocations. Improvement in 2024 land law. Woreda (district) administrations responsible for consulting with and implementing resettlement packages, supporting and ensuring the improvement of the livelihood of displaced farmers and pastoralists (No. 1161/2019 Art. 25).  While threats of private and communal land redistribution of lands have disappeared with new 2024 law  (Art. 25), communities remain  threatened by takings for rural investment projects sheltered by new definition of public purpose in 2019 law.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Titling compulsory Art. 43, 11.2 million Holding Rights issued to 82% of rural persons 2003-18, due to low cost, active state & donor support. Inattention to communal lands remedied under new federal land law 2024, which explicitly includes villge commons & grazing lands of pastoralists. Similar for forests under new Forest Law 2018 & Regs. 2024.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Lands Administration and Use Procl. No. 1324/2024.Forest Proclamation No. 1065 /2018. Forest Regulation No. 544/2024. Afar State Proclamation 49/2009. Somali State Proclamation 128/2013.
indicators.additional_info: Even in earlier land law (Proclamation 456/2005 Art. 6), titling designed as  low-cost and simple rooted in  community-based adjudication. But also 2.4 million ha of common property allocated to investors  (Z. Hailu & others, 2016 'Land Governance Assessment Framework Country Report Ethiopia' The World Bank). New land law (2024) increases protection by clearer provision for Communal Holding Rights. Change led by several pastoral regional state laws seeking to limit disposal to investors (eg. Afar Regional State Rural Proclamation 49/2009 Art. 5). New 2024 law ends regime of commons being 'set aside' for communal use. Holding Rights also enable family rights and polygamous families. Women may secure parcels independently of husbands or fathers: Law 1324/2024 Arts. 22-23.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Families and communities have legal personality to acquire Holding Rights; Federal Law 1324/2024. Federal Forest Regs. 544/2024 enable communities to acquire Holding Rights in perpetuity to rehabilitate degraded lands including from State Forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Rural Lands Administration and Use Proclamation No. 1324/2024. Federal Proclamation No. 1065/2018 on Forest Development, Conservation and Utilization, and Regulation No. 544/2024.
indicators.additional_info: Under section on private property, the Constitution 1995 assured communities that  'in appropriate circumstances' they will be 'empowered to own property in common' (Art. 40.2). Some pastoral regional state laws specifically protected pastures from allocation to investors: e.g. Afar State Proclamation 49/2009, Art. 5, Somali State Proclamation 128/2013, Art. 5. New policy is to issue Holding Rights to communities for grazing lands in Law No. 1324/2024, s. Six. Commons are not divisible or alienable, although community may lease if 3/4 community adults agree.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2024 land law provides for participatory decision-making and adjudication at village cluster level. While Regional States may issue binding administration & management laws Art. 24, law also recognizes 'customary institutions, customary land use and management practices, conflict resolution, and customary rules if these do not contradict constitutional rights including of women (Art. 37).
indicators.law_and_provision: Amhara Regional State Rural Land Administration and Use Law No 456/2005. Federal Rural Lands Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 1324/2024.
indicators.additional_info: In line with Constitution (Art. 52), federal law stipulates regional state authority over land matters and each regional state law devolves some authority further to districts (woreda), then parish (kebele - includes several villages). The Land Law of 2024 does not specify devolutionary administration, leaves this up to each Regional State (Art. 42). e.g. Amhara Regional State Rural Land Administration and Use Law No. 456/2005 stipulates functions at State (Land Authority), district and parish levels, the latter in charge of land use, distribution, keeping of registers, responding to directives of the State Land Authority, and cannot suspend rights to hold or use land without community participation (Arts. 25-27).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Since 2005 Holding Rights of farmers, semi-pastoralists, pastoralists & religious institutions have no time limit, as in new federal land law 2024 Art 6(1). Now also includes Holding Rights to communities for pastoral lands. Forest law 2018 pledges issue of rights in perpetuity to groups & communities rehabilitating & managing degraded lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal  Rural Lands Proclamation No. 1324/2024 and  No. 1065/2018 Forest Development, Conservation and Utilization.
indicators.additional_info: While leases are time-bound, registrable Rural Holding Rights are held in perpetuity, inheritable, transferable, able to rented out (Federal Land Law No. 456/2005 Arts. 7-9, re-entrenched in new Federal law No. 1324/2024, Arts. 6, 7).  The land itself is inalienable as the common property of all Ethiopians. New expropriation law 2019 provides for replacement land and obligatory prior compensation for rural lands taken for public purposes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for consent at compulsory acquisition. 2019 law requires consultation one year in advance & room for negotiating. To be paid before displacement (Arts 8-12). Compensation includes value of improvements & cost of replacing property if alterative is not provided (Art.12).
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Proclamation No. 1161/2019 To Determine Expropriation of Landholdings for Public Purpose, Payment of Compensation and Resettlement.
indicators.additional_info: 2019 Expropriation Law also requires payment of displacement compensation for communal holdings based on calculated use values, lost benefits & livelihoods (Art. 13).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Trees belong to the right holder to the land including  communities as appropriate for Community Forests. Beneficiary communities of allocations for reforestation own carbon but to pay service fee of 5% to the federal govt and 15% to regional govt Regs Art. 5. Consultation  required to gazette new State Forests (Regs. Art. 13). 10% revenue from production forests paid to community (Art 14).
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Rural Land Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 456/2005. Federal Proclamation No. 1065/2018 on Forest  Development, Conservation and Utilization. Forest Regulation No. 544/2024.
indicators.additional_info: Tree planting promoted, and 'Any person who develops forests on his landholding or in a state forest area shall be given assurance of his ownership of the forest' (No. 542/2007 Art. 4.5), further developed in  Forest Proclamation 2018 and Forest Regulation No. 544/2024. Communities are to be provided with Certificate of Titles for Community Forests, may utilize, transact, add value on forest products and share benefits as per community by-laws.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water belongs to Ethiopians in common and domestic use (free) takes priority. Permits required for non-traditional or commercial uses. New community watersheds law (2020) enables communities to secure authority and use rights over community watersheds on basis of an agreed watershed management plan and formation of a Users' Cooperative.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1995. Ethiopian Water Resources Management Proclamation No. 197/2000. Council of Ministers Ethiopian Water Resource Management Regulations No. 115/2005. Proclamation No. 1223/2020 Development, Management and Utilization of Community Watersheds Proclamation.
indicators.additional_info: All natural resources including water belong to the State and people of Ethiopia (Const. 1995 Art. 40.3). Reiterated in No. 197/2000 Art. 5. Domestic uses the priority (Art. 7.1).  Permits not required for digging or use hand-dug wells, traditional irrigation, artisanal mining, traditional animal rearing or water mills (Art. 12.1). Permits needed or commercial uses governed by Water Reg. 115/2005.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Wildlife Strategy & Policy 2011 aims for communities outside Reserves "to own, develop and be beneficiaries of wildlife habitats outside Protected Areas". No law yet. Forest law 2018 provides for Community Forests to be titled in perpetuity Art 2.7. A community or an association may be given part of a Protected or Productive Forest to conserve and utilize.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Proclamation to Provide for Development Conservation and Utilization of Wildlife No. 541/2007. Wildlife Strategy and Policy 2011. Federal Proclamation No. 1065/2018 Forest Development, Conservation and Utilization. Forest Regulation No. 544/2024
indicators.additional_info: Increase in 2018 law for communities to secure forest lands, expanding 2000 & 2007 forest laws . Requirements for participatory management added to with new incentives (Forest Regs. 2024). Benefit-sharing with communities from State Forests required since 2007, added to in 2019 and 2024 Regs. including carbon ownership subject to taxes. Reg. No. 544/2024 Art. 15 (5).

indicators.law_and_provision: Amhara Regional State Rural Land Administration and Use Law No 456/2005. Federal Rural Lands Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 1324/2024.
indicators.additional_info: In line with Constitution (Art. 52), federal law stipulates regional state authority over land matters and each regional state law devolves some authority further to districts (woreda), then parish (kebele - includes several villages). The Land Law of 2024 does not specify devolutionary administration, leaves this up to each Regional State (Art. 42). e.g. Amhara Regional State Rural Land Administration and Use Law No. 456/2005 stipulates functions at State (Land Authority), district and parish levels, the latter in charge of land use, distribution, keeping of registers, responding to directives of the State Land Authority, and cannot suspend rights to hold or use land without community participation (Arts. 25-27).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Since 2005 Holding Rights of farmers, semi-pastoralists, pastoralists & religious institutions have no time limit, as in new federal land law 2024 Art 6(1). Now also includes Holding Rights to communities for pastoral lands. Forest law 2018 pledges issue of rights in perpetuity to groups & communities rehabilitating & managing degraded lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal  Rural Lands Proclamation No. 1324/2024 and  No. 1065/2018 Forest Development, Conservation and Utilization.
indicators.additional_info: While leases are time-bound, registrable Rural Holding Rights are held in perpetuity, inheritable, transferable, able to rented out (Federal Land Law No. 456/2005 Arts. 7-9, re-entrenched in new Federal law No. 1324/2024, Arts. 6, 7).  The land itself is inalienable as the common property of all Ethiopians. New expropriation law 2019 provides for replacement land and obligatory prior compensation for rural lands taken for public purposes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for consent at compulsory acquisition. 2019 law requires consultation one year in advance & room for negotiating. To be paid before displacement (Arts 8-12). Compensation includes value of improvements & cost of replacing property if alterative is not provided (Art.12).
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Proclamation No. 1161/2019 To Determine Expropriation of Landholdings for Public Purpose, Payment of Compensation and Resettlement.
indicators.additional_info: 2019 Expropriation Law also requires payment of displacement compensation for communal holdings based on calculated use values, lost benefits & livelihoods (Art. 13).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Trees belong to the right holder to the land including  communities as appropriate for Community Forests. Beneficiary communities of allocations for reforestation own carbon but to pay service fee of 5% to the federal govt and 15% to regional govt Regs Art. 5. Consultation  required to gazette new State Forests (Regs. Art. 13). 10% revenue from production forests paid to community (Art 14).
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Rural Land Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 456/2005. Federal Proclamation No. 1065/2018 on Forest  Development, Conservation and Utilization. Forest Regulation No. 544/2024.
indicators.additional_info: Tree planting promoted, and 'Any person who develops forests on his landholding or in a state forest area shall be given assurance of his ownership of the forest' (No. 542/2007 Art. 4.5), further developed in  Forest Proclamation 2018 and Forest Regulation No. 544/2024. Communities are to be provided with Certificate of Titles for Community Forests, may utilize, transact, add value on forest products and share benefits as per community by-laws.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water belongs to Ethiopians in common and domestic use (free) takes priority. Permits required for non-traditional or commercial uses. New community watersheds law (2020) enables communities to secure authority and use rights over community watersheds on basis of an agreed watershed management plan and formation of a Users' Cooperative.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1995. Ethiopian Water Resources Management Proclamation No. 197/2000. Council of Ministers Ethiopian Water Resource Management Regulations No. 115/2005. Proclamation No. 1223/2020 Development, Management and Utilization of Community Watersheds Proclamation.
indicators.additional_info: All natural resources including water belong to the State and people of Ethiopia (Const. 1995 Art. 40.3). Reiterated in No. 197/2000 Art. 5. Domestic uses the priority (Art. 7.1).  Permits not required for digging or use hand-dug wells, traditional irrigation, artisanal mining, traditional animal rearing or water mills (Art. 12.1). Permits needed or commercial uses governed by Water Reg. 115/2005.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Wildlife Strategy & Policy 2011 aims for communities outside Reserves "to own, develop and be beneficiaries of wildlife habitats outside Protected Areas". No law yet. Forest law 2018 provides for Community Forests to be titled in perpetuity Art 2.7. A community or an association may be given part of a Protected or Productive Forest to conserve and utilize.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Proclamation to Provide for Development Conservation and Utilization of Wildlife No. 541/2007. Wildlife Strategy and Policy 2011. Federal Proclamation No. 1065/2018 Forest Development, Conservation and Utilization. Forest Regulation No. 544/2024
indicators.additional_info: Increase in 2018 law for communities to secure forest lands, expanding 2000 & 2007 forest laws . Requirements for participatory management added to with new incentives (Forest Regs. 2024). Benefit-sharing with communities from State Forests required since 2007, added to in 2019 and 2024 Regs. including carbon ownership subject to taxes. Reg. No. 544/2024 Art. 15 (5).

indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Finland's statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize and protect the land rights of Sami populations in Finland.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Finland; Act on Metsähallitus 2016
indicators.additional_info: The new Act on Metsähallitus 2016 provides the state broad ownership rights to land in Finland, and does not explicitly protect the livelihoods of Sami populations. Article 17 of the Constitution provides that "The Sami, as an indigenous people...have the right to maintain and develop their own language and culture." NOTE: The Reindeer Husbandry Act Reindeer Husbandry Act 14.9.1990/848 (Finnish RHA) grants reindeer herding rights to the Sami population of Finland.

local_communities_entries.framework: Community land (Aland Islands)
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law states that the Aland Islands are autonomous and the Aland Parliament shall represent the people of the Aland Islands in matters relating to its autonomy. However, ownership rights are limited to the Aland Islands and not other parts of Finland and decision-making power is granted to the Aland Parliament.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Government of Finland. 1991. Act on the Autonomy of Åland 1991/1144. August 16. Available at: http://www.finlex.fi/en/laki/kaannokset/1991/en19911144.
pdf
indicators.additional_info: Section 1 of the Act on the Autonomy of Aland provides that the ""Aland Islands are autonomous."" Section 2 states ""Aland comprises the territory it has at the time of entry into force of this Act and the territorial waters directly adjacent to its land territory according to the enactments in force on the limits of the territorial waters of Finland. If the jurisdiction and sovereignty of the State are extended beyond the limits of the territorial waters the jurisdiction and sovereignty of Aland may be likewise extended.""

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Aland Parliament retains power to decide who can domicile within the islands. The Aland Parliament can acquire real property within Aland under the Act on the 1975 Act on the Acquisition of Real Property in Aland.
indicators.law_and_provision: 1975 Act on the Acquisition of Real Property in Aland; Act on the Autonomy of Island 1991

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law sets out clear requirements for domiciling on the Aland Islands, but it is unclear based on the law whether procedures are affordable and accessible.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Persons domiciled on the Aland Islands are granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act on the Autonomy of the Aland Islands

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Section 3 of the Act provides that ""the Aland Parliament shall represent the people of the Aland Islands in matters relating to its autonomy. The Administration of Aland is vested in the Government of Aland and the officials subordinate to it.""
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec, 3 Act on the Autonomy of Island.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law does not establish durational limits on the rights of those domiciled on the Aland Islands, which indicates that rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act on the Autonomy of Aland, 1991

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law dose not explicitly grant those domicile on the Aland Islands the right to give consent in an inclusive manner before land can be acquired by governments and other outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act on the Autonomy of Aland, 1991

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Aland Parliament has authority over farming and forestry, but it is unclear whether those domiciled on the Aland islands are granted ownership rights to trees.

GAB.name: Gabon

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Only registered parcels are property, most urban, 90% of country is State Domain. No route for customary rights & lands to be registered. Homesteads get Occupancy Permits. Only means to secure collective forest access is via Community Forests, limited in purpose, term & area (5,000 ha). Most forest (88% country) is under foreign logging, agriculture & mining concessions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance 005/2012 on land ownership. Law 03/2012 to improve registration of individual & corporate lands. Decree 00077/1967 on Grant of Concessions and Leases on State Land. Sustainable Development Law 002/2014. Decree No. 192/ 1987 on Exercise of Customary Use Rights. Forest Code 16/2001, Art. 259. Order No. 018/2013 Establish Procedures for Allocation and Management of Community Forests.
indicators.additional_info: By Ordinance 0005/2012, unregistered and 'vacant' land (i.e. not visibly farmed or in recognized roadside settlements with inadequate reach of 3 km) belong to the State. These began in colonial area as forced village removals to aggregate labour. 90% of country is State Domain including Private State Domain which Government may sell, lease or grant concessions; same land is regularly ancestral customary domains  including those of IP forest peoples (1% of pop). 56% of country is under 40 foreign logging companies. Token reference to communal rights: eg constitutional reference to property rights of all people as individuals 'or groups' (Art. 1.10);  Decentralization Law 1996 requiring elected village councils to 'preserve the properties of the community' (Art 80 & 96); Sustainable Development Law, 2014 defining 'community capital' as both natural and cultural assets, Decree No 192/1987 On the Rights of Customary Use of Waters and Forests, lawful for communities who 'follow a tradition way of life'. But zero means for ocmmunities to secure communal lands outside limits of roadside villages.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No equal protection of customary and statutorily titled rights. Seen in: i) legal failure to recognize customary rights as property interests; ii) only occupation & use rights in rural settlements; iii) low compensation for such rights; iv) forests are State property; v) minimal protection from  concessions & leases even invading roadside rural settlements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution (Transitional) 2023. Law . 6/1961 On Expropriation. Decree 00077/1967  Regulating Grant of Concessions and Leases on State Land. Decentralization Law 15/1996. Sustainable Development Law  002/2014. Decree 192/ 1987 on Exercise of Customary Use Rights.
indicators.additional_info: Mixed situation even in formal roadside settlements: occupancy & use rights to family farms in settlements protected but rights to neither communal off-farm forests nor of the IP minority living outside settlements. Those with 'confirmed' customary rights to family farms are paid compensation only for crops (Law No. 6/1961 Arts 9,17,61), Decree 846/1979, Arts. 1,4-6).  But State-paid relocation required (No. 6/61, Arts 42-3). Eviction only after compensation paid (Art. 31). Prior information period is only 8 days (Law No. 6/61 Art. 9). Right to appeal is limited (Art. 29-30). Scope of public purpose is wide ( Art. 46), reinforced by Law  002/2014. As of Law No. 1/2012, communities are consulted prior to issue of concessions.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Title is free, accessible in district offices, but low uptake of 1967 provision of titles for up to 10 ha if 'visibly occupied & used' homesteads within recognized roadside settlements. Joint spousal titles permitted  & both must agree to sale (Civil Code revision2021). Still no provision for issue of collective title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 77 of 1967 On Grant of Concessions and Leases of State Land. Decree No. 249/2012 Establishing the Organization of the Conservation of Land Ownership and Mortgages. Law No. 004/2021 modifying provisions of Law No.15/1972 on the Civil Code.
indicators.additional_info: Ordinance No. 00077/PR-MF-DE of 1967 Regulating the granting of concessions and leasing of state-owned lands offered 'grant of definitive ownership' to those proving occupation peaceful, continuous, public and undisputed to 10 ha rural land on first-come first-served basis. No provision for recognition as community land based on traditional areas, via collective title inclusive of critical forest domains, although there is provision for registration of ownership in common by spousal  joint owners including in revised text the Civil Code by Law No. 004/2021 enabling this (Arts. 335) and new requirement that spouses agree first to sale of land (Art. 336).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No recognition of communities as legal person, despite provision for village settlements to register as collectivities under Local Government Law 15/1996; never implemented. Only provision is for access to  communal lands by traditional forest use, hunting and fishing as "making allowance for their needs" Decree 192/1987.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree No. 192/1987 Art. 1-12) on Exercise of Customary Use Rights. Local Government Law No. 15/1996, Art. 237.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No formal village governance or land committees. Traditional Authorities not recognized. Intention of 1996 law was to delimit village settlements & and elect councils but lacks  implementation decree. Only sustained legal direction is permitting traditional resource uses, with compulsory benefit-sharing by concessions in locality 2013.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree No. 192/1987 on Exercise of Customary Use Rights. Ordinance 001/2012 on Land development Concessions. Ordinance 005/2012 Establishing the Regime for Land Ownership. Decentralization Law 15/1996. Forest Code 16/2001. Decree 105/2013 on Benefit-Sharing.
indicators.additional_info: Local Government Decentralization Law No. 15/1996 Arts. 237-8 provides for communities of 100+ persons to be registered as collectivities, to define village areas and elect village councils with land use powers but no implementation decrees issued. Most villages are in forest zones so provision by Forest Code  No. 16 of 2001 for community managed forests is relevant, also compulsory benefit-sharing by concessionaires with communities (Decree No. 105 of 2013 on Contracts) applying Art. 251 of Forest Code, with official Guidelines May 2016. Both have limitations as low delivery. Doubly constrained by State refusal to enable rural communities to be lawful owners of their settlement and communal lands.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal prescriptions on rural rights but customarily of indefinite term. Statutory private titles of no fixed term are available to rural households for farms but not  promoted, nor sought by most.  Leases, concessions and occupation permits have term limits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 77 of 1967 on Granting Concessions and Leases on State Land. Ordinance on Emphyteutic Leases No. 50 of 1970.
indicators.additional_info: No legal provision on term for customary occupation and use rights but operate as indefinite through inheritance. Ordinance No. 77/1967 enables grant of absolute ownership up to 10 ha to individuals who prove peaceful continuous undisputed occupation (Art.2). Leases and concessions renewable up to 100 years (Ordinance on Emphyteutic Leases, No. 50 of 1970).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Opportunities provided to object to issue of ownership and other grants of land but community consent is not required for any allocation of concessions affecting customary lands nor for Protected Areas or other public projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 77 of 1967 Regulating Grant of Concessions and Leases. Law on National Parks, No. 003 of 2007, Arts. 4, 7,10. Forest Code No. 16 of 2001.
indicators.additional_info: No consent from communities required for issue of concessions and leases from State Property,  in law not permitted to interfere with settlements, within which rights are recognized under Occupancy Permits where 'confirmed' customary rights exist. No community consent required for creation of Protected Areas. Consultation is required.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All forest belongs to the State. Tree use for domestic purposes is granted without permits in the roadside Rural Forest Domain. Logging permits available for up to 50 trees. Community Forests also provided for but only for use, not ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code 16/2001, Art. 259. Order No. 018/2013 Establish Procedures for Allocation and Management of Community Forests. Order N. 106/2014 On the Right to Reserve Area for Community Village Forest. Law on National Parks No. 003 of 2007. Technical Guide for the Delimitation of Community Forests, 2015/2016.
indicators.additional_info: Forest Code, 2001 provides for a Rural Forest Domain 'consisting of forest and forest land whose enjoyment is reserved for village communities, as determined by regulation' (Art. 12). To be used in accordance with customs for individual and collective purposes (Art.14). Art. 252 defines tree use as for timber for houses, firewood, natural latex collection etc. Individuals in this Domain may also acquire logging permits for 50 trees (Art.156).  Rural Forest Domain is still not delimited after 24 years. Community Forests for production and protection provided for (Arts. 156-162 and Application Decree No. 001028 of 2004). Ordinance No. 011 of 2008 includes indigenous communities as villages and permits sale of products as part of domestic use. Order No. 018/ 2013 establishes procedures and attribution of Community Forests. These are not a route to collective tenure, only to collective, or sub-group use of the land.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is public State Property but communities may freely access for domestic use in accordance with customary norms.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 14/963 on State Property. Forest Code 2001.
indicators.additional_info: Water is owned by the State: Art. 109 of Law 14/1963 on State Property stipulates that 'All standing or flowing water, all navigable rivers, floatable or not, natural or artificial, shall be the Public Property of the State'. The Forest Code, 2001 Article 252. permits free water use for individual or collective needs by village communities. Commercial water use is only through permits from Ministry for forests and water (Art. 14).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No rights to own or manage Protected Areas (PA) even when established on customary lands. Affected communities may use PA in designated buffer zones. Community Forests provided for since 2001 but no right to own, only to use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code No. 16 of 2001, Art. 259, Order 018/2013  Procedures for Allocation and Management of Community Forests. Order  106/2014 Right to Reserve Area for Community Village Forest. Law on National Parks No. 003/ 2007. Technical Guide for the Delimitation of Community Forests, 2015/2016.
indicators.additional_info: No use may be made of Protected Areas, Art. 259 Forest Code 2001 other than by prior agreement in specified buffer zones within and on edge of Parks. Environmental Protection Law No. 007 of 2014 makes no reference to community-based rights. Forest Code 2001 provides for Community Forests (up to 10 instituted) but no provisions for community to own these.
