But State-paid relocation required (No. 6/61, Arts 42-3). Eviction only after compensation paid (Art. 31). Prior information period is only 8 days (Law No. 6/61 Art. 9). Right to appeal is limited (Art. 29-30). Scope of public purpose is wide ( Art. 46), reinforced by Law  002/2014. As of Law No. 1/2012, communities are consulted prior to issue of concessions.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Title is free, accessible in district offices, but low uptake of 1967 provision of titles for up to 10 ha if 'visibly occupied & used' homesteads within recognized roadside settlements. Joint spousal titles permitted  & both must agree to sale (Civil Code revision2021). Still no provision for issue of collective title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree 77 of 1967 On Grant of Concessions and Leases of State Land. Decree No. 249/2012 Establishing the Organization of the Conservation of Land Ownership and Mortgages. Law No. 004/2021 modifying provisions of Law No.15/1972 on the Civil Code.
indicators.additional_info: Ordinance No. 00077/PR-MF-DE of 1967 Regulating the granting of concessions and leasing of state-owned lands offered 'grant of definitive ownership' to those proving occupation peaceful, continuous, public and undisputed to 10 ha rural land on first-come first-served basis. No provision for recognition as community land based on traditional areas, via collective title inclusive of critical forest domains, although there is provision for registration of ownership in common by spousal  joint owners including in revised text the Civil Code by Law No. 004/2021 enabling this (Arts. 335) and new requirement that spouses agree first to sale of land (Art. 336).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No recognition of communities as legal person, despite provision for village settlements to register as collectivities under Local Government Law 15/1996; never implemented. Only provision is for access to  communal lands by traditional forest use, hunting and fishing as "making allowance for their needs" Decree 192/1987.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree No. 192/1987 Art. 1-12) on Exercise of Customary Use Rights. Local Government Law No. 15/1996, Art. 237.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No formal village governance or land committees. Traditional Authorities not recognized. Intention of 1996 law was to delimit village settlements & and elect councils but lacks  implementation decree. Only sustained legal direction is permitting traditional resource uses, with compulsory benefit-sharing by concessions in locality 2013.
indicators.law_and_provision: Decree No. 192/1987 on Exercise of Customary Use Rights. Ordinance 001/2012 on Land development Concessions. Ordinance 005/2012 Establishing the Regime for Land Ownership. Decentralization Law 15/1996. Forest Code 16/2001. Decree 105/2013 on Benefit-Sharing.
indicators.additional_info: Local Government Decentralization Law No. 15/1996 Arts. 237-8 provides for communities of 100+ persons to be registered as collectivities, to define village areas and elect village councils with land use powers but no implementation decrees issued. Most villages are in forest zones so provision by Forest Code  No. 16 of 2001 for community managed forests is relevant, also compulsory benefit-sharing by concessionaires with communities (Decree No. 105 of 2013 on Contracts) applying Art. 251 of Forest Code, with official Guidelines May 2016. Both have limitations as low delivery. Doubly constrained by State refusal to enable rural communities to be lawful owners of their settlement and communal lands.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal prescriptions on rural rights but customarily of indefinite term. Statutory private titles of no fixed term are available to rural households for farms but not  promoted, nor sought by most.  Leases, concessions and occupation permits have term limits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 77 of 1967 on Granting Concessions and Leases on State Land. Ordinance on Emphyteutic Leases No. 50 of 1970.
indicators.additional_info: No legal provision on term for customary occupation and use rights but operate as indefinite through inheritance. Ordinance No. 77/1967 enables grant of absolute ownership up to 10 ha to individuals who prove peaceful continuous undisputed occupation (Art.2). Leases and concessions renewable up to 100 years (Ordinance on Emphyteutic Leases, No. 50 of 1970).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Opportunities provided to object to issue of ownership and other grants of land but community consent is not required for any allocation of concessions affecting customary lands nor for Protected Areas or other public projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 77 of 1967 Regulating Grant of Concessions and Leases. Law on National Parks, No. 003 of 2007, Arts. 4, 7,10. Forest Code No. 16 of 2001.
indicators.additional_info: No consent from communities required for issue of concessions and leases from State Property,  in law not permitted to interfere with settlements, within which rights are recognized under Occupancy Permits where 'confirmed' customary rights exist. No community consent required for creation of Protected Areas. Consultation is required.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All forest belongs to the State. Tree use for domestic purposes is granted without permits in the roadside Rural Forest Domain. Logging permits available for up to 50 trees. Community Forests also provided for but only for use, not ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code 16/2001, Art. 259. Order No. 018/2013 Establish Procedures for Allocation and Management of Community Forests. Order N. 106/2014 On the Right to Reserve Area for Community Village Forest. Law on National Parks No. 003 of 2007. Technical Guide for the Delimitation of Community Forests, 2015/2016.
indicators.additional_info: Forest Code, 2001 provides for a Rural Forest Domain 'consisting of forest and forest land whose enjoyment is reserved for village communities, as determined by regulation' (Art. 12). To be used in accordance with customs for individual and collective purposes (Art.14). Art. 252 defines tree use as for timber for houses, firewood, natural latex collection etc. Individuals in this Domain may also acquire logging permits for 50 trees (Art.156).  Rural Forest Domain is still not delimited after 24 years. Community Forests for production and protection provided for (Arts. 156-162 and Application Decree No. 001028 of 2004). Ordinance No. 011 of 2008 includes indigenous communities as villages and permits sale of products as part of domestic use. Order No. 018/ 2013 establishes procedures and attribution of Community Forests. These are not a route to collective tenure, only to collective, or sub-group use of the land.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is public State Property but communities may freely access for domestic use in accordance with customary norms.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 14/963 on State Property. Forest Code 2001.
indicators.additional_info: Water is owned by the State: Art. 109 of Law 14/1963 on State Property stipulates that 'All standing or flowing water, all navigable rivers, floatable or not, natural or artificial, shall be the Public Property of the State'. The Forest Code, 2001 Article 252. permits free water use for individual or collective needs by village communities. Commercial water use is only through permits from Ministry for forests and water (Art. 14).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No rights to own or manage Protected Areas (PA) even when established on customary lands. Affected communities may use PA in designated buffer zones. Community Forests provided for since 2001 but no right to own, only to use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code No. 16 of 2001, Art. 259, Order 018/2013  Procedures for Allocation and Management of Community Forests. Order  106/2014 Right to Reserve Area for Community Village Forest. Law on National Parks No. 003/ 2007. Technical Guide for the Delimitation of Community Forests, 2015/2016.
indicators.additional_info: No use may be made of Protected Areas, Art. 259 Forest Code 2001 other than by prior agreement in specified buffer zones within and on edge of Parks. Environmental Protection Law No. 007 of 2014 makes no reference to community-based rights. Forest Code 2001 provides for Community Forests (up to 10 instituted) but no provisions for community to own these.

GHA.name: Ghana

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary lands constitutionally recognized as lawfully owned & governed by customary authorities, and cannot be alienated into statutory tenure. Ownership is absolute, vested in chiefs, heads of clans & families  as trustees on behalf of members. All rights are recordable by localized Customary Land Secretariats, still in process of establishment.
indicators.additional_info: Since 1890s customary lands have been recognized as the property of communities, vested in traditional authorities including chiefs and their councils ('stools'), first settler family/tendana) or family heads depending on area. These  persons operate as trustee administrators for the owners - communities, clans, families. (Const. 1992 Art 267.1, 36.8) Land Act 2020, sec. 9, 13). The Constitution entrenches (unwritten) customary law as part of the laws of Ghana (Art. 11). The State regulates and may co-opt management (and does so for all forests), paying customary owners fixed percentages of revenue from logging (Art. 267.6).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Constitution 1992 & Land Act 2020 entrench equal status of customary & statutory rights. Both provide for freehold and other possession (customary lease, customary tenancy etc). Customary right legally exist with/without registration. Compulsory for each trustee (eg chief) to insitute Customary Land Secretariat to enable recordation.
indicators.additional_info: Few Customary Secretariats in place yet. Both property systems endure outdated compulsory acquisition rules, such as open-ended definition of public purpose, compensation not payable prior to eviction and often delayed by years (Land Act s. 233-256).The Constitution 1992 & Land Act, 2020 entrench revenue sharing by the Forestry and other State Commissions for use and profit from customary lands through collection  rents, dues, royalties, revenues by the Administrator of Stool Lands, taking 10% for its administration, disbursing the rest to the chief/clan/family head (25%), to the traditional authority (chief and council) (20%) and to the elected District Assembly (55%) to provide development and services to community members (Const. Art. 267.6). NO direct payments to community members as group or individuals.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Localised, cheap & simple recordation ('registration') of customary rights available at Customary Land Secretariats. Recordable interests include: allodial title, customary law freehold, common law freehold, usufructary interest, leasehold, customary tenancy & transfers (s.1,  81). Oral testimony permitted (s. 36-37). Communal areas may also be recorded  for common use (s. 19).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2020. Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands Act, No 481 of 1994. Land Commission Act, No.767, 2008.
indicators.additional_info: Negatives in the cutomary titling regime include the right of Secretariats to charge fees (sec. 17); Secretariat is not elected (sec. 16 (1)); no survey & demarcation required sustaining overlaps (sec. 182 (2)). Also, the allodial title holder - the chief, land chief, head of clan, or head of family - may  take over bare land or farmland subject to usufructuary interests in the 'communal interest' s. 50 (21).  Although he must pay , compensation and provide alternative land where possible (sec. 50 (22) and may be fined if found to be unfair; this is all insufficient given the high values of customary lands. Ideally, Regulations under the Land Act, 2020 will alleviate concerns but no Regulations promulgated as of March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No recognition of the members of chiefdom, sub-chiefdom, clan or family as legal persons in their own right. Chiefs, land chiefs, or heads of clan or family act on their behalf. Sec. 281  describes "land owning group" as 'a stool, skin, family head, clan head or other collection of individuals that holds title to land', "proprietor" is described as 'the person named in the land register'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 Art. 18.  Land Act, 2020 sec. 281
indicators.additional_info: This is reinforced by provision at sec 182 (10) of Land Act, 2020 that at registration 'an entry shall be made in the land register stating the occupant of the stool or skin, or head of clan or family, or any other person authorised by the stool or skin, or clan or family to administer the land or interest in the land'.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities neither directly administer customary lands nor set up/elect or manage the Land Secretariats. These are instituted by the trustee chiefs etc. Land Act s. 13-14. In addition to recording rights & transfers these bodies settle disputes, prepare accounts such as rent from the Forestry Commission, mining concessions etc s. 18. Bound to be transparent, fair and impartial' s. 13.3.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 Arts. 36.8, 267-268, Land Act, 2020. The Office of The Administrator of Stool Land Act, 1994 (Act 481). Head of Family (Accountability) Law, 1985. Mineral Commission Act, 1993 (Act 450) s. 2. Forestry Commission Act, 1999 (Act 571) s.2.
indicators.additional_info: State controls use of minerals, water and timber, natural resources on customary lands (80% of Ghana's land area) through  Commissions, which share a percent of revenue with The Administrator of Stool Lands charged to distribute rent, royalties etc to the stool/skin or head of clan/family. All concessions are subject to Parliamentary approval (Const/ Art. 268). The State Land Registrar cannot register a large scale disposition of a stool, skin, clan or family land unless the Regional Land Commission has agreed (Land Act 2020 s. 102 (3)) taking into account 'protection of indigenous land rights, fairness in terms of agreement, etc.' S. 121 provides for overriding interests including a right of way, a right of water, or rights which may continue to be exercised.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary allodial and customary freehold rights are owned in perpetuity and registrable as such, Land Act 2020, sec 83. Usufructs, which may also be held in perpetuity, are limited to 99 year term at registration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2020.
indicators.additional_info: Although not codified, customary law provides for allodial title and rights in perpetuity, reflected in long history of court rulings and statutes such as the Land Titles Registration Act, 1986 Act 152, s. 19, repealed but much of its content incorporated in 152 sections in the Land Act, 2020 (sec. 80-232)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Consent of owners to compulsory acquisition is not required; only consultation (s. 244-245). Report must show their concerns "are taken into consideration". The State must retain as public land, allocate to a public body or to other entity only as a user right (s. 235). No transfer or eviction until Land Commission has earmarked funds needed & placed compensation in escrow account s. 238.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act 2020; Chapter Seven Secs. 233-267
indicators.additional_info: Claims to be submitted by all persons affected including amount of compensation sought (s. 250). Compensation determined by replacement costs including resettlement on alternative land (sec. 256). Claimant may appeal (s. 258). Compensation is paid at 60% to the customary holder of the land (eg. farmer, plot holder) and 40% to the allodial title holder (chief/council, clan leader, family head) (s. 259). When a tenant is affected, the allodial title holder receives 60%, or where the tenancy is held by the customary usufructary, the latter gets 30% and the tenant 30%. Payment may be delayed (and regularly can take years), only through court claim is interest added (Sec. 261). Resettlement of inhabitants is obligatory and subject to a plan (s. 265).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While ownership of trees is attached to the land and thus owned by customary landowners - or traditional authorities on their behalf (stools, skins, family heads), contradictions as to who permits felling, controls timber, etc. esp. in regard to concessions.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Trees and Timber Act, 1974 (Act 273). The Forestry Commission Act, 1999 (Act 571). The Timber Resources Management Act, 1998 (Act 547). The Concessions Act, 1962 (Act 124).
indicators.additional_info: The Forestry Commission grants timber rights contracts under the Timber Resources Management Act, 1998 Act 547, without mention of constitutional restraint that grants and concessions be ratified by Parliament (Art. 268). Additionally, land subject to timber rights on land with forest plantations, land with timber grown or owned by any individual or group, or land with farms, requires owner's consent in writing (Timber Act, 1997 s. 4.2).Note that Trees and Timber Act, 1974 does not state who owns trees but provides for landowners to register property marks for any trees they wish to fell (s. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is owned by State but domestic use is free, regulated in customary lands by customary norms. Constitution 1992 states that in addition to minerals  "rivers, streams, water courses throughout Ghana ... are the property of the Republic of Ghana and shall be vested in the President on behalf of, and in trust for the people of Ghana" Art.21.6. Reiterated in Water law 1996 s. 12.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 Art. 21.6, 11.1,  Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act No. 522) s 1,.12, 14.1. Land Use and Spatial Planning Act No. 925 of 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Commission regulates use and coordinated policies related to uses. Domestic use protected: "A person who has lawful access to water resources may extract and use such water for domestic purposes" (s.14.1). Given constitutional status of customary tenure as lawful component of the law of Ghana (Art 11.3, 267.1) it may be assumed that domestic use is governed by custom, subject to state policies. Other laws regulate irrigation, reclaimed areas, dams & special zones: Irrigation Development Authority Act, 1977, Volta River Development Act, No. 46 of 1961; Rivers Act, 1903, Land Planning and Soil Conservation Ordinance, 1953, etc.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Designation of forest reserves does not extinguish customary ownership of the land, but signals that the area is controlled & managed by the Forestry Commission. Only compulsory acquisition when creating a Wildlife Protected Areas. No provision for community-owned Protected Areas, only Resource Management Areas outside PA. Wildlife Act s. 16.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Forests Act, 1927 (Act 157, last amended in 1986). The Forestry Commission Act, 1999 (Act 571). Timber Resources Management Act, No. 547 of 1997 (last amended in 2002). The Forest Protection Act, 1974 (Act 243).  Wildlife Resources Management Act, 2023.
indicators.additional_info: New Wildlife Act 2023, sustains management of PA under the Forestry Commission fails to enable communities to own PA -National Park, Strict Nature Reserve, Resource Reserve, RAMSAR site, etc. Distinct from forest reserves which are not classed as PA, where customary ownership remains but is seriously interfered with, including Commission's right to commute rights and restrict use, disallow alienation of the concerned land without written notification. (Forestry Commission Act, 1999, s. 2.2.b, Wildlife Act, 2023 s. 5). Where a recognised fetish grove or tree is included in a reserve, this may not be interfered with (Forests Act, 1927, s. 17.7).  Wildlife Act 2023 assists communities to establish and manage Community Resource Management Areas outside PA.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary lands constitutionally recognized as lawfully owned & governed by customary authorities, and cannot be alienated into statutory tenure. Ownership is absolute, vested in chiefs, heads of clans & families  as trustees on behalf of members. All rights are recordable by localized Customary Land Secretariats, still in process of establishment.
indicators.additional_info: Since 1890s customary lands have been recognized as the property of communities, vested in traditional authorities including chiefs and their councils ('stools'), first settler family/tendana) or family heads depending on area. These  persons operate as trustee administrators for the owners - communities, clans, families. (Const. 1992 Art 267.1, 36.8) Land Act 2020, sec. 9, 13). The Constitution entrenches (unwritten) customary law as part of the laws of Ghana (Art. 11). The State regulates and may co-opt management (and does so for all forests), paying customary owners fixed percentages of revenue from logging (Art. 267.6).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Constitution 1992 & Land Act 2020 entrench equal status of customary & statutory rights. Both provide for freehold and other possession (customary lease, customary tenancy etc). Customary right legally exist with/without registration. Compulsory for each trustee (eg chief) to insitute Customary Land Secretariat to enable recordation.
indicators.additional_info: Few Customary Secretariats in place yet. Both property systems endure outdated compulsory acquisition rules, such as open-ended definition of public purpose, compensation not payable prior to eviction and often delayed by years (Land Act s. 233-256).The Constitution 1992 & Land Act, 2020 entrench revenue sharing by the Forestry and other State Commissions for use and profit from customary lands through collection  rents, dues, royalties, revenues by the Administrator of Stool Lands, taking 10% for its administration, disbursing the rest to the chief/clan/family head (25%), to the traditional authority (chief and council) (20%) and to the elected District Assembly (55%) to provide development and services to community members (Const. Art. 267.6). NO direct payments to community members as group or individuals.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Localised, cheap & simple recordation ('registration') of customary rights available at Customary Land Secretariats. Recordable interests include: allodial title, customary law freehold, common law freehold, usufructary interest, leasehold, customary tenancy & transfers (s.1,  81). Oral testimony permitted (s. 36-37). Communal areas may also be recorded  for common use (s. 19).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2020. Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands Act, No 481 of 1994. Land Commission Act, No.767, 2008.
indicators.additional_info: Negatives in the cutomary titling regime include the right of Secretariats to charge fees (sec. 17); Secretariat is not elected (sec. 16 (1)); no survey & demarcation required sustaining overlaps (sec. 182 (2)). Also, the allodial title holder - the chief, land chief, head of clan, or head of family - may  take over bare land or farmland subject to usufructuary interests in the 'communal interest' s. 50 (21).  Although he must pay , compensation and provide alternative land where possible (sec. 50 (22) and may be fined if found to be unfair; this is all insufficient given the high values of customary lands. Ideally, Regulations under the Land Act, 2020 will alleviate concerns but no Regulations promulgated as of March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No recognition of the members of chiefdom, sub-chiefdom, clan or family as legal persons in their own right. Chiefs, land chiefs, or heads of clan or family act on their behalf. Sec. 281  describes "land owning group" as 'a stool, skin, family head, clan head or other collection of individuals that holds title to land', "proprietor" is described as 'the person named in the land register'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 Art. 18.  Land Act, 2020 sec. 281
indicators.additional_info: This is reinforced by provision at sec 182 (10) of Land Act, 2020 that at registration 'an entry shall be made in the land register stating the occupant of the stool or skin, or head of clan or family, or any other person authorised by the stool or skin, or clan or family to administer the land or interest in the land'.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities neither directly administer customary lands nor set up/elect or manage the Land Secretariats. These are instituted by the trustee chiefs etc. Land Act s. 13-14. In addition to recording rights & transfers these bodies settle disputes, prepare accounts such as rent from the Forestry Commission, mining concessions etc s. 18. Bound to be transparent, fair and impartial' s. 13.3.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1992 Arts. 36.8, 267-268, Land Act, 2020. The Office of The Administrator of Stool Land Act, 1994 (Act 481). Head of Family (Accountability) Law, 1985. Mineral Commission Act, 1993 (Act 450) s. 2. Forestry Commission Act, 1999 (Act 571) s.2.
indicators.additional_info: State controls use of minerals, water and timber, natural resources on customary lands (80% of Ghana's land area) through  Commissions, which share a percent of revenue with The Administrator of Stool Lands charged to distribute rent, royalties etc to the stool/skin or head of clan/family. All concessions are subject to Parliamentary approval (Const/ Art. 268). The State Land Registrar cannot register a large scale disposition of a stool, skin, clan or family land unless the Regional Land Commission has agreed (Land Act 2020 s. 102 (3)) taking into account 'protection of indigenous land rights, fairness in terms of agreement, etc.' S. 121 provides for overriding interests including a right of way, a right of water, or rights which may continue to be exercised.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary allodial and customary freehold rights are owned in perpetuity and registrable as such, Land Act 2020, sec 83. Usufructs, which may also be held in perpetuity, are limited to 99 year term at registration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2020.
indicators.additional_info: Although not codified, customary law provides for allodial title and rights in perpetuity, reflected in long history of court rulings and statutes such as the Land Titles Registration Act, 1986 Act 152, s. 19, repealed but much of its content incorporated in 152 sections in the Land Act, 2020 (sec. 80-232)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Consent of owners to compulsory acquisition is not required; only consultation (s. 244-245). Report must show their concerns "are taken into consideration". The State must retain as public land, allocate to a public body or to other entity only as a user right (s. 235). No transfer or eviction until Land Commission has earmarked funds needed & placed compensation in escrow account s. 238.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act 2020; Chapter Seven Secs. 233-267
indicators.additional_info: Claims to be submitted by all persons affected including amount of compensation sought (s. 250). Compensation determined by replacement costs including resettlement on alternative land (sec. 256). Claimant may appeal (s. 258). Compensation is paid at 60% to the customary holder of the land (eg. farmer, plot holder) and 40% to the allodial title holder (chief/council, clan leader, family head) (s. 259). When a tenant is affected, the allodial title holder receives 60%, or where the tenancy is held by the customary usufructary, the latter gets 30% and the tenant 30%. Payment may be delayed (and regularly can take years), only through court claim is interest added (Sec. 261). Resettlement of inhabitants is obligatory and subject to a plan (s. 265).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While ownership of trees is attached to the land and thus owned by customary landowners - or traditional authorities on their behalf (stools, skins, family heads), contradictions as to who permits felling, controls timber, etc. esp. in regard to concessions.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Trees and Timber Act, 1974 (Act 273). The Forestry Commission Act, 1999 (Act 571). The Timber Resources Management Act, 1998 (Act 547). The Concessions Act, 1962 (Act 124).

GIN.name: Guinea

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities, including Pastoral Code 1995 for Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law (1992) recognizes land owners as those who show peaceful, personal, continuous and bona fide occupation, by property taxes or development of the property Art. 39.3. Only route to formalization is through conversion into  titles extinguishing customary ownership &  jurisdiction. Although registration is compulsory since 1992, not implemented.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010 (2020) Art. 13. Ordinance Q/92 of 30 March 1992 Land and Domain Code (CFD). Decree on Rural Land Policy 2001 D/2001/17 Mai 2001.
indicators.additional_info: French colonial law in the 1920s /early 1930s provided for private customary lands to be registered; in Guinea, this ceased to apply with nationalization (1959) but reintroduced in 1992, the Land and Domain Code still the law in force. The Code implies that individual customary rights are registrable. In practice, only parcels in urban areas are titled (aided by Urbanization Code 1998). The use rights of communities to natural resources is admitted.  Fulani pastoralists have full access to pasture & water under Pastoral Code 1995. Policy Decree 2001 stated need for villages to be legal persons and  to activate devolved land governance  (Arts.12, 15,31). No legal change since 1992.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unequal protection of customary & statutory rights - unless the former registered in the Land Book but limited to family homesteads.  Mass titling planned under 1992 law via decentralizing govt to communes with land authority. Minor delivery since. Customary owners still rely on paying property taxes & developing farms/houses. No protection for commons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance Q/92 of 30 March 1992 Land and Domain Code (also referred to as Ordonnance No.0/92/019. Law No. 2017/040/AN of 24 February 2017 Local Government Code. Pastoral Code, Law L/95/51/CTRN (1995).
indicators.additional_info: Pasturelands defined as "all unenclosed areas normally used lawfully, permanently or seasonally for feeding livestock, as well as areas specially developed for this purpose" Art 4 Pastoral Code 1995 Art 4. May include some forests. Pastoralists must secure permission of owners of cultivated lands to graze. The Code lays down the conditions for transhumance Art. 52-69. The right to pastoral grazing land is assured; Art. 70 describes pasture rights as private; "recognized and protected as such by the law. ... insofar as they are exercised without abuse and respect the rights recognized  to other users" (Art 76)

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No system of simple, accessible, affordable adjudication, mapping and registration of customary rights, although intended by 1992 law. Still intended after Rural Land Policy (2001) but no legal change to remove flaws of law such as exclusion of communal lands and to enable registration of lands as customary properties, only registration in replacement statutory titles.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Domain Code, 1992. Decree Approving Rural Land Policy, 17 Mai 2001.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: There is no intention in the 1992 law in force to recognize a village or family as a legal person for purpose of registration but advised in Land Policy Decree 2001. In any event, registration in rural domains is so limited  despite the law,  this potential has not been tested.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Domain Code, 1992. Decree approving Rural Land Policy, 17 Mai 2001.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The intended administration of land is by local authorities established at the rural commune level. This has not been instituted across the country. In default customary authorities administer and regulate lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance Q/92 of 30 March 1992 Land and Domain Code (also referred to as Ordonnance No.0/92/019. Law No. 2017/040/AN of 24 February 2017 Local Government Code.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The incidents of customary land tenure are not listed in the 1992 law, but due to Article 39.3 it may be assumed that if customary permits inheritance, the law accepts customary rights, registered or unregistered, as owned in perpetuity and/or for so long as the owner is in occupation and develops the land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance  of 30 March 1992 Land and Domain Code (also referred to as Ordonnance No.0/92/019).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not require consent of customary landholders affected by proposed taking of their land. It encourages amicable agreement, negotiation on compensation Art. 56, 63. If no agreement the court will decide Art. 68. The interests of holders are to be entered into the Land Book even should they have no deeds (Art. 60).
indicators.law_and_provision: The Land and Domain Code, Law No. 99/013/AN.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Forest Code states that "Trees outside forests located either on the immediate outskirts of a village or in a collective or individual field, are the property of the collective or the individual property of the owner of the field" (Art. 18).  However, such rights are access & use, not ownership; all forests belong to the nation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law L/2017/060/AN of 12 December 2017 On The Forest Code.
indicators.additional_info: All the forests on national territory form part of the national heritage to which any natural or legal person may have access & use. However these forests may only be owned by the State, local authorities, Guinean individuals or Guinean legal entities governed by private law. Art. 16, Forest Code 2017.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource. Art 4. Only domestic use, satisfying the needs of natural persons for consumption, hygiene, washing and vegetable or animals production is allowed without permit Art 6. Seasonal water use such as by pastoralists requires authorization not permits. Art. 9.  Governance of water by communes, applying customary norms as long as these do not contradict the code. Art 41.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, Law No. L/94/005/CTRN of 15 February 1994

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protected Areas are State property but each to have a buffer zone for local communities to manage & use. The Forest Code 2017 encourages communities to manage forests outside PA. Art 2. Revenue sharing to communities encouraged. Village and individual/family  forests may be classified as under their control. Art 25.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2018/0049/AN Establishing a Code for the Protection of Wild Fauna and the Regulation of Hunting. Law L/2017/060/AN of 12 December 2017 On The Forest Code.
indicators.additional_info: Forest is a national property and Protected Areas PA belong to the State. EachPA must zone a Buffer Zone wherein local communities may practice customary uses as well as conservation and wildlife habitat protection actions (management) (Code for Protection of Wild Fauna and the Regulation of Hunting, 2018, Art. 26, 36, and Forest Act, 2018). Gazettement of a new Protected Area is subject to consultation with local communities where the new PA falls within the domain of a local authority (commune) (Art. 20). The Forest Code 2017 provides for communities to hold and manage forests outside Protected Areas. Art. 2: "Within each village or group of villages, a structure is created to represent the populations in the management of forest resources of local and decentralized authorities and in the distribution of revenues" (Art. 6). Forests owned by a village or individual may be classified (Art 25).

indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010 (2020) Art. 13. Ordinance Q/92 of 30 March 1992 Land and Domain Code (CFD). Decree on Rural Land Policy 2001 D/2001/17 Mai 2001.
indicators.additional_info: French colonial law in the 1920s /early 1930s provided for private customary lands to be registered; in Guinea, this ceased to apply with nationalization (1959) but reintroduced in 1992, the Land and Domain Code still the law in force. Policy Decree 2001 stated need for villages to be legal persons and  to activate devolved land governance  (Arts.12, 15,31). No legal change since 1992.

GMB.name: Gambia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Strong support for customary law and land rights but State may declare any customary land to be state land (1991). Intention from 2007 to devise new policy and law but Commission sworn in only in 2018 and yet to produce reccs. The Lands (Regions) Act 1945 (1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). Art. 7.  The Lands (Regions) Act, 1945 (1991) Cap 57:03, s. 4 & 5.  The State Lands Act, No. 2 of 1991 Cap 57:02, s. 5.
indicators.additional_info: Customary law is constitutionally part of the laws of The Gambia (Art.7e). Customary lands vested in local governments led by chiefs. The Lands (Regions) Act 1945 (1991) states that "The occupation and use of Regions' lands by indigenes shall be governed and regulated by the customary law obtaining in the localities in which such lands are situated' (s. 5) A  weak point comes from the State Lands Act amended in 1991 which enables the Minister to declare any land in the regions to be state land although the land continues to be "for the use and benefit of communities, direct or indirect" (s. 5.2.a). Non-indigenes (from the Province) may acquire rent-paying leases only up to 50 years (s.9).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No Gambian law states that customary lands are properties, or equally protected as land under titles available only in the city area. Nor is compensation equitable at compulsory acquisition. Commission since 2018 is devising new land policy & law. In practice protection of customary land in villages continues, but on an outdated legal foundation from 1945.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). Art. 7 & 22.1.  The Lands (Regions) Act Cap 57:03, s. 4-9. The State Lands Act Cap 57:02, s. 5, 7. Land Acquisition and Compensation Act Cap 57:06 s. 11. Forest Act, Cap. 61:01. s. 39. Biodiversity and Wildlife Act Cap. 62:02. District Tribunals Act Cap 6:03.
indicators.additional_info: The 1945 Lands (Regions) Act has not been significantly amended since 1960s and no regulations have been issued, weakening its force. Loss of lands to State for Forest Parks (66 created in 1950s by Subsidiary Legislation to Lands (Regions) Act). Newer threat from The Gambia Tourism Board Act, 2011 which enables Board to override customary rights. Land Acquisition law compensates only for improvements to lands compared to value of the land for freeholds outside regions (s.11). Communities fully involved when Protected Areas proposed. District Tribunals also led by chief, so conflict of interest adds vulnerability.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No process in place for issued customary land titles to individuals, families or of communities. Consent of Traditional Authorities ('District Authorities') to issue 'deemed' leases required. Chiefs may also issue Certificates of Occupancy but no register for these.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap. 57:03. The State Lands Act Cap. 57:02.
indicators.additional_info: Customary owners in lands designated as State Lands are deemed lessees of the State with 99 year leases for residences, 10 years for agricultural land, and may acquire title deeds accordingly (State Lands Act. s. 7).  Affects limited area of country. Elsewhere District Authorities (traditional authorities comprising district chief (seyfo) & 4 village/clan heads (alkalos) approve applications for leases including by non-local indigenes, but which remain under their jurisdiction (Lands (Regions) Act, s.22). May issue Certificates of Occupancy but not registrable/no Regiater (State Land Regulations, L.I. 17 of 1995).  No regulations to guide these actions.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for families/clans or communities to be legal persons. Traditional authorities lawfully administer customary lands at village & district using customary law. Its use ends when a family or outsider seeks a lease for the land which is then state land, but chiefs/councils continue to administer these 'deemed leases' - in absence of legal support to title parcels as customary properties.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 Art. 22.1. The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap. 57:03. The State Lands Act, Cap 57:02. Land (Registration of Deeds) Act, 1880 (last amended 1972).
indicators.additional_info: By virtue of constitutional protection of customary law and property and provisions of The Lands (Regions) Act, collective landholding is lawful. But no provision for this to be registrable, although cooperatives, companies, friendly societies and NGOs are registrable; rarely formed by families or communities to entrench lands property.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Authority over customary lands is vested in traditional leaders (District chief and village/clan heads). Not elected and no legal guidance on actions or reporting.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap. 57:03. Local Government Act, 2002. Cap.33:01.
indicators.additional_info: Traditional authorities (district chief, seyfo and village heads, alkalos) are referred to as District Authorities, distinct from partially elected District Councils) (Lands (Regions) Act. But they are now appointed by President (Constitution 1996  Art. 58). They have full authority over customary land allocations, transactions, approval for issue certificates of occupancy, applications for statutory leases, etc. but customary land law is not codified and there is no statutory prescription guiding these actions. This invites unaccountability and inconsistency with evidence that some leases are granted without consent of traditional owners (A. Bensouda & Co. 2013, 'Improving Land Sector Governance in The Gambia', World Bank, p. 60).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights are held in perpetuity  and statutes support customary rights as lawful. However, there is no legal provision for these rights to be registered. Until 2025 registrable entitlements are 99 year leaseholds ('deemed leases') which technically means the land becomes state property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 Art. 7, 22.1. The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap. 57:03. The State Lands Act, Cap 57:02. Land (Registration of Deeds) Act, 1880 (last amended 1972).
indicators.additional_info: There is no land registration act describing registrable rights or their incidents and term. The Lands (Regions) Act Cap. 57:03 sections 5, does allow indigenes as well as non-indigenes to acquire leaseholds of specified terms for different land uses. The State Lands Act Cap. allows residents on designated state lands  (tiny area) to acquire 99 year leaseholds for residences but only 10 year renewable leases for farming (s.7).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Although customary laws may require consent of affected persons prior to approval of application for lease, there is no statutory requirement for this. No consultation or consent required at compulsory acquisition but communities are closely involved in deciding upon creation of new Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Acquisition and Compensation Act, 1991, Cap. 57:06. The State Lands Act, Cap. 57:02. Physical Planning & Development Control Act, No. 1/1991. Forest Act, No 3/2018. The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap 57:03. Biodiversity and Wildlife Act, 2003.
indicators.additional_info: Traditional authorities must approve applications for leases but not necessarily with consent of those affected. Local physical plans must be approved and which involve changed land uses but the President may waive requirement for public display of the plan (Cap. 57:08 s. 20.2) for designating an area as State Land and thereby abrogating customary rights, compulsorily acquiring these for public purposes. Exceptionally, the procedures for gazetting Protected Areas requires participation of communities including listing of all their rights and provisions for these to be sustained, or extinguished for compensation for losses, in practice making it difficult to gazette new PA

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Trees outside 'forests' are owned and freely usable by holder but permits required for felling or product sales. Rights to trees in gazetted Forests are obtainable by agreement. Communities own, manage & regulate Community Forests (CF), but which are very small;  by  2000 numbered 233 CF, covering 24,000 ha.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land (Regions) Act Cap/57:03. Forest Act, No. 3 of 2018, s. 4, 24-44.
indicators.additional_info: Forest' covers land with 10%+ natural or planted tree cover. Outside forests, trees owned by holder and  freely useable without permit except when felled or produce removed. Community forests created, owned and managed by communities for timber, firewood, non timber forest produce, grazing and protection (2018, s. 4.4). Communities may manage State Forest as Community Controlled State Forests on basis of Agreement (2018, S. 42-43). 56 Forest Parks created in 1952 in the regions, designated as State Land, although within the customary sector.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water is defined as 'land' and land may be owned by the state, by individuals, or by district authorities (chiefs) in trust for communities in accordance with customary law, which renders domestic use free. Use of all water irrespective of owners is regulated.
indicators.law_and_provision: State Lands Act, Cap. 57:02, s. 2. National Water Resources Council Act, No. 22 of 1999, Cap 66:02.
indicators.additional_info: Land includes lagoons, creeks, rivers, estuaries within The Gambia' (s.2 State Land Act Cap 57:02). Water use is regulated by a National Water Resources Council and administered by the Department of Water Resources in consultation with local governments and traditional authorities (Act. No. 22 of 1999 Cap 66:02 s.7 & 13).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities made party to declaration of Protected Areas. Their rights may be sustained, or extinguished on payment of compensation. Communities may manage State Forests. They may institute, own & manage Community Forests, and co-manage Wildlife Protected Areas on own village lands, and do so.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land (Regions) Act Cap. 57:03. Biodiversity and Wildlife Act, 2003,Cap. 62:02 s. 14-35. Forest Act No. 3 of 2018.
indicators.additional_info: The Lands (Regions) Act allows State to declare Forest Parks, which may be designated for the use and benefit of any community. Prior to gazettement a Reserve, Settlement Committee identifies rights, and recommends either extinction on payment of compensation, alteration of boundaries to enable rights to continue, creation of enclaves within Park or permits non-commercial uses to continue in the Park. Appeal & revival of extinguished rights is possible. Direct provision for communities to manage  a state forest park by agreement. Biodiversity and Wildlife Act, 2003 provide similarly for Protected Wildlife Areas (s.15-32) but with less provision for  autonomous management by communities(s.35-36).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Strong support for customary law and land rights but State may declare any customary land to be state land (1991). Intention from 2007 to devise new policy and law but Commission sworn in only in 2018 and yet to produce reccs. The Lands (Regions) Act 1945 (1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). Art. 7.  The Lands (Regions) Act, 1945 (1991) Cap 57:03, s. 4 & 5.  The State Lands Act, No. 2 of 1991 Cap 57:02, s. 5.
indicators.additional_info: Customary law is constitutionally part of the laws of The Gambia (Art.7e). Customary lands vested in local governments led by chiefs. The Lands (Regions) Act 1945 (1991) states that "The occupation and use of Regions' lands by indigenes shall be governed and regulated by the customary law obtaining in the localities in which such lands are situated' (s. 5) A  weak point comes from the State Lands Act amended in 1991 which enables the Minister to declare any land in the regions to be state land although the land continues to be "for the use and benefit of communities, direct or indirect" (s. 5.2.a). Non-indigenes (from the Province) may acquire rent-paying leases only up to 50 years (s.9).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No Gambian law states that customary lands are properties, or equally protected as land under titles available only in the city area. Nor is compensation equitable at compulsory acquisition. Commission since 2018 is devising new land policy & law. In practice protection of customary land in villages continues, but on an outdated legal foundation from 1945.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). Art. 7 & 22.1.  The Lands (Regions) Act Cap 57:03, s. 4-9. The State Lands Act Cap 57:02, s. 5, 7. Land Acquisition and Compensation Act Cap 57:06 s. 11. Forest Act, Cap. 61:01. s. 39. Biodiversity and Wildlife Act Cap. 62:02. District Tribunals Act Cap 6:03.
indicators.additional_info: The 1945 Lands (Regions) Act has not been significantly amended since 1960s and no regulations have been issued, weakening its force. Loss of lands to State for Forest Parks (66 created in 1950s by Subsidiary Legislation to Lands (Regions) Act). Newer threat from The Gambia Tourism Board Act, 2011 which enables Board to override customary rights. Land Acquisition law compensates only for improvements to lands compared to value of the land for freeholds outside regions (s.11). Communities fully involved when Protected Areas proposed. District Tribunals also led by chief, so conflict of interest adds vulnerability.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No process in place for issued customary land titles to individuals, families or of communities. Consent of Traditional Authorities ('District Authorities') to issue 'deemed' leases required. Chiefs may also issue Certificates of Occupancy but no register for these.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1996 (2018). The Lands (Regions) Act, Cap. 57:03. The State Lands Act Cap. 57:02.
indicators.additional_info: Customary owners in lands designated as State Lands are deemed lessees of the State with 99 year leases for residences, 10 years for agricultural land, and may acquire title deeds accordingly (State Lands Act. s. 7).  Affects limited area of country. Elsewhere District Authorities (traditional authorities comprising district chief (seyfo) & 4 village/clan heads (alkalos) approve applications for leases including by non-local indigenes, but which remain under their jurisdiction (Lands (Regions) Act, s.22). May issue Certificates of Occupancy but not registrable/no Regiater (State Land Regulations, L.I. 17 of 1995).  No regulations to guide these actions.

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All land is nationalized so property means ownership of rights to tracts of land (Decree 6/2018 Art 30). Customary communities acknowledged as discrete territorial entities. (Land Act 1998 Art 3). Boundaries of each to be delimited and registered as an existing entitlement (Decree 6/2018 Arts 41 & 44). To include commons (Art 17).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1984 (amended up to 1996). Land Law No. 5 of 1998. General Land Regulations under 1998 Law,  Decree No 6 of 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution recognizes collective legal persons (Arts 13-14). Land Law 1998 nationalizes land with emphasis on right to use land, and to ensure that local communities can use to fullest extent, with incorporation of customary regime as lawful. Concessions (contracts) to members or outsiders permitted but only for customary private lands, not commons.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Evident from Land Act 1998 & Regs 2018 that customary rights have equal force as non-customary concessions issued by state. No registrtion of parcels, onlu provision for each community domain to be mapped an registered as community property. Individual family rights obtainable only by extinction of customary right in favour of concession.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No. 5 of 1998. General Land Regulations,  Decree No 6 of 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Note that although there is no separate law for Indigenous Peoples the Land Regulations 2018 : "… the state recognizes the right of indigenous peoples to manage and exploit their land, forests and other natural resources in accordance with local customs and practices" Art. 17 (3).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The National Cadastre Service is bound to demarcate each community domain. Art. 41, 44, 46, Decree 6/2018. Perimeter boundaries determined by community with neighbours. The mapped parcel is registered in the Cadastral Atlas as community property. Limitation is that no provision for family parcels to be recorded other than through conversion into state granted concession. Art 45 of 6/2018.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No 5 of 1998. General Land Regulations, Decree 6/2018.
indicators.additional_info: The law 1998 and regulatory Decree 2018 reiterate that communities are responsible for managing their lands in accordance with customs and practices, as well as to decide on requests for concessions over land within their territories. Art 8 Decree 6/2018. No evidence of legally backed system of decision-making, suggestiog possibility of absent majority consultation.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Constitution recognizes collective legal persons (Arts 13-14). This includes communities at registration of their mapped domains as community property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1984 (1996). Land Law, No. 5/1998, Land Regulations, Decree No. 6/2018
indicators.additional_info: Protected Areas may overlap customary lands, and in which instance, customary access and use rights are guaranteed. "Reserved lands are areas classified in the domain of the state or local communities as strategic reserves for forestry, grazing, or pastoral development" (Art. 49, Decree 6/2018). eg. "The right of access for people living in local communities near to Sacred Mato Grosso and other sites of cultural and social importance within the protected areas is guaranteed" (Art. 7(3) Law No 5/1998).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: "Local Communities shall exercise management powers in accordance with their respective uses and customs over the entire area within their territorial boundaries, including inhabited areas, cultivated and fallow areas, areas in common use, pastures, water and sea resources, sacred forests or those designated for other social, cultural and economic purposes..." Art. 6 (4)) Land Law 1998.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No 5/1998. Land Regulations, Decree 6/2018.
indicators.additional_info: The Regs 2018 also stress the right and duty of communities to administer their own lands under customary law; most of country is customary. Land management bodies listed as Government, Municipalities (Communes), Local Communities, Commissions and the Cadastral and Registry Service. Art. 5 Regs 2018.  Potential shortfall in lack of obligation for community members to vet and decide key decisions with high reliance  traditional authorities.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Individual/family rights are owned in perpetuity. "Private land use rights subject to the customary use regime are granted in perpetuity" (Art. 16(2) Decree 6/2018). Concessions or approved by community are also registered as a use right in perpetuity; such rights cannot affect commons, also assumed to be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, No 5/1998. General Land Regulations, Decree No. 6/2018.
indicators.additional_info: While Government is obliged to demarcate and map all community territories, based on community delimitation of area and adjudication with neighbours as to boundaries, failure to do so does not alter the status of the domain as owned by the community in perpetuity (Art. 17 (4), Decree 6/2018). The community domain includes communal use lands for forest, grazing, water and other purposes (Arts. 41-49, Decree 6/2018) - excepting classified forests which are the public domain of the State.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: FPIC does not appear in the laws but communities must give consent to applications for concessions from outside the community, also to any change of use of the land issued, failure resulting in cancellation. Land Law 1998 Art 19. Regs 2018 64-65. Consultation more vaguely required (in mother tongue) at compulsory acquisition. Art 32, 44.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, No 5/1998. General Land Regulations No 6/2018.
indicators.additional_info: "The people living in Local Communities are recognized as having the right to negotiate freely and directly, the transfer of the private rights they hold in accordance with Article 23" and  "Interested third parties must inform the inhabitants of the activities they intend to carry out which may not be altered without their consent, otherwise the right of use will be extinguished" Art. 19 (2) & (3) of Law 1998, Regulations 2018 Art 64-65. Note that if a concession is cancelled, the land does not revert to the community but to the State. Art. 27 1998. Public consultation for applications for land must be held with an affected community within 90 days, and assumed to have been given if no views are forthcoming Art. 32 (4). Note that 20% of land taxes must go to local communities Art. 40 1998.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All trees belong to the landholder including felling trees if domestic and not a protected species. Forest Law 5/2011 Art 14 (1). Forests included in definition of community lands. Land Law 1998 Art 3q. Community Forests encouraged for Protection & for  Sacred Forests. 5-A/2011 Art 4. Communities within State PA retain customary use rights & must be represented on Management Boards. Art. 20, 16.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No 5/1998. Forest Law No. 5 of 2011. Protected Areas Framework Law, Decree-Law No. 5-A/2011.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land under marine and land waters belongs to the State, but the water rights attached to landholder including communities; Land Act 1998. The Water Code 1992 defines the legal regime for all activities related to inland water, including duty to ensure clean water for all.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, No.5/1998. Water Code No 5-A/1992.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No provision for communities to own or co-manage  State Protected Areas (PA) but their own PA added to network of PA. Each PA requires own Decree, including with community agreement of zones, regs, &  compensation if required. Decree 5A/2011, Art 6 (1c). Community reps must be on all State PA Management Boards (Art 16).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Law - Decree-Law No. 5/2011.  Protected Areas Framework Law No 5-A/2011.
indicators.additional_info: A Community Protected Area "aims to promote management based on recovery and updating of traditional and scientific rules for management of natural resources" (Art. 4 (i)).  Classification is by decree specific to forest, boundaries & zones a preservation zone, transition zone & sustainable use zone "to satisfy the spiritual and material needs" Art. 29. Majority community consent required.  Forest law Art. 5 & 6.  A designated Director is responsible for guiding communities to prep mgt. plan incl. rules etc. Art. 14.

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.language: Unofficial translation of Spanish original to English
