indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Constitution establishes land as State property but protects traditional occupation & use. "Lands that have been or shall be demarcated as property of indigenous tribes, peoples or family groups ... shall not be considered private land of the state"; Land Ownership Law Art 4. Includes common lands Art 5. Only agricultural land is registrable but is "unseizable and inalienable" Arts 5,11.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2012. Land Ownership Law, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Only 30% of population is rural  (2019). Communal and family farming lands and residences are classified as 'Traditional Property' Art. 4 & 5 Land  Ownership Law 2009; Family lands as 'Traditional Family Patrimony Lands'. Commons excluding reserves termed 'traditional village lands' or 'village council lands', members exercising exclusive dominion (Report to UNEP from Government of Equatorial Guinea, 2019).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Equity between untitled customary and titled statutorily land, titles limited to farms with same terms for customary & outsider or foreign  applicants. Communal lands unregistrable and defined as inalienable 'traditional  property'; Law 2009 Art 4.  When community lands shown to have been shared by same community for a long time, it is fully unavailable to outsiders; Law 2013 Art. 11.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2012. Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2.009 (2009).  Decree No. 140/2.013 (2013) Regulating the Acquisition of Land by Foreign Individuals and Legal Entities.
indicators.additional_info: Issue of 'concessions' (max 99 years) is free when this involves the "collective property of nationals and those of the traditional agricultural patrimony of each Equatorguinean" (2013 Art. 1). Protection for ancestral lands as unavailable  "even if these are not delimited or registered in the Land Registry provided they continue to belong to the same or natural heirs" (2013 Art. 11).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unclear that titling simpler for customary owners as same procedure applies for others but with special protection in that titles (concessions) may only apply to 'family estates' in customary lands and to land which " not occupied, or the applicant is the occupier, and where no conflict between the applicant and adjacent or third parties, and no projects affecting the land" Law 2009 Cht 4.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2.009 (2009).  Decree No. 140/2013 Regulating the Acquisition of Land by Foreign Individuals and Legal Entities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unclear if the community is a legal person, as the implication of the land law of 2009 is that while a family can register its exclusive dominion, communal land is referred to as 'village land' or 'village council land'. Both held to be 'traditional property'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2009 (2009).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary law is upheld so long as a rule does offend the Constitution. The Civil Code 1899 still applies in recognizing the internal administration of communities and their lands by members under their own systems. While the law does not explicitly designate communities as administrators this is implied in Land Law 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2012. Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2.009 (2009). Civil Code 1899.
indicators.additional_info: NOTE: the 350 page Civil Code could not be accessed in English

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Only concessions have limited duration (max 99 years). Commons are classified along with family lands as traditional property. Customary rights held in perpetuity through inheritance.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 4.2.009, Law for Land Ownership Regime, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: FPIC is not referred to. However, Government is obliged to demonstrate that a land is free from occupation when allocating land to a foreign person or entity Art. 23, Land Law, 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 4./2.009 on Land Ownership Regime

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While forest is owned by the State, rights over natural or planted trees belong to the community or family as clear in provision for Communal Forests as a class of Production Forests as "areas of natural or repopulated forests that the State recognizes, delimits and grants in permanent use to rural communities" Art. 12 Forest Law 1997. However communities may not commercially sell timber Art. 24.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 1.1.997 of 1997 on the Use and Management of Forests.
indicators.additional_info: "Forest land, whether or not covered by natural forests, wild vegetation or man-made plantations is part of the National Forest Reserve ... (this is) of a permanent nature, not alienable of in the public domain; therefore there is no private property…" Arts. 4-5 Forest law 1997. However, use of forests is clearly owned such as in regard to Communal Forests, the use of which belongs solely to the community but for non-commercial purposes. Art. 24.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water falls within the public domain Art. 1-3 Water Law 2007. Private water includes rainwater and ground water including for customary holders. Ponds  on communal lands belong to the villages. Use of rivers, inlets, creeks, bays, inlets for fishing, etc  and wetlands is free for all along withwater for drinking, washing, vessels, bathing, watering livestock Arts. 30-31.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law Regulating Waters and the Coastal Waters, No. 3 of 2003.
indicators.additional_info: Equatoria Guinea has massive inland water sources, and extensive claim to marine waters. However, main urban dwellers have no clean running water. All water falls within the public domain Art. 1-3, Water Law 2007. However private water of owner includes  Rainwater, which may be gathered into ponds, basins, cisterns, reservoirs etc Art. 6 along with groundwater. Art. 6 (3). Ponds located on communal lands belong to the village (Art. 6 (2).  Use of rivers, inlets, creeks, bays, inlets for fishing, etc  and wetlands is free Art. 30 and use of water for drinking, washing, vessels, bathing, watering livestock is generally free to the public Art. 31 .

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for a community to own or co-manage a Protected Areas (PA) although participation and acceptance of local uses & customs provided they cause no harm prevails. Art 9 2003. Only one PA class, Protected Natural Spaces, requires a 'Traditional Zone' Art. 26 & 27. Forest within community land is owned by community and freely used for non-commercial purposes Art. 24.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law Regulating the Environment, No. 7 of 2003

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Constitution establishes land as State property but protects traditional occupation & use. "Lands that have been or shall be demarcated as property of indigenous tribes, peoples or family groups ... shall not be considered private land of the state"; Land Ownership Law Art 4. Includes common lands Art 5. Only agricultural land is registrable but is "unseizable and inalienable" Arts 5,11.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2012. Land Ownership Law, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Only 30% of population is rural  (2019). Communal and family farming lands and residences are classified as 'Traditional Property' Art. 4 & 5 Land  Ownership Law 2009; Family lands as 'Traditional Family Patrimony Lands'. Commons excluding reserves termed 'traditional village lands' or 'village council lands', members exercising exclusive dominion (Report to UNEP from Government of Equatorial Guinea, 2019).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Equity between untitled customary and titled statutorily land, titles limited to farms with same terms for customary & outsider or foreign  applicants. Communal lands unregistrable and defined as inalienable 'traditional  property'; Law 2009 Art 4.  When community lands shown to have been shared by same community for a long time, it is fully unavailable to outsiders; Law 2013 Art. 11.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2012. Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2.009 (2009).  Decree No. 140/2.013 (2013) Regulating the Acquisition of Land by Foreign Individuals and Legal Entities.
indicators.additional_info: Issue of 'concessions' (max 99 years) is free when this involves the "collective property of nationals and those of the traditional agricultural patrimony of each Equatorguinean" (2013 Art. 1). Protection for ancestral lands as unavailable  "even if these are not delimited or registered in the Land Registry provided they continue to belong to the same or natural heirs" (2013 Art. 11).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unclear that titling simpler for customary owners as same procedure applies for others but with special protection in that titles (concessions) may only apply to 'family estates' in customary lands and to land which " not occupied, or the applicant is the occupier, and where no conflict between the applicant and adjacent or third parties, and no projects affecting the land" Law 2009 Cht 4.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Regime of Land Ownership, No. 4/2.009 (2009).  Decree No. 140/2013 Regulating the Acquisition of Land by Foreign Individuals and Legal Entities.

GUF.name: French Guiana

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (indigenous peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not recognize the land rights of indigenous and local communities in French Guiana.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 2005-867 of 28 July 2005 updating and adaptation of the federal law, land law and forest law applicable in Guyana; Ordinance No. 98-777 of 2 September 1998 on specific provisions for gratuitous transfer of land belonging to the private domain of the State in Guyana and amending the code of the domain of the State (Legislative Part)
indicators.additional_info: According to a secondary source, "In French Guiana, native American Indians live on 'terres domaniales', land belonging to the state. Access to communities living inland is restricted since 1971 by prefectural order. A ministerial decree, in 1987, regarding land belonging to the state, makes provision for the concession of territories to 'communities which traditionally rely on the forest for their subsistence'. 496 000 ha have been defined as such at present. They yet have to be definitely granted by the state." Secondary sources: http://lucy.ukc.ac.uk/sonja/rf/ukpr/Report45.htm; http://minorityrights.org/country/french-guiana/ NOTE: French Guiana has not yet ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal People

GUY.name: Guyana

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous communities (Amerindian)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Under the State Lands Act, 1910, President may issue land titles to Amerindian communities. By doing so, statutory ownership rights are transferred to the Amerindian Community. The Amerindian Act 2006 recognizes the traditional ownership rights of Amerindian villages and communities, but these communities are not given the right to exclude others from their lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); State Lands (Amerindians) Regulations (Reg. 10/8/1910, 13/1948, 1/1949); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Section 3 grants the President broad power to grant titles to state land. Under, the Amerindian Act, 2006, these titles can be granted Amerindian communities. The Amerindian Act 2006 grants Amerindians traditional ownership rights, which are defined as any subsistent right or privilege....which is owned legally or by custom by an Amerindian Village or Amerindian Community and which is exercised sustainably in accordance with the spiritual relationship which the Amerindian Village or Amerindian Community has with the land..." (Sec. 2, Amerindian Act, 2006). The Amerindian Act provides that "village lands" means "lands owned communally by a Village under title granted to a Village Council to hold for the benefit of the Village..." Communities are not allowed to dispose of their lands (Sec. 44, Amerindian Act, 2006) and no more than 10 percent of the land can be leased to outsiders for a term no greater than 50 years (sec. 46, Amerindian Act, 2006).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The President retains broad authority to revoke Amerindian land rights granted under the State Lands Act. Amerindian land can be leased and expropriated for large-scale mining projects and other public purposes (Sec. 50, Amerindian Act; Sec. 142, Constitution). Titles to Amerindian land can be revoked in the public interest, or if Amerindians transfer rights to their lands in contravention of laws.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Section 11 of the State Lands Act, 1910 provides that "the President may at any time direct that any land specified on a license or permission shall be taken and used for public purposes, on payment of such compensation as, having regard to all the circumstances of the cases, he deems reasonable." Furthermore, section 14 of the State Lands Act provides that "where any condition of any grant, license, or permission is not fulfilled or where any regulation is not observed, the grant, licence, or permission may be revoked by the President and it shall thereupon cease and determine." Section 8 grants the government authority to allow people to enter Amerindian Village lands. Section 8 states "a person who enters Village lands to conduct official business for the Government or who is acting under the authority of any written law or is otherwise lawful authorized- (a) is deemed to have permission fro the Village from the Village Council"

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Amerindian Act sets out requirements for registering Amerindian village land (Sec. 59-64, Amerindian Act, 2006). However, these procedures are cumbersome and not easily accessible. Also, the Amerindian community must prove that they have been in existence for 25 years and have 150 persons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Sec. 59 of the Amerindian Act provides that a village can apply for titled village land by submitting an application with the name of the village, number of persons, and description of the land, among other pieces of information. Section 60 states that "an Amerindian Community may apply in writing to the Minister for a grant of State lands provided- (a) it has been in existence for at least twenty-five years (b) at the time of the application and for the immediately preceding give years, it comprised at least one hundred fifty persons." The Minister then conducts an investigation of the Amerindian community land to determine whether to grant the community title to their lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Amerindian Villages and Communities are granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Section 64 of the Amerindian Act 2006 states that an Amerindian Village or Community which is dissatisfied with the Minister's decision... may apply to the High Court for a review of the decision.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Authority over Amerindian Lands is vested in the Village Council. Any lease agreement or rules on how land will be used (e.g. forestry, mining, and other purposes) must comply with the Constitution, abide by relevant national laws, and must be approved by the Minister of Amerindian Affairs and the Amerindian village.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: “A Village Council may grant leases of Village lands provided (a) the total amount of land leased does not exceed ten percent of Village lands; (b) the maximum term of a lease is fifty years; (c) the lease is granted at a market rent or above; (d) the purpose of the lease is for agriculture, tourism or other productive and sustainable use of the land, which is consistent with the Village's cultural attachment to the land and provided that it is in the best interests of the Village; and (e) the Village Council obtains the advice and consents required under section 47" (Section 46 (I), Amerindian Act, 2006). Section 47 of the Amerindian Act, 2006 provides that "(1) before granting or amending a lease a Village Council shall obtain the advice of the Minister...If a lease is to be granted to a non-resident or if a lease granted to a non-resident is to be amended, the Village Council shall call a Village general meeting and obtain the consent of at least seventy-five percent of those present and entitled to vote at the Village general meeting. (3) If a lease is to be granted to a resident or if a lease granted to a resident is to be amended, the Village Council shall call a Village general meeting and obtain the consent of at least fifty one percent of those present and entitled to vote at the Village general meeting. (4) If the Village Council does not obtain the advice and consents required by this section, the lease shall not be granted and is void if granted.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land titles to Amerindian lands are granted for an unlimited period of time (these rights are held in perpetuity).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Amerindian communities can veto mining activities and use of forest products on their land (Secs. 47, 55, Amerindian Act 2006) . However, the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission can issue permits, concession, and licenses to Amerindian lands. The State has the power to override the veto by citing a public interest justification. Aside from mining projects, it is not clear that Amerindians have a right to give consent prior to acquisition by the government or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Section 48 of the Amerindian Act provides "a miner who wishes to carry out mining activities on Village lands or in any river, creek, stream or other source of water within the boundaries of Village lands shall provide information, consult, and obtain consent of a least two-thirds of those present and entitled to vote at a Village general meeting." However, Section 8 of the Amerindian Act grants the government authority to allow people to enter onto Amerindian Village lands. Section 8 states "a person who enters Village lands to conduct official business for the Government or who is acting under the authority of any written law or is otherwise lawfully authorized- (a) is deemed to have permission from the Village Council."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Once titles are transferred to Amerindian communities, the community owns the forest resources therein. But the ownership rights are subject to certain restrictions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Section 54 of the Amerindian Act provides that ""a resident who wishes to use forest product from Village lands shall obtain the permission of the Village Council and comply with any conditions attached to that permission."" Section 55 provides that a Village Council must give a consent (two-thirds of the Village) for the use of forest produce by non-residents. Amerindians can also form a community forest management agreement for the purpose of managing forests. Section 11 of the Forest Act 2009 states ""community group"" means persons living within and having strong ties with the community and includes- (a) a registered community forest organisation....other similar society formed under any other law within the community group. The purpose of [a community forest management agreement]...is to provide communities with a means of acquiring clear and secure rights to manage and benefit from their local forests on a sustainable basis in order to help meet local needs.""

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Amerindian water rights can be implied from the State Lands Act. Amerindian Communities are granted traditional water entitlements, which are defined as use rights that are recognized by custom. All communities, as citizens, can obtain use rights as citizens.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water and Sewage Act 2002; Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001).
indicators.additional_info: The State Lands Act assumes that the State is the owner of all water resources, but includes a provision stating "nothing in this Act shall be construed to prejudice, alter or affect any right or privilege legally possessed, exercised or enjoyed by any Amerindian in Guyana." Furthermore, section 18(2) provides that all existing rights to own, use, abstract, manage and control the flow of water are hereby saved upon the terms of their grant or ther= lawful authority under which they are held." Thus, it can be implied that Amerindiana Communities have lawful authority to use water. Section 36 of the Constitution of Guyana provides that the State will protect and make rational use of its water resources. State ownership rights are also established in the State Land Act and the Hydro-electric Power Act (CAP 56:03). Janki, M. Customary Water Las and Practices: Guyana. Available at: http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/templates/legal/docs/CaseStudy_Guyana.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Amerindian Act provides that Amerindian Village may establish their village lands as part of a national protected areas system.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 58, Amerindian Act 2006
indicators.additional_info: Section 58(1) of the Amerindian Act 2006 provides "a Village which wishes to have the whole or any part of its Village lands recognized as a part of a national protected areas system shall comply with the requirements of any written law governing such system." Furthermore, Section 58(2) states that "no protected area may be established over the whole or any part of Village lands without the consent of the Village general meeting (3) If a protected area is established on lands occupied or used by an Amerindian Community- (a) there shall be no alteration or abrogation of any traditional right over such land unless the Amerindian Community which has the right gives its consent in writing; and (b) the Amerindian Community which has a traditional right over such land shall be adequately consulted about the management of the protected area."

local_communities_entries.framework: Non-indigenous communities
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Rights Act grants communities the right to enter into community forest management agreements (CFMAs), but the procedures are not yet established in regulations
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Section 11 of the Forest Act 2009 provides that a "community group" means persons living within and having strong ties with the community. The purpose of community forest management agreements are to "provide communities with a means of acquiring clear and secure rights to manage and benefit from their local forests on a sustainable basis to help meet local needs, stimulate income generation and economic development, and enhance environmental stability."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Commission has broad authority to grant or deny the community group a CFMA. The government may suspend, amend, or revoke State Forest Authorizations (including CFMAs (Sec. 18, Forest Act of 2009)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Section 11(4) of the Forest Act provides that no community forest management agreement may be granted to a group unless the Commission is satisfied that the persons are persons living in close proximity to the forest and have strong ties to use of that forest.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Act does not contain clear procedures for establishing CFMAs. There is no indication that CFMAs are accessible or affordable.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Section 18 of the Forest Act gives due process rights to holders of State Forest Authorizations, which presumably include community groups. However, communities granted rights under CFMAs are not given legal personality for purposes of ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: CFMAs authorize community groups to occupy a specified area of State forest and manage that area in accordance with the CFMAs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009
indicators.additional_info: The specifics of community management rights granted by CFMAs are not spelled out in Guyana's laws or regulations.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: CFMAs have durational limits and the rights expire upon the expiration, revocation, or surrender of a CFMA.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Forest Act does not explicitly state whether communities have the right to give consent prior to acquisition of land and resources by governments and others.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: CFMAs grant community groups the right to manage forest products to "meet local needs, stimulate income generation and economic development, and enhance environmental stability."
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Amerindian water rights can be implied from the State Lands Act. Amerindian Communities are granted traditional water entitlements, which are defined as use rights that are recognized by custom. All communities, as citizens, can obtain use rights as citizens.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water and Sewage Act 2002; Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001).
indicators.additional_info: The State Lands Act assumes that the State is the owner of all water resources, but includes a provision stating "nothing in this Act shall be construed to prejudice, alter or affect any right or privilege legally possessed, exercised or enjoyed by any Amerindian in Guyana." Furthermore, section 18(2) provides that all existing rights to own, use, abstract, manage and control the flow of water are hereby saved upon the terms of their grant or ther= lawful authority under which they are held." Thus, it can be implied that Amerindiana Communities have lawful authority to use water. Section 36 of the Constitution of Guyana provides that the State will protect and make rational use of its water resources. State ownership rights are also established in the State Land Act and the Hydro-electric Power Act (CAP 56:03). Janki, M. Customary Water Las and Practices: Guyana. Available at: http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/templates/legal/docs/CaseStudy_Guyana.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no explicit indication in the law that the rights granted by CFMAs do not apply within protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 11, Forest Act, 2009

By doing so, statutory ownership rights are transferred to the Amerindian Community. The Amerindian Act 2006 recognizes the traditional ownership rights of Amerindian villages and communities, but these communities are not given the right to exclude others from their lands. (Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); State Lands (Amerindians) Regulations (Reg. 10/8/1910, 13/1948, 1/1949); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.)
GUY.Indigenous Q2: Does the law give indigen: Partial, significant progress — The President retains broad authority to revoke Amerindian land rights granted under the State Lands Act. Amerindian land can be leased and expropriated for large-scale mining projects and other public purposes (Sec. 50, Amerindian Act; Sec. 142, Constitution). Titles to Amerindian land can be revoked in the public interest, or if Amerindians transfer rights to their lands in contravention of laws. (Constitution of Guyana 2012; Amerindian Act of 2006; State Land Act of 1910 (1997); Guyanese Constitution of 1980 (2001). Forests Act, Act No. 6 of 2009.)
GUY.Indigenous Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, limited progress — The Amerindian Act sets out requirements for registering Amerindian village land (Sec. 59-64, Amerindian Act, 2006). Any lease agreement or rules on how land will be used (e.g. forestry, mining, and other purposes) must comply with the Constitution, abide by relevant national laws, and must be approved by the Minister of Amerindian Affairs and the Amerindian village. HND.name: Honduras

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2004 Property Law recognizes the ownership rights of  indigenous peoples and Afro-Hondurans.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: Article 346 of the Constitution of Honduras provides "It is the duty of the State to adopt measures to protect the rights and interests of the indigenous communities in the country, especially of the lands and forests in which they are settled". Article 93 of Property Law 2004 provides that "the State, for the special importance for the cultures and spiritual values of their relationship with the land, recognizes the right of indigenous peoples and Afro-Honduran have over the lands they traditionally own and that the law does not prohibit. The process set forth in this Chapter shall be implemented by the Institute of Property (IP) to guarantee these people the full recognition of the rights of communal ownership, use management, land management and sustainable use of natural resources by demarcation and titling in the domain itself". Article 94 states "the rights of ownership over the lands of these people will be entitled to their favor collectively. Members of communities have usufruct tenure according to traditional forms of communal property ownership". NOTE: Honduras ratified ILO Convention 169 (on Indigenous and Tribal peoples) in 1995.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 95 of the 2004 Property Law provides that if the State intends the exploitation of natural resources in indigenous territories, it must inform and consult the affected indigenous populations before authorizing any inspection or exploitation. When the government authorizes exploitation, indigenous people must receive fair compensation for any damages that result from these activities. However, in order to receive protection under the 2004 Property Law, indigenous communities must register following the procedures established in the Property Law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: Article 100 provides that indigenous land is inalienable, indefeasible and imprescriptible. Articles 96-99 establishes additional legal protections that are applicable to indigenous lands in Honduras. Furthermore, Article 102 provides that no person may issue titles to indigenous lands to third parties. Municipal who breach the rights of communal property located within its jurisdiction incur administrative, civil, or criminal liability, notwithstanding the invalidity of their actions.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Property Law 2004 establishes procedures for registering all property within Honduras, including property held by indigenous communities. However, there are no provisions or assistance mechanisms established by law to ensure that indigenous communities are able to easily access and afford registration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: Article 36 indicates that the registration of lands must entail gathering the following information: 1) class title 2) nature, extent, and conditions of the right; 3) the full name, nationality, address, number of the document and identification of the parties; 4) cadastral number or geographic identifier; 5) The area and boundaries of the land parcel

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2004 Property Law indicates that indigenous communities have legal personality for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 100 of the 2004 Property law indicates that communities have the right to govern their lands held under a communal system, and that communities also have power to authorize leases to third parties.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: Article 100 of the Property Law contains language indicating that communities themselves are granted legal authority over their lands.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2004 Property Law does not establish durational limits on indigenous ownership rights to land, which suggests that rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 95 of the 2004 Property Law provides that if the State intends the exploitation of natural resources in indigenous territories, it must inform and consult the affected indigenous populations before authorizing any inspection or exploitation. However, there is no indication from the Property Law that indigenous communities must give consent prior to acquisition of their land by governments and outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: NOTE: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights recently held that the indigenous right to free prior, and informed consent must be upheld and protected by the Honduran government. https://www.culturalsurvival.org/news/indigenous-rights-win-major-steps-forward-honduras

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Indigenous groups have rights to forests on lands that they traditionally inhabit. However, forest regulations that implement these rights have not yet been enacted, so it remains unclear whether indigenous rights to forests constitute full ownership rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 11 of the Forestry Law 2007 recognizes community forest rights. The Forest Law also recognizes a right to establish Social Forestry Systems and 40 Year Management Contracts by which communities can manage forests.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Under the General Water Law (2009), rights to both surface and groundwater vest in the state, but provides a right for all citizens to use water for domestic purposes. Under the Water Framework Law of 2003, municipalities have preference over all other users for the purpose of providing water for human consumption or discharge of sewage.  Indigenous communities, as citizens, have rights to use water for domestic purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: General Water Law (2009); Water and Sanitation Law 2003; Constitution of Honduras
indicators.additional_info: Article 6 of the General Water Law 2009 provides a right to use water for domestic pruposes. This right is granted to all citizens. Article 2 of the General Water Law 2009 provides that "use, expoitation, development, applications, and all other forms of exploitation of water resources and the exploitation or use of ecosstems and related  resources will be administered by the State through the Water Authority..." (Unofficial English translation of law written in Spanish)

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 101 of the Property Law grants indigenous communities rights to co-manage protected areas that are established within indigenous territories. But communities must respect the rules of land use that apply to protected areas. It is unclear whether IPs have full ownership rights in PAs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.

HND.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Partial, significant progress — Article 101 of the Property Law grants indigenous communities rights to co-manage protected areas that are established within indigenous territories. But communities must respect the rules of land use that apply to protected areas. It is unclear whether IPs have full ownership rights in PAs. (Property Law-Decree No. 82-2004; Forest Law, 2007; Resolución Nº 3/10 - Reglamento de la Ley de propiedad.)

IDN.name: Indonesia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous (customary) communities (Adat)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Basic Agrarian Law recognizes ""evidently still existent"" (adat- customary) land rights. The Constitutional Court recognized indigenous peoples as owners of customary forests. The state can convert customary forests to state forest.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 3, 56 Basic Agrarian Law (1960);  Constitutional Court decision "PUTUSAN – Nomor 35/PUU-X/2012"
indicators.additional_info: Articles 18B(2) and 28 of Indonesia's Constitution recognize traditional customary rights broadly, but do not establish indigenous land rights. Historically, the Basic Agrarian Law vested all land in State, but the Constitutional Court recently held that traditional communities are the "right owners" and managers of customary forests. The Constitutional Court decision has not been implemented through legislation. Legal status is  limited to customary forests and the extent that indigenous communities are "evidently still existent".

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Constitutional Court held that customary forests must be included as a category of ""titled forests"" so same level of protection as other titled forests. But State decides on categories.
indicators.law_and_provision: Para. 3.13.3,  3.13. 6, Constitutional Court Decision "PUTUSAN – Nomor 35/PUU-X/2012"; Art. 5, 1999 Forest Law; Art. 5,  Basic Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: Article 24C of the Indonesian Constitution establishes that "the Constitutional Court shall possess the authority of decision in reviewing laws against the Constitution." So the Constitutional Court's decision has a legally binding effect. The State still gets to decide which forests are designated as state forests, private forest, or customary forests (Art. 5, 1999 Forest Law). The Basic Agrarian Law establishes that agrarian law which applies to the earth, water and air space is adat (customary) law as far as it is not conflict with national/state interests (Art. 5).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law requires the Government to conduct land registration throughout the territory of the Republic of Indonesia, and registration covers measuring, mapping and recording of land, registration of rights, and issuance of certificates.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 19, Basic Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: While land registration is a requirement, it is unclear whether the law provides clear, simple, accessible and affordable procedures for indigenous peoples and communities to apply for and receive formal entitlement for their collective property rights.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Basic Agrarian Law recognizes adat law, or customary law, is a source of land law as long as it does not conflict with national interests or other regulations. Indigenous communities are granted legal standing to file claims in court.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 5, Basic Agrarian Law; Art. 51(1) of Law No. 24 of 2003 on the Constitutional Court
indicators.additional_info: Art. 51(1) of Law No. 24 of 2003 on the Constitutional Court provides that community-based customary law groups that are still in existence are provided may be granted legal standing when their constitutional rights are violated.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Law states indigenous communities, if still existent, shall be allowed to manage their forests according to the prevailing indigenous law so long as it does not contravene state law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 67, 1999 Forest Law; Constitutional Court Decision "PUTUSAN – Nomor 35/PUU-X/2012"
indicators.additional_info: Although the Court held that state authority over customary forests is "limited" and customary forests are within the scope of indigenous peoples rights, the Court held that legal authority of customary forests vests to the state if an indigenous community no longer exists within such customary forests. Otherwise, the Court held "the members of a traditional community have the right to clear their customary forests to be controlled and used for the fulfilment of heir individual needs and those of their families. Therefore it is not possible for the rights held by customary law community members to be extinguished or frozen, provided they meet the requirements of a traditional community as referred to in Article 18B(2) of the Constitution."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: With respect to the indigenous community land rights to customary forests, the 1999 Forest Act and the Constitutional Court Decision do not establish durational limits on customary forest rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: 1999 Forest Law; Constitutional Court Decision ""PUTUSAN – Nomor 35/PUU-X/2012""

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Constitutional Court held that forest concession by the State shall keep taking into account the rights of indigenous peoples. The State must consult with the public before expropriating land for a public purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitutional Court Decision "PUTUSAN – Nomor 35/PUU-X/2012"; Art. 18-19; Law No. 2 of 2012, Acquisition of Land for Development in the Public Interest
indicators.additional_info: Indonesia's expropriation law states “an Agency needing land together with the provincial government [to] hold a Public Consultation on a development plan… a public consultation on a development plan…shall be held to achieve agreement on the location of the development plan with the Entitled Parties” Law No. 2 of 2012, Acquisition of Land for Development in the Public Interest, Articles 18-19.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The 1999 Forestry Law provides that indigenous communities shall have the right to collect forest produce to fulfill daily needs relevant to community customary law, but communities do not own trees and cannot use trees for commercial purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 67, 1999 Forest Law
indicators.additional_info: Article 33(3) of the Indonesian Constitution provides that "the land, the waters and the natural resources within shall be under the powers of the State and shall be used to the greatest benefit of the people."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Water Law 7/2004 recognizes traditional communal rights on water resources so long as they actually exist and have been confirmed with local regional regualtions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 16(2), Basic Agrarian Law; Water Law 7/2004; Constitution of Indonesia
indicators.additional_info: Article 16(2) of the Basic Agrarian Law provides that "the rights on water..include the right of using water...the right of breeding and catching fish."Article 33(3) of the Indonesian Constitution provides that "the land, the waters and the natural resources within shall be under the powers of the State and shall be used to the greatest benefit of the people."Articles 6 of the Water Law  7/2004 provide that "(1) water resoruces are controlled by the state and used for the optimal welfare of the people...traditional communal rights on water resources...will be recognized so long as they actually exist and have been confirmed with local regional regualtions." Article 8 provides all citizens with Beneficial Use Water Rights and states "beneficial use water rights ais obtained without any license to fulfill the normal daily needs of individuals adn for small-scale farming within an irrgation system. (2) Beneficial Use Rights requires a license if: a. the manner of its use is bychanging the natural condition of water sources; b. it serves the purposes of a group of people who need water in large amounds; or c. it is used for small-scale farming outside the existing irrigation system."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: None of the laws assessed establish indigenous community ownership rights in protected areas.  However, indigenous communities can manage land within protected areas that is classified as traditional, religious, or particular zones.
indicators.law_and_provision: Government Regulation PP. No.28/2011 regarding the management of nature reserves and conservation areas. , Art 1(7-9) of Minister of Forestry Number: p.56 / Menhut-II / 2006 About Zoning Code National Park. See also, No P 19/Menhut/2004. Regarding collaboration in the management of wildlife sanctuaries and national parks.
indicators.additional_info: Reviewer could not locate the actual regulation; however, according to the 2015 RRI Report entitled "Protected Areas and the Land Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities", indigenous communities have the right to participate in the management of some protected areas classified as traditional, religious, or particular zones.

local_communities_entries.framework: Non-indigenous rural communities (Hutan Kemasyarakatan/ Kemitraan)
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities can form rural forest institutions, collectives or partnerships, and manage/ utilize exploitation rights/ business licenses to forest resources; however the law does not grant communities a proprietary right to the forest area.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 83, 87, 90, 99, Government Regulation  No.6/2007 on Forest Arrangement and Formulation of Forest Management Plan as well as Forest exploitation
indicators.additional_info: Art. 83 of the Regulations states that in order to obtain benefits of forest resources optimally and fairly, local community is empowered through forming rural cooperatives or partnerships. Article 87 provides that local community empowerment through rural forest is realized by granting exploitation rights to rural institutions. Exploitation rights cover area arrangement, formulation of a Management Plan and the utilization and rehabilitation of forests (Art. 87, Regulation No. 6/2007). Exploitation rights to forest areas are not proprietary and cannot be transferred/collateralized. Local community is defined as "social unity consisting of Indonesian citizens living inside and/or around forest, domiciled inside or around forest area having social community with the same source of income dependent on forest and their activities can influence forest ecosystems" (Elucidation on Art. 83, Government Regulation No. 6/2007).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law explicitly states that the exploitation right granted to rural communities is not a proprietary right, so the level of protection is not the same as that given to private property owners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 84-99, Government Regulation, No. 6/2007

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Regulation does not establish clear, accessible, affordable procedures for formally establishing rural community institutions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 84-99, Government Regulation, No. 6/2007

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law is silent about whether rural communities have legal personality, and it can be implied that, since there are no proprietary interests granted by the regulations, rural communities are not legal persons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 84-99, Government Regulation, No. 6/2007
indicators.additional_info: The Regulation states that exploitation rights and business licenses of rural forests is not a proprietary right to forest areas (Art. 90).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Non-indigenous rural communities, through forming rural institutions, can formulate rural-forest management plans.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 89(3), 90(2) Government Regulation, No. 6/2007
indicators.additional_info: The law states that ""rural institutions as holders of the exploitation right of rural forests are obliged to manage forests in accordance with the sustainable forest management principles.""

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Although the law does not establish a specific limit, the nature of the exploitation right/business license implies that there is a durational limit on the license/right.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 84-99, Government Regulation, No. 6/2007
indicators.additional_info: The Regulation states that exploitation rights and business licenses of rural forests is not a proprietary right to forest areas (Art. 90).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Constitutional Court held that forest concessions by the State shall keep taking into account the rights of indigenous peoples. The State must consult with the public before expropriating land for a public purpose, but no consent requirement.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 84-99, Government Regulation, No. 6/2007
indicators.additional_info: The Regulation states that exploitation rights and business licenses of rural forests is not a proprietary right to forest areas (Art. 90).

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress

IND.name: India

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Under the FRA 2006, Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers are granted the right to hold and live in forest land. However, these rights do not extend beyond forest lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3, The Scheduled tribes and other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA 2006)
indicators.additional_info: The law defines "forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes" as members or community of Scheduled Tribes who primarily reside in and who depend on the forest or forest land for bonafide livelihoods." These  include pastoralists and communities. The ownership right is limited to "forest land"---defined as any forest area and includes unclassified forest, undemarcated forests, existing or deemed forest, protected forests, reserved forests, Sanctuaries and National Parks. Also, traditional forest dwellers must have primarily resided for at least three generations prior to Dec. 13, 2005 to obtain rights.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The FRA 2006 gives communities land rights which are equivalent level of protection given to private property owners (compensation from expropriation, etc.), but communities have to register their forest rights before receiving this protection.
indicators.additional_info: The FRA 2006 establishes that the Gram Sabha (local government) shall be the authority to initiate the process for the determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights (Sec. 6). So without government approval through the registration process, community forest rights are not protected by law.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Registration is free. The FRA 2006 provides that the Gram Sabha (traditional village institutions) must receive and decide on claims to community forests, and prepare a map delineating the area of each claim.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 6, FRA 2006; Scheduled Tribes and other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Rules 2007
indicators.additional_info: The law establishes a Forest Rights Committee to assist the Gram Sabha in its functions receive claims, prepare the record of claims and evidence including maps, prepare a list of claimants, and physically verify claims by visiting sits.  The Forest Rights Committee must prepare a map. The Rules include an Annexure with a Claim Form where the names, address, and info of each forest rights claimant must be filled in. The rules provide for assistance to the Gram Sabhas and there are no registration costs.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The FRA 2006 and the Land Acquisition Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 both recognize Scheduled Tribe and other traditional forest dwellers as legal persons for the purposes of land ownership. However, they must register to be recognized.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3, FRA 2006; Sec. 3, LARR Act 2013
indicators.additional_info: "Forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes" means the members or community of Scheduled Tribes who primarily reside in and who depend on the forests or forest lands for bona fide livelihood needs and includes the Scheduled Tribe pastoralists communities" (Sec. 3, FRA 2006)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers are the legal authority over registered "forest lands". The law provides forest dwellers with the right to hold, protect, access, dispose of forest produce within the forest land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3, FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: Along with ownership and use rights, Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers also have rights over disputed lands, community tenures of habitat, rights of settlement and conversion of all forest villages, rights to protected and manage community forest rights, and "any other traditional rights customarily enjoyed by the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes or other traditional forest dwellers.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Once registered, the ownership right to forest land may be held in perpetuity. There are no durational limits established in the FRA 2006.
indicators.law_and_provision: FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: There are no explicit time limits established in India's Forest Rights Act 2006. However, the right held in perpetuity is limited to forest lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Depending on the acquisition project, 70-80% of affected families, including Scheduled Castes and traditional forest dwellers, must consent to land acquisitions. The procedures for gathering consent are not clearly established.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 2, LARR Act 2013; Sec. 5, the LARR Act Ordinance 2014

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Included in the bundle of rights granted by the FRA 2006 is the right of forest dwellers to own, collect, use, and dispose of minor forest produce traditional collected in the village. More than merely a use right.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3(c),  Sec. 2(i), FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: "Minor forest produce" is defined as "all non-timber forest produce of plant origin including bamboo, brush wood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu and kendu leaves, medicinal plants and herbs, roots, tubers and the like". It is unclear whether forest produce can be used for commercial purposes, and there is no explicit ownership right to trees located outside of forest lands.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: India's states have exclusive power to regulate water supplies, irrigation canals, water storage, etc., but there is no explicit recognition of community water rights in federal legislation or regulations (e.g. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956). The Supreme Court of India has interpreted the right to water as included as part of the right to life (Art. 21 of the Constitution). Therefore,  all citizens, including communities, of India have a recognized human right to access and use drinking water (though State retains ownership). Since community ownership is limited to forest lands, it can be implied that community rights to water are also limited to waters located on forest lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; Tekaba AO v. Sakumeren AO (2004) 5 SCC 672; Wasim Ahmed Khan v. Govt. of AP, 2002 (5) ALT 526 (D.B.) Schedule 7, Constitution of India; Art. 262, Constitution of India
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court of India held that state is the soveriegn dominant owner of water (Tekaba AO v. Sakumeren AO (2004) 5 SCC 672). However, the Supreme Court also held that the right to life includes the right to safe and sufficient water (Wasim Ahmed Khan v. Govt. of AP, 2002 (5) ALT 526 (D.B.))

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Scheduled Castes and traditional forest dwellers may protect, regenerate or conserve or manage any "community forest resources", which includes resources in protected areas. "Community Forest Resource" is defined broadly.
indicators.additional_info: The FRA 2006 applies to all protected areas. The law defines "community forest resource" as "customary common forest land" within the traditional or customary boundaries...including reserved forests, protected forest and protected areas such as Sanctuaries and National Parks to which the community had traditional access." The law states "forest rights...in critical wildlife habitats of National Parks and Sanctuaries may subsequently be modified or resettled, provided that no forest rights holders shall be resettled or have their rights in any manner affected [where there is no alternative options, resettlement packages may be prepared]"

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers are the legal authority over registered "forest lands". The law provides forest dwellers with the right to hold, protect, access, dispose of forest produce within the forest land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3, FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: Along with ownership and use rights, Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers also have rights over disputed lands, community tenures of habitat, rights of settlement and conversion of all forest villages, rights to protected and manage community forest rights, and "any other traditional rights customarily enjoyed by the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes or other traditional forest dwellers.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Once registered, the ownership right to forest land may be held in perpetuity. There are no durational limits established in the FRA 2006.
indicators.law_and_provision: FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: There are no explicit time limits established in India's Forest Rights Act 2006. However, the right held in perpetuity is limited to forest lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Depending on the acquisition project, 70-80% of affected families, including Scheduled Castes and traditional forest dwellers, must consent to land acquisitions. The procedures for gathering consent are not clearly established.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 2, LARR Act 2013; Sec. 5, the LARR Act Ordinance 2014

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Included in the bundle of rights granted by the FRA 2006 is the right of forest dwellers to own, collect, use, and dispose of minor forest produce traditional collected in the village. More than merely a use right.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3(c),  Sec. 2(i), FRA 2006
indicators.additional_info: "Minor forest produce" is defined as "all non-timber forest produce of plant origin including bamboo, brush wood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu and kendu leaves, medicial plants and herbs, roots, tubers and the like". It is unclear whether forest produce can be used for commercial purposes, and there is no explicit ownership right to trees located outside of forest lands.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: India's states have exclusive power to regulate water supplies, irrigation canals, water storage, etc., but there is no explicit recognition of community water rights in federal legislation or regulations (e.g. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956). The Supreme Court of India has interpreted the right to water as included as part of the right to life (Art. 21 of the Constitution). Therefore,  all citizens, including communities, of India have a recognized human right to access and use drinking water (though State retains ownership). Since community ownership is limited to forest lands, it can be implied that community rights to water are also limited to waters located on forest lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; Tekaba AO v. Sakumeren AO (2004) 5 SCC 672; Wasim Ahmed Khan v. Govt. of AP, 2002 (5) ALT 526 (D.B.) Schedule 7, Constitution of India; Art. 262, Constitution of India
indicators.additional_info: The Supreme Court of India held that state is the soveriegn dominant owner of water (Tekaba AO v. Sakumeren AO (2004) 5 SCC 672). However, the Supreme Court also held that the right to life includes the right to safe and sufficient water (Wasim Ahmed Khan v. Govt. of AP, 2002 (5) ALT 526 (D.B.))

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Scheduled Castes and traditional forest dwellers may protect, regenerate or conserve or manage any "community forest resources", which includes resources in protected areas. "Community Forest Resource" is defined broadly.
indicators.additional_info: The FRA 2006 applies to all protected areas. The law defines "community forest resource" as "customary common forest land" within the traditional or customary boundaries...including reserved forests, protected forest and protected areas such as Sanctuaries and National Parks to which the community had traditional access." The law states "forest rights...in critical wildlife habitats of National Parks and Sanctuaries may subsequently be modified or resettled, provided that no forest rights holders shall be resettled or have their rights in any manner affected [where there is no alternative options, resettlement packages may be prepared]"
