local_communities_entries.framework: Collective farms
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Collectives in Iraq are granted possession rights to agricultural units for purposes of establishing a collective farm. Collectives are also granted compensation in case their land is requisitioned. However, the Agrarian Reform Authority retains broad authority over these lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Agrarian Reform Law (ARL) No. 1178 of 1970; Constitution of Iraq
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of the ARL provides for the collective distribution of agricultural units. Article 16 provides that ""agrarian reform lands shall be distributed to peasants collectively or individually in accordance with conditions provided in the area when such distribution takes place and within the limits specified"".

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Agrarian Reform Authority has broad discretion to determine the limits of the agricultural land can requisition any excess of such limits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Articles 6, 8 and 9 of The Agrarian Reform Law (ARL) No. 1178 of 1970
indicators.additional_info: Article 6 of the ARL provides "the Agrarian Reform authority shall requisition any excess of the limits specified in Article (2) leave to the land owner the plats vital thereon until the end of requisitioning takes place. However, the owner whose land has bee requisitioned is entitled to reimbursement for the value of trees and installations, pumps and agricultural machinery. Article 9(2) provides that "the owner of the land requisitioned...shall be compensated by an area of equivalent value of the Agrarian Reform....(3) If no such equivalent land were available in the same area, the land owner may claim compensation in another area or cash reimbursement...."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law establishes a process for registering collective farmland, but it is unclear whether the process is accessible and affordable for collectives.
indicators.law_and_provision: Articles 11-13, ARL, 1970
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 provides that "anyone who claims the right of any Miri land and such disposal has been proved as per the domestic agricultural dealing during the five years preceding the implementation of this law, shall be entitled to the registration of the area under his disposal to the maximum of 300 donums of naturally-irrigated land and 150 donums of land cultivated...." Article 12 provides that Agrarian Reform Authority is charged with conducting surveys of the land to determine "1. Definition of land classes and property. 2. Specification of kind and absolute rights related thereto and cultivation rights in orchards. Specification of land demarcation, areas and locations of the rights...Demarcation of the areas allotted for public utility..." Article 3 provides "the land shall be subject to pure possession if registered in the manner provided here above in the land registration records."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law recognizes the legal personality of farming collectives, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 40, ARL
indicators.additional_info: Article 40 provides "the cooperative society and collective...shall have a juristic personality and the right of ownership of moveable and immovable property, and a right to concluding contracts, disputes and all that might lead to fostering their interests."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Collectives have legal authority, but for the specific purpose of carrying out agricultural activities. The Agrarian Reform Authority retains broad legal authority over collective farms. But collective farms can make contracts, settle disputes on collective farmland.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 38, 40, ARL
indicators.additional_info: Article 38 provides that "collective farms shall be established by those who participate their about...with a view of exploiting their resources on the basis of collective ownership of means of production and collective work, for the coordination of their mutual interest and efforts, and the distribution of income"

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 2 recognizes that the ""area of agricultural land possessed by a person Tapu authorized or granted under long lease."" The use of the term long lease that these rights are not granted for an unlimited duration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 2, ARL

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The ARL does not explicitly grant collective farms the right to give consent prior to acquisition of their land by governments or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: ARL

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law indicates that collectives may be granted the right to use trees within the land area authorized and granted as a collective farm.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 2(11), ARL
indicators.additional_info: The law also grants rights to "tenants" which are defined as "person[s] with whom the owner of the land agrees on reclaiming and planting trees in a specific area for a specific period and under specific terms" (Art(1), ARL).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Agrarian Reform Law No. 117 suggests that collective farms have a right to use water located on their properties  for agricultural purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agrarian Reform Law No. 117 of 1970; Ministry of Water Resources Law No. 50 of 2008
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of the ARL provides for the collective distribution of agricultural units. Article 16 provides that ""agrarian reform lands shall be distributed to peasants collectively or individually in accordance with conditions provided in the area when such distribution takes place and within the limits specified"".' NOTE: Reviewer could not translate the MInistry of Water Resources Law No. 50 of 2008 (originally written in Arabic).

indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed. The Israel Land Administration [ILA] manages approximately 93% of Israel's land. The remaining 7% of land is either privately owned or under the protection of religious authorities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Basic Law: Israel lands (1960), Israel Lands Law (1960) and Israel Land Administration Law (1960)
indicators.additional_info: The basic law states that all the lands owned by the state of Israel will remain in state ownership, and will not be sold or given to anyone. Use of land in Israel usually means leasing rights from the ILA for a period of 49 or 98 years. Under Israeli law, the ILA cannot lease land to foreign nationals, which includes Palestinian residents of Jerusalem who have identity cards but are not citizens of Israel. In practice, foreigners may be allowed to lease if they show that they would qualify as Jewish under the law of return.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.
indicators.law_and_provision: Basic Law: Israel lands (1960), Israel Lands Law (1960) and Israel Land Administration Law (1960)
indicators.additional_info: In terms of common lands, such as forests, the KKL-JNF (Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael Jewish National Fund) was established in 1901 in order to buy lands in Israel for Jewish settlers. After Israel was established in 1948, ILA started to manage KKL’s lands but KKL continues to develop the land, in terms of leading the quest for a more environmentally-friendly Israel; creating open spaces, forests and recreation areas, all in appreciation for natural and cultural heritage.

indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.
indicators.additional_info: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.
indicators.additional_info: People in Israel own their houses but not the land that the house is built on.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed. Protection of property is a constitutional right in Israel, yet the right to own land is not protected, and the protection of land occupied is narrowly interpreted in a manner that excludes Bedouin populations.
indicators.law_and_provision: Basic law: Human Dignity and Liberty, article 3
indicators.additional_info: While the right to the protection of property is constitutional, but this protection does not explicitly apply to communities.  Furthermore, as described in the articles linked to below, the Bedouin community tried to use a constitutional interpretation to enforce a claim on land they argued was theirs, but the court rejected it.     http://972mag.com/israel-supreme-court-bedouin-have-no-indigenous-rights/107171/    http://cdi.ulb.ac.be/legal-situation-bedouin-israel-analysis-eric-david/

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal land is not recognized in any of the Israeli laws assessed.
indicators.law_and_provision: the Forest Act 1926
indicators.additional_info: Israel has had specific legislation protecting its forests since the British mandate, the Forests Act from 1926, enacted to protect forest, but there is no community forest rights.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Israeli Water Law Act states that all the water resources in Israel are public property, and there is no private or communal ownership in water resources.
indicators.law_and_provision: Israeli Water Law 1959
indicators.additional_info: Traditionally, Israel has suffered from severe water shortages.  Advances in water conservation and desalination technology, however, have made Israel a net-water producer.  This has strengthened Israel’s ability to meet its legal, which states that all Israelis have a right to water access.  The amount and quality of that water is left to Israeli government to decide.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Israel’s laws do not directly uphold community land rights in formally protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Parks, Nature Reserves and Commemoration Sites Law 1998
indicators.additional_info: The Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) was established to meet the goals of the National Parks, Nature Reserves and Commemoration Sites Law and the Law for the Protection of Wild Animals. The INPA’s goals translate into obligations to protect nature and heritage sites and care for them for the benefit of the public, and to educate the public. The INPA is a government authority held in trust for the public. Its assets, nature reserves and national parks belong to everyone, and the INPA views them as a trust to be protected for the generations to come.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: National-level statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize the land rights of indigenous or local communities. However, collective property rights of rural communities in Northern Italy are recognized by state-level laws in Trentino.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Italy; Act No. 991 on mountain areas; : Provincial Act No. 9 laying down provisions on land reclamation and preservation of farms, and amending certain provincial acts on agriculture, 2007 (Trentino-Alto Adige state-level law); Provincial Act No. 6 laying down new provisions for the management of public lands, 2005 (Trention-Alto Adige state-level law).
indicators.additional_info: State-level legislation applicable to the state of Trentino in Northern Italy recognizes the collective property rights of THE MAGNIFICA COMUNITÀ DI FIEMME. However, since this is a state-level law and LandMark's analyses are limited to national level legislation, this Italian state-level is outside the scope of this study.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Act No. 36 on Water Resources, 1994 recognizes that all citizens of Italy have a right to use water for drinking and human consumption. Therefore, presumably communities, as citizens, are also granted use rights to water in Italy. However, since community land rights are only recognized at the state-level in Trentino, but it is unclear whether collective property rights to water are recognized in other parts of Italy.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act No. 36 on Water Resources, 1994 (Galli); Decree-Law No. 2008 on urgent measures concerning water resources and environmental protection; Constitution of Italy; Act No. 991 on mountain areas; : Provincial Act No. 9 laying down provisions on land reclamation and preservation of farms, and amending certain provincial acts on agriculture, 2007 (Trentino-Alto Adige state-level law); Provincial Act No. 6 laying down new provisions for the management of public lands, 2005 (Trention-Alto Adige state-level law).

VI , Decision, 18 April 2003 n. 2085,
para.4.3, at 3 ). State-level legislation applicable to the state of Trentino in Northern Italy recognizes the collective property rights of THE MAGNIFICA COMUNITÀ DI FIEMME. local_communities_entries.source: Harvard Law and International Development Society (LIDS)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Jamaica's statutory and regulatory frameworks do not recognize the land rights of the Maroons and has not accepted or rejected the treaty between the Maroons and Great Britain
indicators.law_and_provision:
Werner Zips, Law in Competition: Traditional Maroon Authorities within Legal Pluralism in Jamaica, 28 J. OF LEGAL PLURALISM AND UNOFFICIAL L., 279, 279–305 (1996), http://commission-on-legal-pluralism.com/volumes/37-38/zips-art.pdf.
Bilby, Kenneth, Maroon Autonomy in Jamaica, 25.4 CULTURAL SURVIVAL QUARTERLY (2001), https://www.culturalsurvival.org/publications/cultural-survival-quarterly/jamaica/maroon-autonomy-jamaica.
Articles of Pacification with the Maroons of Trelawney Town, Concluded March the first, 1738,   http://cyber.law.harvard.edu/eon/marroon/treaty.html. 
Jean Besson, Folk Law and Legal Pluralism in Jamaica, 31 J. OF LEGAL PLURALISM AND UNOFFICIAL L., 31, 31–56 (1999), http://commission-on-legal-pluralism.com/volumes/43/besson-art.pdf.
indicators.additional_info: The Maroons received communal ownership over their lands in 1738 through a treaty with the British. Once Jamaica gained independence, it did not address the treaty and has allowed the Maroons to keep their lands, but with seeming disapproval. No laws have been enacted that address Maroon lands.

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous and non-indigenous communities
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not adequately recognize or protect indigenous or community land rights in Jordan.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Jordan; Law No. 17 of 1974 on the management of public land; Rangeland Law, 1971
indicators.additional_info: Under the 1971 Rangeland Land Law, the government claims all uncultivated land as belonging to the State. All land receiving less than 200mm of precipitation per year, unless privately owned, is designated for communal pastoral use. The 2002 provisional agricultural law establishes that rangelands are lands registered in the name of the Kingdom's treasury or any other State lands in which the annual rainfall is less than 200 mm, except for: a. Lands permanently irrigated and agricultural projects and housing lands established before the cominto into force of this law. b. Lands exploited for public benefit purposes or allocated to serve the State and its institutions' interests prior to the coming into force of this law, or the lands that the Council of Ministers decided to allocate for this purpose after the implementation of this law's provisions." According to a secondary source, "the pastoral communities continue informal to claim common tribal rights and enjoy free access  and use of natural resources in their rangelands. However, these community claims are only recognized in settled areas. In al the unsettled areas, the State asserts ownership regardless of customary tribal claims. State claims over grazing land changed the traditional welfare system, caused the breakdown of resource allocation mechanisms, and transformed secured access rights into secured-tenured rights. Consequently, customary management rules are often no longer being enforced." See Hadda, F. Rangeland Resource Governance- Jordan. IUCN. Available at: http://cmsdata.iucn.org/downloads/chapter_3.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation only provides for government and private ownership rights. The laws are silent on community land rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 26, Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan; Art. 3, Land Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, 2003; Law on State-owned Property 2011
indicators.additional_info: Article 3 of the Land Code provides that "land in the Republic of Kazakhstan is in the public domain. Plots can also be privately owned..." Article 23 of the Land Code states "plots of land under public ownership can be granted to private ownership to citizens and non-state entities..." Article 23 states that agricultural land may be transferred to individuals/legal entities as ownership rights of private property. NOTE:  Land that is granted to municipalities is sometimes managed by community pastures in practice, but community pastures are not granted explicit legal rights to land.

However, since communities do not have recognized rights to land in Kazakhstan, communal rights to water may be limited and subject to government discretion.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, 2003; Art. 26, Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan;  Land Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, 2003; Law on State-Owned Property, 2011
indicators.additional_info:
Article 4 of the Water Code provides that waters in the Republic of Kazakhstan are the exclusive property of State. However, all citizens are granted the right to use water bodies under Article 22 of the Water Code. Article 22 states "the right to use water bodies
1. The right to use water bodies is available to individuals and legal entities by local executive bodies in coordination with the authorized body in the sphere of use and protection of water resources. 2. Natural and legal persons water bodies are provided on the right: 1) short-term use; 2) long-term use.
3. The right to short-term use is provided for up to five years, the right to long-term use is provided for a period of five to forty-nine years. 4) Natural and legal persons, which provided water bodies in use, can not dispose of the right to use a water body." (Unofficial translation of law originally written in Russia). Article 5 of the Water Code defines "water bodies" as  the concentration of water in the reliefs of the land surface and the depths of the earth, with the boundaries, scope and
water regime. They are: the sea, rivers, canals equivalents, lakes, glaciers and other surface water bodies, of the subsoil, containing groundwater."

KEN.name: Kenya

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Constitution 2010 provides for community land as one of three landholding classes (public, community private) with equal legal force & effect of rights they deliver (Land Act 2012 s. 5). Community Land Act 2016 provides procedures for customary sector with Regs. 2017.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010, Art. 61-63. Land Act, 2012, s. 5. Community Land Act, 2016, s. 5(3). Regulations 2017.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution stipulates that 'all land belongs to the nation, communities or individuals and classified land as public, community or private land' (Art. 61), thereby providing amply for collective & customary rights. Community land mainly comprises land presently vested in county councils in trust for communities (Art. 63 (d) (iii) and registered group ranches (Art. 63 (2) (a)). Together these cover > 50% of country area, mainly pastoral arid/semi-arid lands.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: In law community-based and private statutory based rights to land are equivalent in recognition and protection (Land Act 2012 s. 5). Also equitable protection at compulsory acquisition whether customary lands are titled or not. (Community Land Act 2016 s. 5(3)). Land Values (Amendment) Act 2019 reemphasizes this at s. 107A.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Act, 2016 CLA sec. 5 (3). Land Value (Amendment) Act, 2019 sec. 107A (12)).
indicators.additional_info: Land Value Amendment Act 2019: 'land lawfully held, managed or used by individuals or families as ancestral land and land traditionally occupied by individuals, families or entities pending adjudication must receive prompt payment in full at compulsory acquisition' s. 107A (12).  While registration of community domains is not compulsory, anxiously sought to double-lock protection esp against tendency of State to claim especially remoter lands as public land.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Procedures for adjudication, survey & titling of community lands straightforward & low-cost. Required structure is strong: Community Assembly (CA) of all adults as ultimate decision maker, elected Land Committee (CLC) to administer on community's behalf. Many shortfalls on details, incl. inadequate no. of CA meetings required, too low quorums, poor model by-laws in Regs 2017.
indicators.law_and_provision: Procedure for titling is a main function of the Community Land Act 2016 & Regulations 2017.
indicators.additional_info: A main constitutional and legal objective is formalization of community lands in registered entitlements to end unreliable trustee tenure over half the country (Constitution 2010 & Community Land Act 2016), but slow, unfunded by government, with only 60 community lands registered by Mar 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Legal duty to vest community domain in all members of community in undivided shares (ie held to be a legal person). Members Register to be updated annually. Confirmation at registration that community is a body corporate with perpetual succession, etc.  Members hold transferable, inheritable rights of exclusive occupancy & user to house, farm, business plots etc. may be issued Certificates.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010, Arts. 61 (1), 63 (1). Community Land Act, 2016 sec. 10 (1). Community Land Regulations 2017. Regulation 8.
indicators.additional_info: Recognition of the community as a legal person is a notable achievement of Kenya's Community Land Act 2016  and has been adopted by some new land laws since eg. South Sudan, Liberia, Timor Leste.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community Land Act 2016 s.15 requires the Community Assembly to elect a Community Land Management Committee (CLMC) to administer property on members' behalf. Community Land Regs 2017 stipulate duties, term etc. term, CLMC required to draft Community Land By Laws for Community Assembly approval on all subjects it wishes rules, without which registration of community property cannot proceed.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Act, 2016, section 5. Community Land Regulations  2017, Regulation 4. Regulation 8
indicators.additional_info: Constitution, Land Act & Land Registration Act presume that community as landowner has all the rights of proprietorship, elaborated in the CLA 2016 including zoning the land into farming, settlement, grazing, conservation, and for other purposes (sec 29(1)).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary community land, and derivative rights to individual/family parcels within community property are owned in perpetuity (Community Land Act, 2016 s. 16-17). Also up to community if it seeks registration in freehold, leasehold or customary tenure s. 4 (3).
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Act, 2016
indicators.additional_info: Legal presumption that founding communal customary rights are owned in perpetuity in concordance with existence of community, and law protects customary tenure as a lawful tenure system with non-discrimination in owner and access to land under all tenure systems (Land Act, 2012, s. 5). Delivered fully in the Community Land Act, 2016. Note that a community might seek a leasehold only where the land is definitively public or private land, and transfer required.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution (Art 40) & therefore Land Act 2012 do not require consent at compulsory acquisition. The Fair Administration Act 2015 obliges  government to solicit and consider all views from anyone affected by its action, decision or proposal (s. 5). A Public Participation Bill has failed to reach enactment, largely because of its requirement for consent.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2010, Arts 40, 47.  Land Act, 2012, s. 107-133. Fair Administration Act, 2015. s. 4-5.
indicators.additional_info: No consent to land takings forpublic purposes required. Comunities in Kenya do not enjoy a progressive compulsory acquisition regime, failed first by the Constitution 2010 in not requiring compensation paid prior to eviction (Art. 40 (3b)), too broad definition of public purpose in Land Act 2012 s. 110, 124 (1) (b). Additionally compensation is solely related to the value of the land (and 'in the opinion of the Commission' (Land Act, 2012, s. 113 (2) (a) (ii)). Redeeming factor is that occupants in good faith who may not hold formal title are due compensation (Constitution, Art. 40 (4))  and Land Value (Amendment) Act, 2019, sec. 107A. The  Fair Administration Act, 2015 requires full disclosure and taking views into account.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Ownership of trees is not specified, with presumption that trees are attached to the land and owned accordingly, including communities. CLA  2016, s.16 on Nature of Title. Also obligation of community to protect all natural resources on its land (s. 35).
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Act, 2016. secs 16 & 35
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Conservation and Management Act, 2016 distinguishes between forest cover on public, private and community lands. Sec. 30 (3) lists Community Forests. Sec. 32 (1) states that "All community forests shall be vested in the community…".

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All waters are owned by the nation collectively, vested in the State as trustee. Only domestic abstraction, use, and storage of water is not subject to permit, if within the boundaries of a private or community land  (Water Act, 2016. s.37).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act, 2016. S. 5 on ownership and 37 on exemptions from permits.
indicators.additional_info: Water associations may be formed for collectively used waters beyond owned lands. Definition of landholder amended to include 'any person who by any established right, custom or estate is entitled to be the holder or possessor of land' and 'any person holding or occupying land in accordance with law on promise of title' (s. 2) bringing water law in line with Constitutional provision for customary rights as property. Also note that Constitution makes access to clean and safe water a right.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A community cannot own a State Protected Area but may use under contract. All five forest peoples have submitted restitution claims for Forest Reserves under duty of State to consider remedies for historical land injustices. The CLA requires communities to protect resources. The forest & wildlife laws encourage communities to declare Community Forests & Wildlife Conservancies.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Act (CLA), 2016 s. 35-37. Forest Conservation and Management Act 2016, s. 31(3), 32 (1). Wildlife Conservation and Management Act, 2013, s. 4 (d) & 70, 39-40.
indicators.additional_info: Community Conservancies established since 2013 on community lands but not Community Forests since 2016 forest law. Kenya Forest Service also failing to adhere to constitutional directive that lands traditional occupied by hunter gatherers is community property Art 63 (2) (d) (ii). Matter contested in domestic courts and before the African Court for Human and Peoples Rights in case of Mau Ogiek IP & which ordered restitution as community land in 2022. No implementation with next hearing at ACHPR in June 2025.

(Community Land Act, 2016 CLA sec. 5 (3). Land Value (Amendment) Act, 2019 sec. 107A (12)).)
KEN.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — Procedures for adjudication, survey & titling of community lands straightforward & low-cost. Required structure is strong: Community Assembly (CA) of all adults as ultimate decision maker, elected Land Committee (CLC) to administer on community's behalf. Many shortfalls on details, incl. inadequate no. of CA meetings required, too low quorums, poor model by-laws in Regs 2017.  (Procedure for titling is a main function of the Community Land Act 2016 & Regulations 2017. )
KEN.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Legal duty to vest community domain in all members of community in undivided shares (ie held to be a legal person). Members Register to be updated annually. Confirmation at registration that community is a body corporate with perpetual succession, etc.  Members hold transferable, inheritable rights of exclusive occupancy & user to house, farm, business plots etc. may be issued Certificates. (Constitution, 2010, Arts. 61 (1), 63 (1). Community Land Act, 2016 sec. 10 (1). Community Land Regulations 2017. Regulation 8.)
KEN.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Community Land Act 2016 s.15 requires the Community Assembly to elect a Community Land Management Committee (CLMC) to administer property on members' behalf. Community Land Regs 2017 stipulate duties, term etc. term, CLMC required to draft Community Land By Laws for Community Assembly approval on all subjects it wishes rules, without which registration of community property cannot proceed. (Community Land Act, 2016, section 5. Community Land Regulations  2017, Regulation 4. Regulation 8 )
KEN.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Customary community land, and derivative rights to individual/family parcels within community property are owned in perpetuity (Community Land Act, 2016 s. 16-17). Also up to community if it seeks registration in freehold, leasehold or customary tenure s. 4 (3).  (Community Land Act, 2016)
KEN.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: Partial, limited progress — The Constitution (Art 40) & therefore Land Act 2012 do not require consent at compulsory acquisition. The Fair Administration Act 2015 obliges  government to solicit and consider all views from anyone affected by its action, decision or proposal (s. 5). A Public Participation Bill has failed to reach enactment, largely because of its requirement for consent.  (Constitution, 2010, Arts 40, 47.  Land Act, 2012, s. 107-133. Fair Administration Act, 2015. s. 4-5.)
KEN.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Ownership of trees is not specified, with presumption that trees are attached to the land and owned accordingly, including communities. CLA  2016, s.16 on Nature of Title. Also obligation of community to protect all natural resources on its land (s. 35).  (Community Land Act, 2016. secs 16 & 35)
KEN.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — All waters are owned by the nation collectively, vested in the State as trustee. Only domestic abstraction, use, and storage of water is not subject to permit, if within the boundaries of a private or community land  (Water Act, 2016. s.37).   (Water Act, 2016. S. 5 on ownership and 37 on exemptions from permits.)
KEN.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, limited progress — A community cannot own a State Protected Area but may use under contract. All five forest peoples have submitted restitution claims for Forest Reserves under duty of State to consider remedies for historical land injustices. The CLA requires communities to protect resources. The forest & wildlife laws encourage communities to declare Community Forests & Wildlife Conservancies. (Community Land Act (CLA), 2016 s. 35-37. Forest Conservation and Management Act 2016, s. 31(3), 32 (1). Wildlife Conservation and Management Act, 2013, s. 4 (d) & 70, 39-40.)

local_communities_entries.framework: Pasture User Unions
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Local communities are granted the right to form Pasture User Unions, but communities are only granted use rights to pasture; pastures are owned by the state. Pasture User Unions represent the interests of livestock owners and pasture users.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Article 12(5) of the Constitution provides "The land, its resources, airspace, waters, forests, flora and fauna, as well as other natural resources shall be the exclusive property of the Kyrgyz Republic; these shall be used for the purpose of preserving a unified environmental system as the basis of life and activity of the people of Kyrgyzstan and shall enjoy special protection from the State. Land may also be in private, municipal and other forms of ownership except for pastures which may not be in private property." Article 5 of the Law on Pasture Users Unions states "Local community in the area of a local self-government shall form a Pasture Users Union, which represents the interests of the livestock owners and other pasture users of pastures of this territorial unit with regard to pasture use and improvement. Pasture Users Unions may be established as bodies of territorial public self-government and shall be subject to state registration as legal entities with judicial authorities. All members of Pasture Users Union have the first right to use pastures assigned to their local self-government area within the provisions of the Community Pasture Management and Use Plan." Pasture is defined in Article 2 as a "type of agricultural land, covered with vegetation, used as pasturage for livestock grazing and other purposes, as reflected in the land registry data."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Pasture User Unions are granted the right to represent the interests of pasture users; however, the state retains underlying ownership and Article 4 of the Law on Pastures grants local self-government broad power to control and manage pastures.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Article 4 states "1. Local self-government bodies shall be assigned responsibility and control for management of state pasture resources except for the right of disposal. 2. Local self-government body shall have the right to delegate the pasture management and use authority to Pasture Users Union. 3. Representative local self-government body shall approve community pasture management plan on an annual basis. 4. Government bodies and local state administrations shall not be allowed to interfere in pasture use activities of local self-government bodies and Pasture Users Unions, unless otherwise specified by the legislation of the Kyrgyz Republic."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The registration process for creating Pasture User Unions is compulsory, and the law does not establish assistance mechanisms to ensure registration is affordable and accessible.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Article 16. State Registration of the Right to Pasture Use provides " 1. The right to use pastures of local self-government bodies within the boundaries determined by the Government of the Kyrgyz Republic shall be subject to mandatory state registration of real property rights in accordance with the established procedure.... Article 7 states Community Pasture Management and Use Plan provides "1.The Community Pasture Management and Use Plans contain all the essential information needed to ensure that the pastures are used in a sustainable manner and that all users are aware of their rights and responsibilities. 2.The Community Pasture Management and Use Plans contain the following components: - maps that indicate external and major internal boundaries, excluded and protected areas, stock routes, watering places and other significant objects of pasture infrastructure, pasture conditions and quality of all pasture areas; - carrying capacity;- plans on development and reconstruction of objects of pasture infrastructure;- medium-term pasture management and use, improvement and rehabilitation plan for the term of up to 5 years;- annually updated Pasture Management and Use Plan; - plans of pasture management and use for other purposes. 3. The Community Pasture Management and Use Plan becomes binding on all pasture users upon approval by a representative local self-government body. "

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Law on Pastures grants Pasture User Unions legal personality but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The state retains ownership over pastures. Communities are only given the right to use pastures assigned to their local self-government area within the provisions of the Community Pasture Management and Use Plan developed by the local governments.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009
indicators.additional_info: Article 5 of the Law on Pastures provides that ""all members of Pasture Users Union have the first right to use pastures assigned to their local self-government area within the provisions of the Community Pasture Management and Use Plan"".

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Article 2 provides "Community Pasture Management and Use Plan (CPMUP) - a plan, covering a period of 5 years, for management and use of state-owned pastures." Therefore, use rights to pastures may not be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly provide local community members of Pasture User Unions the right to give consent prior to acquisition by governments and outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly provide communities the right to trees.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment:
The law does not recognize communities or indigenous peoples as owners of water
but does grant Pasture User Unions the right to use water for agricultural/pasture purposes. Article 4 of the Water Code, 2005 provides that all citizens have a right to use water. Presumably, Pasture User Unions, as citizens of Kyrgyzstan, are granted the right to use water.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, 2005; Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures, No. 30, 2009
indicators.additional_info:
Article 4 of the Water Code establishes that "1. The water resources of the Kyrgyz Republic are the exclusive and inalienable property of the State. Every person has the right to use water within the national borders in accordance with the provisions of this Code. 
2. The lands of the water fund occupied by water bodies and state owned water economy constructions and irrigation systems are the exclusive property of the State." Article 21 of the Water Code provides that "2. For the purposes of this Code the use of water resources includes: abstraction of water from a surface water body or an underground water body; conveyance of abstracted water for supply to another person;  use of water for drinking and domestic purposes; use of water for watering household plots; use of water for irrigation and livestock watering; use of sewage and waste water for irrigation; use of water for hydropower generation; use of water for industrial and agro-industrial purposes; use of water for fishing and fish farming; use of water for sport and recreational purposes; impoundment or storage of water bellow a dam or other water economy construction; diversion, restriction or alteration of the flow of water within a water body; alteration of the bed, poima, banks, course or characteristics of a water body, including the abstraction of gravel and other materials from such water bodies; the use of water for irrigation (washing) of salinity lands." Article 5 of the Law on Pasture Users Unions states "Local community in the area of a local self-government shall form a Pasture Users Union, which represents the interests of the livestock owners and other pasture users of pastures of this territorial unit with regard to pasture use and improvement. Pasture Users Unions may be established as bodies of territorial public self-government and shall be subject to state registration as legal entities with judicial authorities.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly provide communities the rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision:
Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic; Kyrgyz Republic. Law on Pastures
No. 30, 2009

KHM.name: Cambodia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities (indigenous and non-indigenous)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Ownership of indigenous community lands are granted by the State to indigenous communities as collective ownership. Collective ownership right limited to cultivated/shifting cultiv. lands, burial land, spiritual forest land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 25-26, Land Law 2001; 2009 Sub-Decree on Procedures of Registration of Land of Indigenous Communities
indicators.additional_info: The Land Law recognizes collective ownership of both indigenous and non-indigenous communities (Art. 10, Ch. 3 Land Law 2001). The law also provides indigenous community ownership rights to areas necessary for shifting cultivation (Art. 25, Land Law 2001).  However, indigenous communities must first register to obtain legal recognition. However, the State has historically granted large-scale concessions of indigenous community lands by justifying its actions based on Art. 12 of the Land Law 2001 and Art. 58 of the Cambodian Constitution, which establish the State as the proprietary owner of land within the territories of Cambodia.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law provides collective ownership and includes all of the rights and protections of owners as are enjoyed by private owners. However, communities with collective ownership rights do not have the right to dispose of any collective ownership that is State public property to any person or group.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 16, 25-26, Land Law 2001; 2009 Sub-Decree on Procedures of Registration of Land of Indigenous Communities; Art. 5, Expropriation Law
indicators.additional_info: The Land Law also grants authorization to communities to occupy and use State property (Art. 16, 2001 Land Law). The State can also expropriate all land for public physical infrastructure purposes and national interests (Expropriation Law).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: There are clear procedures for indigenous communities to register, receive formal entitlement, and collective title certificates (and a detailed map) of their community land rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8- 12, Sub-Decree on Procedures of registration of Land of Indigenous Communities
indicators.additional_info: There are no provisions within the Procedures on Registration which establish mechanisms to assist indigenous populations in registering their community land rights, and the Procedures do not ensure that the registration process will be affordable for indigenous populations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law establishes the ""community as a legal entity"" and defines this legal entity as indigenous communities that have assembled and were officially registered at the Ministry of Interior. So first indigenous community must register.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4, Sub-Decree on Procedures of Registration of Land of Indigenous Communities

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law provides that the exercise of all ownership rights of the community shall be subject to the responsibility of the traditional authorities and mechanisms for decision-making of the community, according to their customs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 26, Land Law 2001

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law does not establish a durational limit on the ownership rights of the indigenous community.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law 2001

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: When the acquiring land, the government "Expropriation Committee" must arrange a public consultation with communities affected  by expropriation. However, the law does not require consent from communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 16, Cambodia Expropriation Law
indicators.additional_info: While consultation is a legal requirement to compulsory acquisition, the law does not require indigenous community consent in a full inclusive and transparent manner.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Traditional users rights are granted to local communities for forest products. These rights include dead wood, timber to build homes, and trees for domestic purposes. However, the law does not include all forest lands within community titled lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 40, Law on Forestry; 2009 Sub-Decree on Procedures of Registration of Land of Indigenous Communities
indicators.additional_info: Local communities cannot harvest or cut down natural trees for commercial purposes without a permit. Based on limitations established in Article 6 of the 2009 Implementing Regulation, few forest areas are eligible for formal designation as community land.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Law on Water Resources Management provides that all water resources in Cambodia are owned by the state (art. 3). The law only grants landowners use rights to water for drinking, washing, bathing, and other domestic purposes (art. 11). The law also provides landowners and occupiers rights to collect and use rainwater and water flowing through their properties. Indigenous community landowners can exercise these rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Cambodia; Law on Water Resources Management of the Kingdom of Cambodia, 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 27 of the Law on Water Resources Management provides "The owner or occupier of upstream land is entitled to collect and use rain-water and the water flowing over his/his property [for domestic purposes] in such a manner that it will not affect the legitimate interest of the downstream users.  The owner or occupier of downstream land is entitled to collect and use rainwater and the water flowing over his/his property from the upstream, but he/she shall not hinder the natural flow of the water by constructing road, large or small dykes or other structures for storing water, unless there is appropriate authorization." Article 28 states "The owners or occupiers of agricultural land shall allow the water flowing over his/her land naturally to neighboring owners or occupiers land to meet their irrigation and other needs." Since the Land Law, 2001 also recognizes ownership rights of indigenous communities, these provisions in the Law on Water Resources Management apply to indigenous landowners. In other words, indigenous landowners have a right to use and collect water for domestic purposes, but must obtain government authorization to use water for commercial purposes.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The State recognizes secure access "within and adjacent to" protected areas for traditional uses, customs, etc. of indigenous communities, but the local communities may not claim title over land in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 22, Art. 26 Law on Protected Areas

local_communities_entries.framework: Non-indigenous communities
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Law (2002) recognizes the traditional user rights of local communities living within Permanent Forest Reserves. Communities can also establish Community Forest Agreements under Article 44 of the Law on Forestry.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
indicators.additional_info: Article 40 of the Forestry Law states "For local communities living within or near the Permanent Forest Reserves, the state shall recognize and ensure their traditional user rights for the purpose of traditional customs, beliefs, religions and living as defined in this article. The traditional user rights of a local community for forest products & by-products shall not require the permit. The traditional user rights under this article consist of: 1- The collection of dead wood, picking wild fruit, collecting bees' honeys, taking resin, and collecting other forest by-products; 2- Using timbers to build houses, stables for animals, fences and to make agricultural instruments; 3- Grass cutting or unleashing livestock to graze within the forests; 4- Using other forest products & by-products consistent with traditional family use; 5- The right to barter or sell forest by-products shall not require the permit, if those activities do not cause significant threat to the sustainability of the forest. The customers or any third party who has collected forest by products from local communities with the purposes of trade, in a manner consistent with the provisions of this law, shall have the permit for forest by-products transportation after royalty and premium payments. A local community can not transfer any of these traditional user rights to a third party, even with mutual agreement or under contract. These traditional user rights shall be: 1- Consistent with the natural balance and sustainability of forest resources and respect the rights of other people; 2- Consistent with permissions and prohibitions under the provisions of this law." Article 45 states "Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries shall recognize the religious forest of local communities, living within or near the forest, as Protection Forest serving religious, cultural or conservation purposes. It is prohibited to harvest any spirit trees, thus they may be specially marked and shall be identified in a Community Forest Management Plan."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Local communities are granted tradional user rights under Community Forest Agreements. However, these rights are not as protected as other tenure regimes e.g. freehold tenure.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 41 of the Forestry Law, the Ministry of Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries has authority to allocate part of the Permanent Forest Reserve to communities, and presumably the Minister has discretion to expropriation, extinguish or otherwise restrict rights to Permanent Forest Reserves. The aw defines "Forestry Community" as a "voluntary community that assembles under a Community Forest Agreement for implementing the sustainable use and development of forest resources conforming to the provisions of this law."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Local communities can obtain rights under a Community Forest Agreement for the purpose of implementing sustainable use and development of forest resources. However, there is no clear process for formalizing, demarcating, and otherwise registering community forests. There are also no provisions in the Forestry Law ensuring that communities are able to easily access and afford registration procedures.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
indicators.additional_info: Article 41 merely states "The Minister of Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries has the authority to allocate any part of the Permanent Forest Reserve to a community living inside or near a forest area in the form of a Community Forest." However, there are no provisions establishing a clear registration process relating to Community Forest Agreements."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Local communities are granted legal personality under the Forestry Law, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communites must follow a Community Forest Management Plan. The Forestry Adminstration has broad authority to determine details of the plan and to monitor community activities. Communities are not allowed to alienate, sell, form a concession or otherwise transfer its rights to third parties (Art. 44, Forestry Law).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 43 of the Forestry Law "A Community Forest shall be managed in the economic and sustainable manner by the local community conforming to the Community Forest Management Plan, rules on Community Forestry and guidelines on Community Forestry. The Forestry Administration shall monitor the implementation of the Management Plan and provide technical assistance, where appropriate, upon the request of the local community. The management plan of the Community Forest shall be prepared by the local community and subject to approval by the Cantonment level of the Forestry Administration. This plan shall be sent to the Central level of the Forestry Administration and be reviewed every five (5) years or earlier if needed. Planted or natural forest established as a Community Forest by a local community shall be consistent with a Community Forest Management Plan and subject to the technical supervision and assistance of the Forestry Administration. The rules for establishment, management and use of a Community Forest shall be determined by the Anu-kret on Community Forestry Management. The guidelines on Community Forestry shall be determined by Prakas of Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Forestry establishes durational limits on Community Forestry Agreements. Article 42 of the Forestry Law states that Community Forest Agreements have a validity not to exceed 15 years. However, such agreements may be extended based on monitoring and evaluation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities the right to give consent in an an inclusive manner prior to acquisition by the government or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law grants communities traditional user rights to forest by-products under Article 40 (Forestry Law).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
indicators.additional_info: Article 40 states "the traditional user rights of a local community for forest products & by-products shall not require the permit. The traditional user rights under this article consist of: 1- The collection of dead wood, picking wild fruit, collecting bees' honeys, taking resin, and collecting other forest by-products; 2- Using timbers to build houses, stables for animals, fences and to make agricultural instruments; 3- Grass cutting or unleashing livestock to graze within the forests; 4- Using other forest products & by-products consistent with traditional family use; 5- The right to barter or sell forest by-products shall not require the permit, if those activities do not cause significant threat to the sustainability of the forest. The customers or any third party who has collected forest by-products from local communities with the purposes of trade, in a manner consistent with the provisions of this law, shall have the permit for forest by-products transportation after royalty and premium payments." Article 44 states " A local community, operating under a Community Forest Agreement, shall have the rights to harvest forest products & by-products within the demarcated forest area stated in the Community Forest Agreement and consistent with the Community Forest Management Plan. A local community can not use the Community Forest in the form of a concession, nor sell, barter or transfer its rights in such forest to a third party."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Law on Water Resources Management provides that all water resources in Cambodia are owned by the state (art. 3). The law only grants landowners use rights to water for drinking, washing, bathing, and other domestic purposes (art. 11). The law also provides landowners and occupiers rights to collect and use rainwater and water flowing through their properties. Indigenous community landowners can exercise these rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Cambodia; Law on Water Resources Management of the Kingdom of Cambodia, 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 27 of the Law on Water Resources Management provides "The owner or occupier of upstream land is entitled to collect and use rain-water and the water flowing over his/his property [for domestic purposes] in such a manner that it will not affect the legitimate interest of the downstream users.  The owner or occupier of downstream land is entitled to collect and use rainwater and the water flowing over his/his property from the upstream, but he/she shall not hinder the natural flow of the water by constructing road, large or small dykes or other structures for storing water, unless there is appropriate authorization." Article 28 states "The owners or occupiers of agricultural land shall allow the water flowing over his/her land naturally to neighboring owners or occupiers land to meet their irrigation and other needs." Since the Land Law, 2001 also recognizes ownership rights of indigenous communities, these provisions in the Law on Water Resources Management apply to indigenous landowners. In other words, indigenous landowners have a right to use and collect water for domestic purposes, but must obtain government authorization to use water for commercial purposes.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry, 2003
