LAO.name: Laos

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Land Law 2003 and implementing decrees recognize use rights to collectively and customarily held land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: The law recognizes use rights to all types of customary land so long as it falls within the government's land use allocation plan. Article 3 of MD 88 recognizes "collective land" and defines it as "all land parcels and natural resources which are available within the territory of the Lao PDR for which the state has granted the right to collectively use by villages, organizations and state organizations..." Article 26 of MD 88 defines "customary land utilization rights" as "the protection and utilization of land through the clearance and development or through the state land allocation plan of the concerned land parcel in a regular, continued and long-term manner until the present time without any documents certifying the land use rights for individual, organization or village communal use." Article 26 further provides that "the state recognizes the customary land use rights of individual, organization or village community by issuing the Land Survey Certificate or Land Title or Land Certificate on a case-by-case basis." MD 88 provides the following documents as evidence of land utilization rights: Land Survey Certificate, Land Certificate, Certificate of Land Ownership History, and Land Development Certificate.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Land Law 2003 provides several ways in which collectively held land use rights can be expropriated, re-allocated, or otherwise extinguished by the government. Land use rights are not as protected as ownership rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 of the Land Law 2003 grants the Land Management Authority to withdraw land use rights. Article 62 states that "persons having the right to use land and persons hold land use right will lose such rights in the following cases: (1) they have used the land or have exercised their land use rights not in accordance with the objectives as allocated by the State (2) they have not paid the land tax consecutively for three years after being warned (3) they have not used the land or not exercised their land use rights as allocated by the State in accordance with the contract (4) land use rights are lost pursuant to a court decision." Article 63 provides that land use rights of an individual or organization shall be terminated in the following cases: (1) the land use rights are voluntarily relinquished; the land is requisitioned by the State for public purposes; (3) transfer to another person; (4) Death without any heir." Article 64 also provides that the Land Management Authority can grant leases and concessions to land in Laos, and presumably this includes to land collectively used land. Article 28 of MD 88 provides communities with compensation for losses of land rights due to expropriation and other reasons.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Individuals and organizations may request and be issued land use certificates, land survey certificates or land title for customary land. However the procedures and legal provisions ensuring affordability and accessibility.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 26 of MD 88 provides that "the application for land registration shall consist of the following evidences: Certification of Land Ownership History, witnesses, land use right holder of neighboring land, and the village administrative authority where he land is located." Under Article 15 of MD 88 provides that the "Land Management Authority is charged with carrying out land registration." Under Article 15 of MD 88 the Village Land Unit is charged with providing data relating to the land for the purpose of forming the land file applying for land, and land documents registration. The land file shall be duly certified by "Naiban" (Chief of village) and, thereafter, sent to the Land Management Authority of district/municipality for consideration, management and protection of state land, collective land within the village territory, and for inspecting the land use by individuals and organization within the village territory. " The law does not specify whether community lands must be mapped or otherwise clearly demarcated to prevent the possibility of disputes.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While villages can apply for collective title, village clusters or groups of villages (kumbahn) that self-identify as a collective group or other groups must first form an association under the Association Decree 2009 to apply for collective rights over customary land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Villages are not granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The level of legal authority varies depending on the land's classification and whether the community is granted a land use certificate, land survey certificate, or a land title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: The law generally provides that the holder of land use rights shall have the right to protect land, right to use land, right of usufruct, right to transfer the land use right, and the inheritance rights (Art. 53, Land Law 2003). Article 16 of MD 88 provides that Land Survey Certificates grant organizations, including community organizations, the right to  use the land for various purposes based on the land category specified by law. However, Organizations granted a Land Survey Certificate shall have no right to transfer, lease out, grant concessions, put in share or collateral. Land Certificates grant land use rights to communities for a period of 3 years after which the community holders can apply for land titles. Land titles confer on communities the right to use land as collateral, and share, sell, exchange, lease and give land as inheritance (MD, Art. 16).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land use certificates are granted for three years, indicating that community use rights may not be held in perpetuity. However, communities can also claim land titles which appear to not have a durational limit.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law is silent on whether communities must give consent prior to the acquisition of their land use right by governments and outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Law 2007 provides for customary use to timber and harvest of forest produces for household use, but this use must conform to village regulations
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Law 2007 (Art. 42).
indicators.additional_info: Article 42 of the Forestry Law 2008 provides "Customary utilization of forests is the use of forest and forest products that has been practiced for a long time in accordance with laws and regulations. The State allows the use of timber and harvest of forest products in nonprohibited forests for household utilization without adverse impact on forest resources, and the environment as well as reflecting the rights and interest of individuals or organizations. Customary utilization of forest and forest products shall be practiced in accordance with a designed plan and with village regulations and laws and regulations on forests."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water belongs to people of Laos, and the Government acts on behalf of the people to manage and allocate water use rights. Use and protection rights to wetland areas may be allocated to individuals or organizations. The Water and Water Resources Law, 1996 provides individual use rights to water, which can be exercised by all citizens (thus, as citizens of Laos, communities are also granted a use right). Community use of water for domestic purposes is free and does not require authorization.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water and Water Resources Law, 1996;  Land Law 2003; Constitution of Laos, 1991
indicators.additional_info: The Land Law 2003 and implementing decrees recognize use rights to collectively and customarily held land." Use and protection rights to wetland areas may be granted to individuals or organizations through an application for a land use certificate by the administrative authority of the village to the district administrative authority. Article 4 of the Water and Water Resourcse Law provides that "Water Resources and Water are the property of the people of Lao PDR as a whole. The Government acts on behalf of the people to manage and to evenly and equitably share the uses of the water. Individuals and organisations will have the right to use water for specific purposes only when authorisation is given by the concerned authority, except for use of a minor nature..." Article 13 provides that "water and water resources may be legally used for different purposes such as: family domestic use, irrigation, fishery; agricultural production; livestock; hydropower; industrial production; navigation; sport, recreation; cultural, medicinal, etc.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Land Law 2003 and implementing decrees recognize use rights to collectively and customarily held land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: The law recognizes use rights to all types of customary land so long as it falls within the government's land use allocation plan. Article 3 of MD 88 recognizes "collective land" and defines it as "all land parcels and natural resources which are available within the territory of the Lao PDR for which the state has granted the right to collectively use by villages, organizations and state organizations..." Article 26 of MD 88 defines "customary land utilization rights" as "the protection and utilization of land through the clearance and development or through the state land allocation plan of the concerned land parcel in a regular, continued and long-term manner until the present time without any documents certifying the land use rights for individual, organization or village communal use." Article 26 further provides that "the state recognizes the customary land use rights of individual, organization or village community by issuing the Land Survey Certificate or Land Title or Land Certificate on a case-by-case basis." MD 88 provides the following documents as evidence of land utilization rights: Land Survey Certificate, Land Certificate, Certificate of Land Ownership History, and Land Development Certificate.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Land Law 2003 provides several ways in which collectively held land use rights can be expropriated, re-allocated, or otherwise extinguished by the government. Land use rights are not as protected as ownership rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 of the Land Law 2003 grants the Land Management Authority to withdraw land use rights. Article 62 states that "persons having the right to use land and persons hold land use right will lose such rights in the following cases: (1) they have used the land or have exercised their land use rights not in accordance with the objectives as allocated by the State (2) they have not paid the land tax consecutively for three years after being warned (3) they have not used the land or not exercised their land use rights as allocated by the State in accordance with the contract (4) land use rights are lost pursuant to a court decision." Article 63 provides that land use rights of an individual or organization shall be terminated in the following cases: (1) the land use rights are voluntarily relinquished; the land is requisitioned by the State for public purposes; (3) transfer to another person; (4) Death without any heir." Article 64 also provides that the Land Management Authority can grant leases and concessions to land in Laos, and presumably this includes to land collectively used land. Article 28 of MD 88 provides communities with compensation for losses of land rights due to expropriation and other reasons.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Individuals and organizations may request and be issued land use certificates, land survey certificates or land title for customary land. However the procedures and legal provisions ensuring affordability and accessibility.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Article 26 of MD 88 provides that "the application for land registration shall consist of the following evidences: Certification of Land Ownership History, witnesses, land use right holder of neighboring land, and the village administrative authority where he land is located." Under Article 15 of MD 88 provides that the "Land Management Authority is charged with carrying out land registration." Under Article 15 of MD 88 the Village Land Unit is charged with providing data relating to the land for the purpose of forming the land file applying for land, and land documents registration. The land file shall be duly certified by "Naiban" (Chief of village) and, thereafter, sent to the Land Management Authority of district/municipality for consideration, management and protection of state land, collective land within the village territory, and for inspecting the land use by individuals and organization within the village territory. " The law does not specify whether community lands must be mapped or otherwise clearly demarcated to prevent the possibility of disputes.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While villages can apply for collective title, village clusters or groups of villages (kumbahn) that self-identify as a collective group or other groups must first form an association under the Association Decee 2009 to apply for collective rights over customary land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: Villages are not granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The level of legal authority varies depending on the land's classification and whether the community is granted a land use certificate, land survey certificate, or a land title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007
indicators.additional_info: The law generally provides that the holder of land use rights shall have the right to protect land, right to use land, right of usufruct, right to transfer the land use right, and the inheritance rights (Art. 53, Land Law 2003). Article 16 of MD 88 provides that Land Survey Certificates grant organizations, including community organizations, the right to  use the land for various purposes based on the land category specified by law. However, Organizations granted a Land Survey Certificate shall have no right to transfer, lease out, grant concessions, put in share or collateral. Land Certificates grant land use rights to communities for a period of 3 years after which the community holders can apply for land titles. Land titles confer on communities the right to use land as collateral, and share, sell, exchange, lease and give land as inheritance (MD, Art. 16).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land use certificates are granted for three years, indicating that community use rights may not be held in perpetuity. However, communities can also claim land titles which appear to not have a durational limit.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law is silent on whether communities must give consent prior to the acquisition of their land use right by governments and outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Laos (Art. 17); Land Law 2003; Ministerial Decree 101 of 2005 on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law (MD 101); Ministerial Decree 88 of 2008 (MD 88) on the Implementation of the 2003 Land Law; Forest Law 2007

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Law 2007 provides for customary use to timber and harvest of forest produces for household use, but this use must conform to village regulations
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Law 2007 (Art. 42).
indicators.additional_info: Article 42 of the Forestry Law 2008 provides "Customary utilization of forests is the use of forest and forest products that has been practiced for a long time in accordance with laws and regulations. The State allows the use of timber and harvest of forest products in nonprohibited forests for household utilization without adverse impact on forest resources, and the environment as well as reflecting the rights and interest of individuals or organizations. Customary utilization of forest and forest products shall be practiced in accordance with a designed plan and with village regulations and laws and regulations on forests."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water belongs to people of Laos, and the Government acts on behalf of the people to manage and allocate water use rights. Use and protection rights to wetland areas may be allocated to individuals or organizations. The Water and Water Resources Law, 1996 provides individual use rights to water, which can be exercised by all citizens (thus, as citizens of Laos, communities are also granted a use right). Community use of water for domestic purposes is free and does not require authorization.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water and Water Resources Law, 1996;  Land Law 2003; Constitution of Laos, 1991
indicators.additional_info: The Land Law 2003 and implementing decrees recognize use rights to collectively and customarily held land." Use and protection rights to wetland areas may be granted to individuals or organizations through an application for a land use certificate by the administrative authority of the village to the district administrative authority. Article 4 of the Water and Water Resourcse Law provides that "Water Resources and Water are the property of the people of Lao PDR as a whole. The Government acts on behalf of the people to manage and to evenly and equitably share the uses of the water. Individuals and organisations will have the right to use water for specific purposes only when authorisation is given by the concerned authority, except for use of a minor nature..." Article 13 provides that "water and water resources may be legally used for different purposes such as: family domestic use, irrigation, fishery; agricultural production; livestock; hydropower; industrial production; navigation; sport, recreation; cultural, medicinal, etc.

LBR.name: Liberia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land Rights Policy 2013 & Law 2018 entrench customary holdings as owned, registrable by individuals, families, communities. Registration in accordance with local norms.  Modernized colonial recognition of community ownership retracted in 1973. 2018 law prefaced by Community Forest Rights Law 2009 which confirmed  Aboriginees deeds still in force & provided for Community Forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1986. Forest Reform Law, 2006. Community Rights Law with Respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Policy 2013. Land Rights Act, 2018 (LRA) & Regulations, No. 57 of 2002.
indicators.additional_info: Until Land Rights Act 2018 customary land  were vulnerable to takings from 1958  in policy to allocate vast lands to commercial investors. Reissue of Law in 1973 excluded 1949-1956 Aborigines Law protecting many of those lands. From 1974-2018 customary lands were registrable only as individual encumbrances on Public Land, as Public Land Deeds. New policy 2013 recognized customary lands as lawfully owned, delivered in Land Rights Act (LRA) 2018 & Regs. 2022. Significant progress in first of two-stage procedure in issue of community titles. Up to 50 final titles issued by March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary tenure has equal force and effect with registered private lands LRA, Art. 32 (2). While law makes registration obligatory (Art.11 (2), 32 (5), 37 (4)), Delay of state survey 'shall not negate the existence or enforceability of Community Ownership of Customary Land'. Explicitly includes forest & other communal lands LRA s.33, 38.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018, (LRA) and Regulations, 2022. Constitution 1986 Art. 20, 22, 24, 26. National Forestry Reform Law 2006 s.9.10.a. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009, s. 2.2.c.
indicators.additional_info: Customary Land ('Community land') includes land owned, used or managed under customary norms, residential, farm, communal forestlands and fallow lands etc. LRA, Art.2. Only minerals, existing parcels owned under fee simple deeds & gazetted National Protected Areas excluded. Art. 5 (4), 33 (3). A statutory Deed of Community Land  is issued in name of the community. Reg 13, 2022.  The communal lnd is communal, never able to be sold without majority consent, and not  even to be considered until after 50 yrs (2068). May be leased,  concessions etc. The exception is residential customary parcels land which may be sold (Art. 49 (1).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: LRA 2018 provides a practical, cheap, inclusive two-step process to issue Community Land Deed in name of community. 2nd step is conduct of Confirmatory Survey by Govt of perimeter boundary & parcels to be excluded as under fee simple titles.  Note: c. 9,000 clans/communities: Up to 500 have completed Stage 1, under 50 have received final titles.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018 and Regulations 2022. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Community-based begins with perimeter boundary agreements, institution of governing land committee, then confirmatory survey of boundary by State, registration of Statutory Deed of Community Lands (Regs 2022). Historically communities were able to secure Aborigines Deeds as registered collective entitlements but after 1973 formalization available only through issue of individual Public Land Deeds (Public Lands Law Cht.3.30).However the Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands 2009 confirmed  Aboriginees deeds in force over vast areas (s.2.3b) as does the LRA, 2018 (Art. 32 (5)).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land Rights Law 2018 recognizes the community as a natural person. It remains "an open class subject to changes as caused by birth, death and migration" Art. 34 (5) & 35 (2). Note that recognition already existed under issue of Aborigines Deeds & communal Public Land Deeds, upheld by the Community Forest Rights Act 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018, Regs 2022. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Under customary law and as acknowledged in statutory laws a community can own registrable land in its own name (actually provided during 1920s-1973) through issue of Aborigines Land Deeds). While new laws did away with that form of tenure, the deeds themselves were upheld  in the Community Forest Rights law 2009 (Art.1.3), now incorporated by the Land Rights Act 2018 as lawful community properties (Art. 32 (5)), and which areas cover several million ha; refer L. Alden Wily, 2007 'So Who Owns the Forest?' SDI & FERN.  Each Community Land is mapped with agreement of neighbours LRA, 2018, Art. 37, subject to Confirmatory Survey, then registered to the community in its own name, owning the land in common but able to transfer or issue private rights under leaseholds but not sell the land LRA, Art. 33.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Authority  is vested in the Community which elects a  Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC) as land manager, to resolve disputes, make by-laws etc. Two-thirds approval of community adults required for approving by-laws, zoning, transfer, leases etc. Land Rights Law 2018 & Regs. 2022.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Act, 2018 Art. 4, 36, 49, 51, 38-45, 50.   Land Rights Regulations, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: Regulations 2022 stipulate procedures for voting, term of CLMDC,  accountability to community members, and drafting of Community By Laws. Zoning advised with rules for each zone - agricultural, residential, cultural shrines & sites, protected areas, commercial area, artisan mining area, public zone max 10% of area. Community Forest Land Rights Law, 2009 s.4 vests authority over community forestlands in community assemblies (all adults) with oversight by Community Forest Management Committee (CFMC). Residential parcels may be registered in Fee Simple Deeds, the soil  remaining the property of the community. Lease up to 50 acres permitted, subject to CLDMC approval. Compulsory acquisition subject to negotiation with legal preference for the State to lease the land.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All customary land owned in perpetuity. Rights to occupy, use, develop parcels within community land are transmissible and transferable, and lands may be overlapped by concessions, but the land remains owned by the community. The exception is residential parcels which may be registered under Fee Simple Deeds and alienable, but sale subject to community approval.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1986. Land Rights Act, 201. Land Rights Act Regulations, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: Land in Liberia is classified as Public, Government, Customary and Private Land (LRA, 2018 Art. 7). Protected Areas co-exist within each of the above, subject to conservation laws (esp. National Reform Forestry Law, 2006 and Community Forest Rights Act, 2009). Constitution allows courts to apply statutory or customary law (Art. 65). While no longer provided for as a form of tenure, Aborigines Deeds (tribal/community based entitlements) issued during 1929-1973 were upheld in 2009 and confirmed in the Community Forest Rights Act, 2009, s.2.2c & 2.3b, and then the Land Rights Act, 2018, Art. 32 (3) (i)) & 5). No communal land within the community property may be sold, but after 50 years holders of Fee Simple Deeds for residential land may sell their parcels subject to community approval.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community consent needed for issue of surface concessions with detailed procedures. Minerals as state property only require FPIC for disturbing surface. No FPIC required for compulsory acquisition under Constitution 1986. Pre-2018 deeded parcels treated as private land. State must first seek to lease communal land from community for intended public purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1986, Art. 24 on compulsory acquisition. Land Rights Law 2018 Arts. 27, 33, 46, 50, 54.Land Rights Act Regulations, 2022, Reg. 20 (1-26).
indicators.additional_info: Detailed  guidance on FPIC when concessions affecting their lands are proposed.  Concessionaire may not enter the community land until payment of agreed compensation, agreement as to benefits, roles, and resettlement effected if required (LRA Regulations, 2022, Art. 20 (1-26). Twenty-four negotiation points must be covered including monitoring, scope for renegotiation, reversion of the lands at the end of the lease period, right to appeal and full provisions for dispute resolution through arbitration during term of the concession.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities own all natural forest/tree resources on community forest lands and planted trees on community or private land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1986. Property Law, Title 29 Cht. 8. National Forestry Reform Law, 2006. Community Rights Law with Respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Act, 2018, and Regulations, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution defines only land under the sea and waterways and minerals as the property of the Republic (Art. 22.b). Property Law defined land as including ''all things growing on land' (Cht 8.3), retained in the Land Rights Act, 2018. The  National Forestry Law 2000 s.2.1 states that all forest resources are held in trust by the Republic other than communal forests or planted trees on private or deeded lands but defines forests so broadly that virtually all community lands are included (s.1.3).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water may be government, private or community property, with its use closely regulated by statute. The Land Rights Act 2018  reemphasizes that only minerals under the land or sea are owned by the state (Art. 33 (3)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1986 Art.22.b. Property Law Title 29 Chapter 8.3. An Act to Amend the Public Authorities Law to Create the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, 1973. Environment Protection and Management Law, 2003. Land Rights Act, 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution 1986 omits water as the property of the Republic (Art. 22.b). Property Law Cht. 8.3 defines land as including water. The Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation Act1973 regulates and administers all water matters,  guided by the National Integrated Water Resources Management Policy, Nov 2007. Enactment of a comprehensive Water Law is intended. The Environmental Protection and Management Agency is also empowered to prescribe measures for protection of rivers, lakes and wetlands (Environment Law, 2003, s.74-75).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities are assured ownership and use of forests within customary lands and may create community protected forests. Gazetted Protected Areas (PA) remain Government Land but may be jointly managed by State and community. Already proposed PA must be negotiated with community. LRA 2018 Art. 42(1). Communities may create Protected Areas owned and managed by themselves. Art. 42 (2)  & (3).
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife and National Parks Act, No.33 of 1988. National Forestry Reform Law, 2006. The Community Rights Law with Respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Act, 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Community forest rights law 2009 recognises that: communities own forests within their customary lands up to 49,999 ha; decisions to allocate require community FPIC; communities are legal persons able to enter Small-Scale and Medium-Scale timber contracts; to be given minimum 55% revenue generated by large-scale contracts, and may manage and regulate their forests (s.2 & 3). The Community Assembly is decision-maker with 5 person Forest Management Committee s. 4. Forests under aboriginal tribal deeds acknowledged as community property but often overlap National Forests. Wildlife law (1987) provides only for local consultation when creating National Parks, removes inhabitants compensating  customary rights, creates Local Advisory Committees to assist Wildlife Authority (1987, s. 11,15,26), diverts local use to buffer zones (s.15).

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land Rights Policy 2013 & Law 2018 entrench customary holdings as owned, registrable by individuals, families, communities. Registration in accordance with local norms.  Modernized colonial recognition of community ownership retracted in 1973. 2018 law prefaced by Community Forest Rights Law 2009 which confirmed  Aboriginees deeds still in force & provided for Community Forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1986. Forest Reform Law, 2006. Community Rights Law with Respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Policy 2013. Land Rights Act, 2018 (LRA) & Regulations, No. 57 of 2002.
indicators.additional_info: Until Land Rights Act 2018 customary land  were vulnerable to takings from 1958  in policy to allocate vast lands to commercial investors. Reissue of Law in 1973 excluded 1949-1956 Aborigines Law protecting many of those lands. From 1974-2018 customary lands were registrable only as individual encumbrances on Public Land, as Public Land Deeds. New policy 2013 recognized customary lands as lawfully owned, delivered in Land Rights Act (LRA) 2018 & Regs. 2022. Significant progress in first of two-stage procedure in issue of community titles. Up to 50 final titles issued by March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary tenure has equal force and effect with registered private lands LRA, Art. 32 (2). While law makes registration obligatory (Art.11 (2), 32 (5), 37 (4)), Delay of state survey 'shall not negate the existence or enforceability of Community Ownership of Customary Land'. Explicitly includes forest & other communal lands LRA s.33, 38.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018, (LRA) and Regulations, 2022. Constitution 1986 Art. 20, 22, 24, 26. National Forestry Reform Law 2006 s.9.10.a. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009, s. 2.2.c.
indicators.additional_info: Customary Land ('Community land') includes land owned, used or managed under customary norms, residential, farm, communal forestlands and fallow lands etc. LRA, Art.2. Only minerals, existing parcels owned under fee simple deeds & gazetted National Protected Areas excluded. Art. 5 (4), 33 (3). A statutory Deed of Community Land  is issued in name of the community. Reg 13, 2022.  The communal lnd is communal, never able to be sold without majority consent, and not  even to be considered until after 50 yrs (2068). May be leased,  concessions etc. The exception is residential customary parcels land which may be sold (Art. 49 (1).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: LRA 2018 provides a practical, cheap, inclusive two-step process to issue Community Land Deed in name of community. 2nd step is conduct of Confirmatory Survey by Govt of perimeter boundary & parcels to be excluded as under fee simple titles.  Note: c. 9,000 clans/communities: Up to 500 have completed Stage 1, under 50 have received final titles.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018 and Regulations 2022. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Community-based begins with perimeter boundary agreements, institution of governing land committee, then confirmatory survey of boundary by State, registration of Statutory Deed of Community Lands (Regs 2022). Historically communities were able to secure Aborigines Deeds as registered collective entitlements but after 1973 formalization available only through issue of individual Public Land Deeds (Public Lands Law Cht.3.30).However the Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands 2009 confirmed  Aboriginees deeds in force over vast areas (s.2.3b) as does the LRA, 2018 (Art. 32 (5)).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land Rights Law 2018 recognizes the community as a natural person. It remains "an open class subject to changes as caused by birth, death and migration" Art. 34 (5) & 35 (2). Note that recognition already existed under issue of Aborigines Deeds & communal Public Land Deeds, upheld by the Community Forest Rights Act 2009.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Rights Act, 2018, Regs 2022. Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009.
indicators.additional_info: Under customary law and as acknowledged in statutory laws a community can own registrable land in its own name (actually provided during 1920s-1973) through issue of Aborigines Land Deeds). While new laws did away with that form of tenure, the deeds themselves were upheld  in the Community Forest Rights law 2009 (Art.1.3), now incorporated by the Land Rights Act 2018 as lawful community properties (Art. 32 (5)), and which areas cover several million ha; refer L. Alden Wily, 2007 'So Who Owns the Forest?' SDI & FERN.  Each Community Land is mapped with agreement of neighbours LRA, 2018, Art. 37, subject to Confirmatory Survey, then registered to the community in its own name, owning the land in common but able to transfer or issue private rights under leaseholds but not sell the land LRA, Art. 33.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Authority  is vested in the Community which elects a  Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC) as land manager, to resolve disputes, make by-laws etc. Two-thirds approval of community adults required for approving by-laws, zoning, transfer, leases etc. Land Rights Law 2018 & Regs. 2022.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Rights Law with respect to Forest Lands, 2009. Land Rights Act, 2018 Art. 4, 36, 49, 51, 38-45, 50.   Land Rights Regulations, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: Regulations 2022 stipulate procedures for voting, term of CLMDC,  accountability to community members, and drafting of Community By Laws. Zoning advised with rules for each zone - agricultural, residential, cultural shrines & sites, protected areas, commercial area, artisan mining area, public zone max 10% of area. Community Forest Land Rights Law, 2009 s.4 vests authority over community forestlands in community assemblies (all adults) with oversight by Community Forest Management Committee (CFMC). Residential parcels may be registered in Fee Simple Deeds, the soil  remaining the property of the community. Lease up to 50 acres permitted, subject to CLDMC approval. Compulsory acquisition subject to negotiation with legal preference for the State to lease the land.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All customary land owned in perpetuity. Rights to occupy, use, develop parcels within community land are transmissible and transferable, and lands may be overlapped by concessions, but the land remains owned by the community. The exception is residential parcels which may be registered under Fee Simple Deeds and alienable, but sale subject to community approval.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1986. Land Rights Act, 201. Land Rights Act Regulations, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: Land in Liberia is classified as Public, Government, Customary and Private Land (LRA, 2018 Art. 7). Protected Areas co-exist within each of the above, subject to conservation laws (esp. National Reform Forestry Law, 2006 and Community Forest Rights Act, 2009). Constitution allows courts to apply statutory or customary law (Art. 65). While no longer provided for as a form of tenure, Aborigines Deeds (tribal/community based entitlements) issued during 1929-1973 were upheld in 2009 and confirmed in the Community Forest Rights Act, 2009, s.2.2c & 2.3b, and then the Land Rights Act, 2018, Art. 32 (3) (i)) & 5). No communal land within the community property may be sold, but after 50 years holders of Fee Simple Deeds for residential land may sell their parcels subject to community approval.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community consent needed for issue of surface concessions with detailed procedures. Minerals as state property only require FPIC for disturbing surface. No FPIC required for compulsory acquisition under Constitution 1986. Pre-2018 deeded parcels treated as private land. State must first seek to lease communal land from community for intended public purpose.

LBY.name: Libya

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Tenure Specialist & Suliman Ibrahim, Director, Centre for Law and Society Studies, Benghazi University

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary rights not a lawful basis of property since 1970s. Focus since 2011 Revolution is on restitution or compensation for urban parcel expropriation under 1978 law achieved in 2015. Constitution & Transitional Justice laws 2012-13 pledge to protect private ownership. No reference to semi-nomadic Bedouin & Amazigh pastoralists. Civil conflict since 2014 limits legal change.
indicators.law_and_provision: Repealed: Law 142/1970 (Tribal Lands & Wells); Law 38/1977 (Real Property); Law 4/1978 (Real Property); Law 21/1984 (Public Use & Disposal of Land); Law 7/1986 (Abolition of Ownership); Law 17/2010 (Re-registration).Transitional Justice Laws No 17/2012, No. 29/2013. Law No 16/2015. Law NO. 20 of 2015.
indicators.additional_info: Context:  (i) rural pop always low, now 17.8% in 2025. (ii)  country arid, only 1% land cultivated. (iii) rural pop in oases or well-based farmers with 2-3 ha. (iv) Pastoralists few, most Bedouin (Arab), handful of Taureg (Amazigh). (v) Focus on urban properties where 4/5 pop live. Gaddafi reduced property to one houseplot per male in 1978. (vi) Reduced all titles to usufructs (intif'a) in 1986. Mass expropriation resulted. (vii) Some restitution permitted from 1990s and compensation available from 2006. (viii) Restitution of urban parcels became central from 2011. (ix)  Law 16/2015 repealed 1978 law but complex as many oroperties long occupied by others. Law 20/2015 repealed related laws but major disputes as to if compensation payable as per Law 29/2013. (x) Civil war since 2014 & mass displacement prevents resolution.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Real rights to land cannot be established unless registered; registration cannot be based on customary rights. No equity in recognition of titled/usufruct rights of urban majority with minority settled/semi-nomadic Bedouin & Taureg. Takeover of oil wells by militias including some ISIS.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 17/2010. Civil Code (1953) Arts. 855ff. Constitution 2012. Transitional Justice Laws 2012, 2013. Laws No 16 & 20 of 2015 repealing 1970s laws.
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 48 of Law 17/2010, all acts that establish, transfer, alter or end original real rights and final judgements thereof must be registered; otherwise, such rights cannot be established, transferred, altered, or ended with regard to the parties concerned or others. Laws in force recognize only the very few registered tribal lands and wells but all records lost in protests in cities. Unregistered properties became state owned from Law 142/1970 and remain so. Law 4/1978 limited ownership one house, a plot of land on which to build a house, a commercial or craft premise, or a productive farm. indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: What were known as tribal lands have become state owned including naturally occurring trees. Registered individual possessors of agricultural land do get compensation for planted trees (ghara) if their land is  reallocated.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is public common property and may be freely used for domestic and stock watering purposes. In practice communal wells in desert are possessed by tribes but without formal recognition.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 3/1982 on the Regulation of the Exploitation of Water repealed by Law No 15/2003 on the Protection and Improvement of the Environment.
indicators.additional_info: Chapter IV of Law No.15/2003 repeals but retains principles of Law No. 3/1982 that (1) Water is shared by all people; (2) Sources of water in Libya are owned by the people and mean all natural water sources whether on or beneath the surface; and (3) that Every person can drink and water his animals from oases, valleys and streams, provided tis causes no harm to water or its source or land or installations built on it or surrounding it; (4) It is allowed to drink or water animals from a private water facility or a facility licensed to one or more beneficiary/ies when a prior permission is obtained and a suitable payment is made  … .”

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Tribes are not recognized land or resource owners, although could use resources for domestic purposes until 1992. Law 15/2003 regulates hunting, under licence only. Cabinet Resolution No. 48/2013 mandates Tourism Ministry in charge of National Parks. De facto resource use continues.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 14/1992 amending Law No. 5/1982 on Protecting Pastures and Forests.  Law No. 15/2003 on  Protection and Improvement of the Environment. Law No 15/1989 on Animals and Trees Protection. Cabinet Resolution No. 48/2013 on National Park Management focused on developing tourism.
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 of Law 5/1982 on Protecting Pastures and Forests read: “Members of communities that have for a long time exercised rights to use forests and public pastures for non-commercial purposes can continue doing so in accordance with conditions to be determined by the Ministry of Agriculture, but it is prohibited for them to exercise any right to use forests and pastures that society or people’s institutions plant or develop, or protected or preserved forests or pastures.” This  article was abrogated by Law 14/1992. Law No.15/1989 on Animals and Tree Protection includes care of pastures as well as trees. Covers which trees may be felled under licence, that female camels may not be killed without a permit, and identifies the General People's Committee for Agricultural Land Reclamation as in charge.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary rights not a lawful basis of property since 1970s. Focus since 2011 Revolution is on restitution or compensation for urban parcel expropriation under 1978 law achieved in 2015. Constitution & Transitional Justice laws 2012-13 pledge to protect private ownership. No reference to semi-nomadic Bedouin & Amazigh pastoralists. Civil conflict since 2014 limits legal change.
indicators.law_and_provision: Repealed: Law 142/1970 (Tribal Lands & Wells); Law 38/1977 (Real Property); Law 4/1978 (Real Property); Law 21/1984 (Public Use & Disposal of Land); Law 7/1986 (Abolition of Ownership); Law 17/2010 (Re-registration).Transitional Justice Laws No 17/2012, No. 29/2013. Law No 16/2015. Law NO. 20 of 2015.
indicators.additional_info: Context:  (i) rural pop always low, now 17.8% in 2025. (ii)  country arid, only 1% land cultivated. (iii) rural pop in oases or well-based farmers with 2-3 ha. (iv) Pastoralists few, most Bedouin (Arab), handful of Taureg (Amazigh). (v) Focus on urban properties where 4/5 pop live. Gaddafi reduced property to one houseplot per male in 1978. (vi) Reduced all titles to usufructs (intif'a) in 1986. Mass expropriation resulted. (vii) Some restitution permitted from 1990s and compensation available from 2006. (viii) Restitution of urban parcels became central from 2011. (ix)  Law 16/2015 repealed 1978 law but complex as many oroperties long occupied by others. Law 20/2015 repealed related laws but major disputes as to if compensation payable as per Law 29/2013. (x) Civil war since 2014 & mass displacement prevents resolution.

(Law 142/1970 (Tribal Land & Wells); Law 38/1977 (Real Property); Law 4/1978 (Real Property);  Law 21/1984 (Public Use and Disposal of Land); Law 7/1986 (Abolition of Ownership). Law No 16/2015 abolishing Law No 4/1978 but with no effect upon tribal land tenure.)
LBY.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — The state does not need the consent of anyone when deciding to use the land for public purposes including allocating to others. Land is deemed state owned, and others can have only a right to usufruct limited to registered holders. (Law 142/1970 (Tribal Land & Wells); Law 38/1977 (Real Property); Law 4/1978 (Real Property);  Law 21/1984 (Public Use and Disposal of Land); Law 7/1986 (Abolition of Ownership))
LBY.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, limited progress — What were known as tribal lands have become state owned including naturally occurring trees. Registered individual possessors of agricultural land do get compensation for planted trees (ghara) if their land is  reallocated.  (Law 142/1970 (Tribal Land & Wells); Law 38/1977 (Real Property); Law 4/1978 (Real Property);  Law 21/1984 (Public Use and Disposal of Land); Law 7/1986 (Abolition of Ownership))
LBY.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water is public common property and may be freely used for domestic and stock watering purposes. In practice communal wells in desert are possessed by tribes but without formal recognition.  (Law No. 3/1982 on the Regulation of the Exploitation of Water repealed by Law No 15/2003 on the Protection and Improvement of the Environment. )
LBY.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: No, the law does not address the issue — Tribes are not recognized land or resource owners, although could use resources for domestic purposes until 1992. Law 15/2003 regulates hunting, under licence only. Cabinet Resolution No. 48/2013 mandates Tourism Ministry in charge of National Parks. De facto resource use continues.   (Law 14/1992 amending Law No. 5/1982 on Protecting Pastures and Forests.  Law No. 15/2003 on  Protection and Improvement of the Environment. Law No 15/1989 on Animals and Trees Protection. Cabinet Resolution No. 48/2013 on National Park Management focused on developing tourism.  )

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All land  vested in the Basotho Nation, power to allocate vested in the King guided by statutes which devolve responsibility to Land Authority, elected District Councils and Community Councils. Implied equivalency of customary rights & statutory leases. Unclarity as to inclusion of communities as legal persons although operates customarily.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1993 (2018, 2022), Art 107-109. Land Act, No. 8 of 2010, s.2, 4, 6. Local Government Act, 1997 (2004) s. 4 & 5.
indicators.additional_info: Existing allocations prior to 1993 Constitution are upheld, but allocations since 2010 registered under Certificate of Occupancy & Use as inheritable 'lifetime usufruct' or a statutory lease. Primarily for residential & agricultural purposes but may finclude orests, pastures, fishing rights etc.  Community Councils may allocate commonage for industrial or commercial use with consent of District Council & Government. 'Person' defined in Land Act 2010 s. 2 as a company, association, or body or persons, corporate or incorporate.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Not strictly equivalent legal force for customary & statutory tenure, in inability of communities to secure communal grazing and forest under collective titles, deemed as unallocated land, and most vulnerable to reallocation.  Statutory leases requiring survey favoured for houses, farms, etc, with 90 yr term. Customary usufructs under Certificates of Occupancy orUse cheaper.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1993, art. 17. Land Act, No.  8 of 2010. Local Government Act, 1997 (amended 2004).
indicators.additional_info: Compensation at compulsory acquisition similar for unregistered household lands, certificated lands and leased.  Exception is 'unallocated' lands including pastures wich have not been made specifically available for resident or agriculture use. Land Act 2010 Art 48.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Accessible, affordable and simple certification for  homesteads, farms etc. available from Community Councils. Leases expensive & require approval by Land Administration Authority. Removes parcel from customary rules to statutory rule. More favourable score if the law provided for collective certificates to cover community grazing areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2010, s. 15, 16. Land Regulations Legal Notice 21 of 2011. Land Authority Act, No. 9 of 2010.
indicators.additional_info: Registration of existing customary house/farm allocations under Certificates or not is compulsory only when  systematic titling launched in area. Leases granted for 30, 60 or 90 years, or longer with Land Administration Authority consent (Land Act 2010 s. 32). Investors including foreigners may be allocated grazing lands by Authority.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communities are not treated as legal persons for purpose of registration & no provision for collective entitlements by Certificate or Lease. Community Councils allocate grazing areas but as a use right. This exposes 60% of country area critical for customary grazing open for allocation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2010, s. 6. Land Regulations, 2011. Local Government Act, 1997, s. 31.
indicators.additional_info: Grazing areas are made available communities by Community Councils as defined by Local Government Act, 1997 (2004) which names their functions as: control of natural resources, land and site allocation, grazing control, burial grounds (S. 5 (2) Second Schedule). Land Act, 2010, s. 15 (1) also makes reference to body corporate and unincorporated bodies able to hold rights for limited or indefinite periods, but within which a community or village does not appear be treated as such.  Nor does the law provide for Communal Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Elected local Community Councils have legal authority to allocate lands to households for agricultural & residential purposes and which may include paddocks and small pastures or woodland. State guidelines with customary norms apply.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2010 s. 14 (1).
indicators.additional_info: Land Act, 2010 devolves the King's prerogative to allocate lands to elected Community Councils under Local Government Act, 1996 (2004). 128 Community Councils in 2012) and higher powers (e.g. to issue leases) in District Councils (10 District Councils in 2012). Community Councils may pass by-laws subject to gazettement on land and natural resource matters including collecting fines (Local Government Act, 1997, s. 42).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: While soil is owned in perpetuity by Basuto nation, rights are for occupation and use and may be revoked for failure to use the land as allocated. Leases available up to 90 years, but lifetime customary usufructs are transmissible to heirs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2010, s. 15, s. 32
indicators.additional_info: Allocations including where formalized as Certificate of Allocation is a lifetime usufruct but passes to spouse, or nominated heir. Corporate entities hold by fixed  or indefinitely period. Agricultural and residential leases are available up to 90 years.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for consent at compulsory acquisition but the state is obliged to enable right to negotiate compensation by the lawful landholder. State may take 'unallocated' land after consultation with councils but no definition of allocated land under customary norms and this makes commons doubly vulnerable to allocation of leases and takings for public purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1993, Land Act, 2010, s. 48-60.
indicators.additional_info: Definition of public interest is broad; Land Act, 2010, s. 51.Principle of negotiation with holder explicit (S. 52) but consent not required for takings for public purpose or public interest (defined separately, s. 51-52). No apparent legal requirement that elected Community Council consult with members to make allocations or negotiate state land takings.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Planted trees explicitly the property of individuals, groups, communities etc. Natural trees as explicitly property of the State but may readily be transferred to individuals, group, communities etc.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2010, s. 2. Forestry Act, 1998, s. 3.
indicators.additional_info: Land defined to cover water, all things natural or man-made growing on land (Land Act, 2010, s. 2). Lawful right-holders presumed to own trees, but modified by Forestry Act, 1998, s. 3 (1): 'Notwithstanding any rule of customary or common law or any legislation to the contrary, individuals, groups of individuals, communities, organisations or cooperatives or their assigns or successors who plant and grow a tree on land lawfully held ... shall own the tree ....' (3(2) '.... ownership of trees not covered by subsection (1) shall vest in the State and it shall be lawful for the Minister to transfer such ownership to individuals, groups of individuals, communities, organizations or cooperatives ... on such terms as he may deem fit'.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the Basotho Nation in common. Domestic use governed by customary law and community councils supervise  water points. Non-domestic use governed by Water Resources Act, 2008.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, No. 15 of 2008, 4, 5 & 6.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community Forests may be declared (1998 s. 17). A Forest Reserve may also be transferred to community by  request & Agreement. Does not apply to National Parks.  The Environment Act 2008 devolves responsibility to District Councils for measures of protection, but required to enable  'traditional forest uses indispensable to the community' to continue (s. 63(5)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Act, 1998. National Parks Act, No. 11 of 1975. Environment Act, No 10 of 2008.
indicators.additional_info: Ownership, control and management of any forest reserve by individuals, groups of individuals, communities, organizations or cooperatives is possible through gazetted written and binding agreement on both parties. Forestry Act, 1998 s. 11 (3). Provision also for Community Forests and Cooperative Forests s. 17. In addition, the Chief Forestry Officer may advise Minister to transfer a forest enterprise to a community, cooperative, etc. if it has 'the required resources and expertise'  (s. 21).  Cutting forest produce, grazing livestock, etc. in reserves is subject to licences (s. 22) but domestic uses such as needing wood to repair a house, firewood, wood to make funeral pyre are unlikely to be subject to fees (s. 23).

local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize the land rights of local communities in Latvia.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Latvia; Law on Land Reform in Rural Areas in the Republic of Latvia, 1990; Law on Privatization in Rural Areas, 1992; Law on Land Title Register; Law On Privatisation of Agricultural Undertakings and Collective Fisheries; Latvia Forestry Law, 2000
indicators.additional_info: The Law on Privatization of Rural Areas only provides private property right to citizens and legal persons. There is no explicit mention of community land rights in the law. Article 105 of Constitution of Latvia "everyone has the right to own property. Property shall not be used contrary to the interests of the public. Property rights may be restricted only in accordance with law. Expropriation of property for public purposes shall be allowed only in exceptional cases on the basis of a specific law and in return for fair compensation." Section 1 of the Forestry Law 2000 defines "lawful forest professor" as "lawful forest possessor -a) a person into whose ownership, in accordance with law and on the basis of a decision by a specific institution, in the course of the land reform, land has been transferred (granted) for payment or whose ownership rights to the land have been restored and the land has been determined (surveyed) on site, or b) a person who has acquired possession of the forest land pursuant to the right of inheritance or on another lawful basis." There is no explicit mention of community or collective rights to forest lands. According to the Eurostat Farm Structure Surveys, Common land in Latvia existed in the 1990s (common land of local municipalities), but since 2000 all such land is leased out to several agricultural holdings, and the Eurostat surveys do not provide their area in a separate category. http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/EN/ef_esqrs_lv.htm
