MAR.name: Morocco

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: By 1919 Royal Decree (Dahir) indigenous lands made inalienable held in trust by State. These terres collectives cover only 15 Mha under 4,631 villages using customary/Sharia rules - with rising limitations: eg. arable land  now 'forcibly' individualized  & available to outsiders. No  collective entitlement making commonage vulnerable. 2019 laws latest to erode local control & area of Soulilayates.
indicators.law_and_provision: Terres Collectives Loi,Dahir 1919. Dahir March 1951. Dahir 1.6.179 of Feb 1963.  Civil Code 1808 (1974). Dahirs 62, 63, 64 of 2019.
indicators.additional_info: Vesting of indigenous tribal collective lands or Soulilayate (descendants) in the State has eroded the rights of customary owners, legally unable to halt takings or issue of leases to outsiders as decided by Central Council in consultation with Provincial Governor (Dahir 1-62-179, 2019). Process began with Dahir March 19 1951 transferring peri-urban collective lands to cities & towns. Dahirs No. 62, 63, 64 of 2019 assign authority to lease soulilyates lands to Central Council. Only positive legal change is that women assured same rights as men modernizing customary norms. Dahir No. 63.17 of 2019 simplifies procedure of delimitation.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unequal rights or authority of terres collectives with state-registered rights under titles. Customary registration in customary and Sharia records of each village have minor standing. As conversion of lands into commercial farms rises, protest increases, without change. Customary seasonal right to move stock within arid & semi-arid lands of terres collectives also now subject to permits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahirs of 27 April 1919, 18 February 1924, and 06 February 1937 on the Delineation of Collective Lands. Dahir No. 1.69.30 of  25 July 1969 on The Collective Land located Within the Perimeter of Irrigation  Areas. Law No. 113-13 27 April 2016 on Pastoral Transhumance and Pastoral and Sylvo-Pastoral Areas.
indicators.additional_info: Limited protection of 10 million customary occupants of the steppes & arid lands peaking with three 2019 laws. No equivalency of individual/family rights  in terres collectives with those holding statutory titles. No protection from compulsory acquisition, no consultation required (Dahir No. 62.17 of 2019). IP Amazigh most affected. Constitution 2011 only recognizes their languages & cultural rights. Less trusteeship than aggressive state control. Yet on paper  'Soulaliyate' (descendants) remain to protect Amazigh rights including right to live according to own norms on own lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary & Sharia documents used within communities to define exclusive individual/family rights to non-communal lands. As State property cannot obtain absolute ownership. May obtain licences in irrigation schemes set up by Government intended to be privatized, removing area from terres collective. Application not limited to members, includes outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Terres Collective Loi, 1919. Registration Laws, 1913 &  1915. Agricultural Investment Code, 1969 and many decrees and orders under this law. Dahir 62.17 (2019) & 63.17 (2019).
indicators.additional_info: Royal Decrees in 1913 &  1915 limited registration to lands outside terres collectives. The 1969 law enabled members to convert customary or sharia documents over irrigated lands into statutory titles. Law No. 63.17 (2019) amends the 1924 law on delimitation of Soulaliyate community property.  Despite  drive to privatize and make more lands available to commercial investors terres collectives or Soulaliyates still exist as a legal form of community land area.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Although customary communities are recognized as the collective owners of all rights to community lands (terres collectives) they are not defined as a legal person able to own land in  own name. Century of progressive reinterpretation of trusteeship under Dahir 1919 as de facto State ownership complete by Dahirs of 2019.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahirs of 27 April 1919, 18 February 1924, and 06 February 1937 on the Delineation of Collective Lands. Dahir No. 1.69.30 of  25 July 1969 on The Collective Land located Within the Perimeter of Irrigation  Areas. Dahir No. 62.17 (2019)
indicators.additional_info: Dahir No. 62.17 of 2019 centralized authority over collective lands, including limiting use of custom, and removing obligation to call for tenders or seek community views to allocating lands to investors.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law describes communities as administrators of their  domains. Village Councils use customary & Sharia rules. Yet these are not elected bodies but comprise State appointees & elected officials. Latest disablement of devolved authority is centralization of decisions in 2019 to take or lease collective lands into the Central Council of the Ministry of Interior.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law of April 27 1919 on administration and supervision of Soulaliyate communities and management limits traditional norms including dictate of election of council members.
indicators.additional_info: Intentions of a Dahir in March 1959  'Reclaiming collective land .. by Terminating Disposals and Concessions of Perpetual Enjoyment Rights..' became law in Dahir No. 62.17 (2019). This assigns power to lease lands within terres collectives to the Minister of Interior and  limits the use of custom to make internal decisions. It does favour gender equity (Art. 6).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: From 1919 until present, members of terres collective own inheritable use rights in perpetuity, transferable within the community under customary norms. However, members decreasingly control how their lands are disposed of and to whom, due to centralization of such decisions to the Ministry of Interior. Chance to become collective owners in the first instance has also receded.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahir on Collective Territories, 1919. Dahirs of 27 April 1919, 18 February 1924, & 06 February 1937 on Delineation of Collective Lands. Dahir No. 1.69.30 of  25 July 1969 on The Collective Land located Within the Perimeter of Irrigation  Areas. Dahir of March 1951 on Alienation of Collective Lands for Construction of Administrative Buildings or to Enable Settlers to Benefit from Fertile Land, and Transfer of collective lands to cities. Circular 103 of July 26 1994 Management and development of Community Lands (Sales, Leases, Projects). Dahir 62.17 (2019) & 63.17 (2019) on Governance of Terres Collectives.
indicators.additional_info: The 1919 pledge to trusteeship of community landholding has become direct state control and de facto ownership of their lands. Customarily, internal management of Soulaliyate (terres collective) remains with the local council, helpfully obliged to include women by Dahir 62.17 of 2019. However, interference with customary rules is rife, such as  implementing decree of 2020 which requires residence of members, impossible for those who have to work in towns if only to earn money to then build the required house in the homeland domain.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Laws also dictate that sectoral decisions are compulsory made with no consultation iavailed n forest, water, grazing and investment laws. Cannot reject State allocation of common land to outsiders. In practice, Government now reinterprets trusteeship over terres collectives as outright ownership. This tutelage is echoed in all laws.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahir No. 62.17 (2019), Implementing Decree No.2.19.973 2020. Dahir 64.17 (2019) and its Circular No. 6303, 13 May 2020.
indicators.additional_info: No provision for collective title over distinct village lands and no requirement for consent or even consultation when lands taken (Law 62.17 (2019). Commons within the 4,631 ethnic communities (10 million people) are most vulnerable to state taking and reallocation to private elites & investors. The law also clarifies that both men and women are 'owners' of occupancy and use rights' within Soulaliyate (terres collective)  diluted by Decree No.2.19.973 (2020) which requires residence in form of a dwelling within the community; difficult for poor members to meet due to habitation in towns for survival.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Forest Law 1917  assures communities rights to manage and use forests on collective lands. Law No 1 of 1976 requires participation on of local populations in the economic development of forests. However, Government also has legal right to allocate their lands for forest projects and may authorise grazing access to forests by stockowners from outside the community.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahir of 10 October 1917 on the conservation and exploitation of forests (amended in April 1959 and 1960). Arts 1, 2.
indicators.additional_info: Exploitation of cork forests has special regulations (Art. 3 of 1917). Forests and trees of private land and by implication community lands may be used (Art 2c). Communal Councils directed to assist  forest management ( Art 2), with power to manage applications for quarrying, hunting and fishing, and  requests for collection of dead wood, timber, brush, grasses for local construction and medicinal plants (Art 10). Community based forest management is reported as barely functional outside traditional regulation.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is an inalienable public asset, unseizable, imprescriptible and governed by Statutes (Water Law 2016 Art 4-5). All persons have the right to use water (Art 5). Private rights to hold, use and regulate water exist (Art. 10). Agricultural water associations instituted for irrigated land Law No. 02-84 of 1990).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Law No. 36-15, 2016. Law on Agricultural Water Associations No. 02-84, 1990.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Protected Areas are State property. Customary landholders permitted to remain within PA subject to rules (Law 2010 Art.3, 15-16). Domestic uses permitted (Art 17). Zones defined within PA wherein agricultural, pastoral and forest activities may continue (Art. 20).  Main impact of Protected Areas on communal lands is helpful limit upon outsider commercial use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No 22-07 of 2010 on Protected Areas.
indicators.additional_info: While there is no  provision for customary communities to declare & manage Protected Areas of their own, a legal entity may apply to manage the PA for a renewable 30 yr. term Art 25-27).  Overlap of PA on terres collective is reported as considerable but no provision for restitution to be considered.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: By 1919 Royal Decree (Dahir) indigenous lands made inalienable held in trust by State. These terres collectives cover only 15 Mha under 4,631 villages using customary/Sharia rules - with rising limitations: eg. arable land  now 'forcibly' individualized  & available to outsiders. No  collective entitlement making commonage vulnerable. 2019 laws latest to erode local control & area of Soulilayates.
indicators.law_and_provision: Terres Collectives Loi,Dahir 1919. Dahir March 1951. Dahir 1.6.179 of Feb 1963.  Civil Code 1808 (1974). Dahirs 62, 63, 64 of 2019.
indicators.additional_info: Vesting of indigenous tribal collective lands or Soulilayate (descendants) in the State has eroded the rights of customary owners, legally unable to halt takings or issue of leases to outsiders as decided by Central Council in consultation with Provincial Governor (Dahir 1-62-179, 2019). Process began with Dahir March 19 1951 transferring peri-urban collective lands to cities & towns. Dahirs No. 62, 63, 64 of 2019 assign authority to lease soulilyates lands to Central Council. Only positive legal change is that women assured same rights as men modernizing customary norms. Dahir No. 63.17 of 2019 simplifies procedure of delimitation.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unequal rights or authority of terres collectives with state-registered rights under titles. Customary registration in customary and Sharia records of each village have minor standing. As conversion of lands into commercial farms rises, protest increases, without change. Customary seasonal right to move stock within arid & semi-arid lands of terres collectives also now subject to permits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Dahirs of 27 April 1919, 18 February 1924, and 06 February 1937 on the Delineation of Collective Lands. Dahir No. 1.69.30 of  25 July 1969 on The Collective Land located Within the Perimeter of Irrigation  Areas. Law No. 113-13 27 April 2016 on Pastoral Transhumance and Pastoral and Sylvo-Pastoral Areas.
indicators.additional_info: Limited protection of 10 million customary occupants of the steppes & arid lands peaking with three 2019 laws. No equivalency of individual/family rights  in terres collectives with those holding statutory titles. No protection from compulsory acquisition, no consultation required (Dahir No. 62.17 of 2019). IP Amazigh most affected. Constitution 2011 only recognizes their languages & cultural rights. Less trusteeship than aggressive state control. Yet on paper  'Soulaliyate' (descendants) remain to protect Amazigh rights including right to live according to own norms on own lands.

MAR.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress — Protected Areas are State property. MDG.name: Madagascar

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Tenure Specialist & Roméo Léandre Tsioritolotra, with translation by Hasiniavo Rasolohery, DELC, Madagascar

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Since laws of 2005-2008 individuals may secure Certificates for homes and farms from Communes. Donor-supported titling ensued.  While a village/community could in theory receive a Land Certificate in common, this could only be for visibly occupied  lands, or since 2021 for still undeveloped land after allocation. No collective ownership of communal lands forests, rangelands, etc.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi n° 2005-019 du 17 octobre 2005 fixant les principes régissant les statuts des terres. Law No. 2006-031 of 24 November 2006 setting the legal regime for untitled private land ownership and its implementing decree (Decree No. 2007-1109). Law 2008-013 of 23 July 2008 on the public domain of the State and its implementing decree. Law 2008-014 of 23 July 2008 on the private domain of the State, Decentralized Communities and legal entities of Public Law and its implementing decree. Law No. 2021-016 Amending Law No. 2006-013 of November 24 2006.
indicators.additional_info: Legal changes to property law from 2005 removed presumption that untitled customary lands were state property and established land offices at Commune level to issue titles. Titling limited to: individuals & families with 10+ yrs occupation & use on land shown not be public or privately titled lands, or Protected Areas. 2021 Amendment  retained 2006 as the period from which development on farms & house plots must have taken place; no undeveloped lands since permitted under Certificate (Art. 9).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Art 23 of Law 2006 & 2021 assert that "the Land Certificate is a deed constituting proof of ownership rights and is enforceable against third parties". Improves compensation and protection against mining which required owner's consent. However, less equity of Certificates with private Titles as boundaries thru lack of survey may be challenged & lack of development can result in cancellation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2006-031 of 24 November 2006 setting the legal regime for untitled private land ownership and its implementing decree (Decree No. 2007-1109); Ordinance No. 62-023 of 19 September 1962 on expropriation for public purposes. Law No. 2021-016 Amending Law No. 2006-013 of November 24 2006.
indicators.additional_info: Land is either public property, private property of government, privately titled lands, or Protected Areas. No provision for group title. Participatory natural resource management requires group of local persons to register an NGO or CBO to manage customary forest as per 1996 law.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Procedure for issue of Land Certificates is subject to a Local Land Use Plan through participation of farmers. Process  straightforward & cost-effective. Shortfalls in substance; only covers occupied & now developed lands, no provision to bring unfarmed commons under lawful community ownership. Also Certificate doesnt have equal force with Titles.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2006-031 of 24 November 2006 setting the legal regime for untitled private land ownership and its implementing decree (Decree No. 2007-1109). Law 2021-016 revised Law 2006-031.
indicators.additional_info: The recognition procedure is explicit, simple and low-priced as the commune determines the cost of the land certificate. Price is based upon a balance between the certificate of deliverance right and the power purchase of the community. Procedure provides measures to be taken in case there is a conflict. A “Property Counter” is created at the level of Communes to process requests for certificates. The law does not specify good governance requirements.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No recognition of community as a legal person. A community could apply to hold only occupied and developed lands under one Certificate but has be certified by authorities (Art. 9 Law 2021-016).
indicators.law_and_provision: Art 5, Law N° 2006-31 fixing the legal regime of non-titled private property.
indicators.additional_info: Villages have no identity as discrete entities or legal persons. In theory, a village could register itself as a CBO or Association but only useful to collective farm and house tenure, not common.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision in the land law for village to legally administer holdings or to establish an elected Committee for this. Nor is such a body established at the Commune, its land functions focused only on issuing Certificates.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2006-031 of 24 November 2006 setting the legal regime for untitled private land ownership and its implementing decree (Decree No. 2007-1109); Law 2008-013 of 23 July 2008 on the public domain of the State and its implementing decree; Law 2008-014 of 23 July 2008 on the private domain of the State, Decentralized Collectivities (Communes) and legal entities of Public Law and its implementing decree
indicators.additional_info: Legislation from 2006 promotes decentralization of land governance.  Governance of untitled private lands is entrusted to Communes which have responsibility for many villages. Local land offices are autonomous in terms of budget, decision-making policy and in the recruitment of their staff.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary rights are held in perpetuity and assumed so for Certificate. This does not make it fully secure, as plot boundaries are easily challenged as not surveyed, or owner may have plot taken away for failing to develop the land. Security is only obtainable through (expensive) conversion into a state-registered Land Title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2006-031 of 24 November 2006 setting the legal regime for untitled private land ownership and its implementing decree (Decree No. 2007-1109), Amendment to above law by Law No. 2021-016.  Law 2008-014 of 23 July 2008 on the private domain of the State, Decentralized Communities and legal entities of Public Law and its implementing decree.
indicators.additional_info: Recognition of property rights with certificate indicates the existence of occupancy rights, the personal and exclusive use of established land parcels. This is provisional security if contested and contestant wins, the Certificate is easily cancelled by the Commune or  Court. For right to be permanent, the holder must survey land in state format and registration, which converts recognition of occupancy certificate to a property title.  This protects the property in perpetuity, except when expropriated for a public purpose.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No consent of affected landholders is required at compulsory acquisition. A survey is required to establish the validity and effects of the intended public purpose but no formal or recorded consultation is required. Those holding mining permits must secure the permission of the owner of the Land Certificate prior to mining (2021, Art. 21).
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 62-023 of 19 September 1962 on expropriation for public purposes. Law 2021-016 Art.. 22 on Expropriation.
indicators.additional_info: If the land subject to intended compulsory acquisition, both holders of Land Titles and Land Certificates are eligible for compensation. Where there is no Property Counter (Guichet Foncier) in the Commune, Government is required to assist holders with no Certificates to secure  Land Certificate or Land Title (Certificate Foncier, or Titre Foncier) (2021, Art. 22).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Planted trees are owned but require permits to be felled. No ownership of natural trees, all protected. No commercial use may be made of trees without a permit. GELOSE law (1996) enables a hamlet or village to make agreement to manage and sustainably use its forest - but not own it. Art. 1 Decree 1998. Numerous contracts between forest authorities, communes and communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 1996-025 on Local Magement of Renewable Natural Reosurces (GELOSE law). Forest Code No. 97-017 of 1997 Art. 41. Decree N°98-782 (1998) governing procedures applied to forestry exploitation. Decree No. 2000=027 on Local Communities Responsible for Local Mansgement of Renwable Natural Resources.  Law 2007-036 of 2008 on investments in Madagascar.
indicators.additional_info: Trees and natural forests existing in the Malagasy ground are considered protected. Local populations may use trees for specified domestic purposes. Agreement may be suspended if the user has not followed conditions (Art 3). Provision for community natural resource domains under GELOSE law (1996) compensates to an extent for lack of legal provision for an inclusive approach to certificates for community ownership & use of communal domains - but only management of forest, not ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No person or community may own water which is a national public good but may use it free for domestic purposes and secure management and other use rights through agreements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law N ° 98-029 of January 20th, 1999 bearing the Code of the Water.
indicators.additional_info: Water is declared a common national patrimony and cannot be privatized (Art. 2 Water Code). Access and use of water is  free. Groups, associations or individuals may manage or exploit water through agreement on terms & conditions.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The state owns all natural resources. 2015 Protected Areas Code allows NGOs and private agencies to contract to manage part of a Protected Area under strict conditions. GELOSE law 1996 enables a registered village or hamlet group to lawfully access, use and manage local forest using local rules. c. 1,500 formed, helping to overcome failure of  law to recognize commons as community property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 96-025 of 30 September 1996 on the local management of renewable natural resources. Decree No. 2000-027 of 1996 Law. Law No. 97-017 of 8 August 1997 revising forest legislation. Decree N ° 98-782 On rules applied to logging. Law 2008-028 on the recasting of the Protected Areas Code and its implementing decree. . Law No. 2015-005 Code for Management of Protected Areas.
indicators.additional_info: A community may be a registered association or an interest group,  obeying the community rules as a hamlet, village or group of villages. They may hold rights over trees, forest products, and other resources, subject to statutory rules. The agreement defines the local communities’ usage of their economic, cultural and cultural activities and their duties managing unprotected and protected forest.  While one-sided in decision-making these popular contractual agreements open a legal route to secure traditional use rights to customary forest and rangeland domain.

MEX.name: Mexico

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples (Comunidades)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Comunidades are classified as either common land or human settlement land, and legally all members of the comunidad are considered to have equal ownership claims in the land. Unlike ejido land, there is no explicit right to alienate comunidad land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 75, 101-104, Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 27(VII) of the Constitution states " law protects the integrity of lands of indigenous groups." Comunidades are granted the right to determine the use of their lands and their division into separate portions (art. 101, Agrarian Law). All legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to Ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 73, 107, Agrarian Law 2008). However, comunidades cannot sell or lease their land, but convert their land into ejido land (Art. 104, Agrarian Law). NOTE: In 1990 Mexico ratified ILO Convention 169, which deals specifically with the rights of indigenous and tribal peoples. Article 7 of the Conventions calls for states to respect indigenous land rights.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution and the Agrarian Law establish that comunidad land must be protected by law. However, comunidades must register to receive protection and the gov't retains broad power to expropriate their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 100, 106-107 Agrarian Law; Art. 27(VII), Constitution
indicators.additional_info: All legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 107, Agrarian Law 2008). Article 106 of the Agrarian Law provides that "the land belonging to indigenous groups should be protected by authorities under [the Constitution]."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Registration is free. The law establishes clear, accessible procedures for demarcating, mapping, and registering ejido/ comunidad land. Federal agencies must assist ejidos/ comunidades in securing land.
indicators.additional_info: All legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 73, 107, Agrarian Law 2008). The law establishes that the Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN) must register and provide documentary evidence of ejido and comunidad land. The program of registration is called Procede (established in 1993), ejido/ comunidad assemblies vote on boundaries and the Instituto Estadistica Geografia e Informatica demaractes and maps ejido/comunidad land. The PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA is a federal agency charged with assisting ejidos and comunidades in registering their lands. REGLAMENTO INTERIOR DE LA PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA provides that the Procuraduria Agraria must ensure the prompt, speedy, and effective delivery of agrarian justice, seeking to guarantee the legal security of tenure of ejido and comunidad land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Comunidades are granted legal personality by the Constitution and the Agrarian Law, but must first register to obtain legal personality.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 27(VII), Constitution; Art. 9, 107, Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution recognizes the legal personality of communal populations, including comunidades (Art. 27(VII). The Agrarian Law also explicitly provides that comunidades and ejidos have legal personality (Art. 9 , 107, Agrarian Law). Art. 49 of the Agrarian Law provides that members of the ejidos that have been or are illegally deprived of their lands or waters may come directly to the agrarian tribunal to seek restitution (all legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 107, Agrarian Law 2008)).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law grants the community the right to determine the use of its land, the division of separate portions, and other rules governing the land. However, management of the land is left up to the comunidad through a representative body.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. Art. 74, 100, Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: Under Article 101 of the Agrarian Law, comunidad land owners can use and enjoy their land transfer rights to their families. Article 105 of the Agrarian Law stipulates that communities may establish groups or sub-communities with representative bodies that can lay down internal rules for the comunidad. Art. 49 of the Agrarian Law provides that members of the ejidos that have been or are illegally deprived of their lands or waters may come directly to the agrarian tribunal to seek restitution.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Agrarian Law does not establish durational limits on land held by comunidades.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agrarian Law, 1992

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Comunidad land may be acquired through expropriation for a public purpose, and the consent of the comunidad is not a prerequisite. Ejidos are entitled to compensation when their land is expropriated.
indicators.additional_info: All legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 73, 107, Agrarian Law 2008). State can expropriate comunidad land for a public purpose (Art. 93, Agrarian Law).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not establish restrictions on comunidad use of trees and other forest produce for subsistence purposes, but commercial use requires government authorization. No explicit ownership rights to trees on comunidad land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 104-106, Law on Forest Sustainable Development (Ley General de Desarrollo Forestal Sustentable), 2008; Agrarian Law

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Ownership of water is vested in the State. The Agrarian Law grants ejidos/ comunidades rights to use water located on or near their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 55, Agrarian Law 1992 (amended 2012); Ley de Aguas Nacionales, Arts. 16, 20
indicators.additional_info: The law provides that the water falling within ejido lands, where legally assigned individual, are in common use and their use will be provided for in the rules of procedure of the ejido as long as laws and regulations are not violated (Art. 55, Agrarian Law). All legal articles in the Agrarian Law that apply to ejidos also apply to comunidades (Agrarian Communities) unless there is a specific contradiction in the law (Art. 107, Agrarian Law 2008).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Federal protected areas can contain land held under any tenure type and are divided into core zones and buffer zones. Buffer zones are designated for sustainable resource use, including use by ejidos/ comunidades.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63, 77bis, General Law on Ecological Balance and Protection of Environment
indicators.additional_info: Ejidos and comunidades can establish voluntary conservation zones within their territories.

local_communities_entries.framework: Communities (Ejidos)
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Ejidos land is divided into three classifications, and the degree of ownership and management depends on the classification, but the law provides for ownership of ejido lands. However, ownership is vested in assemblies.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 27(VII), Constitution of Mexico; Art. 9, 44, 68 Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: Article 9 of the Agrarian Law provides that ejidos own the land that is provided to them. Art. 76 of the Agrarian Law provides that landowners on ejidos have the right harvest, use and enjoy the land. The Constitution of Mexico also provides that "the juridicial personality of the [ejidos] is recognized, and their property attached to the land used for human settlements as well as for productive activities is protected." Ejido land is recognized/protected by law and divided into three separate categories of tenure: I. land for human settlement, II. common lands, and III. parcels of arable land (Art. 44, Agrarian Law). Common lands are managed by a comisariado (elected governing body), arable land and land for human settlements is held by recognized ejido members. With landowner consent, Ejido land can be sold, leased, used as collateral, and privatized with approval from the ejido "general assembly" (Art. 75-76 Agrarian Law).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution and the Agrarian establish that ejido land must be protected by law, but ejidos must be registered to receive protection and cannot sell or lease their land as freely as private property owners (need to go through Ejido assemblies).
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 27(VII) Constitution of Mexico; Arts. 14, 93, 75, 152 of the Agrarian Law
indicators.additional_info: Art. 27(VII) of the Constitution states "the law, taking into consideration the respect for and strengthening of the community life of agricultural corporations (ejidos) and communities shall safeguard for human settlement and regulate the usage of common lands, forests, and waters..." Article 14 provides that ejido landowners have the right to use and enjoy their land, and other rights granted to them by the ejido. The state retains power to expropriate Ejido land for a public purpose, but must compensate ejidos (Art. 93, 94, 96, Agrarian Law). NOTE: Mexico ratified ILO Convention 169- Indigenous and Tribal People's Convention in 1990.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Registration is free. The law establishes clear, accessible procedures for demarcating, mapping, and registering ejido/comunidad land. Federal agencies must assist ejidos/comunidades in securing land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 90, 92, 150-152, Agrarian Law; Regulations establishing PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA
indicators.additional_info: The law establishes that the Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN) must register and provide documentary evidence of ejido and comunidad land. The program of registration is called Procede (established in 1993), ejido/comunidad assemblies vote on boundaries and the Instituto Estadistica Geografia e Informatica demarcates and maps ejido/comunidad land. The PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA is a federal agency charged with assisting ejidos and comunidades in registering their lands. REGLAMENTO INTERIOR DE LA PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA provides that the Procuraduria Agraria must ensure the prompt, speedy, and effective delivery of agrarian justice, seeking to guarantee the legal security of tenure of ejido and comunidad land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution recognizes the legal personality of communal populations, including ejidos. The Agrarian Law also explicitly provides that the ejidos have legal personality, but must register first.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 27(VII) Constitution, Art. 9, Agrarian Law 1992 (amended 2012)
indicators.additional_info: Art. 49 of the Agrarian Law provides that members of the ejidos that have been or are illegally deprived of their lands or waters may come directly to the agrarian tribunal to seek restitution.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Ejido land is governed in accordance with the internal rules of the ejidos as long as the rules do not violate laws or regulations. However, the Ejido "general assemblies" are given legal authority to manage ejido land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 2 of the Constitution states that "communities of indigenous people are those which constitute a social, economic, and cultural unit, are situated in a territory, and have their own authorities in accordance with their traditions and customs." Art. 27(VII) of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 14 of the Agrarian Law stipulate that the law should allow ejidos (and comunidades) to convey parcels of their land among individual community members and establish procedures which may grant community members ownership of land tracts. Art. 76-77 of the Agrarian Law grants ejido landowners to use and enjoy the land and veto power over assembly decisions relating to the "collective exploitation of their land." Art. 17 of the Agrarian grants ejidos the right to determine rules for succession. Decisions relating to the conveyance, sale, or lease of ejido lands must be made by the ejido "general assembly" (Art. 23, 74, 75, Agrarian Law). Article 56 provides that assemblies have decision-making authority relating to the delimitation of ejido land.

MEX.Indigenous Q8: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, limited progress — The law does not establish restrictions on comunidad use of trees and other forest produce for subsistence purposes, but commercial use requires government authorization. No explicit ownership rights to trees on comunidad land. (Art. 104-106, Law on Forest Sustainable Development (Ley General de Desarrollo Forestal Sustentable), 2008; Agrarian Law)
MEX.Indigenous Q9: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, limited progress — Ownership of water is vested in the State. The Agrarian Law grants ejidos/ comunidades rights to use water located on or near their land. (Art. 55, Agrarian Law 1992 (amended 2012); Ley de Aguas Nacionales, Arts. 16, 20)
MEX.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Federal protected areas can contain land held under any tenure type and are divided into core zones and buffer zones. Buffer zones are designated for sustainable resource use, including use by ejidos/ comunidades.  (Arts. 63, 77bis, General Law on Ecological Balance and Protection of Environment)
MEX.Communities Q1: Does the law recognize a: Partial, significant progress — Ejidos land is divided into three classifications, and the degree of ownership and management depends on the classification, but the law provides for ownership of ejido lands. However, ownership is vested in assemblies. (Art. 27(VII), Constitution of Mexico; Art. 9, 44, 68 Agrarian Law)
MEX.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: Partial, significant progress — The Constitution and the Agrarian establish that ejido land must be protected by law, but ejidos must be registered to receive protection and cannot sell or lease their land as freely as private property owners (need to go through Ejido assemblies). (Art. 27(VII) Constitution of Mexico; Arts. 14, 93, 75, 152 of the Agrarian Law)
MEX.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Registration is free. The law establishes clear, accessible procedures for demarcating, mapping, and registering ejido/comunidad land. Federal agencies must assist ejidos/comunidades in securing land. (Arts. 90, 92, 150-152, Agrarian Law; Regulations establishing PROCURADURÍA AGRARIA)
MEX.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — The Constitution recognizes the legal personality of communal populations, including ejidos. The Agrarian Law also explicitly provides that the ejidos have legal personality, but must register first. (Art. 27(VII) Constitution, Art. 9, Agrarian Law 1992 (amended 2012))
MEX.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — Ejido land is governed in accordance with the internal rules of the ejidos as long as the rules do not violate laws or regulations. However, the Ejido "general assemblies" are given legal authority to manage ejido land. (Art. 2 of the Constitution states that "communities of indigenous people are those which constitute a social, economic, and cultural unit, are situated in a territory, and have their own authorities in accordance with their traditions and customs." Art. 27(VII) of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 14 of the Agrarian Law stipulate that the law should allow ejidos (and comunidades) to convey parcels of their land among individual community members and establish procedures which may grant community members ownership of land tracts. Art. 76-77 of the Agrarian Law grants ejido landowners to use and enjoy the land and veto power over assembly decisions relating to the "collective exploitation of their land." Art. 17 of the Agrarian grants ejidos the right to determine rules for succession. Decisions relating to the conveyance, sale, or lease of ejido lands must be made by the ejido "general assembly" (Art. 23, 74, 75, Agrarian Law). Article 56 provides that assemblies have decision-making authority relating to the delimitation of ejido land.)
MEX.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The Agrarian Law does not establish durational limits on land owned by ejidos. (Agrarian Law 2002)
MEX.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — Ejido land may be acquired through expropriation for a public purpose, and the consent of the ejidos is not a prerequisite. Ejidos are entitled to compensation when their land is expropriated. (Art. 93, 94, 96, Agrarian Law)
MEX.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, limited progress — The law does not establish restrictions on Ejido use of trees and other forest produce for subsistence purposes, but commercial use requires government authorization. No explicit ownership rights to trees on ejido land. (Art. 104-106, Law on Forest Sustainable Development (Ley General de Desarrollo Forestal Sustentable), 2008; Agrarian Law)
MEX.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, limited progress — Ownership of water is vested in the State. The Agrarian Law grants the ejidos community rights to use water located on or near their land. (Art. 55, Agrarian Law 1992 (amended 2012); Ley de Aguas Nacionales, Arts. 16, 20)
MEX.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Federal protected areas can contain land held under any tenure type and are divided into core zones and buffer zones. Buffer zones are designated for sustainable resource use, including use by ejidos/comunidades.  (Arts. 63, 77bis, General Law on Ecological Balance and Protection of Environment)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory framework does not explicitly recognize community land rights in Macedonia.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Macedonia; Law on Ownership and Other Real Rights; Law on privatization of state agricultural land, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 30 of the Constitution provides "The right to property and the right to inheritance are guaranteed. Ownership of property creates rights and duties and should serve the wellbeing of both the individual and the community. None may be deprived or limited of his/her property, or of the rights deriving from it, except in the public interest determined by law. If property is expropriated or restricted, just compensation, not lower than its market value, is guaranteed. " Article 2 of the Law on Ownership and Other Real Rights provides "the right to ownership can be acquired by all domestic and foreign natural persons and legal entities, including the state and the units of the local self-government, under conditions and in a manner stipulated by this and other laws." The Forest Law 1997 only provides for state and privately owned forest rights.

MLI.name: Mali

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Agricultural Law 2017 enables customary lands to be removed from the State domain - but only through issue of Certificates, confimed by 2020 Land Law. A village may obtain a Certificate including communal pasture, woodland and reserve lands for expansion. Problematic lack of implementing Decree. Pastoralists secure rights of use, access, transit & water under Pastoral Charter 2001.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2023 Arts. 12,13,42,174,176,179. Ordinance No. 2020-014 Governing Public Property and Land Ownership,  2020 Arts 1, 3, 28, 71-74. Agricultural Law 2017-001 Arts. 7-11, 34-42. Pastoral Charter 2001.
indicators.additional_info: Neither the repealed Constitution 1992 nor new Constitution July 2023 protect customary rights. The latter introduces Traditional Authorities as contributing to social cohesion (Art. 179). The Agricultural Law 2017 still lacks  implementation Decree. Land Ordinance 2020 sustains exclusion of unregistered customary lands from recognition as owned; Art 28 (b) confirms certification prerequisite to exclusion from the State private domain. Only individual rights demonstrating development & construction may be registered in Ownership Titles (Art 73).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unequal legal force and effect between lands with Land Titles (mainly urban), proposed customary lands with Certificates, and lands with no covering Certificate or Title. eg. Unregistered customary parcels may be taken immediately at compulsory acquisition (Land 2020 Art. 75). Certified customary lands will have similar protection to land under title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2023 Art.13, Land Ordinance 2020 Art. 28, 71- Arts.
indicators.additional_info: Limitation remains for villages, families and individuals who do not hold Certificates of Customary Possession or Ownership - ie all at this point. All communities are protected from chiefs using their position to claim rights other than personal rights under customary law (2020 Art. 72).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Issue of Customary Certificates has not begun due to lacking Decree. Communes not well equipped to lead or aid communities to set up required Village Land Commissions. Pastoralists have improved access & use under Pastoral Charter 2001 & Transhumance Decree 2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2023-004 on the Territorial Collecitivities. Ordinance No. 2020-014 Governing Public Property and Land Ownership. Law No. 2017-001 On Agricultural Land. Pastoral Charter 2001, Decree on Transhumance, 2010.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Villages are legal persons. The law does not require villages, tribes or other community groups to register corporate entities in order receive a Certificate of Land Possession. Nor must villages register entities for allocation of Village Hunting Zones or right to rehabilitate local forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance No. 2020-014. Agricultural Law No. 2017-001. Law No. 2018-036 on Wildlife and Habitat Protection. Law No. 10-028 on the National Forest Estate.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Titular land administrator is not communities but the 667 Commune Councils headed by Mayors whose jurisdictions include villages & hamlets. Under 2017 law each to set up Village Land Commission, unclear if any instituted. Customary rules operate, governance village-based supervised by Commune. New land records to be kept by Commune.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agricultural Law No. 2017-001. Territorial Collectivities Code Law No. 2023-004.  Land Ordinance No. 2020-014.
indicators.additional_info: Devolutionary governance in Mali began in 1990s, latest legal framework in 2023. Rural communes comprise 'fractions'  (villages & sub-villages). Neighbouring villages by their own agreement comprise the Commune (1990s). Agricultural Law 2017 provides for Village Land Commissions but not main source of authority (Art. 43). Elected Commune Councils responsible for land rights, titling, forest, wildlife and fisheries management. Must consult villages on all land issues, land use plans, management of natural resources, management of public and private communal domains  (2023 Collectivities Law, Arts 2-4 22-26).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All land belongs to the State (Art 3 of Land Code 2020-014). so property rights are rights to the national domain under customary or statutory rules. Both may be held in perpetuity, transferred but the land itself never sold. Leases  & concessions for commercial purposes available including for foreign enterprise. Pastoralists may secure access to local pastures, often on annual fee basis.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance No. 2020-014. Agricultural Law No. 2017-001.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal requirement for consent but consultation obligatory prior to compulsory acquisition or change of land use.  Foreign investments or mining are not subject to consent of the community although must consult with village & Commune. The Mining Law 2023 requires a Local Content Plan be prepared, listing infrastructure & benefits for affected communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance 2020-014 Art. 75. Agricultural  Law No. 2017-001. Mining Code 2023-040, Arts. 1, 119, 121. and Mining: Local Content Law No. 2023-041.
indicators.additional_info: FAO held a workshop in Mali on the terms of the Voluntary Guidelines for Land etc. including FPIC but while its content was agreed in principle , FPIC has not yet been adopted into laws.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Under Agricultural and Collectivities Law 2023 communities own all local trees and govern use under customary rules. Protected species listed under Forest Law subject to permits & fees to fell. Authority over natural resources overlaps among village, commune, and ministry.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agricultural Law 2017-001 Art. 2(6), 7, 11. Territorial Collectivities Law 2023-004 Arts 2, 22-26. Forest Law 2010-028, Arts.  Art. 6 (22-25), 20-24, 41-44.
indicators.additional_info: Community rights under Agricultural Law include lands used for agricultural, pastoral, forestry and fishing activities (2017 Art. 2.6).Forests within Communes classified and protected by Commune (Forest Law 2010) . Villages already create Community Forests, although no specific legal provision for this.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All water belongs to the Public Domain (Land Law 2020 Art.. 9). "Its use belongs to everyone provided that it is not contrary to the public interest' (Water Code 2002 Art. 2). Water use associations are common at village and commune levels under traditional rules.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law 2020-014, Art. 9. Water Code 2002-006, Art. 2-4. Pastoral Code 2001 and Presidential Decree on Transhumance 2010. Agricultural Law 2017-001.
indicators.additional_info: "Water can only be the subject of private appropriation under the conditions set by the provisions in force and in the respect for customary rights recognized for rural populations provided that they are not contrary to the public interest" (Water Code 2002 Art 3). Pastoral communities assured access to water and can control water use within their home territories as do farming communities. Village Land Commissions must include pastoral reps under 2017 law, still not implemented in Mar 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protected & Classified Forests held at national & commune levels. Communes manage buffer zones & subsistence hunting zones for community use and villages may make own Village Hunting Zones (Wildlife Law 2018 Art 12-13, 44). Forests classed as State, Commune & Private, with use rights in Commune Forests (Forest Law 2010 Art. 28-29).
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife Management Law No. 2018-036. Forest Law No 2010-028. Agricultural Law 2017-001.
indicators.additional_info: There is no legal provision for Community Forests in the Forest Code 2010 but communities could declare these due to their authority over village lands inclusive of forest/woodlands under the Agricultural Law 2017. Communes include protected and unprotected forests (confusingly termed 'classified forests' mainly for reforestation and plantations). A village may define a Hunting Zone within its customary domain (2018 Art 12-13). Buffer zones for subsistence also attached to Wildlife Reserves (Art. 44). The 2018 law promotes Community Village Hunting Zones in Protected Forests  Art. 45-50) managed by  Village Hunting Associations. Forest Law 2010 allows forest and riparian communities  to graze, collect dry wood and non-wood products in State and Commune Forests (Art. 42). No legal provision for restitution of any lands.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Agricultural Law 2017 enables customary lands to be removed from the State domain - but only through issue of Certificates, confimed by 2020 Land Law. A village may obtain a Certificate including communal pasture, woodland and reserve lands for expansion. Problematic lack of implementing Decree. Pastoralists secure rights of use, access, transit & water under Pastoral Charter 2001.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2023 Arts. 12,13,42,174,176,179. Ordinance No. 2020-014 Governing Public Property and Land Ownership,  2020 Arts 1, 3, 28, 71-74. Agricultural Law 2017-001 Arts. 7-11, 34-42. Pastoral Charter 2001.
indicators.additional_info: Neither the repealed Constitution 1992 nor new Constitution July 2023 protect customary rights. The latter introduces Traditional Authorities as contributing to social cohesion (Art. 179). The Agricultural Law 2017 still lacks  implementation Decree. Land Ordinance 2020 sustains exclusion of unregistered customary lands from recognition as owned; Art 28 (b) confirms certification prerequisite to exclusion from the State private domain. Only individual rights demonstrating development & construction may be registered in Ownership Titles (Art 73).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unequal legal force and effect between lands with Land Titles (mainly urban), proposed customary lands with Certificates, and lands with no covering Certificate or Title. eg. Unregistered customary parcels may be taken immediately at compulsory acquisition (Land 2020 Art. 75). Certified customary lands will have similar protection to land under title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2023 Art.13, Land Ordinance 2020 Art. 28, 71- Arts.
indicators.additional_info: Limitation remains for villages, families and individuals who do not hold Certificates of Customary Possession or Ownership - ie all at this point. All communities are protected from chiefs using their position to claim rights other than personal rights under customary law (2020 Art. 72).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Issue of Customary Certificates has not begun due to lacking Decree. Communes not well equipped to lead or aid communities to set up required Village Land Commissions. Pastoralists have improved access & use under Pastoral Charter 2001 & Transhumance Decree 2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2023-004 on the Territorial Collecitivities. Ordinance No. 2020-014 Governing Public Property and Land Ownership. Law No. 2017-001 On Agricultural Land. Pastoral Charter 2001, Decree on Transhumance, 2010.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Villages are legal persons. The law does not require villages, tribes or other community groups to register corporate entities in order receive a Certificate of Land Possession. Nor must villages register entities for allocation of Village Hunting Zones or right to rehabilitate local forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance No. 2020-014. Agricultural Law No. 2017-001. Law No. 2018-036 on Wildlife and Habitat Protection. Law No. 10-028 on the National Forest Estate.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Titular land administrator is not communities but the 667 Commune Councils headed by Mayors whose jurisdictions include villages & hamlets. Under 2017 law each to set up Village Land Commission, unclear if any instituted. Customary rules operate, governance village-based supervised by Commune. New land records to be kept by Commune.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agricultural Law No. 2017-001. Territorial Collectivities Code Law No. 2023-004.  Land Ordinance No. 2020-014.
indicators.additional_info: Devolutionary governance in Mali began in 1990s, latest legal framework in 2023. Rural communes comprise 'fractions'  (villages & sub-villages). Neighbouring villages by their own agreement comprise the Commune (1990s). Agricultural Law 2017 provides for Village Land Commissions but not main source of authority (Art. 43). Elected Commune Councils responsible for land rights, titling, forest, wildlife and fisheries management. Must consult villages on all land issues, land use plans, management of natural resources, management of public and private communal domains  (2023 Collectivities Law, Arts 2-4 22-26).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: All land belongs to the State (Art 3 of Land Code 2020-014). so property rights are rights to the national domain under customary or statutory rules. Both may be held in perpetuity, transferred but the land itself never sold. Leases  & concessions for commercial purposes available including for foreign enterprise. Pastoralists may secure access to local pastures, often on annual fee basis.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance No. 2020-014. Agricultural Law No. 2017-001.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No legal requirement for consent but consultation obligatory prior to compulsory acquisition or change of land use.  Foreign investments or mining are not subject to consent of the community although must consult with village & Commune. The Mining Law 2023 requires a Local Content Plan be prepared, listing infrastructure & benefits for affected communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Ordinance 2020-014 Art. 75. Agricultural  Law No. 2017-001. Mining Code 2023-040, Arts. 1, 119, 121. and Mining: Local Content Law No. 2023-041.
indicators.additional_info: FAO held a workshop in Mali on the terms of the Voluntary Guidelines for Land etc. including FPIC but while its content was agreed in principle , FPIC has not yet been adopted into laws.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Under Agricultural and Collectivities Law 2023 communities own all local trees and govern use under customary rules. Protected species listed under Forest Law subject to permits & fees to fell. Authority over natural resources overlaps among village, commune, and ministry.
indicators.law_and_provision: Agricultural Law 2017-001 Art. 2(6), 7, 11. Territorial Collectivities Law 2023-004 Arts 2, 22-26. Forest Law 2010-028, Arts.  Art. 6 (22-25), 20-24, 41-44.
indicators.additional_info: Community rights under Agricultural Law include lands used for agricultural, pastoral, forestry and fishing activities (2017 Art. 2.6).Forests within Communes classified and protected by Commune (Forest Law 2010) . Villages already create Community Forests, although no specific legal provision for this.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All water belongs to the Public Domain (Land Law 2020 Art.. 9). "Its use belongs to everyone provided that it is not contrary to the public interest' (Water Code 2002 Art. 2). Water use associations are common at village and commune levels under traditional rules.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law 2020-014, Art. 9. Water Code 2002-006, Art. 2-4. Pastoral Code 2001 and Presidential Decree on Transhumance 2010. Agricultural Law 2017-001.
indicators.additional_info: "Water can only be the subject of private appropriation under the conditions set by the provisions in force and in the respect for customary rights recognized for rural populations provided that they are not contrary to the public interest" (Water Code 2002 Art 3). Pastoral communities assured access to water and can control water use within their home territories as do farming communities. Village Land Commissions must include pastoral reps under 2017 law, still not implemented in Mar 2025.

MMR.name: Myanmar

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities (indigenous and non-indigenous)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Myanmar has not yet enacted a law that recognizes community or indigenous land rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Vacant, Fallow and Virgin Lands Management Law 2012; Farmland Law 2012; National Land Use Policy (May 2015 draft); Constitution of Myanmar; Association Law (2014)
indicators.additional_info: A recent USAID report (Feb. 2016) discusses the current legal framework of Myanmar and how new legislation to respect and protect community tenure rights can be implemented. See Report: http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/USAID_Land_Tenure_Community_Tenure_Report.pdf
