MNG.name: Mongolia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All rural communities
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Tenure Specialist & Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Tenure classes are State and Private land. Pasturelands at 75% of country area are the major State asset. Their use along with use of public lands in villages and urban areas are defined as 'common purpose and use lands', including water points, wells and salt licks within pasture lands. The State may also issue possession licences to citizens as individuals, families or organizations for farms, houses, and other premises, for winter and spring camps, and enclosed hayfields or breeding areas. However, pastureland is open to all users, unavailable for ownership or exclusive possession (Art. 6.2.1 Law on Possession of Land, 2002), in practice encroached by rising number of commercial use contracts issued to foreigners. Exclusive ownership of houses and farms etc are available to citizens at higher cost, largely taken up in urban domains. No legal provision for collective rural landholding inclusive of pasturelands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997. Civil Code 2002.
indicators.additional_info: "The State may give for private ownership only land other than pastures and areas under public use or reserved for the State's special needs and only to citizens of Mongolia" (Constitution, 1992, Art. 6.3). Art. 54. of Law on Land 2002 permits pastureland users 'to take land use traditions into consideration to protect the land' and in resolving conflicts (Art. 54.10).  The Civil Code 2002 provides for family tenure as a default (Art. 125) and recognizes herder and other groups as legal persons for activities (Civil Code 25-26). Annual allocation of rights to pastureland by local authorities occurs outside of issue of possession licences. Art.54.1 provides that soum (village or ward) and district Governors, taking land use traditions and other factors in management activities, and in Art. 54.2 direct that "summer and autumn settlements and rangelands shall be allocated to baghs and hot ails and shall be used collectively. Winter and spring pastures shall be prevented from livestock grazing during summer and autumn, and shall be carefully protected with public efforts"  Draft Rangeland law to conserve diminishing and degrading pasturelands through issue of exclusive rights has not materialized, likely due todifficulties of significant multiple community use of many seasonal pastures, and with nomadic pastoralists moving up to four or more times a year.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Tenure over pastureland is insecure for other than issued annual occupation rights to specific camps or use of pastures, and although take precedence, do not extinguish use contracts issued to foreigners to the same land for mining or commercial agriculture. Compulsory acquisition is also unfavourable to unregistered possessors and those relying on common purpose and use of pasturelands as they receive no compensation. Registered owners are eligible for compensation by negotation, including replacement land of comparable size, location, status and quality
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997. Government Notice No. 34 of 2020 on National Shepherds Programme.
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution and Law on Land 2002 only provides private ownership rights to citizens-families, and excludes pasture land and common tenure land from the categories of land that can be vested in families or communities as owners, even on a temporary Possession Licence basis (15-60 years, renewable). Customary norms of tenure and management may be used by families and groups in using and managing pasturelands (Art 54.1). Support for 'traditional customs and norms of use' of pasture land in Law on Land 2002 and of disseminating traditional knowledge to shepherds under approved Shepherds Programme 2020. This does not add up to communal or collective pasture ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Articles 31- 34 of Law on Land 2002 provides clear procedures for requesting a possession contract and issue of licence on its basis. The contract must include a map, description of the land, etc. This is conducted at district level. Affordability is addressed through issue of gratis licences of possession if application is the first by the family, and/or in other unelaborated circumstances which may include lack of finance.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 32 provides procedures for communities to acquire licenses to land. Article 34.6 provides that contracts must include "a map showing the size, locations and boundaries of the land" and "characteristics of the land and its quality." Article 36 indicates that there are fees associated with obtaining a licence.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law is insufficiently clear on status of social groups larger than families as legal persons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Code, 2002. Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Government Resolution No. 34 of 2020 on National Shepherds Programme.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 25.1 of Civil Code 2002 describes legal persons as an 'organized unity with concrete mission and engaged in regular activities, which is entitled to own, possess, use and dispose of its property'. Art. 25.4 provides that "if not otherwised in the Law, several legal persons may merge with the purpose to coordinate their activities, thus merging they will retain their legal person status". This could mean that a herding group or village, or other social entity could be acknowledged as a legal person. Art. 125 specifically treats the family as a legal person (Art. 125). Art. 126 lists the common property of family members. Article 23.1.1 of Law on Land Ownership 2002 provides for family or part of the family if specified to be the registered owner. No provision for this in respect of groups, villages in respect of use of pasturelands. Promotion of pastoral cooperatives is one task of the Mongolia Shepherd Programme 2020 but for activities not ownership. Scored as 3 as the law is insufficiently clear on status of social groups larger than families as legal persons.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Articles 17-24 of the 2002 Law on Land indicates that government bodies retain authority over land allocated under a possession contract, which indicates that communities do not have ultimate legal authority. However, in respect of pasturelands, customary norms of use and management are legally encouraged to be applied by the family, group or village. Herder associations have legal status under Art. 481.1 of the Civil Code, not as owners, only as pasture land managers. Self governance is supported across Mongolia under the Administrative Law 2006, including considerable citizen public meetings at all levels.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law of Mongolia on Administrative and Territorial Units and Their Governance, Dec. 2006. Civil Code 2002.
indicators.additional_info: By 2017 more than 2000 herder groups for community based rangeland management (CBRM) existed as mobiized by donors, with various names from group to partners, to association or water user associations. Support for these self-organized groups as legal persons is provided by Article 481.1 of Civil Code which states that 'People are allowed to build up an association or a community and run their acitivites under a co-mangement contract'. Much debate on forms of allocating rights to at least home winter and spring pasturelands but no law on pasturelands resulting until the present.  Note that terminology of administrative units varies by urban and rural domains: overall, 21 Provinces (Aimag); 333 sub-provinces (Districts, Soum, or Duureg), and 1664 hamlets/settlements (Bagh). Khot ail are family based winter and spring campsites (excluding pasture).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Mixed. Ownership entitlements held by families for houseplot or farm have no time limit. However, more affordable possession licences, and dominant in rural areas, are for 15-60 years only, renewable only 40 years at a time. Art. 30, 54, Law on Land. Neither ownership, licences or contracts are available over pasturelands for rangeland use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997.
indicators.additional_info: Article 30.1 of the 2002 Law on Land provides that "the state-owned land may be given possession with a license to Mongolian citizens...for a duration of 15 to 60 years. The land possession license may be extended for not longer than 40 years at a time."

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership does not provide for a public consultation process when the government decides to acquire land for "special needs of the state."
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 35- 37, Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Art.. 42-43 Law on Law 2002 (Possession).
indicators.additional_info: Under Arts 35-37 of Law on Land Ownership, no provision for consultation at compulsory acquisition. Under Arts. 42-43 Law on Land 2002 (Possession) 2002, does provide for payment of compensation for removal of citizens under possession licences prior to expiration of the contract for a public purpose. Art. 43.6 is explicit that there is no compensation for use contracts with citizens, companies or organizations (mainly foreigners). The law does not explicitly grant communities the right to give consent prior to acquisition by governments and outsiders. Note that while the law is lacking, reports suggest that consultation is widely practised by district administrations (duureg).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A Mongolian citizen-landowner may acquire ownership and use rights to forests planted on his or her property under a possession licence.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4.2, 4.4.1, 4.4.2,  Mongolian Law on Forests 2012; Law on Land 2002
indicators.additional_info: Art. 4.4.1 establishes that State Administrative Central Body shall grant ownership of forest resources to aimags, capital, and soums' (villages)'. Article 4.4.2 provides that district governments shall grant tenure rights and right to use forest resources to forest user groups, economic entities or organizations on a contractual basis indicating specific duration and conditions (covers possession licences and user rights, and 'tenure' in these instances is not absolute ownership.)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly establish indigenous or local community rights to water. However, in the original water law of 1995, communities are entitled to use rights as citizens, and are free to use water for domestic purposes (Art. 8, The Mongolian Law on Water and Mineral Water Use Fees (1995). This law is now replaced with Law on Water, May 17, 2012, but which does give details under Chapter Four at Art 29 where Water User is listed but not defined.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 3, 8, The Mongolian Law on Water and Mineral Water Use Fees (1995), REVI
indicators.additional_info: Art. 3 of Law on Water of 1005 provided "citizens of Mongolia, foreign citizens, persons with no citizenship, economic entites, and organizations using water, mineral waters and/or riparian zones in Mongolia for any purpose shall be fee payers." However, Art. 8  provided fee exemptions for water used for domestic purposes- household needs, livestock, animals, and family vegetable gardens, extinguishing fires, and reuse of water for industrial technological needs; this is highly likely to remain the case but is not provided in the official English text of the consolidated Water Law, 2012.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: All natural resources belong to the State (on behalf of the people).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Special Protected Areas, 1994. Forest Law, 2012. Environmental Protection Law, 1995.
indicators.additional_info: Mongolian law enables forest user group to manage and use so-called 'tenure forests' which mean forests which they are allocated under possessory contracts. (Art. 3.1.5, Forest Law, May 2012 (as amended).  There is also provision for granting ownership of a planted forests and its non-timber forest products to provinces or district authorities (Art. 4.3, 4.4 and which shall grant tenure rights and the right to use the forest to a forest user group, economic entity or organization on a contractual basis (Art. 4.4.2).  This excludes Protected Areas as defined by the Law of Special Protected Areas, 1994. The Environment Law, 1995, enables village representatives to develop rules for protecting hayfields, pasture and water sources which are not under possession certificates (Art. 18,). The Law on Special Protected Areas permits rural households members to use Strictly Protected Areas in Limited Use Zones (Art. 11.10, including for grazing (Art. 17)) and Nature Reserves for domestic, traditional uses (Art. 21.1). Art. 38 of the Law on Special Protected Areas provides  that "citizens or economic entities using land in special protected areas have the rights described in Art. 45 of the Law on Land" and in addition have the obligation to "[take] measures to preserve the land and restore it to its original conditions at their own expense." Note that pastoralist families form formal associations to manage if not own pastures to limit rampant degradation.. By 2017 more than 2000 herder groups for community based rangeland management (CBRM) existed; support as legal entities for both forest user groups and herder associations exists in Article 481.1 of Civil Code which states that 'People are allowed to build up an association or a community and run their acitivites under a co-mangement contract'. Sustained debate since 2000s on significant level of request by pastoralists to be allocated possession rights to  at least home winter and spring pasturelands but no law on this has eventuated as of 2024.

local_communities_entries.framework: All rural communities
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Tenure Specialist & Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Tenure classes are State and Private land. Pasturelands at 75% of country area are the major State asset. Their use along with use of public lands in villages and urban areas are defined as 'common purpose and use lands', including water points, wells and salt licks within pasture lands. The State may also issue possession licences to citizens as individuals, families or organizations for farms, houses, and other premises, for winter and spring camps, and enclosed hayfields or breeding areas. However, pastureland is open to all users, unavailable for ownership or exclusive possession (Art. 6.2.1 Law on Possession of Land, 2002), in practice encroached by rising number of commercial use contracts issued to foreigners. Exclusive ownership of houses and farms etc are available to citizens at higher cost, largely taken up in urban domains. No legal provision for collective rural landholding inclusive of pasturelands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997. Civil Code 2002.
indicators.additional_info: "The State may give for private ownership only land other than pastures and areas under public use or reserved for the State's special needs and only to citizens of Mongolia" (Constitution, 1992, Art. 6.3). Art. 54. of Law on Land 2002 permits pastureland users 'to take land use traditions into consideration to protect the land' and in resolving conflicts (Art. 54.10).  The Civil Code 2002 provides for family tenure as a default (Art. 125) and recognizes herder and other groups as legal persons for activities (Civil Code 25-26). Annual allocation of rights to pastureland by local authorities occurs outside of issue of possession licences. Art.54.1 provides that soum (village or ward) and district Governors, taking land use traditions and other factors in management activities, and in Art. 54.2 direct that "summer and autumn settlements and rangelands shall be allocated to baghs and hot ails and shall be used collectively. Winter and spring pastures shall be prevented from livestock grazing during summer and autumn, and shall be carefully protected with public efforts"  Draft Rangeland law to conserve diminishing and degrading pasturelands through issue of exclusive rights has not materialized, likely due todifficulties of significant multiple community use of many seasonal pastures, and with nomadic pastoralists moving up to four or more times a year.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Tenure over pastureland is insecure for other than issued annual occupation rights to specific camps or use of pastures, and although take precedence, do not extinguish use contracts issued to foreigners to the same land for mining or commercial agriculture. Compulsory acquisition is also unfavourable to unregistered possessors and those relying on common purpose and use of pasturelands as they receive no compensation. Registered owners are eligible for compensation by negotation, including replacement land of comparable size, location, status and quality
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997. Government Notice No. 34 of 2020 on National Shepherds Programme.
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution and Law on Land 2002 only provides private ownership rights to citizens-families, and excludes pasture land and common tenure land from the categories of land that can be vested in families or communities as owners, even on a temporary Possession Licence basis (15-60 years, renewable). Customary norms of tenure and management may be used by families and groups in using and managing pasturelands (Art 54.1). Support for 'traditional customs and norms of use' of pasture land in Law on Land 2002 and of disseminating traditional knowledge to shepherds under approved Shepherds Programme 2020. This does not add up to communal or collective pasture ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Articles 31- 34 of Law on Land 2002 provides clear procedures for requesting a possession contract and issue of licence on its basis. The contract must include a map, description of the land, etc. This is conducted at district level. Affordability is addressed through issue of gratis licences of possession if application is the first by the family, and/or in other unelaborated circumstances which may include lack of finance.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 32 provides procedures for communities to acquire licenses to land. Article 34.6 provides that contracts must include "a map showing the size, locations and boundaries of the land" and "characteristics of the land and its quality." Article 36 indicates that there are fees associated with obtaining a licence.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law is insufficiently clear on status of social groups larger than families as legal persons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Code, 2002. Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Government Resolution No. 34 of 2020 on National Shepherds Programme.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 25.1 of Civil Code 2002 describes legal persons as an 'organized unity with concrete mission and engaged in regular activities, which is entitled to own, possess, use and dispose of its property'. Art. 25.4 provides that "if not otherwised in the Law, several legal persons may merge with the purpose to coordinate their activities, thus merging they will retain their legal person status". This could mean that a herding group or village, or other social entity could be acknowledged as a legal person. Art. 125 specifically treats the family as a legal person (Art. 125). Art. 126 lists the common property of family members. Article 23.1.1 of Law on Land Ownership 2002 provides for family or part of the family if specified to be the registered owner. No provision for this in respect of groups, villages in respect of use of pasturelands. Promotion of pastoral cooperatives is one task of the Mongolia Shepherd Programme 2020 but for activities not ownership. Scored as 3 as the law is insufficiently clear on status of social groups larger than families as legal persons.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Articles 17-24 of the 2002 Law on Land indicates that government bodies retain authority over land allocated under a possession contract, which indicates that communities do not have ultimate legal authority. However, in respect of pasturelands, customary norms of use and management are legally encouraged to be applied by the family, group or village. Herder associations have legal status under Art. 481.1 of the Civil Code, not as owners, only as pasture land managers. Self governance is supported across Mongolia under the Administrative Law 2006, including considerable citizen public meetings at all levels.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law of Mongolia on Administrative and Territorial Units and Their Governance, Dec. 2006. Civil Code 2002.
indicators.additional_info: By 2017 more than 2000 herder groups for community based rangeland management (CBRM) existed as mobiized by donors, with various names from group to partners, to association or water user associations. Support for these self-organized groups as legal persons is provided by Article 481.1 of Civil Code which states that 'People are allowed to build up an association or a community and run their acitivites under a co-mangement contract'. Much debate on forms of allocating rights to at least home winter and spring pasturelands but no law on pasturelands resulting until the present.  Note that terminology of administrative units varies by urban and rural domains: overall, 21 Provinces (Aimag); 333 sub-provinces (Districts, Soum, or Duureg), and 1664 hamlets/settlements (Bagh). Khot ail are family based winter and spring campsites (excluding pasture).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Mixed. Ownership entitlements held by families for houseplot or farm have no time limit. However, more affordable possession licences, and dominant in rural areas, are for 15-60 years only, renewable only 40 years at a time. Art. 30, 54, Law on Land. Neither ownership, licences or contracts are available over pasturelands for rangeland use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Mongolia, 1992 (amended 2001, 2019). Law To Regulate Possession and Use of State-Owned Land and Other Issues, 2002 ('Law on Land'). Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Law on Registration of Immovable Property, 1997.
indicators.additional_info: Article 30.1 of the 2002 Law on Land provides that "the state-owned land may be given possession with a license to Mongolian citizens...for a duration of 15 to 60 years. The land possession license may be extended for not longer than 40 years at a time."

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership does not provide for a public consultation process when the government decides to acquire land for "special needs of the state."
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 35- 37, Law on Allocation of Land to Mongolian Citizens for Ownership, 2002. Art.. 42-43 Law on Law 2002 (Possession).
indicators.additional_info: Under Arts 35-37 of Law on Land Ownership, no provision for consultation at compulsory acquisition. Under Arts. 42-43 Law on Land 2002 (Possession) 2002, does provide for payment of compensation for removal of citizens under possession licences prior to expiration of the contract for a public purpose. Art. 43.6 is explicit that there is no compensation for use contracts with citizens, companies or organizations (mainly foreigners). The law does not explicitly grant communities the right to give consent prior to acquisition by governments and outsiders. Note that while the law is lacking, reports suggest that consultation is widely practised by district administrations (duureg).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A Mongolian citizen-landowner may acquire ownership and use rights to forests planted on his or her property under a possession licence.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4.2, 4.4.1, 4.4.2,  Mongolian Law on Forests 2012; Law on Land 2002
indicators.additional_info: Art. 4.4.1 establishes that State Administrative Central Body shall grant ownership of forest resources to aimags, capital, and soums' (villages)'. Article 4.4.2 provides that district governments shall grant tenure rights and right to use forest resources to forest user groups, economic entities or organizations on a contractual basis indicating specific duration and conditions (covers possession licences and user rights, and 'tenure' in these instances is not absolute ownership.)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly establish indigenous or local community rights to water. However, in the original water law of 1995, communities are entitled to use rights as citizens, and are free to use water for domestic purposes (Art. 8, The Mongolian Law on Water and Mineral Water Use Fees (1995). This law is now replaced with Law on Water, May 17, 2012, but which does give details under Chapter Four at Art 29 where Water User is listed but not defined.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 3, 8, The Mongolian Law on Water and Mineral Water Use Fees (1995), REVI
indicators.additional_info: Art. 3 of Law on Water of 1005 provided "citizens of Mongolia, foreign citizens, persons with no citizenship, economic entites, and organizations using water, mineral waters and/or riparian zones in Mongolia for any purpose shall be fee payers." However, Art. 8  provided fee exemptions for water used for domestic purposes- household needs, livestock, animals, and family vegetable gardens, extinguishing fires, and reuse of water for industrial technological needs; this is highly likely to remain the case but is not provided in the official English text of the consolidated Water Law, 2012.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: All natural resources belong to the State (on behalf of the people).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Special Protected Areas, 1994. Forest Law, 2012. Environmental Protection Law, 1995.
indicators.additional_info: Mongolian law enables forest user group to manage and use so-called 'tenure forests' which mean forests which they are allocated under possessory contracts. (Art. 3.1.5, Forest Law, May 2012 (as amended).  There is also provision for granting ownership of a planted forests and its non-timber forest products to provinces or district authorities (Art. 4.3, 4.4 and which shall grant tenure rights and the right to use the forest to a forest user group, economic entity or organization on a contractual basis (Art. 4.4.2).  This excludes Protected Areas as defined by the Law of Special Protected Areas, 1994. The Environment Law, 1995, enables village representatives to develop rules for protecting hayfields, pasture and water sources which are not under possession certificates (Art. 18,). The Law on Special Protected Areas permits rural households members to use Strictly Protected Areas in Limited Use Zones (Art. 11.10, including for grazing (Art. 17)) and Nature Reserves for domestic, traditional uses (Art. 21.1). Art. 38 of the Law on Special Protected Areas provides  that "citizens or economic entities using land in special protected areas have the rights described in Art. 45 of the Law on Land" and in addition have the obligation to "[take] measures to preserve the land and restore it to its original conditions at their own expense." Note that pastoralist families form formal associations to manage if not own pastures to limit rampant degradation.. By 2017 more than 2000 herder groups for community based rangeland management (CBRM) existed; support as legal entities for both forest user groups and herder associations exists in Article 481.1 of Civil Code which states that 'People are allowed to build up an association or a community and run their acitivites under a co-mangement contract'. Sustained debate since 2000s on significant level of request by pastoralists to be allocated possession rights to  at least home winter and spring pasturelands but no law on this has eventuated as of 2024.

MOZ.name: Mozambique

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: While land belongs to the nation, rights to exclusive hold & use land may be under customary or statutory law, confirmed by issue of same type of deed, DUAT; follows  survey & mapping. Not compulsory to register but  since 1997 nearly 3,000 of est. 5,000 communities have secured DUATS in interim/final form. Governed by customary law. National Land Policy 2022 confirms approach.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004, Art. 109. Land Law No. 19 of 1997. Land Law Regulations Decree No. 66 of 1998. Decree 43 of 2010. Land Policy and Its Implementation Strategy, Resolution 45/2022.
indicators.additional_info: Customary law is an acknowledged element of Mozambican law (Constitution Art.4, 223).Community lands protected  to same degree as  non-customary acquisition with same title mechanism. Lack of registration does not prejudice rights of land use and benefit on basis of customary rights, or occupation in good faith for 10+ years (Land Law Art. 12-14). DUATS for economic activities are subject to maximum term of 50 years renewable, whereas DUATS acquired by local communities have no fixed term (Art. 17).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Equitable protection of customary/statutory rights as  communities are recognised owners of rights of use & benefit with/without formalization, includes off-farm resources. Same compensation at compulsory acquisition but more vulnerable to reclassification of lands for investors, conservation, etc. reduced,  but not removed by 2010 law. Law 181/2010 & Decree 31/2012. Law 16/2014.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004. Decree on Benefit-Sharing, No. 93 of 2005. Land Planning Law, No. 19 of 2007. Planning Decree No. 23 of 2008. Regulation Land Management, Expropriation for Land, Planning Diploma No. 181 of 2010. Resettlement Regulation Decree No. 31 of 2012. Conservation Law No. 16 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Positive protection as (a) legal owners of rights of use and benefit without registration, provision to delimit and register lands as communities (Land Law 1997, Regulations 1998, Technical Annex 2000); (b) equitable compensation and resettlement at compulsory acquisition for economic projects (Land Planning Law, No. 19/2007, Regulations Decree No. 23 /2008, Ministerial Diploma No. 181/2010 Directive of Expropriation for Land Planning, Resettlement Regulation Decree 31/2012); (c) revenue sharing from protected areas, opportunities for public-private-community partnerships (Decree No. 93/2005). But wide grounds for compulsory acquisition or restrictive zoning for economic projects, tourism, etc sustaining vulnerability of community based land rights.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Formalization of rights is voluntary, straightforward, cheaper since 2009 and more inclusive of community members. Communities, groups, individuals may apply. Formalization encouraged and donor-funded NGOs remain prominent facilitators.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No. 19 of 1997. Regulations of Land Law Decree 66 of 1998. Technical Annex to Regulations on community delimitation and titling (2000). Law of State Local Bodies No. 8 of 2003. Ministerial Diplomas No. 67 of 2009, No. 158 of 2011 and No. 43 of 2010.
indicators.additional_info: Communities are now to participate in delimitation of community area, costs to be decided by local Public Administration (Diplomas 2009, 2010, 2011). Procedure straightforward, but costly. NGO support key to progress. Law of State Local Bodies, No. 8/2003, Ministerial Diploma No. 67/2009 require Local Consultative Councils. Diploma No. 158/2011 requires minimum two consultative meetings. Diploma No. 43/2010 makes delimitation  a joint effort of the District Administrator,  Cadastre Service, Advisory Councils of Villages and Towns, members of community, owners or occupant neighbours, and the applicant.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities and groups for purpose of formalization recognized as legal persons. Communities may acquire title on basis of custom or occupancy for 10+ years. Community chooses its own name to be registered.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law, No. 19 of 1997, Art. 10, 13. Land Law Regulations No. 66 of 1998, Art. 12.
indicators.additional_info: The title issued to local communities shall be issued in the name of the community, which name shall be decided upon by the community' Art. 13.4. Land Law, No. 19/1997. Joint holding by several local communities is governed by co-ownership of property in Arts. 1403 ff of Civil Code.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Strong Constitutional recognition of Traditional Authorities and customary law, but weak definition of TA roles & no requirement to elect advisory committees. Local Authorities Law 2023 only reaches District level.  Land & Natural Resource Management Committees exist, triggered by projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004.  Law on Local State Organs & Regulations No. 8 of 2003. Decree 15 of 2000 on liaison between State bodies and communities. Ministerial Diplomas No. 67 of 2006 and No. 43 of 2010. Land Law No. 19 of 1997 and Regulations 1998. Local Authorities Act, No 12 of 2023.
indicators.additional_info: Mild improvement towards devolutionary governance by requirement for Local Consultation Councils required under Diplomas 67/2006 and  43/2010.  Communities are to 'participate' in management of natural resources, conflict resolution, titling, and identification of community land areas (Art. 24 Land Law19/1997).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Rights of land use and benefit have no fixed term if acquired by communities through occupation, or for residential or family use. The right to inherit lands is constitutionally entrenched (Art. 83) and in Land Law (Art. 17).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law No. 19 of 1997 Art. 17.2.
indicators.additional_info: Right acquired for economic activities are limited to terms of 50 years, renewable once. Lands may be held perpetuity by communities on the basis of customary law (Art. 17 Land Law No. 19 of 1997).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No consent of communities required at reclassification of their lands for public interests, active for tourism, conservation, commercial faring, mining, etc. Improved requirements to consult (Decree 31/2012) and intentions under 2022 land policy to conduct takings only with participatory planning from outset, compensation to include valuation of lost uses and customs etc (Pillar 6).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004. Land Planning Law, 19 of 2007, Decree 23 of 2008 Regulation Land Management, Expropriation for Land Planning Diploma 181 of 2010. Resettlement Regulation Decree 31 of 2012. Diploma 67 of 2009 under Land Law 1997. National Land Policy  Resolution 45/2022.
indicators.additional_info: Interference in community lands derives from laws dealing with disasters, declaration of protected areas, special development zones including for tourism,  security, land use planning for developments incl. for private investors. Consultation requirements rising as in Decree 31/ 2012 on Resettlement (Art. 13-14). Procedures for inclusive decision-making at community level improving (Ministerial Diploma No. 67/2009 ). But the Constitution has not been amended to require compensation be paid prior to forced removal. Nor is relocation indicated as the last resort.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: While all land & natural resources are national property, access, use and benefit belongs to community on whose land trees fall. Own consumption subject to customary rules and exempt from forest exploitation fees (Forest Act 2023 Art. 51). Compensation at compulsory acquisition includes planted trees; Diploma 181/2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Act, No. 17 of 2023. Conservation Act No. 16 of 2014. Ministerial Diploma No. 181 of 2010 On  Process of Expropriation for Purposes of Land Planning.
indicators.additional_info: Local communities recognized as having rights to beneficial use in the forest heritage of their respective areas (2023 Art. 13).  Government required to organize participatory forest  management, and which 'presupposes the safeguarding of their rights, including that of free, prior and informed consents in the decision-making process' (Art. 25). Provision for 'community conservation areas' under The Conservation Act 2014 enables communities to manage natural resources by customary rules as long as compliant with national legislation (Art. 22).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water as all land & resources belong to nation. Distinction  drawn between common and private use. Common use includes domestic & personal use, stock watering and small scale irrigation. Not subject to permits or fees, conducted locally in accordance with traditional norms.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2004. Water Law, No. 16 of 1991. Regulations on Water Licences and Concessions, Decree No. 43 of 2007.
indicators.additional_info: Water Law 1991 stipulates that all water constitutes the public water domain (Art. 1) Divides water in common and private use, the latter subject to licences (Art.21.1). Common use means water is achieved without mechanised means, meets domestic, persons and family needs, livestock watering and small-scale irrigation (Art. 21.2). Common water use is free, not subject to permits, and undertaken in accordance with general of traditional (customary) systems  (Art. 22).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities may request part of a state Protected Area be set aside for them, also must be paid shares from conservation efforts incl. tourism operations (Conservation Act 2014 Arts. 11, 49).  Community defined Forests of Use, Historical & Cultural Value & Community Conservation Areas within community domains governed by customary laws (Forest Act 2023. Conservation Act 2014.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004, Art. 98.3. Forest Act, No 17 of 2023. Conservation Law No. 16 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: The founding framework for conservation lies in  constitutional definition of 'public domain' as existing in the public, local authority and community domains (Art. 98.3). 'Forest heritage' includes forests on community lands of Local Use, Historical and Cultural Value (Forest Law 2023 Art. 31) Also Community Conservation Areas (Conservation Law Art. 18, 22). Communities affected by State or Local Authority Protected Areas have rights to access use & benefit, to request special parts to be allocated to themselves, to be engaged and paid for conservation activities and to gain shares from commercial operations (Conservation  Law Art. 11,49).

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: While land belongs to the nation, rights to exclusive hold & use land may be under customary or statutory law, confirmed by issue of same type of deed, DUAT; follows  survey & mapping. Not compulsory to register but  since 1997 nearly 3,000 of est. 5,000 communities have secured DUATS in interim/final form. Governed by customary law. National Land Policy 2022 confirms approach.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2004, Art. 109. Land Law No. 19 of 1997. Land Law Regulations Decree No. 66 of 1998. Decree 43 of 2010. Land Policy and Its Implementation Strategy, Resolution 45/2022.
indicators.additional_info: Customary law is an acknowledged element of Mozambican law (Constitution Art.4, 223).Community lands protected  to same degree as  non-customary acquisition with same title mechanism. Lack of registration does not prejudice rights of land use and benefit on basis of customary rights, or occupation in good faith for 10+ years (Land Law Art. 12-14). DUATS for economic activities are subject to maximum term of 50 years renewable, whereas DUATS acquired by local communities have no fixed term (Art. 17).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully

Law 16/2014.

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Tenure Specialist & Prof. M. Baro, Arizona State University

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary law abolished in 1983 law. Ownership recognized only if under registered private title. Chief-allocated private parcels must be developed & registered. Art. 36-44. Rest is 'vacant' (Indirass) land. Extra  'living space' allocated to each settlement of 50+ dwellings but not under collective title. Pastoral Code 2000 protects rights of 5% of pop who are pastoralists, using 55% country.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 (2017) Art. 15. Land Ordinance 1983 No. 83.127. Application Decree No. 2010-080. Land Code  Decree of 25 Nov 1930 governing expropriation.  Pastoral Code Law No. 2000-044. Arts. 12, 13, 24, 25).
indicators.additional_info: Constitution protects individually registered property only (Art. 15, 1991). Art. 3 of Land Ordinance abolished customary tenure to eliminate landlordism & slavery pervading  Arab-African relationships. In practice tribal & community leaders allocate rights according to custom. Traditional leaders also members of district & provincial decision-making bodies. Art. 6 of 1983 law orders  subdivision of group arable lands Senegal Valley, including making these available to Arabs not local to the area. Pastoral Code protects clan lands, aims to limit conflicts with farmers via arbitration forums but disputes continue over scarce arable lands in 38% country, between violently evicted but returned black farmers & pastoralists.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unequal legal effect of customary & statutory tenure (the latter exisr as registered parcels). Undeveloped lands (commons) are State land but pastoralists guaranteed access. Compensation at takings given to those holding licences, concessions or titles. Pro-investor Code since 2012 accelerating losses. Land Ordinance 1983 (Decree 2010), Pastoral Code 2000. Expropriation Decree 1930.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2017, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code. Decree of 25 Nov 1930 governing expropriation.
indicators.additional_info: Law provides for compensation in cash or kind to those holding licences to occupy, or for allocated rural concessions, including issue of land of same value.  LGAF 2014 reports that "Where the right is not registered but exists on a continual basis on rural or urban land, the holder may be issued a certificate of ownership after an investigation into the date and condition  of the land". One case of compensation to a group recorded where held by a registered agricultural group LGAF 2014 also reports that "the riparian populations cannot protect their land against the installation of latifundia type farms". Customary lands vulnerable to aggressive state policy co-opting 'undeveloped' land as State property, pro-investor strategy & law, lack of collective land titles, and sustained conflict between Arab & African communities over cultivable lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal opportunity for clans or communities to register lands collectively. The exception is where the land was held by a Cooperative prior to 1960 as cultivated land. An exception for pastoralists who may secure contracts for exclusive grazing zones, otherwise unregistered access guaranteed. Pastoral Code, 2000.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code
indicators.additional_info: No legal provision for communities to register land as a customary entitlement. Orientation of laws entirely to individual holders. Only one case of a pre-1960 farming cooperative issued collective title. Pastoralists hold usufructs as groups, not registrable under Pastoral Code 2000.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for traditional communities to be recognized as legal persons, exception being  farming Cooperatives registered prior to 1960 who still share the cultivated land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code
indicators.additional_info: No legal route for tribe, clan or village to register as a legal person, an effect of 1983 law abolishing customary tenure. Meanwhile registration of large or smaller estates in names of feudal landlords, chiefs & notables, taking from poorer customary owners. Some rural communities still hold land but without legal backing.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communities are de facto if not legal land administrators. No legal provision for a tribe, clan or village (communities) to regulate land relations, although in practice do so.  Additionally, special areas allocated to pastoral groups, and 'vital spaces' up to 100 ha to farming settlements, regulated by these groups.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code
indicators.additional_info: There is no national registry of land in Mauritania and a plethora of state authorities with duties and powers over land. Reported as conflicting and conflicted. Main theme is legal centralization of authority to the national government.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The State owns the soil & 'property rights' to the soil exist only if granted/registered by State. Customary rights held in perpetuity principally via inheritance has no legal force. No term specified for usufructs given to pastoral clans. Declining utility of long-term occupancy & use as protection. Civil discontent continues between Arab semi-nomadic & African farming communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code
indicators.additional_info: Only individuals have legally acknowledged rights (if registered) and these re limited to farm and house lands. Also state issued concessions, licences or permits to occupy a specific parcel.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The consent of landholders is not required when land is taken for a public purpose. This applies to registered individual landholders on cultivated lands, urban plots and to unregistered land holders - the rural majority. No legal requirement for consultation. Appeal is possible but the law does not specify if this includes unregistered landholders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2017, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code.
indicators.additional_info: The law and practice are different. On the whole, both pastoral and farming communities still operate under  customary law - until the State intervenes. In addition, while collective rights are denied these are in effect recognized by provisions of the pastoral code, and also in a minor way  by  issue of  100ha of 'vital space' around each village.  Following procedures of colonial laws, two districts (Trarza and Dakhlet Mouadhibou) are still registered as the collective property of the inhabitants.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: By omission of otherwise in law, titled and untitled landholders own and may use trees on their respective lands;  limitations on tree use  specified only for Protected Forests as held by national or local governments. Forest Code 2007 Arts 44-46.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, Law No. 97-007, Articles 44-46.
indicators.additional_info: Article 44: "User rights are strictly limited to the personal and family needs of users". Article 45: "The rights of use exercised in the forests of the State or a Commune may be restricted or suspended only for reasons of safeguarding the forest heritage by the relevant forestry services". Article 46: "The rights of use of the riparian populations for reforestation and restoration must comply with this law and its implementing regulations. Exercise of these rights is subordinated to the condition of the stands and vegetation and may be restricted or suspended to safeguard forest heritage".

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the State and is inalienable and imprescriptible. Use rights recognized, with priority on socio-economic needs, then stock watering, then industrial needs. Customary, community-based water rules acknowledged for pastoralists. Water Code 1986. Land Ordinance 1983. Pastoral Code 2000.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code as Ordinance No. 85-144 of 4 July 1986. Order 83.127 of June 1983 nationalizing land and abolishing customary tenure (Art. 3).  Pastoral Code, Act. 444 of 2000.
indicators.additional_info: Water is a national resource (Water Code of 1986 Art. 3).  Property rights including water converted into use rights (1983, 1986). Socio-economic needs of the population take precedence in allocation of water (1986, Art. 105), followed by needs related to cattle rearing, agriculture, silviculture, fishing and reafforestation projects, and finally for industrial and agro-industrial needs (Art. 106). The Pastoral Code 2000 recognizes the collective basis of pastoralism and community based regulation of resource access and use including  water; pastoral lands were recognized as inalienable national lands, reserved for pastoralism. Water developments to be in accordance with traditional pastoral needs (Arts. 13, 26)

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No provision for communities to own Protected Areas but communities may form Wildlife Management Associations and Communes (local governments) or one community as appropriate may own & manage protected forests called 'Communal Parks'. Art. 6 of Law 2018. Only vague implication that any community could declare a Protected Community Forest.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 041 of 2018 Hunting and Wildlife Management. Implementation Decree No. 066 of 2023  Law No. 045 of 2000 Environmental Code. Forest Code No. 055 of 2007.
indicators.additional_info: Natural resources are national property (Environmental Code 2000 Art. 4). Law on Hunting and Wildlife Management (No. 2018-041) allows wilaya (districts) or communes (village clusters, occasionally a single village) to control/manage Communal Parks. Forest Act 2007 provides for State Forests, Forests of Local Collectivities (Districts &  Communes) & Specially Protected Forests (Art. 4).  No commercial use, grazing, hunting or clearing permitted. Other access and use permitted (Arts 34-54).

Pro-investor Code since 2012 accelerating losses. Land Ordinance 1983 (Decree 2010), Pastoral Code 2000. Expropriation Decree 1930.  (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2017, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code. Decree of 25 Nov 1930 governing expropriation. )
MRT.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — No legal opportunity for clans or communities to register lands collectively. The exception is where the land was held by a Cooperative prior to 1960 as cultivated land. An exception for pastoralists who may secure contracts for exclusive grazing zones, otherwise unregistered access guaranteed. Pastoral Code, 2000. (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code)
MRT.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — No provision for traditional communities to be recognized as legal persons, exception being  farming Cooperatives registered prior to 1960 who still share the cultivated land. (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code)
MRT.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — Communities are de facto if not legal land administrators. No legal provision for a tribe, clan or village (communities) to regulate land relations, although in practice do so.  Additionally, special areas allocated to pastoral groups, and 'vital spaces' up to 100 ha to farming settlements, regulated by these groups. (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code)
MRT.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Partial, limited progress — The State owns the soil & 'property rights' to the soil exist only if granted/registered by State. Customary rights held in perpetuity principally via inheritance has no legal force. No term specified for usufructs given to pastoral clans. Declining utility of long-term occupancy & use as protection. Civil discontent continues between Arab semi-nomadic & African farming communities. (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2012, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code)
MRT.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — The consent of landholders is not required when land is taken for a public purpose. This applies to registered individual landholders on cultivated lands, urban plots and to unregistered land holders - the rural majority. No legal requirement for consultation. Appeal is possible but the law does not specify if this includes unregistered landholders.  (Constitution 1991 as amended up to 2017, Art. 15. Ordinance No. 83.127 of 5 June 1983 On Reorganization of Land & Property. Application Decree No. 2010-080 of 31 March 2010 for Ordinance No. 83.127. Law No. 2000-044 Pastoral Code.)
MRT.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, limited progress — By omission of otherwise in law, titled and untitled landholders own and may use trees on their respective lands;  limitations on tree use  specified only for Protected Forests as held by national or local governments. Forest Code 2007 Arts 44-46. (Forest Code, Law No. 97-007, Articles 44-46.)
MRT.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water belongs to the State and is inalienable and imprescriptible. Use rights recognized, with priority on socio-economic needs, then stock watering, then industrial needs. Customary, community-based water rules acknowledged for pastoralists. Water Code 1986. Land Ordinance 1983. Pastoral Code 2000. (Water Code as Ordinance No. 85-144 of 4 July 1986. Order 83.127 of June 1983 nationalizing land and abolishing customary tenure (Art. 3).  Pastoral Code, Act. 444 of 2000.)
MRT.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress — No provision for communities to own Protected Areas but communities may form Wildlife Management Associations and Communes (local governments) or one community as appropriate may own & manage protected forests called 'Communal Parks'. Art. 6 of Law 2018. Only vague implication that any community could declare a Protected Community Forest.  (Law No. 041 of 2018 Hunting and Wildlife Management. Implementation Decree No. 066 of 2023  Law No. 045 of 2000 Environmental Code. Forest Code No. 055 of 2007.)

MWI.name: Malawi

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land law 1965 reformed by three laws in 2016. All land vested in Republic. Customary individuals, families & groups may register as private landowners. Unallocated & communal lands remain public property, governed by local committees. Customary Land Act 2016. Land Act 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1994 (2017), Art. 28, 44. Land Act No. 16 of 2016. Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. Customary Land Regulations, No. 18 of 2018. The Registered Land (Amendment) Act, 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Chiefs protested original new land law 2013 which vested commons in the members of the village; President did not sign into law. Revisions increased power of Traditional Authorities (TA). A Certificate of Customary Lands is issued to each Traditional Management Area (TLMA) in the name of the TA. Confers management  on elected Committees as chaired by Village Headmen. Certificates of Customary Estate are issued to individuals, families, or to a registered group.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Lands under Certificates of Customary Estate have more equivalency with freehold and leasehold entitlements than untitled customary lands, still the majority. eg. compensation at compulsory acquisition now includes value of certificated lands. Communal lands even more vulnerable, as 'unowned public land'.  CLA, 2016.
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Act (CLA), No. 19 of 2016. Land Acquisition (Amendment ) Act, 2016.
indicators.additional_info: A new protection for customary estates is that every member of the family must be listed on the Registration Certificate when title issued to the family unit, and additionally that the consent of all is required to sell the land (CLA, 2016 s. 28(4).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: A Certificate of Customary Lands for each Traditional Land  Management Area (TLMA) issued in name of the Traditional Authority (TA), conferring management functions on the elected Customary Land Committees, which Village Headman chair. Supervised  by TLMA Land Clerk; main function is to process Customary Certificates based on Committee decisions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Act, No 19 of 2016. Customary Land Regulations, Government Notice No 18 of 2018.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Village/communities not recognized as legal persons. Interest groups may register customary or statutory associations. No opening for villages to secure  communal lands under Certificate.The remain 'unallocated public land' under the control of the Headman and State land officials. Customary Land Regulations 2018.
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. Regulations, No. 9 of 2018

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The elected village Customary Land Committees are  official administrators, chaired by the  Headman and supervised by the Land Clerk, a public land official. There is no legal requirement for the Committee to be accountable to all adult members of the community. TA retain right to halt any issue of title or transaction.
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Act, No. 19of 2016. Regulations, Government Notice No. 9 of 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Customary land interests are denied status as owned unless the parcel is subject to an adjudicated and registered Certificate of Customary Estate, for which a fee is paid. Focus of assisted titling is exclusively on private individual/family farms and houses.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Lands with Certificate of Customary Estate are 'of indefinite term and transmissible'. Also the case under cusatomary norms. Parcels may also be leased out pending consent of the Traditional Authority (TA).  Sale of the right to the parcel is only with permission of the District Land Clerk.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, No. 16 of 2016. Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016.
indicators.additional_info: "Irrespective of what (unwritten) customary law might dictate, rights on customary lands are limited to usufructs, assigned to lineages, families or individuals and may be transferred to heirs, with reports of over half rights being transferred through inheritance, with differences between matrilineal and patrilineal systems" World Bank Malawi Land Governance Assessment Framework, 2012.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Consent of community prior to proposed compulsory acquisition is not required. The Commissioner must attend a meeting in the community  on plan and take comments into account (CLA, 2016 s. 17 (7)). Chiefs  have authority over allocations of use & occupation rights and may defeat wrongful occupancy via new Customary Land Tribunals at village and district levels.
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016.
indicators.additional_info: An attempt to limit exposure of customary lands to involuntary change of owner and use is made by requirement to allocate the taken land to the investment and Travel Centre which gives the investor only a derivative right (Land Act, 2016 s. 11).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land is defined as including water, all things growing on land and other things permanently affixed and although all land ('the soil itself') is vested in the Republic (Land Act s. 8) Rights to trees  belong to the owner of the land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2016 s. 2 & 8. Forestry Act No. 11 of 1997, s. 34. as amended in 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Forestry Act No. 11 of 1997 (as amended 2016) s. 34 provides 'Any person or community which protects a tree or forest whether planted or naturally growing in any land which that person or community is entitled to use shall acquire and retain the ownership of the tree and forest with the right to sustainably harvest and dispose of the produce'. Section 37 confirms this.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Although attached to the land, water is vested in the Republic . Domestic rights to use public water assured.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, No. 15 of 1969 (CAP: 72:03),s. 2, 3, 6 (1) & 7.
indicators.additional_info: Domestic purposes includes watering of stock. Public water means ground and underground water but excludes stagnant pan or swamp wholly contained within private land (Water Resources Act, 1969, s. 2). No prescriptive rights to water permitted (s. 7).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Protected Areas (PA) are national property. A communities may co-manage with the state authority. Customary Land Committees (CLC) may establish 'Village Forest Areas'  (VFA) on unallocated communal lands (1997, s.29-30). Minister makes rules (s. 32). CLC by-laws must be approved by Minister (s. 33). Ownership of trees is assured subject to rules  (s. 34).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Act No. 11 of 1997 as amended in 2017, 2019, 2020, s. 22-23, 26, 29-34.
indicators.additional_info: Provision for co-management of public forest reserves with communities (s. 25) provided agreement with govt excludes commercial extractive use. Taking of communal lands to create new public reserves requires consultation with but not consent of the Traditional Authority (s. 23, 26). Compensation very limited where no houses or farms. Village Forest Areas (VFA) not owned by village, only managed by it, but treted as de facto possession, until Chief orders reallocation.

(Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. )
MWI.Indigenous Q8: Does the law explicitly r: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Land is defined as including water, all things growing on land and other things permanently affixed and although all land ('the soil itself') is vested in the Republic (Land Act s. 8) Rights to trees  belong to the owner of the land. (Land Act, 2016 s. 2 & 8. Forestry Act No. 11 of 1997, s. 34. as amended in 2016.)
MWI.Indigenous Q9: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, significant progress — Although attached to the land, water is vested in the Republic . Domestic rights to use public water assured. (Water Resources Act, No. 15 of 1969 (CAP: 72:03),s. 2, 3, 6 (1) & 7.)
MWI.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Partial, significant progress — Protected Areas (PA) are national property. A communities may co-manage with the state authority. Customary Land Committees (CLC) may establish 'Village Forest Areas'  (VFA) on unallocated communal lands (1997, s.29-30). Minister makes rules (s. 32). CLC by-laws must be approved by Minister (s. 33). Ownership of trees is assured subject to rules  (s. 34). (Forestry Act No. 11 of 1997 as amended in 2017, 2019, 2020, s. 22-23, 26, 29-34.)
MWI.Communities Q1: Does the law recognize a: Partial, significant progress — Land law 1965 reformed by three laws in 2016. All land vested in Republic. Customary individuals, families & groups may register as private landowners. Unallocated & communal lands remain public property, governed by local committees. Customary Land Act 2016. Land Act 2016. (Constitution 1994 (2017), Art. 28, 44. Land Act No. 16 of 2016. Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. Customary Land Regulations, No. 18 of 2018. The Registered Land (Amendment) Act, 2016. )
MWI.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: Partial, significant progress — Lands under Certificates of Customary Estate have more equivalency with freehold and leasehold entitlements than untitled customary lands, still the majority. eg. compensation at compulsory acquisition now includes value of certificated lands. Communal lands even more vulnerable, as 'unowned public land'.  CLA, 2016.  (Customary Land Act (CLA), No. 19 of 2016. Land Acquisition (Amendment ) Act, 2016. )
MWI.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — A Certificate of Customary Lands for each Traditional Land  Management Area (TLMA) issued in name of the Traditional Authority (TA), conferring management functions on the elected Customary Land Committees, which Village Headman chair. Supervised  by TLMA Land Clerk; main function is to process Customary Certificates based on Committee decisions. (Customary Land Act, No 19 of 2016. Customary Land Regulations, Government Notice No 18 of 2018. )
MWI.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — Village/communities not recognized as legal persons. Interest groups may register customary or statutory associations. No opening for villages to secure  communal lands under Certificate.The remain 'unallocated public land' under the control of the Headman and State land officials. Customary Land Regulations 2018. (Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. Regulations, No. 9 of 2018)
MWI.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — The elected village Customary Land Committees are  official administrators, chaired by the  Headman and supervised by the Land Clerk, a public land official. There is no legal requirement for the Committee to be accountable to all adult members of the community. TA retain right to halt any issue of title or transaction. (Customary Land Act, No. 19of 2016. Regulations, Government Notice No. 9 of 2018. )
