Also the case under cusatomary norms. Parcels may also be leased out pending consent of the Traditional Authority (TA).  Sale of the right to the parcel is only with permission of the District Land Clerk.  (Land Act, No. 16 of 2016. Customary Land Act, No. 19 of 2016. )

MYS.name: Malaysia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Federal Court and High Court of Malaysia recognized that indigenous communities have a proprietary interest in their ancestral lands. However, there is no federal statute which recognizes indigenous/ community land rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Malaysia Land Code, 1965; Superintendent of Land v. Gov't of Sarawak (2007); Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia (2002), Adong bin Kuqua & Ors v. Kerajaan Negeri Johor & Anor (1997)
indicators.additional_info: The Land Code vests ownership of all Malaysia land in the state (Art. 40, Land Code, 1965). In 2007, the Federal Court of Malaysia (Malaysia' highest court) endorsed the view that the common law respects the pre-existence of land rights under native laws or customs. In 2002, the High Court of Malaysia held the Orang Asli Aboriginal peoples have a proprietary interest in and to their customary and ancestral lands in Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia. The Organg Asli's interest in land was limited only to the area that formed the Orang Asli's settlement, and did not include hunting or roaming areas. In Adong bin Kuqua & Ors v. Kerajaan Negeri Johor & Anor (1997), the High Court of Malaysia held that Organ Asli ("original peoples") have a common law right to their ancestral land based on a continuous and unbroken occupation and enjoyment of rights to the land. However, these decisions have not been implemented through legislation. NOTE: Land is governed at the state-level.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Federal Court held indigenous communities (ICs) have proprietary interest in their land, but ICs do not have statutory protection at the federal level.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 8, 12 Aboriginal Peoples Act 1954
indicators.additional_info: There is no federal-level legislative protection for indigenous communities in Malaysia. NOTE: State-level legislation- the Aboriginal Peoples Act (APA) 1954---which only applies to states in Peninsular Malaysia--grants ICs rights to use and occupy their ancestral lands, but not ownership rights. Sec. 8 of the APA grants occupancy rights. Sec. 9 of the APA states that "no aborigine shall transfer, lease, charge, sell, convey, assign, mortgage or otherwise dispose of any land except with the consent of the Director General..."  Section 12 of the APA provides that "if any land is excised from any aboriginal area or if any land in any aboriginal areas is alienated, granted, leased, the State Authority may grant compensation therefor may pay such compensation to persons entitled in his opinion thereto." In the state Sarawak, the Land Code 1958 recognizes rights to native customary land.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Malaysia has not enacted federal legislation or regulations that allow for indigenous communities to formally receive formal title to their lands.
indicators.additional_info: Under Article 74(2) land tenure is listed as under the umbrella of state governments, not the federal government. NOTE: Although the case was in 2002, the High Court stated in Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia that "it is evident that the government is moving towards issuing permanent titles to orang asi lands, but is administratively hampered..."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While there is no federal legislation granting legal personality to indigenous communities (ICs), the High Court of Malaysia has granted legal standing to ICs in several cases involving land rights disputes.
indicators.law_and_provision: High Court Decisions- Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia (2002), Adong bin Kuqua & Ors v. Kerajaan Negeri Johor & Anor (1997) and Adong and in Sagong Tasi & Ors. v. Kerajaan Negeri Selangor & 3 Or (1992)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on this issue, but the High Court suggested that indigenous communities have legal authority over their customary and ancestral land.
indicators.law_and_provision: High Court Decisions- Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia (2002), Adong bin Kuqua & Ors v. Kerajaan Negeri Johor & Anor (1997) and Adong and in Sagong Tasi & Ors. v. Kerajaan Negeri Selangor & 3 Or (1992)
indicators.additional_info: In Sagong Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia (2002), the High Court stated that "land occupied under customary right" can be defined as land which was continuously occupied and maintained by indigenous populations to the exclusion of others in pursuance of their culture and inherited by them from generation to generation in accordance with their customs..." This holding suggests a recognition of indigenous communities' legal authority over their land.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on this issue, but the High Court held that land which is continuously occupied by Orang Asali for generations grants them an interest in the land--the Court did not impose any durational limit.
indicators.additional_info: The High Court's holding, in Sagon Bin Tasi v. Government of Malaysia, suggests that Orang Asli have an interest in and to the land on which they settle, and this interest may be held in perpetuity (no durational limits were imposed by the Court).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Land Acquisition Act 1960 permits the government to expropriate land for a public purpose and does not need to consult or obtain consent from indigenous communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Acquisition Act 1960
indicators.additional_info: The law stipulates that "The State Authority may acquire any land which is needed--(a) for any public purpose; by any person or corporation for any purpose which in the opinion of the State Authority is beneficial to the economic development of Malaysia or any part thereof or to the public generally or any class of the public; or for purpose of mining or for residential, agricultural, commercial, industrial or recreational purposes or any combination of such purposes..." (Sec. 3, Land Acquisition Act 1960).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly grant indigenous/community rights to trees. Forests resources are governed by state law in Malaysia.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 14, National Forestry Act 1984, Art. 74(2) of the Constitution
indicators.additional_info: Sec. 14 of the National Forest Management Act states that "all forest produce situated, lying, growing or having its origin within n a permanent reserved forest or State land shall be the property of the State Authority." Sec. 15 requires that individuals must obtain licences to take forest produce from state land. NOTE: The Aboriginal Peoples Act states that "where an aboriginal community establishes a claim to fruit or rubber trees on State land which is alienated, granted, leased for any purpose, occupied temporarily under license or otherwise disposed of, then such compensation shall be paid to the aboriginal community..." (Sec. 11, APA 1954). This Act only applies to Peninsular Malaysia though and does not grant land ownership rights to aboriginal peoples---only use and occupancy rights.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The  Water Act, 1920 and the Water Services Industry Act, 2006 do not establish that individuals have a right to use water for domestic purposes. The Act only provides that ownership and control of rivers in each State are vested solely in the Ruler of such State (Sec. 3). Presumably, water resource governance is established at the state-level, but LandMark's legal indicator assessment is limited to national-level laws. Obstructon or interference with Malaysia's rivers requires a license (sec. 5, Waters Act, 1920).
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 3, Waters Act 1920- amended 1989; Water Services Industry Act, 2006
indicators.additional_info: The law establishes that "Subject to the terms of any express grant made by or on behalf of the Ruler of a State, the entire property in and control of all rivers in any State is and shall be vested solely in the Ruler of such State; provided that in the case of lands held by the Government under grant or lease or reserved for a public purpose and maintained by a Government Department, such control may be exercised by the Head of such Department, under the direction of the State Authority (Sec. 3, Waters Act, 1920 (amended 1989)).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly grant indigenous groups/communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Protected Areas and Protected Places Act 1959- amended 2006

NAM.name: Namibia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communal lands (38% country) vested in Government; customary owners may only register usufructs for houses and farms (2002 law). Corporate entities may obtain leaseholds over expansive commonge for privste & cooperative ranches(2013). Traditional Authorities (TA) resist efforts to introduce collective village titles to protect local grazing lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1990 (2014), Art. 100 & Schedule 5: s. (1). Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of  2002, s. 17. (CLRA). Amendment Act No 13 of 2013. Ministerial Notice of Change to Regulations under The  Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, Gazette Notice 15 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Compulsory registration of customary rights for farming & residential units to individuals; 2002 law  delivers a registered lifetime usufruct, inheritable with approval of chief. Collective customary property in form of village & village cluster commonages now registrable for leaseholds if village registered a Coop or other entity  for commercial purposes eg. lodges, ranches (CLRA Amdt Act, 2013). Amendment to Regulations in 2014 also redrafts Application Forms for Certificate of Customary Rights for Residential and Farming Units or 'Other' purposes to allow families & groups to apply; limited to farming, residential & commercial purposes. Draft Ministerial Policy on Group Rights (June 2014) never applied & aim for new land law including collective entitlement has stalled; TA do not support losing control over commonage. The Prescription Act No. 68 of 1969 (1993) does not apply to communal areas (S. 20).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unequal treatment of freehold and communal land, absolute ownership under the former, Communal Lands (38% country area) are vested in State, limiting rights to lifetime usufructs or leaseholds for commercial groups. Authority is vested in unelected chiefs, controlling vast rangelands & conversions to private ranches. Enclosure forbidden but ignored.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1990, Art. 66, 144, Schedule 5 (1). Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 20, 21, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29. Communal Act & Traditional Authorities Act, 2000, s. 18, 20. (Government Circular on Compensation Guidelines, Ministry of Lands, 2010).
indicators.additional_info: Constitution Art 66 protects customary law but interpreted as the right of chiefs to allocate rights as lifetime usufructs for residential & farmlands. No provision for grazing as common properties of communities, only available under commercial lease to registered entities. Traditional Authorities have powers of allocation & cancellation. Compensation inequitable; due for land if freehold as per Constitution Art. 144, but customary occupants receive value of improvements only.  Rates improved in 2010 but still exclude involuntary loss of traditional grazing lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Compulsory registration of customary rights to houses & farms as Certificates. Procedure straightforward &  low cost with application to Traditional Authority, ratified by the Communal Land Board, & registered. Customary Right is a heritable lifetime usufruct to cultivation or residential land. Law 2002 still lacks provision for exclusive village or ward rights to local grazing areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act No. 5 of 2002, s. 2-14 (Boards), s.20-29 (Chiefs), Amendment Act, No. 13 of 2013, s. 1& 5. Government Notice No. 15 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Communal Land Reform Act, 2002 provided only for registration of individually held housing and farm rights, and for leaseholds for commercial groups (e.g. ranches) with weak legal provision in 2013 via minor changes to application forms) to enable families and groups to secure certificates for shared homesteads & farmlands. Although the form does not exclude grazing lands, group applications by several villages in 2023 rejected. Although chief decides allocations, Land Boards (government agencies) keep register of certificates and issue leaseholds directly.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are spatially and socially discrete, but no provision as legal persons. A family or group may acquire farm land since 2014, and a community may register a trust or association and obtain a leasehold over grazing land for commercial development. Group rights policy of 2014 to enable each community to secure its local grazing unimplemented.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 20 ff. Agricultural Commercial Land Reform Act, No. 6 of 1995.
indicators.additional_info: Group rights limited until 2013 to commercial farms outside communal areas for resettlement schemes of groups, with potential to be a group  legal entity or to hold their private lands as a group (Agricultural Commercial Land Reform Act, 1995 (2014), s. 37). Also provision for group tenure in Rehoboth District (Subdivision of Agricultural Land Act, No. 70 of 1970) to meet collective tenure customs of the Baster community (origins in South Africa). Still no main law provision for clans, villages, village clusters, tribes to hold land collectively, other than via establishing legal entity (cooperative, trust, corporation).  Gazetted change in 2014 in application forms for leasehold and customary certificates in Communal Areas allows spouses, families and groups to apply for rights without forming legal entity but limited to residential and farm lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Vested in regional chief who consult with village headmen. No village land committee provided for. Traditional authorities actively maintain authority and decision-making in the domains they manage, the land itself owned in trust by the State.
indicators.law_and_provision: Traditional Authorities Act, No. 25 of 2002, s. 3.Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 20-29.
indicators.additional_info: As legally designated land authorities, chiefs hold substantial powers. The grassroots village, village cluster (ward), hunter-gatherer band, pastoral group, have no authority autonomous of the appointed chief. Chiefs appoint headmen at community level to represent them. This is especially contentious in pastoral zones such as Kunene Region.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: By custom, rights owned in perpetuity. Compulsory registration limited to houses & farms issued in lifetime usufructs which may be inherited.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 26.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for consent. Chief consults with communities prior to allocations of new customary rights or approval for Board to issue leaseholds and which may be granted for commercial and public service purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 22 (3), s, 40. Government Circular on Compensation Policy Guidelines for Communal Land (2010).
indicators.additional_info: Limited protection of interests especially for communal grazing lands and unregistered house & farm parcels. No obligatory for Traditional Authority (Chief) to seek local comments; he may make inquiries prior to allocation of a new customary right and if a member of the community objects, he may conduct a hearing and may take the result into account (Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 22). Little protection against grant of leaseholds of large areas of commonage; only the Traditional Authority must give consent (s. 30 (4)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Outside communal lands, freeholders own trees on their lands, trees owned by Government in communal lands (Constitution Art. 100). However customary occupants may freely use trees outside Protected Areas for domestic needs   customary rules. Community Forests established by Agreement with Government for local management and use (Forest Act 2001).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 100, Schedule 5(1). Forest Act, No. 12 of 2001, s.15,  33.
indicators.additional_info: Constitutional provision (Art. 100) for land, water and natural resources above and below the surface to belong to the State unless otherwise lawfully owned (ie excludes  freehold & leasehold lands). communal lands (38% of country) are owned by Government (Const. Schedule 5 (1)). Strong provision for Community Forests within which community may dispose of forest produce under a gazetted Agreement by which Community Forest established for community management and use (Forest Act,200, s. 15). Requires consent of traditional authority, and community defined as the tribe with TA as key actor. Community Forests exist mainly within vast  Wildlife Conservancies (17Mha) run by  Associations of self-selected members who work with private safari and hunting companies.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource administered by government. Free rights to use for domestic purposes. Includes  stock watering. Water Resources Management Act 2013.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Management Act, No. 11 of 2013, s. 38-40
indicators.additional_info: Water owned by State (Constitution, 1990, Art. 100). Persons have free right to take water for own domestic use without licence, as does an owner or occupier of land outsider a local authority area, subject to health and safety restrictions (s. 38, 39). An owner or occupier  including on communal land also has right to collect rainwater on land for domestic but not to an extent that affects environment or downstream users (s. 40). Domestic use includes drinking, cooking, washing, watering a household garden and watering animals for reasonable own use (s. 2).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community Forests  & Wildlife Conservancies on communal lands controlled by self-selected groups of members. Co-management  promoted in State Protected Areas but mainly for jobs and benefits, not equal decision-making. Unsuccessful restitution claim by Hai//om San for Etosha National Park. Positive Presidential Commission Report on Ancestral Land Claims and Restitution (2020) not acted upon.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Act, No. 12 of 2001. Nature Conservation Amendment Act, No. 151 of 1996, s. 24 A.
indicators.additional_info: By 2024 there were 86 Community Wildlife Management Areas (WMA) covering 17 Mha (20% of country) within Communal Lands/  Communities do not own the land, only rights to manage, use & benefit - vested in voluntary WMA Boards. Around 30 Community Forests exist within WMA.  Applications by conservancies to hold communal lands under lease from Tribal Land Boards have failed. Some WMA cover much of the local tribal area (eg 25 + villages) defeating inclusive decision-making.WMA Boards also control revenue distribution.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communal lands (38% country) vested in Government; customary owners may only register usufructs for houses and farms (2002 law). Corporate entities may obtain leaseholds over expansive commonge for privste & cooperative ranches(2013). Traditional Authorities (TA) resist efforts to introduce collective village titles to protect local grazing lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1990 (2014), Art. 100 & Schedule 5: s. (1). Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of  2002, s. 17. (CLRA). Amendment Act No 13 of 2013. Ministerial Notice of Change to Regulations under The  Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, Gazette Notice 15 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Compulsory registration of customary rights for farming & residential units to individuals; 2002 law  delivers a registered lifetime usufruct, inheritable with approval of chief. Collective customary property in form of village & village cluster commonages now registrable for leaseholds if village registered a Coop or other entity  for commercial purposes eg. lodges, ranches (CLRA Amdt Act, 2013). Amendment to Regulations in 2014 also redrafts Application Forms for Certificate of Customary Rights for Residential and Farming Units or 'Other' purposes to allow families & groups to apply; limited to farming, residential & commercial purposes. Draft Ministerial Policy on Group Rights (June 2014) never applied & aim for new land law including collective entitlement has stalled; TA do not support losing control over commonage. The Prescription Act No. 68 of 1969 (1993) does not apply to communal areas (S. 20).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unequal treatment of freehold and communal land, absolute ownership under the former, Communal Lands (38% country area) are vested in State, limiting rights to lifetime usufructs or leaseholds for commercial groups. Authority is vested in unelected chiefs, controlling vast rangelands & conversions to private ranches. Enclosure forbidden but ignored.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1990, Art. 66, 144, Schedule 5 (1). Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 20, 21, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29. Communal Act & Traditional Authorities Act, 2000, s. 18, 20. (Government Circular on Compensation Guidelines, Ministry of Lands, 2010).
indicators.additional_info: Constitution Art 66 protects customary law but interpreted as the right of chiefs to allocate rights as lifetime usufructs for residential & farmlands. No provision for grazing as common properties of communities, only available under commercial lease to registered entities. Traditional Authorities have powers of allocation & cancellation. Compensation inequitable; due for land if freehold as per Constitution Art. 144, but customary occupants receive value of improvements only.  Rates improved in 2010 but still exclude involuntary loss of traditional grazing lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Compulsory registration of customary rights to houses & farms as Certificates. Procedure straightforward &  low cost with application to Traditional Authority, ratified by the Communal Land Board, & registered. Customary Right is a heritable lifetime usufruct to cultivation or residential land. Law 2002 still lacks provision for exclusive village or ward rights to local grazing areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act No. 5 of 2002, s. 2-14 (Boards), s.20-29 (Chiefs), Amendment Act, No. 13 of 2013, s. 1& 5. Government Notice No. 15 of 2014.
indicators.additional_info: Communal Land Reform Act, 2002 provided only for registration of individually held housing and farm rights, and for leaseholds for commercial groups (e.g. ranches) with weak legal provision in 2013 via minor changes to application forms) to enable families and groups to secure certificates for shared homesteads & farmlands. Although the form does not exclude grazing lands, group applications by several villages in 2023 rejected. Although chief decides allocations, Land Boards (government agencies) keep register of certificates and issue leaseholds directly.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are spatially and socially discrete, but no provision as legal persons. A family or group may acquire farm land since 2014, and a community may register a trust or association and obtain a leasehold over grazing land for commercial development. Group rights policy of 2014 to enable each community to secure its local grazing unimplemented.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 20 ff. Agricultural Commercial Land Reform Act, No. 6 of 1995.
indicators.additional_info: Group rights limited until 2013 to commercial farms outside communal areas for resettlement schemes of groups, with potential to be a group  legal entity or to hold their private lands as a group (Agricultural Commercial Land Reform Act, 1995 (2014), s. 37). Also provision for group tenure in Rehoboth District (Subdivision of Agricultural Land Act, No. 70 of 1970) to meet collective tenure customs of the Baster community (origins in South Africa). Still no main law provision for clans, villages, village clusters, tribes to hold land collectively, other than via establishing legal entity (cooperative, trust, corporation).  Gazetted change in 2014 in application forms for leasehold and customary certificates in Communal Areas allows spouses, families and groups to apply for rights without forming legal entity but limited to residential and farm lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Vested in regional chief who consult with village headmen. No village land committee provided for. Traditional authorities actively maintain authority and decision-making in the domains they manage, the land itself owned in trust by the State.
indicators.law_and_provision: Traditional Authorities Act, No. 25 of 2002, s. 3.Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 20-29.
indicators.additional_info: As legally designated land authorities, chiefs hold substantial powers. The grassroots village, village cluster (ward), hunter-gatherer band, pastoral group, have no authority autonomous of the appointed chief. Chiefs appoint headmen at community level to represent them. This is especially contentious in pastoral zones such as Kunene Region.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: By custom, rights owned in perpetuity. Compulsory registration limited to houses & farms issued in lifetime usufructs which may be inherited.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 26.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for consent. Chief consults with communities prior to allocations of new customary rights or approval for Board to issue leaseholds and which may be granted for commercial and public service purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Communal Land Reform Act, No. 5 of 2002, s. 22 (3), s, 40. Government Circular on Compensation Policy Guidelines for Communal Land (2010).
indicators.additional_info: Limited protection of interests especially for communal grazing lands and unregistered house & farm parcels. No obligatory for Traditional Authority (Chief) to seek local comments; he may make inquiries prior to allocation of a new customary right and if a member of the community objects, he may conduct a hearing and may take the result into account (Communal Land Reform Act, 2002, s. 22). Little protection against grant of leaseholds of large areas of commonage; only the Traditional Authority must give consent (s. 30 (4)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Outside communal lands, freeholders own trees on their lands, trees owned by Government in communal lands (Constitution Art. 100). However customary occupants may freely use trees outside Protected Areas for domestic needs   customary rules. Community Forests established by Agreement with Government for local management and use (Forest Act 2001).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 100, Schedule 5(1). Forest Act, No. 12 of 2001, s.15,  33.
indicators.additional_info: Constitutional provision (Art. 100) for land, water and natural resources above and below the surface to belong to the State unless otherwise lawfully owned (ie excludes  freehold & leasehold lands). communal lands (38% of country) are owned by Government (Const. Schedule 5 (1)). Strong provision for Community Forests within which community may dispose of forest produce under a gazetted Agreement by which Community Forest established for community management and use (Forest Act,200, s. 15). Requires consent of traditional authority, and community defined as the tribe with TA as key actor. Community Forests exist mainly within vast  Wildlife Conservancies (17Mha) run by  Associations of self-selected members who work with private safari and hunting companies.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource administered by government. Free rights to use for domestic purposes. Includes  stock watering. Water Resources Management Act 2013.

NER.name: Niger

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities, with additional pastoral code for IP pastoralists
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Rural Land Code, 1993 provides for individual, family and collective tenure including under customary law, chiefs as custodial managers. Protection of rights whether recorded in Commune Rural Land Dossier or owner has secured Certificate of Customary Right. Pastoralists have free access to pasture and may be granted priority rights over home areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Land Policy 2021, revised in 2023. Constitution 2010 (2017) Arts 28, 148, 167). Rural Land Code 1993 (No 93-015 on Principles) Arts.  passim. Law No. 2008-22 amending Ordinance No. 93-28 of 1993 on Status of Traditional Chieftaincy. Pastoral Code, No. 29-2010
indicators.additional_info: With provision of village land plans and registers, usual for farming communities to distinguish between farmed/house lands and common property of the village for grazing, watering, plant and wood collection, etc. All land belongs ultimate to State/national community so level playing field for all rightholders, statutory or customary. However, administrative overlaps & inconsistencies in laws thwart  their application.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Lands held under customary and statutory rights deemed equal in legal force and effect. Law of Administrative Territories 2001 references groups holding common lands. Compensation equitable at compulsory acquisition (Const. 2010, with obligatory fully paid relocation for communities (Law 2008-37).
indicators.law_and_provision: Const.2010  Art. 28. Rural Land Code 1993 Arts 129-133. Law of Administrative Territories No. 03/2001 Arts 140-148. Law No. 2008-37 of 2008 amending and supplementing Law No. 61-37 Regulating Expropriation for Public Use and Temporary Occupation. Pastoral Code No. 29-2010.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Process of devising rural land plans and issuing certificates has been slow but speeding up & less costly. Dossier includes files on each landholder including groups using communal land.  Customary Certificates issued by Chief but registered at Commune. Commune Land Commission may also issue Title Deeds with survey and more cost.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Code No 15 of 1993. Territorial Planning Law No 03 of 2001. Decree No. 97-367 of Feb 1997 established procedure for registering  land rights in the Rural File and Rural Land Register.  Law No 048 of 2004 on livestock breeding. Ordinance on pastoralists, No. 29 of 2010. Law on Water, No 09 of 2010. Law on Forests No. 040 of 2004.
indicators.additional_info: The anchor Rural Land Code 1993 provides principles for  tenure & governance. Now that Commune Land Commissions in place issue of Certificates speeding up. Groups often secure temporary farming rights from communal land. Role of chiefs curtailed by local committee involvement and rnew consultation requirements.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for family, group, tribe, or village to establish corporate personality to be recognized as lawful customary owner or to secure a Certificates of Possession. These can cover farmed, settled, or shared forest, grazing of other commons, or land set side for pastoral use by pastoralists in home territories. Rural Land Code 1993. Pastoral Code 2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Code No. 1993-015 Arts. 23-31. Pastoral Code, 2010-29 Arts 11-12.
indicators.additional_info: Recently more promotion of the ability of groups to secure Certificates of Possession issued by Commune Land Authorities (Cofocom), but without precise guidelines, or clarity of extent of rights.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Strong but slow devolution of rural land governance via establishment of Village Land Commissions (Cofob) to drive consultation and create Village Rural Plan, and  Commune Commissions (Cofocom) to hold Registers and issue Certificates and Titles as certified by local Chief. 40% of villages or tribal groups had Cofob by 2020.
indicators.law_and_provision: No 93-015 Principles of the Rural Land Code. Ordinance No. 93-028 on the status of Chiefs, amended by Law No. 2008-22.Law of Territorial Planning, No. 2001-03 of 2001. Law No 2001-32 of 2001 , Code on Local Authorities No. 2010-54 of 2010.
indicators.additional_info: Rural Land Policy 2020 aims to promote deeds of possession and collective land ownership for lineages, extended families, village communities and tribes under locally defined land tenure rules. Some concern that Traditional Authorities automatically head the village/tribal Cofob.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights have no term, inheritable, assumed as held in perpetuity. Right may voluntarily be formalized in a Certificate issued by a village chef du canton (chief) at village level (Cofob) or at higher cost and requirements for a Title Deed issued by Commune Land Authority (Cofocom).
indicators.law_and_provision: Code of Principles of Rural Land No 1993-015. Pastoral Code No.2010-09.  Territorial Planning Code No. 2001-32.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law does not specify consent as obligatory, only consultation, at compulsory acquisition for public purposes. Consultation requirements are precise, including involvement of those affected in planning the relocation and supporting services.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2008-37 of 2008 amending and supplementing Law No. 61-37 Regulating Expropriation for Public Use and Temporary Occupation.
indicators.additional_info: Eviction may proceed only after a resettlement plan has been established, full consultation required for resettlement planning. Land, water points & 'cultural asset) compensated (Arts. 13, 137). Resettlement includes allowances, technical assistance, transport allowances, loans (Art. 137-138, Law 2008-37 on Expropriation). Pastoralists must be consulted and granted compensation prior to oil and mining developments in their home territories (Pastoral Code, 2010 Art. 11-12).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Rural Land Code covers land and attached resources. Planted and natural trees are assumed as property. Rights include gathering forest products where logging is underway in Unclassified State Forests (Forest Law 2004). A village or tribe may be assisted to rehabilitate forests & manage wildlife for the state in their own area.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law No. 040 of 2004.Wildlife Law No. 07-2008. Pastoral Code No. 29 of 2010. Law No. 5 of 1961 on Northern Line (defining State arid lands).
indicators.additional_info: All undeveloped lands belong to the State (Ordinance 1993-015). Concessionaires must respect the customary use rights of communities and groups in allocated Classified Forests (Art. 51). Wildlife law does not permit customary uses in national parks, wildlife reserves, integral reserves, or unless within the specific order for that Protected Area. Occupaton of Forests and Wildlife PA is not permitted but both farmers and pastoralists may be allocated concessions for pasture, farming, hunting, fishing or forestry (Wildlife Law No. 07-2008 Art. 3).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: While all water is state property, communities have right to regulate its use within customary domains, certificated or titled domains in accordance with Water Law. Access to a public well is free for all.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ordinance No. 2010-09 on the Niger Water Code.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protected Areas  (PA) are classified as the public domain of the State, but cannot be declared without community consultation & participation and to whom access and use rights are granted. This is also so under the Pastoral Code for pastoralist home areas. Both forest and pastoral laws permit use of PA during drought.
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife Law No. 07-1998. Forest Law No. 040-2004. Pastoral Code No. 29-2010.
indicators.additional_info: Gazettement of new Protected Areas must take account of pastoral home territories to ensure their priority rights of use, occupation, management (Art 11-12, Pastoral Code 2010). No provision for Community Protected Forests or Community Wildlife Reserves, although a village or tribe may be assisted to rehabilitate forest lands and manage wildlife for the State in its own area.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Rural Land Code, 1993 provides for individual, family and collective tenure including under customary law, chiefs as custodial managers. Protection of rights whether recorded in Commune Rural Land Dossier or owner has secured Certificate of Customary Right. Pastoralists have free access to pasture and may be granted priority rights over home areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Land Policy 2021, revised in 2023. Constitution 2010 (2017) Arts 28, 148, 167). Rural Land Code 1993 (No 93-015 on Principles) Arts.  passim. Law No. 2008-22 amending Ordinance No. 93-28 of 1993 on Status of Traditional Chieftaincy. Pastoral Code, No. 29-2010
indicators.additional_info: With provision of village land plans and registers, usual for farming communities to distinguish between farmed/house lands and common property of the village for grazing, watering, plant and wood collection, etc. All land belongs ultimate to State/national community so level playing field for all rightholders, statutory or customary. However, administrative overlaps & inconsistencies in laws thwart  their application.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Lands held under customary and statutory rights deemed equal in legal force and effect. Law of Administrative Territories 2001 references groups holding common lands. Compensation equitable at compulsory acquisition (Const. 2010, with obligatory fully paid relocation for communities (Law 2008-37).
indicators.law_and_provision: Const.2010  Art. 28. Rural Land Code 1993 Arts 129-133. Law of Administrative Territories No. 03/2001 Arts 140-148. Law No. 2008-37 of 2008 amending and supplementing Law No. 61-37 Regulating Expropriation for Public Use and Temporary Occupation. Pastoral Code No. 29-2010.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Process of devising rural land plans and issuing certificates has been slow but speeding up & less costly. Dossier includes files on each landholder including groups using communal land.  Customary Certificates issued by Chief but registered at Commune. Commune Land Commission may also issue Title Deeds with survey and more cost.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Code No 15 of 1993. Territorial Planning Law No 03 of 2001. Decree No. 97-367 of Feb 1997 established procedure for registering  land rights in the Rural File and Rural Land Register.  Law No 048 of 2004 on livestock breeding. Ordinance on pastoralists, No. 29 of 2010. Law on Water, No 09 of 2010. Law on Forests No. 040 of 2004.
indicators.additional_info: The anchor Rural Land Code 1993 provides principles for  tenure & governance. Now that Commune Land Commissions in place issue of Certificates speeding up. Groups often secure temporary farming rights from communal land. Role of chiefs curtailed by local committee involvement and rnew consultation requirements.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No requirement for family, group, tribe, or village to establish corporate personality to be recognized as lawful customary owner or to secure a Certificates of Possession. These can cover farmed, settled, or shared forest, grazing of other commons, or land set side for pastoral use by pastoralists in home territories. Rural Land Code 1993. Pastoral Code 2010.
indicators.law_and_provision: Rural Land Code No. 1993-015 Arts. 23-31. Pastoral Code, 2010-29 Arts 11-12.
indicators.additional_info: Recently more promotion of the ability of groups to secure Certificates of Possession issued by Commune Land Authorities (Cofocom), but without precise guidelines, or clarity of extent of rights.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Strong but slow devolution of rural land governance via establishment of Village Land Commissions (Cofob) to drive consultation and create Village Rural Plan, and  Commune Commissions (Cofocom) to hold Registers and issue Certificates and Titles as certified by local Chief. 40% of villages or tribal groups had Cofob by 2020.
indicators.law_and_provision: No 93-015 Principles of the Rural Land Code. Ordinance No. 93-028 on the status of Chiefs, amended by Law No. 2008-22.Law of Territorial Planning, No. 2001-03 of 2001. Law No 2001-32 of 2001 , Code on Local Authorities No. 2010-54 of 2010.
indicators.additional_info: Rural Land Policy 2020 aims to promote deeds of possession and collective land ownership for lineages, extended families, village communities and tribes under locally defined land tenure rules. Some concern that Traditional Authorities automatically head the village/tribal Cofob.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights have no term, inheritable, assumed as held in perpetuity. indicators.law_and_provision: Code of Principles of Rural Land No 1993-015. Pastoral Code No.2010-09.  Territorial Planning Code No. 2001-32.

NGA.name: Nigeria

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Land Use Decree 1978 (now 2004) nationalized land so formal rights termed either Customary Rights of Occupancy (rural) or Statutory Rights of Occupancy (urban). Equivalent in legal force. Registration voluntary, administered by District Governments. Customary land covers >75% country area. Each village may designated >5,000 ha as communal land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1999  Art. 44 (3);  Land Use Act, 1990, CAP 202 reissued in 2004,  s. 1, 2, 6) originally the Land Use Decree No 6 of 1978, s. 36 (2).
indicators.additional_info: National Domain is divided into State/Public Land (10-15%), Private Land (70-75% including customary rights) and Communal Land (5%, also under customary tenure). Most customary land held by families as houses and farms. Village commons administered by village Traditional Authority.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Claimed equivalency of statutory and customary rights is not confirmed in terms of the 2004 law. Excuse is that from original law of 1978, the Land Use Act is still tied to the Constitution, impeding changes.
indicators.additional_info: Legal shortfalls: (i) only Governor or Local Government Authority may consent to transfers, subleasing, assignment or mortgaging of customary rights of occupancy while no consent required to secure statutory right of occupancy (2004 s. 21); (ii) Governor may convert customary land into urban domain extinguishing customary rights (s. 5) or issue licences for quarrying to outsiders, not possible when land under statutory titles (s. 12.1); (iii) compensation at comp. acquisition is less for customary lands, limited to improvements (s. 29); and (iv) undeveloped lands in customary sector less protected (s. 36 (3)).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Low level of application and issue of Customary Certificates of Occupancy as procedure is cumbersome & expensive.  Traditional Authorities (TA) continue to administer unregistered customary parcels. Missing legal provision for the rights of migrating nomads (Fulani), a critical issue in northern states.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 5, 6, 10, 36 (3).
indicators.additional_info: Expensive: Certificate requires payment for unexhausted improvements and annual rent, grant depends on assent of unelected committee, limits on size, and holding of undeveloped lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law treats an individual, family and community as equally eligible for issue of Customary Certificates, meaning the latter are legal persons for purposes of land law. Outdated law fails to  protect customary lands near towns from informal settlements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 51
indicators.additional_info: Land Use Act, s. 51: "customary right of occupancy" means the right of a person or community lawfully using or occupying land in accordance with customary law and includes a customary right of occupancy granted by a Local Government under this Act".

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition of customary law as basis of authority deceptive, as Governor and Local Government hold significant powers. The law also fails to specify the powers of Traditional Authorities as de facto administrators of local customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act (1978) as reissued in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: The law leaves decisions to customary law, as limited by Bill of Rights in Constitution (1999). The Constitution makes customary law the source of jurisdiction in State and Federal Customary Courts. This has a long tradition begun in Privy Court Ruling in 2021 that customary law is founded on the assent of the people.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights governed by customary law including inheritance norms. These accept customary rights are held in perpetuity if not voluntarily surrendered, transferred etc.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act 2004
indicators.additional_info: Alienation of customary rights is not possible without Governor's consent,  and may occur only by assignment, transfer or lease. Land Use Act, 2004 s. 21. The Constitution provides for Customary Courts to rule on customary law disputes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal provisions for consent for land takings. Governor may extinguish customary rights virtually at will for broadly defined public purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, 2004 s.28 (3), 51.
indicators.additional_info: Compensation must be prompt, not prior. While Constitution allows negotiation through tribunals (Art. 44), Land Use Act (s. 47 (2) denies court jurisdiction to inquire into any matter relating to compulsory acquisition or compensation.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Individual State Forest laws list protected trees with implication that other trees on customary lands may be  freely harvested  (eg. Kaduna State Forestry Law, 2019, Cross River State Establishment of Forestry Commission 2010). Villages may declare Community Forests, norms different in each State Forest Law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 14. Cross River State Forest Act, Law No. 3 of 2010.  Kaduna State Forestry Law, 2019.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is public land under Federal and State control but access and use for domestic purposes is guaranteed, including stock watering & personal irrigation. New water and sanitation laws in each state require rural communities to establish Water Committees to manage, regulate and improve water provision.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, No. 101 of 1993, Section 2(a) (iii). Ekiti State Water Supply and Sanitation Law No. 8 of 2013.
indicators.additional_info: All land and resources are nationalized including water, and control vested in the federal or state governments, so communities obtain either free or licenced use rights (commercial).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Gazettement of National Parks and Reserves does not require consent of affected communities. Rights of access and use granted to adjacent communities in buffer zones and where participatory management activated. Communities may establish and seek gazettement for Community Forests on their own lands. Most advanced in Cross River State.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Park Service Act, No. 46 of 1999 (2006). Cross River State Forestry Commission Act, No.3 of 2010.
indicators.additional_info: National Parks are managed by the federal government. All other PA governed by the 36 State Governments. Wildlife regulated  under the National Park Service Act 1999 (amended 2006). Hunting banned. Each Park Management Plan must specify buffer zones for local use & participation in management (1999 s.27). No provision for restitution of Protected Areas to communities against claims.

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Land Use Decree 1978 (now 2004) nationalized land so formal rights termed either Customary Rights of Occupancy (rural) or Statutory Rights of Occupancy (urban). Equivalent in legal force. Registration voluntary, administered by District Governments. Customary land covers >75% country area. Each village may designated >5,000 ha as communal land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1999  Art. 44 (3);  Land Use Act, 1990, CAP 202 reissued in 2004,  s. 1, 2, 6) originally the Land Use Decree No 6 of 1978, s. 36 (2).
indicators.additional_info: National Domain is divided into State/Public Land (10-15%), Private Land (70-75% including customary rights) and Communal Land (5%, also under customary tenure). Most customary land held by families as houses and farms. Village commons administered by village Traditional Authority.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Claimed equivalency of statutory and customary rights is not confirmed in terms of the 2004 law. Excuse is that from original law of 1978, the Land Use Act is still tied to the Constitution, impeding changes.
indicators.additional_info: Legal shortfalls: (i) only Governor or Local Government Authority may consent to transfers, subleasing, assignment or mortgaging of customary rights of occupancy while no consent required to secure statutory right of occupancy (2004 s. 21); (ii) Governor may convert customary land into urban domain extinguishing customary rights (s. 5) or issue licences for quarrying to outsiders, not possible when land under statutory titles (s. 12.1); (iii) compensation at comp. acquisition is less for customary lands, limited to improvements (s. 29); and (iv) undeveloped lands in customary sector less protected (s. 36 (3)).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Low level of application and issue of Customary Certificates of Occupancy as procedure is cumbersome & expensive.  Traditional Authorities (TA) continue to administer unregistered customary parcels. Missing legal provision for the rights of migrating nomads (Fulani), a critical issue in northern states.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 5, 6, 10, 36 (3).
indicators.additional_info: Expensive: Certificate requires payment for unexhausted improvements and annual rent, grant depends on assent of unelected committee, limits on size, and holding of undeveloped lands.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law treats an individual, family and community as equally eligible for issue of Customary Certificates, meaning the latter are legal persons for purposes of land law. Outdated law fails to  protect customary lands near towns from informal settlements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 51
indicators.additional_info: Land Use Act, s. 51: "customary right of occupancy" means the right of a person or community lawfully using or occupying land in accordance with customary law and includes a customary right of occupancy granted by a Local Government under this Act".

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition of customary law as basis of authority deceptive, as Governor and Local Government hold significant powers. The law also fails to specify the powers of Traditional Authorities as de facto administrators of local customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act (1978) as reissued in 2004.
indicators.additional_info: The law leaves decisions to customary law, as limited by Bill of Rights in Constitution (1999). The Constitution makes customary law the source of jurisdiction in State and Federal Customary Courts. This has a long tradition begun in Privy Court Ruling in 2021 that customary law is founded on the assent of the people.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights governed by customary law including inheritance norms. These accept customary rights are held in perpetuity if not voluntarily surrendered, transferred etc.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act 2004
indicators.additional_info: Alienation of customary rights is not possible without Governor's consent,  and may occur only by assignment, transfer or lease. Land Use Act, 2004 s. 21. The Constitution provides for Customary Courts to rule on customary law disputes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal provisions for consent for land takings. Governor may extinguish customary rights virtually at will for broadly defined public purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, 2004 s.28 (3), 51.
indicators.additional_info: Compensation must be prompt, not prior. While Constitution allows negotiation through tribunals (Art. 44), Land Use Act (s. 47 (2) denies court jurisdiction to inquire into any matter relating to compulsory acquisition or compensation.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Individual State Forest laws list protected trees with implication that other trees on customary lands may be  freely harvested  (eg. Kaduna State Forestry Law, 2019, Cross River State Establishment of Forestry Commission 2010). Villages may declare Community Forests, norms different in each State Forest Law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Use Act, CAP 202, s. 14. Cross River State Forest Act, Law No. 3 of 2010.  Kaduna State Forestry Law, 2019.
