NIC.name: Nicaragua

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities in Nicaragua are granted ownership rights that are recognized and protected by the 1987 Constitution. The Statute Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (187) and the Communal Land Law(2003) provide indigenous peoples with the right to own and use communal lands based on their traditional and customary patterns of land and resource use and occupancy.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 5 of the Constitution provides “The State recognizes the existence of indigenous peoples who enjoy the rights, duties and guarantees designated in the Constitution, and especially those to maintain and develop their identity and culture to have their own forms of social organization and administer their local affairs, as well as to preserve the communal forms of land property and their exploitations, use, and enjoyment, all in accordance with the law. […] The various forms of public, private, associative, cooperative, and communal property shall be guaranteed and encouraged without discrimination in order to produce wealth and shall serve social needs by operating freely." Article 24 of Law 445 provides "the State recognizes the right of the indigenous and ethnic communities over the lands they traditionally occupy. Likewise, it recognizes and guarantees the inalienability, the imprescriptibility and the inability to attach said property." Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...." NOTE: In 2010, Nicaragua ratified ILO Convention 169- the Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution grants community ownership rights the same level of protection as those granted under other tenure regimes (private property). However, the government retains authority to limit property rights to expropriated property (Art. 44). The government can also grant concessions to communal lands so long as it consults the indigenous community (Article 16, Law 445). Communities must register to receive protection (Art. 39-51, Law 445).
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 15 of Law 445 provides that "Autonomous Regional Councils and Autonomous Regional Governments shall respect the rights of ownership that the indigenous and ethnic communities...have over their communal lands and over the natural resources they contain." Article 16 of Law 445 provides that "in cases regarding the granting of concessions and contracts for the rational exploitation of the resources found in the subsoil of the ethnic and indigenous communities lands, by the State, the corresponding Regional Council shall issue the resolution upon consultation with the indigenous communities on whose lands the natural resources are located. As a result of the consultation, the communities shall respond positively or negatively to the request of the Autonomous Regional Council." Article 25 of Law 445 establishes "in the contracts to exploit the natural resources on the indigenous and ethnic communal properties, the State shall recognize the right of ownership of the community or territory where theses are to be found."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law 445 establishes clear procedures for formalizing indigenous and community land, but is unclear whether these procedures are affordable and accessible for communities. Communities can either demarcate land as a community or as a territory.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous and ethnic communities are recognized as legal persons for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 60 of Law 544 provides "the administrative remedies established in Articles 39 through 45 No. 290, Law of Organizations, Jurisdiction and Procedures of the Executive Power, may be invoked by the communal and territorial authorities or any other citizen who considers that his rights have been violated in the process of demarcation and titling."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution, Statute of the Autonomy of the Atlantic Cost, and Law 445 recognizes the legal authority and autonomy of indigenous populations in Nicaragua. Authority over and administration of the tenure regime is vested in the communal assemblies, territorial assemblies, traditional community authorities, and territorial authorities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 181 of the Constitution delegates autonomy and authority to communities (through traditional community authorities. Article 4 of Law 445 establishes that ""the Communal Assembly constitutes the maximum authority of the indigenous and ethnic communities. The Legal Representation of the communities corresponds to the communal authorities. Every community will define which communal authority shall legally represent them. The territorial Assembly is the maximum authority of the territory and it is summoned according to the procedures established by the group of communities which integrate the territorial unit."" Article 10 of Law 445 provides that ""traditional community authorities may grant authorizations for the exploitation of communal lands in favor of third parties. This authorization will not be required in order to carry out subsistence activities.""

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law does not establish duration limits on the ownership rights of indigenous and ethnic communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law 445 requires consultation and negotiation with communities whenever the government grants a concession to a third party for the purpose of natural resource extraction. However, community consent is not a prerequisite to land acquisition by governments and others.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 16 of Law 445 provides that "in cases regarding the granting of concessions and contracts for the rational exploitation of the resources found in the subsoil of the ethnic and indigenous communities lands, by the State, the corresponding Regional Council shall issue the resolution upon consultation with the indigenous communities on whose lands the natural resources are located. As a result of the consultation, the communities shall respond positively or negatively to the request of the Autonomous Regional Council". Article 17 further states "In the cases where the community is opposed to the performance of the project, the granting of the concession, or the contract for exploitation, the Regional Council shall initiate a negotiation process within the community. In this negotiation process, the communities shall be represented by their traditional authorities, who shall be assisted by technical advisors of their choice. In all cases, the negotiation of the Regional Council shall foresee indemnification for eventual damages to the community, regardless of their participation in the project. Displacement or resettlement of the community will not be considered under any circumstances. In each off these procedures, and for the purpose of further protecting the natural resources, the Central Government shall directly participate in supporting the communities in their negotiations." Article 18 states "when the consultation process is completed for the execution of the project or the granting of the concession or contract, the community, the respective Autonomous Regional Council and the interested entity or company shall sign an agreement specifying the technical terms and the participation in the economic benefits of the community." Article 2 of Law 445 defines "consultation" as "the expression and delivery of the technical information regarding the operation or project, followed by a process of discussion and decision making. The communities shall have interpreters to translate everything that is said during said process into their own languages and shall be assisted by technicians, experts on the subject matter. Both the interpreter as well as the technician, shall be chosen by communities." NOTE: According to USAID's land tenure profile of Nicaragua, some local government officials have entered into agreements with private commercial enterprises without local community knowledge or participation in negotiations or benefits http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/country-profiles/full-reports/USAID_Land_Tenure_Nicaragua_Profile.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law 445 indicates that ownership rights to trees are included within the bundle of communal property rights. Under the Forest law, indigenous and ethnic communities have rights to forest resources, including access, withdrawal, management, and exclusion, but not rights of alienation, meaning that rights are not-transferable and non-mortgageable.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2003 Forest Law; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law 445 indicates that ownership rights to water are included within the bundle of communal property rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Law 2007; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz);
indicators.additional_info: Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The State may designate communal property as protected areas, but indigenous communities may not be evicted from protected areas. While the government retains ultimate control and authority over protected areas, communities retain rights to manage land within protected areas. Article 59 of the 1999 Law on Protected Areas provides that "in the event that the lands [designated as protected areas] are of indigenous communities, the right of ownership thereof will be respected."
indicators.law_and_provision: Reglamento de áreas protegidas de Nicaragua (1999); Law on the Conservation, Development and Sustainable Forestry (Law No. 462); Coastal Law 2009; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 21 of El Reglamento de areas protegidas de Nicaragua 1999 obliges government authorities to ensure the participation of local inhabitants when formulating the management plans of protected areas. The following protected areas may be established in Nicaragua: Biological Reserve, National Park, National Monument, Historical Monument, Wildlife Refuge, Nature Reserve, Reserve of Genetic Resources, Protected Landscape/Seascape, and Biosphere Reserve. NOTE: One successful example of a co-management scheme, involving local communities, is the Voluntary Indigenous Forest Rangers Corps of Bosawas, Nicaragua was created in the mid-1990s to manage natural reserves in Nicaragua. This is a voluntary organization of indigenous ranger corps that administer and manage land within the Bosawas Natural Reserves (https://www.cbd.int/doc/pa/tools/Indigenous%20peoples%20and%20protected%20areas%20management.pdf)

local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.comment: Indigenous communities in Nicaragua are granted ownership rights that are recognized and protected by the 1987 Constitution. The Statute Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (187) and the Communal Land Law(2003) provide indigenous peoples with the right to own and use communal lands based on their traditional and customary patterns of land and resource use and occupancy.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 5 of the Constitution provides “The State recognizes the existence of indigenous peoples who enjoy the rights, duties and guarantees designated in the Constitution, and especially those to maintain and develop their identity and culture to have their own forms of social organization and administer their local affairs, as well as to preserve the communal forms of land property and their exploitations, use, and enjoyment, all in accordance with the law. […] The various forms of public, private, associative, cooperative, and communal property shall be guaranteed and encouraged without discrimination in order to produce wealth and shall serve social needs by operating freely." Article 24 of Law 445 provides "the State recognizes the right of the indigenous and ethnic communities over the lands they traditionally occupy. Likewise, it recognizes and guarantees the inalienability, the imprescriptibility and the inability to attach said property." Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...." NOTE: In 2010, Nicaragua ratified ILO Convention 169- the Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution grants community ownership rights the same level of protection as those granted under other tenure regimes (private property). However, the government retains authority to limit property rights to expropriated property (Art. 44). The government can also grant concessions to communal lands so long as it consults the indigenous community (Article 16, Law 445). Communities must register to receive protection (Art. 39-51, Law 445).
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 15 of Law 445 provides that "Autonomous Regional Councils and Autonomous Regional Governments shall respect the rights of ownership that the indigenous and ethnic communities...have over their communal lands and over the natural resources they contain." Article 16 of Law 445 provides that "in cases regarding the granting of concessions and contracts for the rational exploitation of the resources found in the subsoil of the ethnic and indigenous communities lands, by the State, the corresponding Regional Council shall issue the resolution upon consultation with the indigenous communities on whose lands the natural resources are located. As a result of the consultation, the communities shall respond positively or negatively to the request of the Autonomous Regional Council." Article 25 of Law 445 establishes "in the contracts to exploit the natural resources on the indigenous and ethnic communal properties, the State shall recognize the right of ownership of the community or territory where theses are to be found."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law 445 establishes clear procedures for formalizing indigenous and community land, but is unclear whether these procedures are affordable and accessible for communities. Communities can either demarcate land as a community or as a territory.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous and ethnic communities are recognized as legal persons for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 60 of Law 544 provides "the administrative remedies established in Articles 39 through 45 No. 290, Law of Organizations, Jurisdiction and Procedures of the Executive Power, may be invoked by the communal and territorial authorities or any other citizen who considers that his rights have been violated in the process of demarcation and titling."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution, Statute of the Autonomy of the Atlantic Cost, and Law 445 recognizes the legal authority and autonomy of indigenous populations in Nicaragua. Authority over and administration of the tenure regime is vested in the communal assemblies, territorial assemblies, traditional community authorities, and territorial authorities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 181 of the Constitution delegates autonomy and authority to communities (through traditional community authorities. Article 4 of Law 445 establishes that ""the Communal Assembly constitutes the maximum authority of the indigenous and ethnic communities. The Legal Representation of the communities corresponds to the communal authorities. Every community will define which communal authority shall legally represent them. The territorial Assembly is the maximum authority of the territory and it is summoned according to the procedures established by the group of communities which integrate the territorial unit."" Article 10 of Law 445 provides that ""traditional community authorities may grant authorizations for the exploitation of communal lands in favor of third parties. This authorization will not be required in order to carry out subsistence activities.""

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law does not establish duration limits on the ownership rights of indigenous and ethnic communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law 445 requires consultation and negotiation with communities whenever the government grants a concession to a third party for the purpose of natural resource extraction. However, community consent is not a prerequisite to land acquisition by governments and others.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 16 of Law 445 provides that "in cases regarding the granting of concessions and contracts for the rational exploitation of the resources found in the subsoil of the ethnic and indigenous communities lands, by the State, the corresponding Regional Council shall issue the resolution upon consultation with the indigenous communities on whose lands the natural resources are located. As a result of the consultation, the communities shall respond positively or negatively to the request of the Autonomous Regional Council". Article 17 further states "In the cases where the community is opposed to the performance of the project, the granting of the concession, or the contract for exploitation, the Regional Council shall initiate a negotiation process within the community. In this negotiation process, the communities shall be represented by their traditional authorities, who shall be assisted by technical advisors of their choice. In all cases, the negotiation of the Regional Council shall foresee indemnification for eventual damages to the community, regardless of their participation in the project. Displacement or resettlement of the community will not be considered under any circumstances. In each off these procedures, and for the purpose of further protecting the natural resources, the Central Government shall directly participate in supporting the communities in their negotiations." Article 18 states "when the consultation process is completed for the execution of the project or the granting of the concession or contract, the community, the respective Autonomous Regional Council and the interested entity or company shall sign an agreement specifying the technical terms and the participation in the economic benefits of the community." Article 2 of Law 445 defines "consultation" as "the expression and delivery of the technical information regarding the operation or project, followed by a process of discussion and decision making. The communities shall have interpreters to translate everything that is said during said process into their own languages and shall be assisted by technicians, experts on the subject matter. Both the interpreter as well as the technician, shall be chosen by communities." NOTE: According to USAID's land tenure profile of Nicaragua, some local government officials have entered into agreements with private commercial enterprises without local community knowledge or participation in negotiations or benefits http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/country-profiles/full-reports/USAID_Land_Tenure_Nicaragua_Profile.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law 445 indicates that ownership rights to trees are included within the bundle of communal property rights. Under the Forest law, indigenous and ethnic communities have rights to forest resources, including access, withdrawal, management, and exclusion, but not rights of alienation, meaning that rights are not-transferable and non-mortgageable.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2003 Forest Law; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law 445 indicates that ownership rights to water are included within the bundle of communal property rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Law 2007; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz);
indicators.additional_info: Article 2 of Law 445 defines "communal property" as "the collective property constituted by the lands, waters, forests, and other natural resources contained therein which have traditionally belonged to the community...."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The State may designate communal property as protected areas, but indigenous communities may not be evicted from protected areas. While the government retains ultimate control and authority over protected areas, communities retain rights to manage land within protected areas. Article 59 of the 1999 Law on Protected Areas provides that "in the event that the lands [designated as protected areas] are of indigenous communities, the right of ownership thereof will be respected."
indicators.law_and_provision:
Reglamento de áreas protegidas de Nicaragua 
(1999); Law on the Conservation, Development and Sustainable Forestry (Law No. 462); Coastal Law 2009; Article 5, 89-91, 107, 181 Constitution of Nicaragua, 1987; Statute of Autonomy of the Atlantic Coast (1987); Law 445 (Law of Communal Property Regime of the Indigenous Peoples and Ethnic Communities of the Autonomous Regions of the Atlantic Coast of Nicaragua and of the Rivers Bocay, Coco, Indio and Maiz)
indicators.additional_info: Article 21 of El Reglamento de areas protegidas de Nicaragua 1999 obliges government authorities to ensure the participation of local inhabitants when formulating the management plans of protected areas. The following protected areas may be established in Nicaragua: Biological Reserve, National Park, National Monument, Historical Monument, Wildlife Refuge, Nature Reserve, Reserve of Genetic Resources, Protected Landscape/Seascape, and Biosphere Reserve. NOTE: One successful example of a co-management scheme, involving local communities, is the Voluntary Indigenous Forest Rangers Corps of Bosawas, Nicaragua was created in the mid-1990s to manage natural reserves in Nicaragua. This is a voluntary organization of indigenous ranger corps that administer and manage land within the Bosawas Natural Reserves (https://www.cbd.int/doc/pa/tools/Indigenous%20peoples%20and%20protected%20areas%20management.pdf)

NOR.name: Norway

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous land (Sami)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court in 2001 found that the Sami population in Svartskogen (in northern Norway) were the rightful owners of their lands. The Finmark Act 2005 recognizes Sami territorial rights to use lands and water held in Finnmark County, but these rights do not extend beyond the county of Finnmark.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Norway; Sec. 5, Act of 17 June 2005 No. 85 relating to legal relations and management country of Finnmark (Finnmark Act) 2005; Supreme Court of Norway. 2001. Norwegian Supreme Court Ruling Rt. 2001 s.1229
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution of Norway provides that "it is the responsibility of authorities of the State to create conditions enabling the Sami people to preserve and develop its language, culture and way of life" (Article 108, Constitution of Norway). The Constitutional Court held "the [Sami's] land use has had a varied form given what has been a natural utilisation in the different periods. In a nutshell, the land use is characterised by continuity, and has been all-embracing and intensive as well as flexible. The conditions regarding the scope and length of the land use for establishment of ownership are maintained" (Unofficial translation). Section 5 of the Finnmark Act provides that "through prolonged use of land and water areas, the Sami have collectively and individually acquired rights to land in Finnmark." (the doctrine of immemorial usage applies meaning Sami's acquired rights through using the land over a long time period.) NOTE: section 3 of the Finnmark Act must abide by the ILO Convention No. 169 concerning Indigenous and Tribal Peoples in Independent Countries (ILO Convention 169 was ratified by Norway in 1990). NOTE ALSO: The Reindeer Husbandry Act of 1987 (amended 1997) recognizes that Sami have an exclusive right to herd reindeer with pasture areas, this is essentially a usufruct right.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The laws states that it does not interfere with the individual rights acquired by Sami and other people through prescription or immemorial usage. However, the government bodies: Sami Parliament, the Finnmark estate, the Finnmark Commission, and the Land Consolidation Court retain broad authority over lands held by the Sami population.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 5, 10 Act of 17 June 2005 No. 85 relating to legal relations and management country of Finnmark (Finnmark Act) 2005
indicators.additional_info: Section 10 of the Finnmark Act provides that "In matters concerning changes in the use of uncultivated land, Finnmarkseiendommen shall assess the significance a change will have for Sami culture, reindeer husbandry, use of non-cultivated areas, commercial activity and social life. The guidelines of the Sami Parliament pursuant to section 4 shall be followed in the assessment of Sami interests pursuant to the first sentence. Decisions concerning changes in the use of uncultivated land require the support of at least four board members if the whole minority bases its opinion on consideration for Sami culture, reindeer husbandry, use of non-cultivated areas, commercial activity and social life assessed on the basis of the guidelines of the Sami Parliament. If the majority consists of four or less, a collective minority may during the board meeting demand that the matter be placed before the Sami Parliament. If the Sami Parliament does not ratify the decision of the majority or does not consider the matter within a reasonable time, a collective majority of the board may demand that Finnmarkseiendommen place the matter before the King, who shall then decide whether the decision shall be approved. Such approval of the decision has the same effect as such a decision by the board."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: There is a clear process for formalization. The Finnmark Commission investigates rights to land and water in Finnmark and a special court (the Uncultivated Land Tribunal for Finnmark) to settle disputes concerning rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 29, 32, 36, 45 Finnmark Act
indicators.additional_info: Section 32 of the Finnmark Act provides that "the Finnmark Commission is itself responsible for obtaining sufficient information concerning a matter. The Commission may in the manner it finds appropriate obtain statements, documents, and other materials and conduct surveys and investigations". Section 45 of the Finnmark Act provides that the Land Consolidation Court carries out boundary markings on the ground, fixing of coordinates and survey of the boundaries in accordance with the judgment, declaration or agreement"

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Sami population is granted legal personality, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 36, Finnmark Act

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Sami Parliament has authority to issue guidelines on the use of community lands, but these guidelines must be approved by the Ministry. Sami land is administered through the Finnmark Estate.
indicators.law_and_provision: Section 4-6, Finnmark Act 2005
indicators.additional_info: Section 4 of the Finnmark Act states "The Sami Parliament may issue guidelines for assessing the effect of changes in the use of uncultivated land on Sami culture, reindeer husbandry, use of non-cultivated areas, commercial activity and social life. The guidelines shall be approved by the Ministry. The Ministry shall examine whether the guidelines lie within the framework laid down in the first sentence and whether they have been drawn up in an appropriate manner. In matters concerning changes in the use of uncultivated land, state, county and municipal authorities shall assess the significance such changes will have for Sami culture, reindeer husbandry, use of non-cultivated areas, commercial activity and social life. The guidelines of the Sami Parliament shall be followed in the assessment of Sami interests pursuant to the first sentence." Section 5 of the Finnmark Act provides "In order to establish the scope and content of the rights held by Sami and other people on the basis of prescription or immemorial usage or on some other basis, a commission shall be established to investigate rights to land and water in Finnmarkand a special court to settle disputes concerning such rights, cf. chapter 5." Section 10 also grants decision-making authority over land use of uncultivated lands to the Finnmark Estate using the guidelines established by the Sami populations.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Finnmark Act 2005 does not impose durational limits on the land rights of Sami Populations which indicates that rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Finnmark Act 2005

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant the Sami population rights to give consent prior to acquisition. Changes in the use of uncultivated land must be assessed by the Finnmark Estate and allowed on a case-by-case basis following the guidelines of the Sami Parliament.
indicators.law_and_provision: Finnmark Act 2005

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law grants Sami the right to remove timber for home crafts, fell deciduous trees for domestic fuel, remove deciduous trees for use as fence posts and poles for hay-drying racks in the reindeer husbandry and agriculture industries.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 22-23 of the Finnmark Act 2005, Sec. 2 of the Forestry Act 2005
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Act 2005 provides that the ""[Forestry Act] may not be applied in contravention of the rights of Sami reindeer herders to timber and fuel.""

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The same legal protections that apply to land also apply to water. Sami can use watercourse for fishing and other domestic purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 2, Finnmark Act; Water Resources Act 2000
indicators.additional_info: Section 2 of the Finnmark Act provides that ""The Act shall apply to real property and watercourses with natural resources in the county of Finnmark.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law is silent on whether Sami Population has rights to land in protected areas, but are entitled to compensation for loss of land if land is designated as a national park.
indicators.law_and_provision: Section 19, Finnmark Act 2005; Nature Conservation Act 1970
indicators.additional_info: Section 19 provides "Land owned by Finnmarkseiendommen may be designated as national parks pursuant to the provisions of the Nature Conservation Act. When drafting rules of use, emphasis shall be placed on the possibility of continuing traditional use. Finnmarkseiendommen and affected holders of rights of use may demand compensation for financial loss pursuant to the provisions of section 20b of the Nature Conservation Act.

local_communities_entries.framework: Community land (community commons or Bygdeallmenning)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law grants communities the rights use Bygd commons for agricultural purposes. Bygd commons are defined as "community-owned commons (as opposed to state-owned) where farmers living in a “bygd” have certain use rights (profits) tied to their cadastral farm units (rights of common appendant) such as fishing, grazing, logging, etc.
indicators.law_and_provision: Government of Norway. 1992. Act relating to Bygd Commons. June 19. Translated by Julie Wille in Legislation on Commons (Statsallmenning/Bygdeallmenning) in Norway: Center for Land Studies Report, edited by Berge, Erling, Gaku Mitsumata, and Daisaku Shimada. 2011. Norwegian University of Life Sciences (UMB). Available at: http://www.umb.no/statisk/clts/reports/CLTS_Report_1_2011.pdf .
indicators.additional_info:
The owner of the holding with rights of 
common appendant may only exercise the 
right to the extent necessary to cover needs of the holding for agriculture-related operations. Section 1-1 of the Act relating to bygd commons provides that "bygd commons is commons where property rights to the ground and reminder vest in at least half of the agricultural holdings which since ancient times have rights of common A right “appendant” to a Bygd common is inalienable and established by prescription and not by any grant. It means in this case
that the rights of common, including the fraction of the ground, are inalienably attached to a cadastral farm unit. Section 2-2 of the Act relating to Bygd Commons provides that "the owner of the holding with the rights of common appendant may only exercise the right to the extent necessary to cover needs of the holding for agriculture-related operations. Furthermore, Section 2 of the Montain Act provides "Rights of common in the state commons belong to communities (bygdi ) or parts thereof, which from ancient times have had such rights. The rights shall be used in a way that at any time is in accordance with rational use and which is natural according to the times and circumstances."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Section 1-2 of Act relating to bygd commons provides circumstances in which bygd commons can be sold, leased, and expropriated.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act relating to byd commons 1992; Act relating to the exploitation of rights and entitlements in the state commons (The Mountain Act)
indicators.additional_info:
Loss of rights of common according to this
paragraph occurs only when the commons
board has made a decision about this, and the owner of the holding in question is notified of the decision (Sec. 2-6 of the Act relating to bygd commons). Furthermore, Section 2-6 provides that rights of common lapses: 1. if farming on the holding will be terminated, and a) the land is used for other purposes, or b) remains unused for a continuous period of five years or 2. If the holding through the sale, other voluntary surrender, expropriation or reassignment loses its character of agriculture

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law provides that land held within bygd commons must be registered, but it is unclear whether this process is accessible and inexpensive for commoners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act relating to bygd commons 1992; Act relating to the exploitation of rights and entitlements in the state commons (The Mountain Act)
indicators.additional_info: Section 2-5 of the Act relating to Bygd Commons provides that "for each bygd commons there will be a register of holdings with rights of common appendant. The register shall contain information on the cultivated area, about the allocation of benefits that were made from the commons, and what any time exercises the rights of common. The rights of common register is the basis for the census for election of the commons board." If change in ownership and other events that result in changes with respect to the exercise of rights of common or voting rights at the commons board election (tenancy, moving, liquidation or resumption of agricultural operations, entering into or dissolution of marriage, death, etc.), notification shall be given to the commons board.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law grants bygd commoners with legal personality, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act relating to Bygd commons 1992

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Section 3-1 of the Act relating to bygd commons provides that ""management of the bygd commons belongs to the commons board."" Bylaws of the common board must be approved by the Ministry.
indicators.law_and_provision: Section 3-1, 3-8 of the Act relating to Bygd Commons
indicators.additional_info: The Mountain Act 1992 grants the mountain board authority to administer the usage and exploitation of rights and entitlements (Sec. 3).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law grants bygd commoners with legal personality , but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act relating to Bygd commons 1992

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant Bygd commoners with the right to give consent prior to acquisition by governments or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Act relating to Bygd commons 1992

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: With approval from the bygd commons board, logging may take place within the commons. However, there is no indication commoners are owners of the trees within the commons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Section 2-7 Act relating to Bygd Commons 1992; Forest Act, 2005
indicators.additional_info:
Section 2-7 of the Bygd Commons provides that logging can only be done after allocation from the commons 
board and grants from the state forestry 
management.

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: With approval from the bygd commons board, fishing may take place within waterways in Bygd Commons. Communities, as citizens, can also use water for domestic purposes.

indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue

NPL.name: Nepal

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land is divided into three tenure types: state land, private land, and Guthi (religious) land. Communities are granted user rights to forests, but the state retains broad power to extinguish forest areas collectively held and used by communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended) Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Communities are granted the right to create Community Forest User Groups for the development, conservation, and utilization of collectively-managed forests. However, community user groups are limited to the rights set out in their work plants (Forest Regulation, 2051). The state retains ownership and authority over Community Forests and retains power to extinguish Community Forest User Groups upon the granting of notice to the community. NOTE: In practice, community-based tenure is also provided through the handing over of Religious Forests, community-based conservation including Buffer Zone Areas, Community Leasehold Forests, and Collaborative Forests.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rights granted to Community Forest User Groups are not given the same level of protection as private ownership rights. Community Forests are easily extinguishable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Article 27 of the Forest Act provides that the District Forest Officer may cancel or take back the forest rights granted to Community User Groups. NOTE: Article 30 of the Forest Act provides that priority shall be given to Community Forests. The law states "Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, any part of the National Forest suitable to handover to the Users' Group as Community Forest shall not be handed over as Leasehold Forest."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: There are clear procedures for establishing Community Forest User Groups, and the Work Plan must include maps and details of the forests granted to communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Section 28 of the Forest Regulations provides that "Users' Group shall have to prepare a Work Plan of Community Forest by including the following matters: (a) Details of the Forest-name, boundaries, areas...(b) Map of the Forest..."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly provide communities with the rights to legal personality for the purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Act provides communities some authority over the forest area, but this is subject to the rights specified in the Work Plan. Communities have no authority beyond hat granted by the Work Plan.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Section 31 of the Forest Regulation provides that communities are prohibited from clearing forest areas, building huts and houses, and other activities in community forest areas. Additionally, the law provides that "the Users' Group shall collect, sell and distribute only those Forest products which are available pursuant to the Work Plan" (Sec. 32, Forest Regulation).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Under the Forest Regulation, 2051, community forest rights are durational in nature, and the District Forest Officer retains authority to cancel or extinguish Community Forests at any time.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The District Forest Officer can extinguish community-held forests without consulting or obtaining consent from the community
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended) Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Act provides for the creation of community and religious forests for the collective management, conservation, and use of forest resources. But state retains broad discretion to take back collectively managed forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Communities may apply to the District Forest Officer to become a Community Forest User Group (Art. 25, Forest Act). This right entitles them to "develop, conserve, use and manage the Forest and to sell and distribute the Forest Products." However, the Forest Regulation states that "Forest Products [of User Groups] shall not be collected, sold and distributed exceeding the quantity of collection, sale and distribution specified in the Work Plan for the whole year" (Sec. 6, Forest Regulation, 2051). Communities may also apply for "religious forest" and, if handed over to the community by the District Forest Officer, communities may "utilize Forest products contained in the Religious Forest for the religious purposes (Art. 35-36, Forest Act 2049). The District Forest Officer has broad discretion to take back religious forests as long as s/he notifies the community (Art. 37, Forest Act; Forest Regulation, 2051).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Under the Water Resources Act, 2049 (1992) citizens are granted rights to use water for domestic pruposes, which means that communities are also granted the right to use water on an individual or collective basis. However, since community land use rights are limited to forest areas, it can be implied that water rights are limited to such areas as well.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, 2049 (1992); Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995); Constitution of Nepal
indicators.additional_info: Article 35 of the Constitution states "Every citizen shall have the right of access to clean drinking water and sanitation." Sec. 3 of the Water Resources Act, 2049 provides that "the ownership of the water resources available in Nepal shall be vested in Nepal."  However, individuals are granted beneficial use rights. Article 4 provides that "no license shall be erquierd for the following uses of water resources. (a) for one's own drinking and other domestic use on an individual or collective basis, (b) for irrigation of one's own land on an individual or collective basis, (c) for the purpose of running water-mill or water-grinder as cottage industry, (d) for the use of boat on personal basis for local transportation, (e) or the use, as prescribed, of water resources confided to a land by the owner of such land." Article 14 states that indiviudals, communities, and organisations have the Right to use Water and Water Resources for family or business purposes."" As discussed in indicator 1, Land is divided into three tenure types: state land, private land, and Guthi (religious) land. Communities are granted user rights to forests, but the state retains broad power to extinguish forest areas collectively held and used by communities.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While communities are not granted ownership rights in protected areas, the law provides rights to communities to manage land held within buffer zone areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Parks and Wildlife Act, 1973; Buffer Zone Management Regulation 2052 (1996)
indicators.additional_info: Communities are legally permitted to manage and co-manage protected areas, provided they are organized as institutions (Section 16(b), National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 1973). However, there are no explicit rights in Protected Areas granted to communities by law. Section 16(b) of the Act states "His Majesty's Government may, by publishing a notification in the Nepal Gazette, entrust the management of any conservation area...to any institution established with the objective of conserving nature and natural resources..."

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land is divided into three tenure types: state land, private land, and Guthi (religious) land. Communities are granted user rights to forests, but the state retains broad power to extinguish forest areas collectively held and used by communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended) Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Communities are granted the right to create Community Forest User Groups for the development, conservation, and utilization of collectively-managed forests. However, community user groups are limited to the rights set out in their work plants (Forest Regulation, 2051). The state retains ownership and authority over Community Forests and retains power to extinguish Community Forest User Groups upon the granting of notice to the community. NOTE: In practice, community-based tenure is also provided through the handing over of Religious Forests, community-based conservation including Buffer Zone Areas, Community Leasehold Forests, and Collaborative Forests.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Rights granted to Community Forest User Groups are not given the same level of protection as private ownership rights. Community Forests are easily extinguishable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Article 27 of the Forest Act provides that the District Forest Officer may cancel or take back the forest rights granted to Community User Groups. NOTE: Article 30 of the Forest Act provides that priority shall be given to Community Forests. The law states "Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, any part of the National Forest suitable to handover to the Users' Group as Community Forest shall not be handed over as Leasehold Forest."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: There are clear procedures for establishing Community Forest User Groups, and the Work Plan must include maps and details of the forests granted to communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Section 28 of the Forest Regulations provides that "Users' Group shall have to prepare a Work Plan of Community Forest by including the following matters: (a) Details of the Forest-name, boundaries, areas...(b) Map of the Forest..."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly provide communities with the rights to legal personality for the purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Act provides communities some authority over the forest area, but this is subject to the rights specified in the Work Plan. Communities have no authority beyond hat granted by the Work Plan.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Section 31 of the Forest Regulation provides that communities are prohibited from clearing forest areas, building huts and houses, and other activities in community forest areas. Additionally, the law provides that "the Users' Group shall collect, sell and distribute only those Forest products which are available pursuant to the Work Plan" (Sec. 32, Forest Regulation).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Under the Forest Regulation, 2051, community forest rights are durational in nature, and the District Forest Officer retains authority to cancel or extinguish Community Forests at any time.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The District Forest Officer can extinguish community-held forests without consulting or obtaining consent from the community
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended) Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Act provides for the creation of community and religious forests for the collective management, conservation, and use of forest resources. But state retains broad discretion to take back collectively managed forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Nepal, 2015; The Lands Act, 2021 (1964); The Land (Measurement and Inspect) Act (1963, as amended)Arts. 25-27 and 35-37, Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995)
indicators.additional_info: Communities may apply to the District Forest Officer to become a Community Forest User Group (Art. 25, Forest Act). This right entitles them to "develop, conserve, use and manage the Forest and to sell and distribute the Forest Products." However, the Forest Regulation states that "Forest Products [of User Groups] shall not be collected, sold and distributed exceeding the quantity of collection, sale and distribution specified in the Work Plan for the whole year" (Sec. 6, Forest Regulation, 2051). Communities may also apply for "religious forest" and, if handed over to the community by the District Forest Officer, communities may "utilize Forest products contained in the Religious Forest for the religious purposes (Art. 35-36, Forest Act 2049). The District Forest Officer has broad discretion to take back religious forests as long as s/he notifies the community (Art. 37, Forest Act; Forest Regulation, 2051).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Under the Water Resources Act, 2049 (1992) citizens are granted rights to use water for domestic pruposes, which means that communities are also granted the right to use water on an individual or collective basis. However, since community land use rights are limited to forest areas, it can be implied that water rights are limited to such areas as well.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, 2049 (1992); Forest Act, 2049 (1993); Forest Regulation, 2051 (1995); Constitution of Nepal
indicators.additional_info: Article 35 of the Constitution states "Every citizen shall have the right of access to clean drinking water and sanitation." Sec. 3 of the Water Resources Act, 2049 provides that "the ownership of the water resources available in Nepal shall be vested in Nepal."  However, individuals are granted beneficial use rights. Article 4 provides that "no license shall be erquierd for the following uses of water resources. (a) for one's own drinking and other domestic use on an individual or collective basis, (b) for irrigation of one's own land on an individual or collective basis, (c) for the purpose of running water-mill or water-grinder as cottage industry, (d) for the use of boat on personal basis for local transportation, (e) or the use, as prescribed, of water resources confided to a land by the owner of such land." Article 14 states that indiviudals, communities, and organisations have the Right to use Water and Water Resources for family or business purposes."" As discussed in indicator 1, Land is divided into three tenure types: state land, private land, and Guthi (religious) land. Communities are granted user rights to forests, but the state retains broad power to extinguish forest areas collectively held and used by communities.
