NZL.name: New Zealand

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous communities (Maori)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Title to customary land is recognized by statute (the TTWA 1993) and New Zealand also recognizes the doctrine of aboriginal title (same as Australia, Canada, USA) under common law. The TTWA 1993 recognizes Maori customary land and Maori freehold land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Act, 1986; Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997; Treaty of Waitangi (1840)
indicators.additional_info: The TTWA 1993 provides for recognition and protection of customary Maori land. Section 129 of the TTWA 1993 establishes two categories of indigenous land: Maori customary land ("land that is held by Maori in accordance with tikanga Moari" and Maori freehold land "land, the beneficial ownership of which has been determined by the Maori Land Court by freehold order." Alienation of Maori customary and freehold land is prohibited by law (Secs. 145-146, TTWA 1993). The TTWA also provides for the establishment of "Maori reserve land" which is defined as "any lands that for the time being vested in the Maori reserve." The government retains underlying ownership and authority over Maori customary and freehold land. NOTE: The Treaty of Waitangi was first signed in 1840 and was an agreement between Britain and Maoris. The Treaty recognized Maori ownership of their lands, forests, and other properties.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Maori customary landholders can obtain ownership rights to Maori freehold land by applying to the Maori Land Court for "Maori freehold status", but the Court has discretion to approve or deny.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997
indicators.additional_info: Section 132 of TTWA 1993 provides that "the Maori Land Court shall continue to have exclusive jurisdiction to investigate the title to Maori customary land and to determine the relative interest of the owners of the land." Section 135-137 grants the Maori Land Court power to change the status of Maori Land--for instance Maori freehold land can be changed to Moari General land. Subject to restrictions on alienation, Maori freehold land has the same level of protection as freehold land held in fee simple. In other words, owners of Maori freehold land can exclude others from their property, and exercise other rights generally held by fee simple owners. However, Section 144 provides that Maori freehold land may be deemed Crown land for certain purposes. Section 141 of the TTWA 1993 provides that vesting orders (whereupon Maori customary land vests in the landowners and obtain freehold status) has the effect of "freeing the land, and every part of the land, from any trusts, restrictions, or conditions to which the land was subject immediately before making the order."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The TTWA 1993 provides clear procedures for applying to the Maori Land Court for declarations of Maori freehold status, but there are no legal provisions indicating that these procedures must be affordable and accessible for Maori landholders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997
indicators.additional_info: Section 132 establishes the application process for changing the status for land from Maori customary land to freehold land. The provision states "in any application for the exercise of the court's jurisdiction under this section, the applicant may specify- (a) the person or persons in whom it is proposed the land shall be vested; and (b) any trusts, restrictions or conditions to which it is proposed the land shall be subject....On any investigation of title and determination of relative interests... the court may make an order defining the area dealt with and vesting the land in---(a) such person or persons as the court may find to be entitled to the land in such relative shares as the court thinks fit...." (Sec. 132(3)-(4)), TTWA 1993).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Maori freehold landowners are given legal personality for the purposes of land ownership. The Court has recognized the Maoris as legal persons in several cases.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Maori communities retain authority over their customary and freehold lands; however, this authority is subject to certain restrictions imposed by the state.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997
indicators.additional_info: According to Section 132 of the TTWA "every title to and interest in Maori customary land shall be determined according to tikanga Moari, meaning the customary law governs the land. However, under Section 144 of the TTWA 1993 Maori customary land is deemed crown land for certain purposes. The TTWA 1993 also sets restrictions on alienation (Sec. 145- 147, TTWA 1993). Section 141 of the TTWA 1993 provides that vesting orders (whereupon Maori customary land vests in the landowners and obtain freehold status) has the effect of "freeing the land, and every part o the land, from any trusts, restrictions, or conditions to which the land was subject immediately before making the order."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The TTWA act does not impose durational limits on the rights of Maoris to hold customary and freehold Moari land, which indicates that these rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant Maori communities the right to give consent in an inclusive manner prior to acquisition of their lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary ownership rights to trees are not explicitly provided by law, but the TTWA 1993 indicates that Maori landowners have some forestry rights over Maori freehold land. It is unclear what is these extent of these forestry rights and whether they extend to ownership of the trees on Maori land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Act 1949; Forestry Rights Registration Act, 1983; Crown Forests Assets Act 1989; Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997
indicators.additional_info: Section 150B of TTWA 1993 indicates that a Maori incorporation can alienate forestry rights to forests on Maori on freehold land. The Forestry Rights Registration Act 1983 does specifically define whether forestry rights are rights to the trees located on land or establish whether Maoris have rights to trees on their properties. Section 67DA of the Forests Act 1949 provides that the Governor-General may make an Order granting the right to mill indigenous timber harvested from forests on Maori land.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 recognizes customary titles to the foreshore and seabed held by the Maori, but Moari have to apply to the Maori land court to achieve legal recognition.
indicators.law_and_provision: Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (MCAA 2011)
indicators.additional_info: The MCAA 2011 recognizes customary marine title areas and protect customary rights in marine and coastal areas. Protected customary rights and customary marine titles can be recognized by law through entering into an agreement with the Crown (Secs. 95-99, MCAA 2011) and applying to the Maori Land Court (Sec. 100-103). In Attorney-General v. Ngati Apa (2003), the Court of Appeal held that the Maori Land Court had jurisdiction to determine claims of customary ownership to areas of the foreshore and sea bed. Section 2 of the MCAA 2011 defines "customary title group" as "means the part of the common marine and coastal area where customary title order applies or in respect of which an agreement is made and brought into effect."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Reserves Act 1977 grants Maoris the right to take or kill birds and establish burial grounds within scenic reserves under certain circumstances. Maoris are also granted the right to establish agreements with the Crown for the purpose of protecting the environment and wildlife.
indicators.law_and_provision: Secs. 46, 77AReserves Act 1977; Conservation Act 1987; National Parks Act 1980
indicators.additional_info: Section 46 of the Reserves Act 1977 provides that "the Minister may from time to time, by notice in the Gazette, grant to the Maori the right to take or kill birds within any scenic reserve which immediately before the reservation or taking thereof was Maori land, provided the taking and killing of birds would no be in contravention of the Wildlife Act 1953 or any regulations or Proclamation or notification under that act....Where any scenic or historic reserve includes any ancestral burial grounds of Maori, the Minister may, by notice in the Gazette, grant the right to bury or inter the remains of deceased Maori in a place to be specified therein." Section 77A of the Reserves Act provides Maoris with the right to establish co-management agreements on Maori land. Section 77A states that "if satisfied that any Maori land or Crown land held under a Crown lease by Maori should be managed so as to preserve and protect- (i) the natural environment, landscape amenity, wildlife or freshwater-life or marine-life habitat, or historical value of the land; or (ii) the spiritual and cultural values which Maori associated with the land---the Minister may... agree with the owner or the lessee for a Nga Whenua Rahui Kawenate to provide for the management of the land in a manner that will achieve those purposes..."

NZL.value_label: Average score of 10 legal indicators for Indigenous Peoples' land rights (1 = law fully protects, 4 = law does not protect)
NZL.Indigenous Q1: Does the law recognize al: Partial, significant progress — Title to customary land is recognized by statute (the TTWA 1993) and New Zealand also recognizes the doctrine of aboriginal title (same as Australia, Canada, USA) under common law. The TTWA 1993 recognizes Maori customary land and Maori freehold land. (Constitution Act, 1986; Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997; Treaty of Waitangi (1840))
NZL.Indigenous Q2: Does the law give indigen: Partial, significant progress — Maori customary landholders can obtain ownership rights to Maori freehold land by applying to the Maori Land Court for "Maori freehold status", but the Court has discretion to approve or deny. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — The TTWA 1993 provides clear procedures for applying to the Maori Land Court for declarations of Maori freehold status, but there are no legal provisions indicating that these procedures must be affordable and accessible for Maori landholders. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q4: Does the law recognize th: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Maori freehold landowners are given legal personality for the purposes of land ownership. The Court has recognized the Maoris as legal persons in several cases. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q5: Does the law recognize th: Partial, significant progress — Maori communities retain authority over their customary and freehold lands; however, this authority is subject to certain restrictions imposed by the state. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q6: Do the law and formal tit: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — The TTWA act does not impose durational limits on the rights of Maoris to hold customary and freehold Moari land, which indicates that these rights may be held in perpetuity. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — The law does not explicitly grant Maori communities the right to give consent in an inclusive manner prior to acquisition of their lands. (Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q8: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, limited progress — Customary ownership rights to trees are not explicitly provided by law, but the TTWA 1993 indicates that Maori landowners have some forestry rights over Maori freehold land. It is unclear what is these extent of these forestry rights and whether they extend to ownership of the trees on Maori land. (Forestry Act 1949; Forestry Rights Registration Act, 1983; Crown Forests Assets Act 1989; Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 (TTWA 1993); Ngati Apa v. Attorney-General 1997)
NZL.Indigenous Q9: Does the law explicitly r: Partial, significant progress — The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 recognizes customary titles to the foreshore and seabed held by the Maori, but Moari have to apply to the Maori land court to achieve legal recognition. (Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (MCAA 2011))
NZL.Indigenous Q10: Does the law uphold indi: Partial, significant progress — The Reserves Act 1977 grants Maoris the right to take or kill birds and establish burial grounds within scenic reserves under certain circumstances. Maoris are also granted the right to establish agreements with the Crown for the purpose of protecting the environment and wildlife. (Secs. 46, 77AReserves Act 1977; Conservation Act 1987; National Parks Act 1980)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no explicit legal recognition of land rights held by indigenous peoples and local communities in  Oman
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Law (Royal Decree 5/80), 1980; The Law of Expropriation of Property for Public Utility (Royal Decree 64/78), 1978;
indicators.additional_info: The law states that all land in the country is the property of the state, unless specified otherwise. Government land plots are routinely granted on usufruct by the ministry for what are regarded as public utility or infrastructure projects. The Law permits Omani nationals to enjoy the benefits of owning land on freehold and leasehold bases. The owner of real estate property may lease it for residential or commercial purposes in Oman. A lease under Omani law does not provide any real rights in the property, but confers upon the lessee a leasehold right to occupy a land or a building. Pursuant to the Usufruct Law, usufruct rights over land are granted by the owner of the land to a third party for a consideration to utilize and develop it. Again, under a lease mechanism and no recognition of indigenous people. NOTE: The population in Oman consists of Muslim - with about 75% of these following the Ibadi sect, and 25% Sunni (especially in the Dhofar Governorate) (CIA WorldFactbook, 2007). There is a small Shiia presence, while Hindus (non-nationals) make up 13% of the total population. None of these groups are considered as indigenous peoples of Oman.

indicators.additional_info: Ownership of water being separate from land so that it can be freely exchanged among farmers. Rights are perpetual and are transferred from one generation to another through inheritance. Rights have the characteristic of private goods. Falaj water rights are recognized at the national level and have the same legal aspects as any other private asset. Thus, an explicit water right may be sold, inherited, or donated.

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution recognizes customary law and the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, which follow customary tenure systems (Pashtunwali) and provide for collective tenure and community based land governance by villages, clans and shura.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Pakistan; Land Reforms Act 1977; Land Control Karachi Division Act 1952; Land Acquisition Act 1894; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Registration Act, 108, Stamp Act 1899.
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of the Constitution of Pakistan recognizes the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATAs) as territories within Pakistan. The Constitution recognizes Pakistan's customary legal system and applicable in court cases (Art. 8 of the Constitution). NOTE: In practice, FATAs are governed by customary laws, which provide for collective tenure by the village, clan (qaum), shura (councils). Since this study is limited to national-level statutory law (constitutions, legislation, regulations, court decisions), the indicators do not measure customary law.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Pakistan's statutory legal system grants the government broad power to expropriate land within the territory of Pakistan. Statutory laws are silent on the extent to which community lands held under customary tenure are protected.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Pakistan; Land Reforms Act 1977; Land Control Karachi Division Act 1952; Land Acquisition Act 1894; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Registration Act, 108, Stamp Act 1899.
indicators.additional_info: Article 152 of the Constitution grants the government power to acquire land within the "Province" for Federal purposes. The national Land Acquisition Act 1894 provides that "whenever it appears to the Collector of the District that land in any locality is needed or likely to be needed any public purpose or for a Company" the Collector of the District can compulsorily acquire that land. Presumably, this means that customary community land can be expropriated for a public purpose. Article 1 of the Constitution of Pakistan recognizes the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATAs) as territories within Pakistan. The Constitution recognizes Pakistan's customary legal system and applicable in court cases (Art. 8 of the Constitution). NOTE: In practice, FATAs are governed by customary laws, which provide for collective tenure by the village, clan (qaum), shura (councils). Since this study is limited to national-level statutory law (legislation, regulations, court decisions), the indicators do not measure customary law.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Pakistan's statutory legal system does not provide a formal process of registering or titling community property held under customary tenure.

According to a USAID article, forests are that are not protected or reserved are considered the common property of a village, tribe, or clan under customary law. indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Pakistan has not enacted a comprehensive water statutory law at the national-level that defines property rights to water. Water belongs to the landowner under customary law, but LandMark assessment is limited to national level legislative and regulatory frameworks.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Accord 1991; Constitution of Pakistan; Canal and Drainage Act; Land Reforms Act 1977; Land Control Karachi Division Act 1952; Land Acquisition Act 1894; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Registration Act, 108, Stamp Act 1899.
indicators.additional_info: Water rights are recognized under customary law, but Pakistan's national and regulatory framework does not address water resource rights. The 1991 Water Accord establishes how water must be allocated between the different provinces, but does notdefine property rights to water. Under customary law, consistent with Islamic law principles, groundwater is owned by respective landowners. NOTE: LandMark's legal indicators do not assess customary laws. See USAID Propetry Rights and Resource Governance Profile on Pakistan.  (http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/country-profiles/full-reports/USAID_Land_Tenure_Pakistan_Profile_0.pdf).

PAN.name: Panama

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous communities (comarcas)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution of Panama recognizes the ownership rights of indigenous communities to their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Law No. 72 of 2008 on the establishment of a special procedure for granting collective title to indigenous lands; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Article 127 of the Constitution provides "The State guarantees to indigenous communities the reservation of necessary lands an collective ownership thereof, to ensure their economic and social well-being. Procedures to be followed for obtaining this purpose, and the definition of boundaries within which private appropriation of land is prohibited, shall be regulated by law." Furthermore, Article 124 of the Constitution provides "the State shall give special attention to indigenous farming communities, with the purpose of promoting their economic, social, and political participation in the national life." The indigenous groups- the Embera-Wounaan, Madungandi, Ngodbe-Bugle comarcas have their own charters, and Panama's Legislative Assembly has recognizes the rights of each of these indigenous groups through legislative decrees.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: According to Art. 9 of Act No. 72 of 2008, the land title awarded to indigenous communities is collective, indefinite, non-transferable, irrevocable and inalienable. Registration following the procedures established in Act No. 72 of 2008 is required to receive formal legal protection.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Art. 3 of Act No. 72 of 2008 provides that "the title of collective land ownership ensures the economic, social and cultural well-being of people living in the indigenous community. "Traditional Occupacion" in Art. 2 of Act No. 72 of 2008 is defined as "possession, use, conservation, management, ownership and use of land of indigenous peoples defined in this article, handed down from generation to generation." "Indigenous Peoples" are defined in Art. 2 as "human communities that descended from populations that inhabited the country from the time of conquest." Art. 12 of Act No. 72 of 2008 establishes that "in case of usurpation or invasion of recognized land title through the collective property, the competent authorities shall enforce property rights of these areas."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Act No. 72 of 2008 provides clear procedures for formalizing indigenous community land rights. The cost of applying for title is free, but it is unclear whether there are robust assistance mechanisms ensuring communities are able to easily access registration processes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Article 5-6 of the Act. No. 72 of 2008 provides the application for collective title must be submitted to the La Direccion Nacional de Reforma Agraria accompanied by the following documents: 1. The plan or sketch of the area that is the subject of the application. 2. The certification of the Comptroller General of the Republic of population census of the community. 3. The certification of the National Indigenous Policy Directorate of the Ministry of Government and Justice of the existence of the community or communities applicants based on previous reports and studies. The respective state institutions issue the documents mentioned in no more than thirty days and for free. Article 8 establishes negotiation procedures for the resolution of disputes when applications are contested.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities are granted legal personality for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities are granted legal authority to manage their lands according to customary norms and practices.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: "Traditional Occupacion" in Art. 2 of Act No. 72 of 2008 is defined as "possession, use, conservation, management, ownership and use of land of indigenous peoples defined in this article, handed down from generation to generation."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: According to Art. 9 of Act No. 72 of 2008, the land title awarded to communities is indefinite, meaning community ownership rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 14 of Act. No. 72 of 2008 establishes that governments and private entitles must ensure the free, prior and informed consent of indigenous communities prior to acquiring their land for development projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Although Panama's Act No. 72 of 2008 contains an FPIC requirement, Panama has not yet ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples (which recognizes indigenous rights to give consent prior to acquisition of their lands by governments and outsiders).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Forestry laws stipulate that government agencies are to work in conjunction with the relevant indigenous communities when granting licences for forestry development in comarcas and indigenous territories.
indicators.law_and_provision: Articles 44 and 45, Forest Law, 1994 (Decree Law No. 1); Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Article 44 of Resource rights are not clearly defined within Panama's legislative and regulatory framework, which is why Panama did not receive the highest score for this indicator.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: In 2012, the Government enacted Act No. 11 of 26 March 2012 which allowed the Ngobe-Bugle comarca indigenous communities to manage mineral, water, and environmental resources. But its unclear whether other communities have ownership or use rights to water located on their lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000); Act No. 11 of 26 March 2012.
indicators.additional_info: Resource rights are not clearly defined within Panama's legislative and regulatory framework, which is why Panama did not receive the highest score for this indicator.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 13 of Act No. 72 of 2008 suggests that indigenous communities are granted the right to co-manage land within protected areas if the protected area overlaps with indigenous land. However, indigenous rights within protected areas are not clearly defined by Panamanian statutory and regulatory frameworks.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 127, Constitution of Panama, 1972; Ley 72 de 2008; Act No. 2 of 16 September 1938; Act No. 16 of 19 February 1953 on the establishment of San Blas comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 12042 (7 April 1953); Act No. 99 of 23 December 1998 on the renaming of San Blas comarca as Kuna Yala comarca, Gaceta Oficial No. 23701 (29 December 1998); Act No. 22 of 8 November 1983 on the establishment of the Emberá comarca in Darién, Gaceta Oficial No. 19976 (17 January 1984); Act No. 24 of 12 January 1996 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Madungandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 22951 (15 January 1996); Act No. 10 of 7 March 1997 on the establishment of the Ngobe-Bugle comarca and other measures, Gaceta Oficial No. 23242 (11 March 1997); Act No. 34 of 25 July 2000 on the establishment of the Kuna comarca in Wargandi, Gaceta Oficial No. 24106 (28 July 2000).
indicators.additional_info: Article 13 of Act No. 72 of 2008 establishes that the National Environmental Authority shall coordinate with traditional indigenous authorities in each community to develop actions and strategies for implementing a plan for sustainable use of natural resources and community development, in case that the lands are recognized as part of a national protected area. Land and resource rights within protected areas are not clearly defined within Panama's legislative and regulatory framework, which is why Panama did not receive the highest score for this indicator.

PER.name: Peru

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Adriana Vidal, Independent Land Tenure and Natural Resource Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Recognized communities: coastal peasant communities, sierra peasant communities, and native communities of the jungle (Law 26505 Art. 10). They are recognized as entities under the law with guaranteed property rights over their lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 89, Art 90; Law Decree 22175, Art. 7, Art. 10; Law 24656, Art. 1, Art. 2
indicators.additional_info: The legal difference between coastal, sierra and jungle communities is related to the rules for the transfer of their lands. For sierra peasant communities and jungle communities, more demanding criteria is established when transferring lands than for the coastal communities. Non-contacted native communities from the jungle are recognized as well and have a special regime (Law 28736).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The integrity of their customary land rights is secured and recognized over third party land possession. Community land rights have a constitutional level of recognition and receive protection the same as other type of property, but must register to receive protection.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 89; Law 22715, Art. 10; Law 24657, Art. 2
indicators.additional_info: In order to clear any community land that has overlapping possession rights of third parties, communities have to follow an administrative procedure of titling. For non-contacted native communities legal land titling is provided by the State by means of the creation of 'reservations' (Law 28736 Art. 2, Art. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land titling administrative procedure is free of cost for communities. Formal entitlement of community lands is of national interest (Law 24657, Art. 2) and has preference over previous legal title granted to third parties (Law 22175, Art. 12).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 24657, Art. 18
indicators.additional_info: Administrative procedure is defined and clear.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Peasant and Native Communities have legal existence and are legal entities according to the Constitution. Nevertheless, in order to have legal standing and receive land title communities have to register.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 149; Law 2656, Art. 2; Law 22175, Art. 14

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Autonomy and freedom of the communities with respect to the use and free disposition of their lands. Communities' customary practices, traditions, and cultural identity are respected.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 89, Art. 149; Law 26505, Art. 10
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous communities have the right to sell, lease, apply mortgages, and other disposition acts over their lands, as long as they do so with the approval of at least half of the members of the community (for coastal communities) and at least two thirds of the members for rural and native communities of the sierra and jungle. This disposition is regardless of their customary rules for adopting agreements.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Communities' land rights are vested in perpetuity by the Constitution and special laws for the different types of communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 89; Law 24656, Art. 7; Supreme Decree 11-97-AG, Art. 24

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Rules of free, prior and informed consent are applied accordingly to ILO 169 Convention. Expropriation only allowed by public interest and compensation according to value market. (Law 26505)
indicators.law_and_provision: Legislative Resolution 26253; Law 29785, Art. 2; Law 26505, Art. 10.
indicators.additional_info: Free, prior and informed consent is applied with regard to the legislative or administrative measures coming from the government that have the potential to affect communities' rights. For land transfer agreements between communities and third parties, the law requires that the community reaches an agreement with a majority of votes (coastal communities) or with two thirds of the votes (sierra and jungle communities).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Forest resources belong to the Nation. However, communities have the right to use forest resources located within their lands subject to the approval of a management plan. Management plans are not needed for non contacted communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law Decree 22175, Art. 11; Law 26821, Art. 17, Art. 18; Law 27308, Art 12.
indicators.additional_info: Rules applied for the use of areas with forestry potential are not determined by customary rules but by forest regulations. Rural and native communities with the land title have preference (not exclusivity) over the sustainable harvesting of the natural resources, except for areas that are explicitly reserved by the State or in which third parties have previous exclusive rights. In lands that are not titled, communities have free access to natural resources on the surface or subsurface for sustenance uses as long as they are not preempted by State disposition of the land or third-parties rights. Communities have to apply for a permit to use forest resources with commercial purpose even if it is within their legal lands and only in forests categorized as 'production forests'.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water resources belong to the Nation. However, customary rules are respected as well as their right to use water resources within their lands including commercial and sustenance purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 29338 Art III, Art 64, Art 107, Art 117, Art 118.
indicators.additional_info: This right is granted in perpetuity and it has preeminence over other rights and uses (e.g. uses for hydro structures). There is special protection for non-contacted native communities, in which lands the national authority will not grant any authorization of water use for any third party.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Recognition of property and protection of traditional uses, self-determination and lifestyles. Limited to compatibility with the protected area's objectives.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 28611 Art. 108, Art. 110; Law 26834 Art. 31; Supreme Decree 038-2001-AG, Art. 1, Art. 9, Art. 14, Art. 43.
indicators.additional_info: The State promotes the participation of communities in the establishment and design of the purposes and objectives of natural protected areas (Law 26834 Art. 31).

(Law Decree 22175, Art. 11; Law 26821, Art. 17, Art. 18; Law 27308, Art 12.)
PER.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water resources belong to the Nation. However, customary rules are respected as well as their right to use water resources within their lands including commercial and sustenance purposes. (Law 29338 Art III, Art 64, Art 107, Art 117, Art 118. )
PER.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress — Recognition of property and protection of traditional uses, self-determination and lifestyles. Limited to compatibility with the protected area's objectives. (Law 28611 Art. 108, Art. 110; Law 26834 Art. 31; Supreme Decree 038-2001-AG, Art. 1, Art. 9, Art. 14, Art. 43.)

PHL.name: Philippines

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Cultural Communities/ Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Celine Salcedo-La Viña, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Right of ownership by ICCs/IPs to ancestral domains and lands explicitly recognized. Expansive definition of ancestral domains, including the commonage, even if no longer exclusively occupied by ICCs/IPs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Republic Act (R.A.) No. 8371, Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA), Sec. 3 (a) & (b), 4-8.
indicators.additional_info: Recognition of ICCs/IPs land rights is rooted in the Constitution (Art. XII, Sec. 5). Constitutionality of the IPRA was upheld by the Philippine Supreme Court in Cruz v. Secretary, G.r. No. 135385, 12/06/2000.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Ancestral domains regarded as private but community property, owned under native title (title/pre-conquest rights), but formal registration encouraged.  Relocation and displacement for any reason is subject to consent and compensation. However, scope of ancestral domains may be limited by the provision in law recognizing existing or vested rights within ancestral domains (Sec. 56).
indicators.additional_info: WRT compensation, Administrative Order (A.O.) No. 1, Series of 1998, Rules & Regulations Implementing the IPRA (IRR) provides that compensation for relocation or displacement of ICCs/IPs (including compulsory acquisition) applies to both individually-owned and communally-owned ancestral lands (IRR, Sec. 4). WRT to existing rights, the IRR also provides for recognition of existing contracts, concessions and leases within ancestral domains (Rule VIII, Part II, Sec. 6).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Clear procedures for delineation and recognition of ancestral domains provided, with self-delineation as a guiding principle. Procedure is complex but ICCs/IPs are assisted in the process by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and/or NGOs authorized by them.  Costs are borne by NCIP, unless shouldered by the community  directly or through another entity.
indicators.law_and_provision: R.A. 8371, IPRA, Sec. 51-53; NCIP A.O. No. 4, Series of 2012, Revised Omnibus Rules on Delineation and Recognition of Ancestral Domains and Lands of 2012
indicators.additional_info: Law emphasizes decisive/active role played by ICCs/IPs in all activities related to the process of delineation and titling (Sec. 51).  NCIP may initiate the delineation process with the consent of the concerned ICC/IP (Sec. 52, IPRA).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: ICC/IP community explicitly recognized as a legal person for purposes of delineation and issuance of ancestral domain/land titles. Title is issued in the name of the community, containing a list of all members identified in the census undertaken for the purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision: R.A. 8371, IPRA, Sec. 52; A.O. 4
indicators.additional_info: Authorized community elders/leaders submit a written intention to apply for title, identifying the person(s)--who must be residents of the community--who shall act as authorized representative(s) in the filing and processing of the application (A.O. 4, Rule II).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Right to self-governance and self-determination explicitly recognized, including right to determine and decide priorities for development, and freely pursue own economic, social and cultural development. Customary systems compatible with Constitution and internationally-recognized human rights recognized and supported.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Right to ancestral domains follow indigenous concept of ownership, i.e., as private but community  property which belong to all generations.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Free and prior informed consent (FPIC) explicitly provided. FPIC Includes right to give or withhold consent to a project or acquisition, government or private. ICC/IP community entitled to internal consensus building using its own traditional structures and processes.
indicators.law_and_provision: R.A. 8371, IPRA, Sec. 7 (b) & (c); NCIP A.O. No. 3, Series of 2012, Revised Guidelines on Free and Prior Informed Consent, Sec. 5(f), 19-24.
indicators.additional_info: Primacy of customary processes in community consensus-building may result in marginalization of women and other vulnerable groups in communities with male-dominated decision-making traditions.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Definition of ancestral domain explicitly includes forests, pasture, hunting grounds, and other natural resources within its boundaries. But the provision on natural resources exploitation and development within ancestral domains is ambiguous, merely granting priority rights to ICCs/IPs.
indicators.additional_info: Note that under the Constitution, all natural resources including forests and timber are owned by the State (Art. XII, Sec. 2). This effectively limits the scope of ancestral domains.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Definition of ancestral domain explicitly includes bodies of water, including inland waters and coastal waters within its boundaries. But the provision on natural resources exploitation and development within ancestral domains is ambiguous, merely granting priority rights to ICCs/IPs.
indicators.additional_info: Note Constitutional provision declaring state ownership of all waters (Art. XII, Sec. 2). Similarly, under Presidential Decree No. 1067, the Water Code, all waters are state owned (Art. 3-6). This effectively limits the scope of ancestral domains.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Ancestral lands that overlap with protected areas are subject to protected areas law. This conflicts with ICCs/IPs management & control rights under IPRA. Although, NIPAS law prohibits eviction without consent and calls for ICC/IP participation in  delineation and management planning and governance of the protected area.  Formulation and implementation of plans, policies, rules and regulations to be done in partnership with ICC/IPs and shall consider their livelihood sources, among others.
indicators.law_and_provision: R.A. No. 7586, National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act of 1992, Sec. 13; Department Administrative Order No. 25, Series of 1992, NIPAS Implementing Rules & Regulations, Sec. 44-49
indicators.additional_info: Joint Department of Environment & Natural Resources (DENR) and NCIP Memorandum Circular No, 2007-01 on Management of Overlapping Protected Areas And/or Their Buffer Zones And Ancestral Domains/ Lands seeks to harmonize IPRA and NIPAS Act. It calls for the establishment of a harmonized plan, with ICC/IPs to have primary responsibility for overlapping areas with assistance from DENR and other gov't agencies.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law provides clear ownership rights to communities that hold customary land.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Constitution of Papua New Guinea (arts. 5 and 53); Land Act 1996, secs. 2, 4 and 133-135
indicators.additional_info: Schedule 2 of the Constitutions (and arts. 5 and 53) recognized customary land. The 1996 Land Act defines "customary land " as land that is "owned and possessed by an automatic citizen or community of automatic citizens by virtue of rights of a proprietary or possessory kind that belong to that citizen or community and arise from and are regulated by custom" (sec. 2). The definition of "citizen" refers to "a customary local group or community" (Sec. 2). Furthermore, the Forest Rights Act 1991 defines "customary owners" in relation to an area of customary land, means persons having customary rights- (a) of ownership over the land; or (b) of ownership over forest produce growing on the land."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary land is granted the same level of legal protection as state land. Customary land rights are legally recognized without registration, but the state has broad authority to expropriate and issue leases to customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Secs. 4, 10, 11, 12 Land Act 1996; Art. 53, Constitution
indicators.additional_info: Section 4 of the Land Act 1996 provides that "all land in the country other than customary land is the property of the State..." Section 10(2) of the Land Act provides that the "Minister (of Lands) on behalf of the State, may acquire customary land on such terms and conditions as are agreed on between him and the customary landowners. Furthermore, the law states that "the Minister shall not acquire customary land unless he is satisfied, after reasonable inquire, that the land is not required or likely to be required by customary landowners or person on whom the land will or may devolve by custom." However, the Land Act grants the Minister power to issue business and agriculture leases to customary lands (Secs. 11, 87, 92, Land Act 1996) . The government retains power to expropriate customary lands (sec. 12, Land Act; Art. 53, Constitution).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Registration and delimitation of community lands in order to establish ownership is voluntary. The procedures are clear, accessible, and free.
indicators.law_and_provision: Voluntary Customary Land Registration Act 2009; Land Groups Incorporation (Amendment) Act 2009; Land (Tenure Conversion) Act 1963
indicators.additional_info: Schedule 2 of the Land Groups Incorporation (Amendment) Act 2009 provides that "(1) An application to the Registrar for the incorporation of a land group shall be accompanied by a sketch, drawing, or plan of the land and containing a general description of the land including: (a) its size and location; (b) use; and (c) boundaries; and (d) the names of the village and clan....If there is any dispute over the boundary or boundaries, the exact location of the disputed boundary or boundaries must be identified and the nature of the dispute noted on the document." Under the 2009 Land Registration Act, the Director of Customary Land Registration must verify the membership of an ILG and make a preliminary check of the proposed boundaries of the ILG's land (Sec. 34E, Land Registration (Customary Land) Amendment Act 2007).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Only legal entities, known as Incorporated Land Groups (ILGs), are recognized as legal persons for the purpose of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Groups Incorporation (Amendment) Act 2009
indicators.additional_info: Once a community takes the corporate form of an ILG, it can sue and be sued, hold assets in its name, sign contracts and govern itself through corporate constitutions.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Authority over customary lands vested in incorporated land groups.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Groups Incorporation (Amendment) Act 2009 (LGI Act 2009)
indicators.additional_info: Decision-making relating to customary lands is granted to Incorporated Land Groups (ILGs). ILGs are empowered to "(a)acquire, hold and dispose of customary land and rights in or in respect of customary land, in the manner (if any) and to the extent (if any allowed by custom...(c) use and manage the land, or enter into agreements for the use or management of it;...(e) distribute any product of the land or any profits arising out of the use or management of it" (Sec. 13 LGI Act 2009). Furthermore, Schedule 12 of the LGI Act 2009 provides that "the land group shall act in accordance with the customs of the people, but on incorporation, custom cease to apply." This means that the executive committee of the ILG can disregard community customs when making decision affecting customary lands. All actions taken by the ILG are binding on all members of the ILG (Sec. 15, LGI Act 2009)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Land Act 1996 does not establish durational limits on customary ownership rights to land, which indicates that community rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act 1996

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The state must obtain the consent of Incorporated Land Groups when entering into Forest Management Agreements with private actors that involve that forests held by customary landowners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 57, Forestry Act, 1991; Sec. 10, The Land Act 1996
indicators.additional_info: Section 57 of the Forestry Act provides that title of the land to which the Forest Management Agreement must be "vested in the [ILG] and "registered under a law providing for the registration of title to customary land." Section 57 further provides that "where it is impractical [grant title to customary owners of that land]" agents of the group may execute the agreement on the customary groups behalf provided that 75 percent of the adult member residents on the land of the ILG give written consent to their group entering into the agreement." The Land Act, 1996 provides that "the Minister, on behalf of the State, may acquire customary land on such terms and conditions as are agreed on between him and the customary landowners." However, the Minister retains authority to grant agriculture and business leases to customary lands without the customary landowner's consent.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Act 1991 recognizes community ownership rights to "forest produce" growing on customary lands. The state retains authority to grant leases, licenses, and concessions to trees on customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 2, Forestry Act 1991
indicators.additional_info: The Forestry Act 1991 defines "customary owners" in relation to an area of customary land, means persons having customary rights- (a) of ownership over the land; or (b) of ownership over forest produce growing on the land" (sec. 2, Forest Act 1991). Forest produces are defined as "(a) growing or dead trees, whether standing or fallen; and (b) any part of or any product of such trees; and (c) any other vegetable growth, whether alive or dead, and in a National Forest includes stone, gravel, limestone, lime salt, sand, loam, brick earth, but does not include oil, metal or minerals..."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary rights to use water are recognized by the Water Resources Act, 1982. However, communitiy landowners are not given full ownership rights to water located on their land. Instead, the law provides only a right to use water for domestic purposes, fire fighting purposes, and recreational purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, 1982
indicators.additional_info: The Water Resources Act, 1982 recognizes "customary rights to the use of water" which are defined as "rights to the use of water- (a) that are authorized by custom; and (b) that are being availed of at the time in question, or in the normal course of land managaement, would be availabed of in a customary manner within a reasonable period after that time." Section 5 of the Water Resources Act, 1982 provides "the right to the use, flow and control of water is vested in the State. (2) This Act does not affect customary rights to the use of water by citizens resident in the area in which those customary rights are exercised." The Act indicates that use rights may be used for domestic purposes, prescribed recreational use, and other prescribed purposes. Section 21 of said Act states "a person may take water without charge for (a) domestic purposes; or (b) watering stock; or (c) fire fighting."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: National Parks Act, 1982 provides for the establishment of reserves, parks, and gardens, but only on state-owned land, and not on customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Parks Act, 1982
indicators.additional_info: Papua New Guinea does not have an extensive set of protected areas since non-customary land only constitutes 3% of the country and urban areas take up much of this 3% area. Source: http://www.rightsandresources.org/wp-content/uploads/RRIReport_Protected-Areas-and-Land-Rights_web.pdf

indicators.law_and_provision: Land Groups Incorporation (Amendment) Act 2009 (LGI Act 2009)
indicators.additional_info: Decision-making relating to customary lands is granted to Incorporated Land Groups (ILGs). ILGs are empowered to "(a)acquire, hold and dispose of customary land and rights in or in respect of customary land, in the manner (if any) and to the extent (if any allowed by custom...(c) use and manage the land, or enter into agreements for the use or management of it;...(e) distribute any product of the land or any profits arising out of the use or management of it" (Sec. 13 LGI Act 2009). Furthermore, Schedule 12 of the LGI Act 2009 provides that "the land group shall act in accordance with the customs of the people, but on incorporation, custom cease to apply." This means that the executive committee of the ILG can disregard community customs when making decision affecting customary lands. All actions taken by the ILG are binding on all members of the ILG (Sec. 15, LGI Act 2009)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Land Act 1996 does not establish durational limits on customary ownership rights to land, which indicates that community rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act 1996

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The state must obtain the consent of Incorporated Land Groups when entering into Forest Management Agreements with private actors that involve that forests held by customary landowners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 57, Forestry Act, 1991; Sec. 10, The Land Act 1996
indicators.additional_info: Section 57 of the Forestry Act provides that title of the land to which the Forest Management Agreement must be "vested in the [ILG] and "registered under a law providing for the registration of title to customary land." Section 57 further provides that "where it is impractical [grant title to customary owners of that land]" agents of the group may execute the agreement on the customary groups behalf provided that 75 percent of the adult member residents on the land of the ILG give written consent to their group entering into the agreement." The Land Act, 1996 provides that "the Minister, on behalf of the State, may acquire customary land on such terms and conditions as are agreed on between him and the customary landowners." However, the Minister retains authority to grant agriculture and business leases to customary lands without the customary landowner's consent.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Forestry Act 1991 recognizes community ownership rights to "forest produce" growing on customary lands. The state retains authority to grant leases, licenses, and concessions to trees on customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 2, Forestry Act 1991
indicators.additional_info: The Forestry Act 1991 defines "customary owners" in relation to an area of customary land, means persons having customary rights- (a) of ownership over the land; or (b) of ownership over forest produce growing on the land" (sec. 2, Forest Act 1991). Forest produces are defined as "(a) growing or dead trees, whether standing or fallen; and (b) any part of or any product of such trees; and (c) any other vegetable growth, whether alive or dead, and in a National Forest includes stone, gravel, limestone, lime salt, sand, loam, brick earth, but does not include oil, metal or minerals..."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary rights to use water are recognized by the Water Resources Act, 1982. However, communitiy landowners are not given full ownership rights to water located on their land. Instead, the law provides only a right to use water for domestic purposes, fire fighting purposes, and recreational purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Act, 1982
indicators.additional_info: The Water Resources Act, 1982 recognizes "customary rights to the use of water" which are defined as "rights to the use of water- (a) that are authorized by custom; and (b) that are being availed of at the time in question, or in the normal course of land managaement, would be availabed of in a customary manner within a reasonable period after that time." Section 5 of the Water Resources Act, 1982 provides "the right to the use, flow and control of water is vested in the State. (2) This Act does not affect customary rights to the use of water by citizens resident in the area in which those customary rights are exercised." The Act indicates that use rights may be used for domestic purposes, prescribed recreational use, and other prescribed purposes. Section 21 of said Act states "a person may take water without charge for (a) domestic purposes; or (b) watering stock; or (c) fire fighting."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: National Parks Act, 1982 provides for the establishment of reserves, parks, and gardens, but only on state-owned land, and not on customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Parks Act, 1982
indicators.additional_info: Papua New Guinea does not have an extensive set of protected areas since non-customary land only constitutes 3% of the country and urban areas take up much of this 3% area. Source: http://www.rightsandresources.org/wp-content/uploads/RRIReport_Protected-Areas-and-Land-Rights_web.pdf
