indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Law No. 68/93 (Law on Baldios) states that vacant land (wasteland) in Portugal is owned and managed by local communities (Art. 1). However, communities must abide by use plans that are developed in cooperation with Portuguese administrative bodies (Art. 6).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)
indicators.additional_info: Article 2 of Law No. 68/93 (Law on Baldios) states "the provisions of this law are applicable to the wastelands, even when composed of discrete areas, in particular those which are as follows: a) land considered vacant and as such communally owned and managed by residents of one or more parishes, or part of them, even if occasionally not being subject, in whole or in part, of exploitation by these residents, or lack of organ management regularly constituted; b) land eligible for use and enjoyment by local community which, having previously been used and fruídos as wastelands". Article 3 states "The wastelands are, as a rule, common grounds, notably for apascentação cattle, firewood, collection or bushes, crops and other fruitions, including agricultural nature, forestry, forest-pastoral or apiculture."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 4 of the Law on Baldios provides that acts of legal ownership or seizure are void. However, the government can still expropriate wasteland for public purposes (Art. 29, Law on Baldios; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 14 of the Law on Baldios establishes that compartes assemblies are empowered to decide on matters relating to registration. However, there is no clear registration process established in the Law on Baldios (and no implementing regulations establishing demarcation or registration processes). There are no provisions ensuring registration will be affordable and accessible for local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law grants local communities legal personality for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)
indicators.additional_info: Communities can submit legal claims relating to wasteland disputes. Article 32 of the Law on Baldios provides that "it is the responsibility of the territorially competent ordinary courts hear disputes which directly or indirectly have as their object wastelands, in particular for the area, boundaries, use, occupation or appropriation, assignment agreements, decisions of its organs or omissions of compliance provisions of the law. They are exempt from preparation and court costs organs and members of local communities rights over wastelands, including entities that have been delegated its administrative powers."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 5 of the Law on Baldios indicates that the customs of local communities determine how vacant land is used and enjoyed. However, the state has authority to develop use plans in cooperation with local communities (Art. 6-8). Also, land is administered by governing bodies (assembleia de compartes) as opposed to the community members themselves and a governing board (Art. 20).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 states "the wastelands are administered in their own right, by their compartes, in accordance with applicable customs and habits or, in their absence, through organ or democratically elected bodies. Local communities are organized, for the exercise of representation of acts, provision, management and supervision for the corresponding vacant through an assembly of compartes, a governing board and a supervisory board. The members of the board of compartes assembly and the governing board and the supervisory board are elected for periods of two years, renewable, and remain in office until they are replaced."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: There are no durational limits established by the Law on Baldios, which indicates that rights granted to Baldios may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Article 29 of the Law on Baldios provides that wasteland can be expropriated for a public purpose or if the land is abandoned. There is no explicit right granted to communities to give consent in an inclusive manner if the government decides to acquire land in a compulsory manner.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 3 indicates that local communities have rights to the use of enjoyment of pastoral forests and firewood located on wasteland.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 1 of the Law No. 54/2005 on the legal regime of water domain establishes that water in the public domain belongs to the state. However private property owners can obtain ownership rights to water located on their property (Law No. 54/2005 on the legal regime of water domain). Since communities have legal rights own and manage wastelands in Portugal, they presumably also have rights to own water resources located within these areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act No. 58/2005; Law No. 54/2005 on the legal regime of water domain; Decree-Law No. 226-A/2007 on the use of water resources; Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)
indicators.additional_info: Law No. 68/93 (Law on Baldios) states that vacant land (wasteland) in Portugal is owned and managed by local communities (Art. 1). However, communities must abide by use plans that are developed in cooperation with Portuguese administrative bodies (Art. 6). Article 2 of Law No. 68/93 (Law on Baldios) states "the provisions of this law are applicable to the wastelands, even when composed of discrete areas, in particular those which are as follows: a) land considered vacant and as such communally owned and managed by residents of one or more parishes, or part of them, even if occasionally not being subject, in whole or in part, of exploitation by these residents, or lack of organ management regularly constituted; b) land eligible for use and enjoyment by local community which, having previously been used and fruídos as wastelands". Article 3 states "The wastelands are, as a rule, common grounds, notably for apascentação cattle, firewood, collection or bushes, crops and other fruitions, including agricultural nature, forestry, forest-pastoral or apiculture."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant local communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Portugal; Law No. 168/99 on Land Expropriation; Law No. 68/93 on Uncultivated Land (Law on Baldios)

PRY.name: Paraguay

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous communities
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 64 of the Constitution recognizes the communal ownership rights of the indigenous communities of Paraguay. Indigenous peoples access to land is regulated in the Indigenous Communities Statute (1981). However, the constitutional rights granted to indigenous communities have not been supported by legislation or regulations, resulting in potential conflict between communities and the state.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay 1992; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: Article 64 of the Constitution states the indigenous peoples have [the] right to communal ownership of the land in [an] extension and quality sufficient for the preservation and the development of their  forms of lifestyles. The State will provide them gratuitously with these lands, which will be non-seizable [inembargables], indivisible, non-transferrable, imprescriptible, not susceptible to guarantee contractual obligations nor to be leased; likewise, they will be exempt from taxes. The removal or transfer of [the indigenous peoples] from their habitat without their express consent is prohibited." Article 7 of the Indigenous Communities Statues establishes that "the State recognizes the legal existence of indigenous communities and grants them legal status under the provisions of this law." NOTE: Paraguay ratified ILO Convention 169 (on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) in 1993.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 64 of the Constitution provides that lands owned by indigenous peoples are non-seizable, indivisible, non-transferrable, imprescriptible, not susceptible to guarantee contractual obligations nor to be leased. Furthermore the removal or transfer of the indigenous peoples from their habitat without their express consent is prohibited. However, indigenous communities must register under the 1981 Indigenous Communities Statute to receive legal protection. Legislation implementing indigenous constitutional rights has not yet been passed.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: Article 14 of the Indigenous Communities Statute provides that the settlement of indigenous communities should, as much as possible, attend to the current or traditional possession of the community's land. Free and express consent will be essential to their usual location, except for in situations when natural security reasons apply. Article 26 of the Statute and Article 109 of the Constitution grants indigenous communities the right to receive compensation for expropriation. NOTE: In practice, except for certain areas that are managed by indigenous communities, lands must be purchased from private owners at potentially high costs or expropriated by an act of Congress. As of 2002, communities were only granted legal title to 66,000 hectares of the minimum 240,000 hectares held and used by communities. See Ortega, R. 2004. Models for Recognizing Indigenous Land Rights in Latin America. Washington, DC: World Bank. Available at: http://siteresources.worldbank.org/GLOBALENVIRONMENTFACILITYGEFOPERATIONS/Resources/Publications-Presentations/Biopublication2005ModelsforRecognizing.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Indigenous Communities Statute provides for the formalization and demarcation of indigenous community lands, but the procedures are vague. Also, the law does not provide assistance mechanisms or ensure that indigenous communities will be able to easily access registration procedures.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution suggests that registration processes are free for communities (Article 64 provides "the State will provide [communities with lands] gratuitously", but this is not entirely clear under the Indigenous Communities Statute 1981. Article 9 of the Indigenous Communities Statue (1981) provides that "the request for recognition of legal personality will be presented by the Paraguayan Indigenous Institute by community leaders, with the following data: a) name of the community; payroll families and their members, stating age, marital status and sex; b) geographical location of the community if it is permanent, or sites frequented by the community; c) the names of name community leaders and justification of their authority". Once an indigenous community has recognized legal status, it must register land titles with the Agrarian Register, General Property Registry and the National Registry of Indigenous Communities (Art. 20, Indigenous Communities Statute, 1981). Article 22 of the Statute provides that the Paraguay Indigenous Institute must obtain a report containing information on community land, including location, time of residency, crops, etc. The Paraguay Indigenous Institute must then conduct a survey, measurement, and demarcation of the land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities are recognized as legal persons for the purpose of ownership once they register following the procedures established in the Indigenous Communities Statute (1981).
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: Article 12 of the Indigenous Communities Statute, 1981 states that community leaders legally represent communities. Community leaders' names must be given to the Institute I.B.R. and included in the National Register of Indigenous Communities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution and Indigenous Communities Statute grants indigenous communities legal authority over their lands (Art 64, Constitution; Art 3, Indigenous Communities Statute). Authority over the community is vested in the community leaders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: Article 5 of the Indigenous Communities Statute, 1981 provides that "indigenous communities may apply to regulate their coexistence following customary laws as long as it not inconsistent with the principles of public order." Article 28 of the Statute establishes the Paraguay Indigenous Institute (INDI), a government body designed to handle government relations with indigenous communities.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Indigenous Communities Statute does not establish durational limits, which suggest that indigenous community land rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 64 of the Constitution provides ""the removal or transfer of [the indigenous peoples] from their habitat without their express consent is prohibited."" However the process for gathering consent is not clearly established through legislation or regulations. It is unclear whether consent must be gathered in an inclusive or transparent manner.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities." Law No. 234/94 (Ratifying ILO Convention 169).
indicators.additional_info: Paraguay ratified ILO Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) in 1993--see Law No. 234/93. ILO Convention 169 contains a right to give consent. However, the procedures for gathering indigenous community consent have not been implemented or established in Paraguay's national laws (the Indigenous Communities Statute was passed in 1981 before ILO Convention 169 was ratified.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Paraguay's statutes and regulations do not explicitly recognize that indigenous community property includes rights to trees on the land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Law -Law No 542/93, Law No. 422/73, and Law No. 4890; Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements)
indicators.additional_info: Article 24 of the Law on Forest Resources (No. 542/93) indicates that forest areas can be expropriated for the purpose of establishing indigenous community settlements. But this law does not explicitly indicate that communities may be given rights to trees or forest resources located within their lands.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Article 3 of Ley No. 3.239/07 (Water Resources Law) provides that "the waters, surface and ground, are owned by the public domain and its domain is inalienable and imprescriptible. The Water Resources Law grants all citizens the right use and drink water to fulfill their daily needs and for household/domestic purposes (Arts. 13, 15, 16). Therefore, it can be implied that community landowners, as citizens of Paraguay, have rights to use water for basic needs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley N° 3.239/07 - De los recursos hídricos del Paraguay. ; Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements); Law No. 919/96 amending and extending several articles of Law No. 904 dated December 18, 1981 "Statute of indigenous communities."
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 15 of the 2007 Water Law, the "The surface and ground water resources use for domestic purposes and basic household production that are used directly by the user, without the intervention of any kind, are freely available, are not subject to permits or concessions or taxes of any kind."  Paraguay ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples in 1993.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Paraguay's statutes and regulations do not explicitly recognize that indigenous community property includes rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Laws -Law No. 4.014, Law No. 542/93, Law No. 422/73, and Law No. 4890; Arts. 63-66, Constitution of Paraguay; Indigenous Communities Statute (Act. No 94/81); Act NO. 43/89 (Regularization of title to indigenous settlements)
indicators.additional_info:
NOTE: According to IFAD's technical note on indigenous peoples issues in Paraguay (https://www.ifad.org/documents/10180/6f8cdf30-12a7-479a-9e02-aee9be26f784). In 2007 after various letters of concern were sent to UNDP, GEF and the Ministry of the Environment, the Asociación de Comunidades Indígenas de Itapúa (Association of Indigenous Communities of Itapúa- ACIDI), CAPI and the UK-based Forest Peoples Programme issued a formal complaint to the GEF Council regarding the violations of the rights of the Mbyá Guaraní indigenous peoples caused by the implementation of the GEF project. As part of the project, the Reserve for the San Rafael National Parkwas created; however, the entire area of the reserve was superimposed directly on top of the ancestral lands of the Mbyá Guaraní people without consulting the indigenous communities or obtaining their free, prior and informed consent. The organizations seek full information disclosure regarding the project‘s plans, full participation of the indigenous communities and assurance that the rights of the indigenous peoples as enshrined in national law will be respected. 
Source: Letter from the rep. of ACIDI, CAPI and FPP http://www.forestpeoples.org/sites/fpp/files/publication/2010/08/gefparaguayiprightsletnov07eng.pdf

local_communities_entries.framework: Non-indigenous communities
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, reviewed & amended by Monica Vasile

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Refers to forest & pasture commons.  Restitution Law 2000 provides for community ownership rights to forest & pasture lands. However, communities must form an association to obtain these rights (Arts. 93-95, Forest Code, 2008).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Restitution Law, No 1 of 2000; Forest Code, 2008 Art 9-95.
indicators.additional_info: The 2008 Forest Code grants  ownership rights to community associations for forest and pasture lands (Art. 94-95). Associations founded on village communities, or descent groups, which have legal personality as private owners once registered as an association with independent locally elected bodies. Common properties are called obste, composesorat, or urbariala.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Articles 94-95 of the 2008 Forest Code establishes that community forests are guaranteed, indivisible and inalienable. Registered in National Register of Forest Owners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Restitution Law, No. 1 of 2000;  Forest Code, 2008

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Code establishes a registration process for formalizing rights held by community forests. The procedures for registration are in 3 steps: validation,putting into possession, and warranting of property title. There are no assistance mechanisms, schematic maps are provided by local commissions.
indicators.law_and_provision: Government Decisions HG 890/4.08.2005, Law 247/2005.
indicators.additional_info: Community property nciently existed but was nationalized by Socialist State in 1950-1957.  Procedure is bureaucratic and costly, dpendent upon community initiative which hands in documents to municipality commissions, which demarcates, then passes to regional commissions for title. Then cadastral maps required to register in the Land Book (public register of lands, Law No. 7 of 1996 on Cadastre and Land Registry). Also strict conditions for harvesting, control vested in specialists.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Clear legal personality once registered the Association (Forestry Code, Art. 92). Community or group not directly recognized as a legal person. The 1898 Transylvania Law and Romanian Principalities Law (Forestry Code, 2010) had  same complex requirements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008, Art. 92
indicators.additional_info: The laws that first recognized collective landowning rights required the formation of legal entities (at the end of 10th century until beginning of the 20th century), formed of individual members, enlisted in tables; in most cases the common property came to be expressed in a sum of individual shares, although the property was not divided on the ground (Forestry Code, 1910); thus the 'common' was not a collectivity but a sum of parts. The process of establishing who was a member proved to be extremely cumbersome.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Forest Code (2008) indicates that communities have  authority over how to use common property. Law explicitly grants authority of community lands to the community itself. Power is devolved to the local level, commons govern themselves through elected councils and general assemblies, according to locally created and approved by-laws, upheld by state courts (Law 1/2000, Art. 29).  Forest harvesting is regulated by state laws, communities are bound to follow imposed management plans (Forestry Code 2008).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008
indicators.additional_info: Article 93 of the 2008 Forest Code provides that "community forest owners associations may operate in accordance with the Government Ordinance no. 26/2000 on associations and foundations, approved by Law No. 246/2005.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No law related to community properties limits term, which suggests that community rights to land may be held in perpetuity. Most legal by-laws establish 'unlimited duration'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008
indicators.additional_info: Neither Forestry Code, 2008 nor the Restitution Law, No. 1 of 2000 even mention limited terms of title to registered associations as owners of commons.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Legal regulations, the local by-laws recognized by state courts, require consent of the general assembly of commoners, following detailed procedures, in case of ‘dissolving’ of the legal entity (according to by-laws, law 1/2000). But community lands cannot be sold partly or wholly, or acquired by outsiders (Law 1/2000).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008
indicators.additional_info: Land cannot be acquired, ‘alienated’ by outsiders, according to law 1/2000, and also members cannot sell their shares to outsiders (modification introduced by law 400/2002). In case the legal landholding entity ‘dissolves’, the land becomes property of the municipality, enters the public domain, but does not become state property.  The ‘dissolving’ procedure is detailed in the by-laws (according to law 1/2000, art. 28). Most by-laws specify that the dissolving has to be decided by the general assembly, following detailed voting procedures.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law recognizes property of collectives over the ‘forestry fund’, which includes trees. The commons can log trees for household consumption, and derive benefits from commercial logging. However, the powers of regulation and decisions on felling trees are externally vested in forestry specialists (Forestry Code, 2008).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008
indicators.additional_info: Article 93 states "forest owners associations are established according to Art. 92 para. (1) and operates in accordance with the provisions of Government Ordinance no. 26/2000 on associations and foundations, approved by Law no. 246/2005". Article 94 states "to qualify for support under the law, forest owners associations and associative forms provided by art. 92 para. (1) must enroll in the National Register of forest owners associations, held at the central public authority responsible for forestry. (2) content, model and registration procedure in the National Register of forest owners associations approved by order of the head of the central public authority responsible for forestry". Article 95. states "(1) community of Mosneni in joint property, brotherhoods of Mosneni in possession, brotherhoods razesesti undivided, composesoratele, frontier forests, forest land records, political communes, communities and other associative forms with different names existing before 1948, are part of historical treasure Romania. (2) Property referred to in paragraph associative forms. (1) is guaranteed, indivisible and inalienable. (3) associative forms provided in par. (1), a result of the event will of local communities, are legal, organization and functioning shall be regulated by special law. NOTE: M. Vasile overves that the official 2015 figure of 788,694 ha is likely less when only traditional commons are considered, which she estimates as c. 640,000 ha.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Collectives own the ponds and streams on their lands, of less than 5 km long and with a hydrographic basin of less than 10 sq km. Over this size, they are owned by the state. The right to use the water is free for all. The community may not use the water for commercial purposes without formal authority from the government. (Law of Waters 107/1996) .
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Law, 1996 (Law No. 107); Constitution of Romania, 1991; Law on Land Resources No. 81/1991; Law on Cadastre and Land Registry (Law 7/1996); Forest Code, 2008
indicators.additional_info: According to article 3 of the the Water Law, 1996 provides that "(1) the Public domain shall own the surface waters and their minor beds, with lengths bigger than 5 km, and river basins larger than 10 square kilometers, the banks and basins of the lakes, as well as the ground waters, the inland marine waters, the sea beach and the cliff, with their natural riches and the energetic potential that can be reevaluated, the territorial sea and the marine waters beds. (2) The minor river beds of lengths below 5 km, and river basins that do not exceed 10 square kilometers, on which waters do not flow permanently, shall belong to the holders of any title of the lands, where the waters are formed or flow. The owners of such minor river beds must use these waters in accordance with the general water use conditions in the respective basin." Article 9 of the Water Law states "Art.  9 – (1) The right to use the surface or ground waters, including the artesian wells, is established by the water management licence and is exercised according to the legal provisions. Such right also includes the discharge into the water resources of waste water, drainage water, meteoric water, mine or deposit water, after being used. (2) The surface or ground waters may be freely used, by complying with the sanitary and water quality protection norms, for drinking, watering, washing, bathing, and other household needs, if for such activities no installations, or low capacity installations are used of less than 0.2 litre/sec., for exclusively meeting the needs of one’s own household."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Protected areas may contain land held under any tenure type, including collective entities, and are divided into core zones and buffer zones. In these zones, restrictions of use apply and compensations should be paid to owners (Government Decree on Protected Areas OUG 57/2007).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 5/2000 on Approval of the National Territorial Arrangement Plan-Protected Areas; Law 1995- 137 on the Environmental Protection; Law 2000-183 regarding the protection of the movable national heritage;  Forest Code, 2008. Government Decree on Protected Areas, no. 57/2007.

RUS.name: Russia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous communities
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Federal legislation grants indigenous communities the right to freely use land and renewable natural resources in their traditionally occupied territories. Law No. 104-FS grants indigenous peoples """"Territories of Traditional Natural Use"""".
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous communities are granted the right to obtain compensation in the event that their traditional environment is damaged by industrial activities (Art. 8, Federal Law No.82-FS) Article 69 of the Russian Constitution provides that "the Russian Federation shall guarantee to all of its peoples the rights of the indigenous small peoples according to the universally recognized principles and norms of international law and norms of international law and international treaties and agreements of the Russian Federation." IPs are not granted ownership rights, since Article 8 of the Land Code classifies land as federally-owned land, land owned by Russian regions, land owned by municipal entities, privately-owned land, and agricultural-purpose land (owned by local government bodies).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Federal Laws No. 49-FS, No. 104-FS, and No. 82-FS provide some legal protection to indigenous community land, but the gov't maintains broad authority over these lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no indication that the federal laws provide clear, accessible procedures for indigenous communities to register their land rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Art. 14 of the Law "On Guarantees" provides that customary law may be used in court proceedings as long as it does not contradict federal or regional legislation, which suggests legal personality.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The laws do not establish that communities have legal authority over their land. (Federal Law No.82-FS) "On Guarantees" established the right to self-government for indigenous peoples, but was amended.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ; Federal Law on  “On Changes in Federal Acts of the Russian Federation” (2004). Federal Law no. 122- FS.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Federal Law "On Guarantees" provides indigenous peoples with use rights in perpetuity. However, Federal Law No. 104-FS "On Territories" grants "Territory of Traditional Natural Use".
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly grant communities the right to give consent prior to acquisition.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly grant indigenous groups/ communities rights to trees.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code
indicators.additional_info: Indigenous peoples have the right freely use land and renewable natural resources in their traditionally occupied territories and areas where they engage in traditional economic activities (Law "On Guarantees, art. 8, para. 1).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Water Code of Russia, 2008 provides state ownership of surface waters and public water bodies (art. 6). However, article 6 further provides that "everyone person has the right of access to public waer bodies and can use them free of charge for personal and domestic needs..." Based on this provision, it can be presumed that indigenous communities in Russia have a right to use water for domestic purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, 2008; Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code
indicators.additional_info: Article 6 of the Water Code states "1. State- or municipality-owned surface water bodies are public water bodies, i.e. publicly accessible water bodies, except as otherwise provided in this Code. 2.  Every  person  has  the  right  of  access  to  public  water  bodies  and  can  use  them  free  of  charge  for personal and domestic needs, except as otherwise provided in this Code and other federal laws." Under Chapter 3 of the Water Code, the government can also grant water use rights for various purposes, such as recreational, and electric power generation.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation does not explicitly grant indigenous groups/ communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 8, On Guarantees of the Rights of Numerically Small Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation (Federal Law No.82-FS) ;  Federal Law No. 104-FS ("On Obshchina"); Federal Law No. 49-FS ("On Territories'); Constitution; Land Code

RWA.name: Rwanda

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary tenure over house/farms extinguished by compulsory issue of renewable leaseholds since 2005 in parcels up to 2 ha, to couple, each spouse or family; conversion complete. Communal valley lands nationalized, some allocated to sugar companies but new provision for groups or communities to secure concessions. Batwa forest IP relocated from ancestral areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution (rev. 2015) Arts. 34-35, 44. Law Governing Land, 2021, Arts. 2, 6, 9, 10, 29-33.
indicators.additional_info: Extinction of customary tenure due partly to displacement during civil war 1990s resulting in plots occupied by others. Issued titles either emphyteutic leases or freeholds for urban plots (Art. 9). While the Law on Land No. 43/2013 (previously 2005 law) was repealed by Land Law 2021, its Orders remain in force. Changes enable names of both spouses on title, or titles to separate farms. Also opening for groups to recover use of nationalized valley commons under concessions, limited to individuals or registered groups  (2021 Art. 33).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary rights no longer exist so comparison with statutory rights impossible. Equality within house & farm leaseholds is significant as if payment of compensation at compulsory acquisition, but rural inequality with urban freeholds. Key loss was communal valley lands for seasonal rice & grazing. Land rights no longer governed by customary law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land, No. Law No. 18/2007 on Expropriation.
indicators.additional_info: Customary law applies to inheritance and some goverance aspects of landholding; ie. not extinguished completely, only for definition of lawful landholding, entirely statutory and state-defined. Reason was complexities of pre-war and post-war overlaps in landholdings, found easier to begin with clean slate.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land admin. is devolved to District Land Bureaux, executing systematic parcel identification & administration of transfers/sales. Well-funded, subsidized, cheaper for poor,  and swift (largely achieved by 2012). Provisional Certificates mainly replaced by final leases. Rural concessions issued to investors on State Land, incl. nationalized valley commons.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land No. 27/2021. Ministerial Order No. 002/2008 Determining Modalities of Registration.
indicators.additional_info: Rwanda is the first African state to achieve 100% formalization of property rights in rural domain, but through a procedure which abolished customary tenure & excluded communal lands. Ministerial Order No. 002/2008 determining the modalities of land registration.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Other than married spouses, only individuals, and associations with legal personality may register ownership. Communities may only be recognized as legal persons if register as Association or other corporate entity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Law, No. 27/2021. Ministerial Order No. 001/2008 On Land Leasing. Ministerial Order No. 002/2008 Determining the Modalities of Land Registration.
indicators.additional_info: Rwanda regularly updates new land law to reflect lessons and changing policies, notably hardening distinction between private and state lands, reduction to only two forms of property in land (state and private). Began with 2003 law, then the Organic Land Law, 2005, Arts. 2, 4-5 (repealed but largely retained as  Land Law of No. 43/2013), repealed by new Law on Land, No, 27/2021. Orders under the 2013 remain in force.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: A decentralized regime for land governance, but not fully to 15,000+ villages. Land Committees only assist District Land Bureaus and closer Cell Land Offices (385 in place by 2016). No role for Traditional Authorities. Leeway to use customary norms in appointing village councils (not only for land matters) and to guide inheritance of lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land, No. 27/2021. Law No. 87/2013 Determining the Organization and Functioning of Decentralized Administrative Entities.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 68 of Law on Land 2021 states that land committees are responsible for monitoring land management and use (Art. 68). Law No. 87/2013 defines rural decentralized governance as Districts, Cells and Villages (Art. 2); the Cell and Village do not have legal personality (Art. 4). Councillors are elected except at Village level where customary processes used to appoint members (Art. 5).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Private home/farm parcels owned under 99 year emphyeutic leases, automatically renewed, thus potentially owned in perpetuity. Land Law 2021 Art 10. State is the owner-lessor. Customary inheritance norms may be applied.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land, No. 27/2021.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No legal requirement to secure consent to take lands for public purposes. Local consultation required including to create State Protected Areas but decision lies with state agencies.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No.18/2007 Relating to Expropriation in the Public Interest. Law No.47/2013 on Forests.
indicators.additional_info: No consent of owners or communities required when compulsorily acquiring lands for public purposes including creation of Protected Areas. Law No. 47/2013 on Forests, Law No. 18/2007 On Expropriation. Consultation and related procedures stipulated in Articles 12ff of Law No. 18/2007. Adequate forward information and right to appeal provided for, compensation is limited to listed losses but must be paid prior to eviction.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All natural forest including in valleys belongs to the State. 2021 Art. 31. And "lands that do not belong to individuals" is Private Domain of  the State". Art. 32.  However, planted trees on private land belong to the plot owner and may be used in accordance with rules under 2013 land law Art. 43. Access and use to trees outside private lands requires permits. Art. 10.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land, No. 27/2021. Law Determining the Management  and Utilization of Forests in Rwanda No. 47/2013.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 43 of Land Law 2021 states: "Notwithstanding personal land rights and other related properties, all rights of ownership and control of natural resources on, under, or upon any land in Rwanda are vested in the State...".

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the State but access assured for domestic/farm livelihood uses without permits required. Law No. 49/2018. The principle of subsidiarity, whereby planning and implementation is exercised at the lowest appropriate level is established; Art 7. Permits required for non-domestic uses.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 48/2018 on The Environment. Law No. 49/2018 Determining the Use and Management of Water Resources in Rwanda.
indicators.additional_info: The state owns and controls water resources. Art. 11 of Law No. 48/2018 and Art. 18, Law  No. 49/2018.  Domestic use takes priority, livestock watering second priority. Land owners must use water for irrigation 'rationally'. Art. 12. Powers of management may be delegated by districts to local water associations. Permits requires for other than domestic uses.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Protected Areas cannot be owned by communities, groups or individuals but if they form a legal entity, they may help manage forest subject to agreement by the Minister.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 47/2013 Determining the Management & Utilization of Forests. Law No. 48/2018 on The Environment. Law No. 064/2021 Governing Biodiversity.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 40-42 of Law No. 47/2013 requires groups or villages to form legal entities to assist State to manage natural resources. Incentives offered but no attempt to devolve authority to communities. No provision for restitution.

RWA.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: No, the law does not address the issue — Customary rights no longer exist so comparison with statutory rights impossible. Equality within house & farm leaseholds is significant as if payment of compensation at compulsory acquisition, but rural inequality with urban freeholds. Key loss was communal valley lands for seasonal rice & grazing. Land rights no longer governed by customary law. (Law on Land, No. Law No. 18/2007 on Expropriation. )
RWA.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — Land admin. is devolved to District Land Bureaux, executing systematic parcel identification & administration of transfers/sales. Well-funded, subsidized, cheaper for poor,  and swift (largely achieved by 2012). Provisional Certificates mainly replaced by final leases. Rural concessions issued to investors on State Land, incl. nationalized valley commons.  (Law on Land No. 27/2021. Ministerial Order No. 002/2008 Determining Modalities of Registration.)
RWA.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — Other than married spouses, only individuals, and associations with legal personality may register ownership. Communities may only be recognized as legal persons if register as Association or other corporate entity.   (Law on Law, No. 27/2021. Ministerial Order No. 001/2008 On Land Leasing. Ministerial Order No. 002/2008 Determining the Modalities of Land Registration.)
RWA.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — A decentralized regime for land governance, but not fully to 15,000+ villages. Land Committees only assist District Land Bureaus and closer Cell Land Offices (385 in place by 2016). No role for Traditional Authorities. Leeway to use customary norms in appointing village councils (not only for land matters) and to guide inheritance of lands. (Law on Land, No. 27/2021. Law No. 87/2013 Determining the Organization and Functioning of Decentralized Administrative Entities.)
RWA.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Private home/farm parcels owned under 99 year emphyeutic leases, automatically renewed, thus potentially owned in perpetuity. Land Law 2021 Art 10. State is the owner-lessor. Customary inheritance norms may be applied. (Law on Land, No. 27/2021. )
RWA.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — No legal requirement to secure consent to take lands for public purposes. Local consultation required including to create State Protected Areas but decision lies with state agencies. (Law No.18/2007 Relating to Expropriation in the Public Interest. Law No.47/2013 on Forests.)
RWA.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — All natural forest including in valleys belongs to the State. 2021 Art. 31. And "lands that do not belong to individuals" is Private Domain of  the State". Art. 32.  However, planted trees on private land belong to the plot owner and may be used in accordance with rules under 2013 land law Art. 43. Access and use to trees outside private lands requires permits. Art. 10. (Law on Land, No. 27/2021. Law Determining the Management  and Utilization of Forests in Rwanda No. 47/2013.)
RWA.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water belongs to the State but access assured for domestic/farm livelihood uses without permits required. Law No. 49/2018. The principle of subsidiarity, whereby planning and implementation is exercised at the lowest appropriate level is established; Art 7. Permits required for non-domestic uses. (Law No. 48/2018 on The Environment. Law No. 49/2018 Determining the Use and Management of Water Resources in Rwanda.)
RWA.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, limited progress — Protected Areas cannot be owned by communities, groups or individuals but if they form a legal entity, they may help manage forest subject to agreement by the Minister. (Law No. 47/2013 Determining the Management & Utilization of Forests. Law No. 48/2018 on The Environment. Law No. 064/2021 Governing Biodiversity. )

SDN.name: Sudan

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Since 1925 customary rights reduced to occupancy on government property. Opportunities to register as usufructs not taken up outside urban areas. No progress on 2005 & 2019 constitutional commitments to upgrade to full rights but 1970 & 1984 laws downgraded non-customary titled lands on government land to usufructs. Customary norms lawfully operate over 90% country.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Settlement & Registration Act, 1925, s. 13, 16. Prescriptions & Limitations Ordinance, 1928. Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990). Constitution 2005. Sudan Constitutional Charter for the 2019 Transitional Period.
indicators.additional_info: Law of 1928 deems use of waste, forest or unregistered lands as usufruct. Unregistered Land Act 1970 made  unregistered Government property, repealed  by Civil Transactions Act, 1984 but which retained most 1970's  content. Redefined Government ownership ('public property') as trustee ownership on behalf of God (s. 27, 559 (1)). Allows usufructs to be registered and to have same force as registered ownership (s. 560, 568, 570). Reduced freehold & leasehold to 'hikr'-  registered usufruct (s. 559).  1990 Amendment forbade courts or authorities t  hear applications or complaints connected with land owned by the State (s. 559 (8)). Provision for common and family property limited to urban parcels ( s. 532-37, 538-542) .

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Equality of registered customary and non-customary rights in that all registered parcels under single regime as usufructs. Almost no cust. lan registered, remain as permissive occupancy. A communal usufruct may in law be granted for grazing 'for the benefit of the whole community and protection of animals resources' (1984 s. 565 (b).
indicators.additional_info: All unregistered land belong to Government, but with opportunity through settlement and adjudication procedures to be registered as usufructs. Some protection at ocmpulsory accquisitio as  'lawful users or occupiers. Also, an applicant for registered right must not interfere with immediate areas of villages or cause injury to farms and settlements (1984, s.559, 560, 561(3), (4) & (5)). Government retains power to evict any person in occupation of land belonging to Government (s. 8).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Formalization occurs through systematic titling but inaction on this for decades. Provision for registration of individual, family and communal rights (grazing only) exists in law but not implemented, with 1990 amendment implying unregistered occupants & users are 'deemed' registered.This does not limit right of owner (Government) to evict at will.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Settlement and Registration Act, 1925, s. 21. Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990) s. 538-539.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Villages, communities, tribes, clans or other customary associations do not have legal personality although 1990 enables grazing land to be allocated to community. No requirement to establish a legal entity unless for registered usufruct. Vast majority are unregistered rural landholders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act 1984 (amended 1990).
indicators.additional_info: Co-ownership developed for condominium and family business purposes, difficult to apply to a customary land area (Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990) Chaps. 3-4).The law implies however that a family or clan or community can be registered as usufructary of a common area, especially grazing, but is not precise on the status as landholder, who remains a usufructary of Government land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Indirect provision for a People's Administration to be created at quarter, village or tribal camp level by local government (Locality) and endowed with powers. Also titular provision for Native Administration but powers unstated. Decentralization to States and then within States was  favoured in 2005 Constitution, but minimal implementation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Regional Government Act, 1980. Local Government Act, 1998, s. 19 & 20.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary tenure permits holding of right in perpetuity via inheritance. No term specified for registered usufructs, except for business purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990).
indicators.additional_info: Family ownership (mainly for business purposes) only for 15 years (Civil Transactions Act, 1984, Cht. 4). In rural domains where customary norms accepted as lawful use, holdings in perpetuity may be assumed despite absence of legal statement.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No consent requirements in the law. Consultation is  encouraged  including in Local Government Act.  Exploiters of mawaat (wasteland) by drilling water drilling, cultivation, building, etc. entitled to register usufruct, only requirement is that they do not interfere with settlements.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act, s. 561, 599.  Land Settlement and Registration Act, 1925, s. 13. Land Acquisition Act, 1930, s. 9).
indicators.additional_info: Since Land Settlement and Registration Act, 1925 & Land Acquisition Act 1930 'land subject to village or tribal rights' refers to Government owned lands, and no compensation required (1925, s. 13 (ii), 1930 (s. 9 (1)). Investor-friendly law welcoming Sudanese & non-Sudanese investors, with facilitation for finding land, likely to be customarily occupied (National Investment Encouragement Act, 2013).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Natural trees belong to state and permit required to fell and utilize (timber contract or concession for area). However, communities may define People's' Forests within and around villages and sustainable domestic use does not require permits. Communities may apply for concessions under contracts for timber.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act, 1984, s. 565 (1) (e). Law on Forests and Renewable Natural Resources, 2002, s. 40. Timber Utilization and Management Act, 2003, s. 4, 11.
indicators.additional_info: The 1989 Forests Acts was progressive in introducing community forests, to be managed by local committees, a large number established, status in 2025 unknown. Regulation and supervision is by the Forest Commission.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All water is public property. Under Islamic Sharia, customary law & formal enactments, communities have rights of access including for irrigation & stock watering. Permits variously required.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990), s. 59-601.
indicators.additional_info: Public property in Sudan's law is deemed registered as property of Government. Constitution 2005 focuses only on management (Art. 11) while 1998 Constitution had stated  that water is public property (i.e. government property), Art. 9. Constitution 2005 respects terms of 1998 Constitution (2005, Art. 226). States run water corporations, regulate, allocate rights. Note that Nile waters are subject to international water-sharing treaty under Nile Basin Initiative.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Forests divided into National, State, Private. Peoples' Forests may control forests in village locality subject to Forest Corporation direction. Grazing permitted (2002, Sec. 32). Commercial use governed by Timber Act, 2003. Rangelands Act 2015 provides for grazing areas including in Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law of Forests and Renewable Resources 2002, s. 33.Timber Utilization and Management Act, 2003.  Environmental Protection Act, 2001.Rangelands and Forage Resource Development (Rationalization) Act 2015.
indicators.additional_info: Forests Act 1989 and 2002 law encourages  'People's Forests' managed by committees outside Protected Areas. Some National Parks occupied by traditional communities, subject to rules, permitted to graze animals, but no cultivation or tree cutting permitted (Rangelands Law, 2015). Once a national or state protected area is gazetted it cannot be reclaimed (Forest law 2002, s. 28).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Since 1925 customary rights reduced to occupancy on government property. Opportunities to register as usufructs not taken up outside urban areas. No progress on 2005 & 2019 constitutional commitments to upgrade to full rights but 1970 & 1984 laws downgraded non-customary titled lands on government land to usufructs. Customary norms lawfully operate over 90% country.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Settlement & Registration Act, 1925, s. 13, 16. Prescriptions & Limitations Ordinance, 1928. Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990). Constitution 2005. Sudan Constitutional Charter for the 2019 Transitional Period.
indicators.additional_info: Law of 1928 deems use of waste, forest or unregistered lands as usufruct. Unregistered Land Act 1970 made  unregistered Government property, repealed  by Civil Transactions Act, 1984 but which retained most 1970's  content. Redefined Government ownership ('public property') as trustee ownership on behalf of God (s. 27, 559 (1)). Allows usufructs to be registered and to have same force as registered ownership (s. 560, 568, 570). Reduced freehold & leasehold to 'hikr'-  registered usufruct (s. 559).  1990 Amendment forbade courts or authorities t  hear applications or complaints connected with land owned by the State (s. 559 (8)). Provision for common and family property limited to urban parcels ( s. 532-37, 538-542) .

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Equality of registered customary and non-customary rights in that all registered parcels under single regime as usufructs. Almost no cust. lan registered, remain as permissive occupancy. A communal usufruct may in law be granted for grazing 'for the benefit of the whole community and protection of animals resources' (1984 s. 565 (b).
indicators.additional_info: All unregistered land belong to Government, but with opportunity through settlement and adjudication procedures to be registered as usufructs. Some protection at ocmpulsory accquisitio as  'lawful users or occupiers. Also, an applicant for registered right must not interfere with immediate areas of villages or cause injury to farms and settlements (1984, s.559, 560, 561(3), (4) & (5)). Government retains power to evict any person in occupation of land belonging to Government (s. 8).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Formalization occurs through systematic titling but inaction on this for decades. Provision for registration of individual, family and communal rights (grazing only) exists in law but not implemented, with 1990 amendment implying unregistered occupants & users are 'deemed' registered.This does not limit right of owner (Government) to evict at will.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Settlement and Registration Act, 1925, s. 21. Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990) s. 538-539.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Villages, communities, tribes, clans or other customary associations do not have legal personality although 1990 enables grazing land to be allocated to community. No requirement to establish a legal entity unless for registered usufruct. Vast majority are unregistered rural landholders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act 1984 (amended 1990).
indicators.additional_info: Co-ownership developed for condominium and family business purposes, difficult to apply to a customary land area (Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990) Chaps. 3-4).The law implies however that a family or clan or community can be registered as usufructary of a common area, especially grazing, but is not precise on the status as landholder, who remains a usufructary of Government land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Indirect provision for a People's Administration to be created at quarter, village or tribal camp level by local government (Locality) and endowed with powers. Also titular provision for Native Administration but powers unstated. Decentralization to States and then within States was  favoured in 2005 Constitution, but minimal implementation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Regional Government Act, 1980. Local Government Act, 1998, s. 19 & 20.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary tenure permits holding of right in perpetuity via inheritance. No term specified for registered usufructs, except for business purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Civil Transactions Act, 1984 (1990).
indicators.additional_info: Family ownership (mainly for business purposes) only for 15 years (Civil Transactions Act, 1984, Cht. 4). In rural domains where customary norms accepted as lawful use, holdings in perpetuity may be assumed despite absence of legal statement.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No consent requirements in the law. Consultation is  encouraged  including in Local Government Act.  Exploiters of mawaat (wasteland) by drilling water drilling, cultivation, building, etc. entitled to register usufruct, only requirement is that they do not interfere with settlements.
