SEN.name: Senegal

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Senegal abolished customary law in 1964, nationalized rural lands, permitted communities to allocate use certificates for developed lands only. Sales & transfers banned. Failure to support commune (cluster of villages) saw return to customary norms and unlawful sales. Community control of communal lands undermined,able to be allocated by State to others than community.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on the National Domain. Law No. 72-1888 of 1972 withdrawing Land from National Domain incl. under rural communities. Amended in 2020 by  Decree No.1773. Law No. 2011-07 on Land Ownership.  Law No. 2013-10  General Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 2021-38  Centralizing allocation of rural lands to municipal councils and higher bodies.
indicators.additional_info: Aim of abolishing customary tenure was to rid country of landlordism and to even up Arab-African relations. Despite sustained commitment to devolution, weak to poor over 60 years. Village may allocate parcels below 10 ha, commune 10-50 ha, Governor 50+ ha (Law No. 2021-38). No cheap alternative to statutory titles under 1964 law still in force, and disallowed in nationalized rural domain.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Unequality tenure secure for rural occupancy & titled lands in urban domains. While the law abolished customary land tenure in 1964, the same law endorses the existing occupancy of communities and their members on their (customary) lands. Titles are not available in the nationalized and inalienable rural domain.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2004-16 On Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development, 25 May, 2004.
indicators.additional_info: There has been periodic state acknowledgement since 1964 that the absence of legal mechanisms for families to secure and transfer parcels is unhelpful for productivity. Law No. 2004-16 pledged to "protect the operating rights of rural actors and the land rights of rural communities" and to  introduce "controlled transferability of land to enable land mobility and creation of more viable farms" and "inheritance of land to encourage sustainable investment in family farms" (Art. 22). None of these pledges have eventuated but inheritance is the main means of transfer in practice.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Issue of certificates for rural farms/houses is straightforward but expensive, low uptake since 1964. No legal means for  individual, family or collective lands to be mapped, adjudicated and subject of issue of Titles. Law No. 2011-07 On Land Ownership retains rural domain as national, inalienable land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2011-07 of March 30, 2011 On Land Ownership.
indicators.additional_info: The French colonial administration provided for registration of individual and collective rural lands in 1925 & 1956. No uptake in customary sector, then replaced in 1964 and since by accepted occupancy and use for development (farms etc) and exclusive rights to commons (pioneer zones) only via State use allocations to villages, communes & investors.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no legal provision for rural communities to be recognized as legal persons for the purpose of registering lands held in common. Allocation of collective use rights to customry commons may  be made to village or several village communities (commune).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on the National Estate.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The intention in the Land Code of 1964 and its Implementing Decree was for elected rural committees to administer lands. Village and commune do administer farm/settlement lands but commons under Commune and higher state bodies. Stark difference between practice and legal practice; customary norms and rights pursued, such as original first settler retaining allocation rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2013-10 of 28 December 2013 on the Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on The National Estate.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No explicit legal text on inheritance of customary parcels but the dominant mode of transfer in practice, and more legal acceptance; eg. Law No 2004 for Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development states "inheritance of land to encourage sustainable investment in family farms" would be provided through land reforms. Not applied after the closure of the National Land Reform Commission in May 2017.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 2004 for Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development. Decree No. 2017-998 of 16 May 2017 Dissolving the National Land Commission.
indicators.additional_info: The majority of rural landholders practice customary land tenure, irrespective of its illegality, including norm that a family or individual land allocation is inheritable and thus potentially held in perpetuity.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No consent from villagers required to reallocate any rural land, nationalized since 1964. State limited by 'public purpose'  loosely defined. Regular takings of communal lands for private or government projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2013-10 of 28 December 2013 on the Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on The National Estate.
indicators.additional_info: Senegal's rural population was recorded in 2022 as 9 million people; with only 385 local governments (Communes, or now called Municipal Councils), averages  23,000 persons, suggesting a large number of villages within each Commune/Municipal Council domain.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Free domestic use of trees. Exact types of use defined by Forest Code 2018 (Art 29). Only available to village families (Art 32). Only valid in unclassified forests, classified forests withdrawn from the municipality (Commune) and its village components (Art. 30-31).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, Law No. 2018-25 of 02 November 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Forest/tree use rights limited to: collecting dead wood and straw; harvesting fruits, leaves, roots, bark, gums, resins and honey for food and medicinal purposes; grazing livestock and pruning forage species; cutting of wood for construction and repair of dwellings, and use of sacred woods for worship (Art. 29 Forest Code). Management of protected forests is by district and commune authorities: these include community nature reserves, communal woods, communal nature reserves and communal forests, sites of local interest (Art. 2.16). Communities may only enter conventions (agreements) with forestry departments to execute management (Art. 2.10).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource and cannot be owned (Art. 2 Water Code 1981).  Allocation of water places priority on the supply of water to the population (Art. 75). "When human water needs have been met, priority is given to the needs of livestock farming, agriculture, forestry, fish farming and reforestation projects"(Art. 76).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, 1981. 4 March 1981.
indicators.additional_info: Note that Senegal's rural population was recorded in 2022 as 9 million people; with only 385 local governments (Communes, or now called Municipal Councils), averages  23,000 persons, suggesting a large number of villages within each Commune/Municipal Council domain.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unclassified Protected Areas are those delegated to Municipalities to manage. Originate in villages wish to set aside local commons as  communal nature reserves, communal woods, communal forests, sites of local interest (Art. 2.16). By Agreements, the village/s may manage under rules approved by Forest Ministry. Hundreds exist, many donor-funded for charcoal & other income projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, 2018 Law No. 2018-25 of 02 November 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Classified Protected Areas are owned by the State. Within the unregistered rural land sector domain, villages may set aside areas for protection or production (Art. 2.16). However, it is the Municipality, not village, which is charged with management.

Amended in 2020 by  Decree No.1773. Law No. 2011-07 on Land Ownership.  Law No. 2013-10  General Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 2021-38  Centralizing allocation of rural lands to municipal councils and higher bodies.
indicators.additional_info: Aim of abolishing customary tenure was to rid country of landlordism and to even up Arab-African relations. Despite sustained commitment to devolution, weak to poor over 60 years. Village may allocate parcels below 10 ha, commune 10-50 ha, Governor 50+ ha (Law No. 2021-38). No cheap alternative to statutory titles under 1964 law still in force, and disallowed in nationalized rural domain.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Unequality tenure secure for rural occupancy & titled lands in urban domains. While the law abolished customary land tenure in 1964, the same law endorses the existing occupancy of communities and their members on their (customary) lands. Titles are not available in the nationalized and inalienable rural domain.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2004-16 On Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development, 25 May, 2004.
indicators.additional_info: There has been periodic state acknowledgement since 1964 that the absence of legal mechanisms for families to secure and transfer parcels is unhelpful for productivity. Law No. 2004-16 pledged to "protect the operating rights of rural actors and the land rights of rural communities" and to  introduce "controlled transferability of land to enable land mobility and creation of more viable farms" and "inheritance of land to encourage sustainable investment in family farms" (Art. 22). None of these pledges have eventuated but inheritance is the main means of transfer in practice.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Issue of certificates for rural farms/houses is straightforward but expensive, low uptake since 1964. No legal means for  individual, family or collective lands to be mapped, adjudicated and subject of issue of Titles. Law No. 2011-07 On Land Ownership retains rural domain as national, inalienable land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2011-07 of March 30, 2011 On Land Ownership.
indicators.additional_info: The French colonial administration provided for registration of individual and collective rural lands in 1925 & 1956. No uptake in customary sector, then replaced in 1964 and since by accepted occupancy and use for development (farms etc) and exclusive rights to commons (pioneer zones) only via State use allocations to villages, communes & investors.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no legal provision for rural communities to be recognized as legal persons for the purpose of registering lands held in common. Allocation of collective use rights to customry commons may  be made to village or several village communities (commune).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on the National Estate.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The intention in the Land Code of 1964 and its Implementing Decree was for elected rural committees to administer lands. Village and commune do administer farm/settlement lands but commons under Commune and higher state bodies. Stark difference between practice and legal practice; customary norms and rights pursued, such as original first settler retaining allocation rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2013-10 of 28 December 2013 on the Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on The National Estate.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No explicit legal text on inheritance of customary parcels but the dominant mode of transfer in practice, and more legal acceptance; eg. Law No 2004 for Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development states "inheritance of land to encourage sustainable investment in family farms" would be provided through land reforms. Not applied after the closure of the National Land Reform Commission in May 2017.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 2004 for Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral Development. Decree No. 2017-998 of 16 May 2017 Dissolving the National Land Commission.
indicators.additional_info: The majority of rural landholders practice customary land tenure, irrespective of its illegality, including norm that a family or individual land allocation is inheritable and thus potentially held in perpetuity.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No consent from villagers required to reallocate any rural land, nationalized since 1964. State limited by 'public purpose'  loosely defined. Regular takings of communal lands for private or government projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2013-10 of 28 December 2013 on the Code of Local Authorities. Law No. 64-46 of 17 June 1964 on The National Estate.
indicators.additional_info: Senegal's rural population was recorded in 2022 as 9 million people; with only 385 local governments (Communes, or now called Municipal Councils), averages  23,000 persons, suggesting a large number of villages within each Commune/Municipal Council domain.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Free domestic use of trees. Exact types of use defined by Forest Code 2018 (Art 29). Only available to village families (Art 32). Only valid in unclassified forests, classified forests withdrawn from the municipality (Commune) and its village components (Art. 30-31).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, Law No. 2018-25 of 02 November 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Forest/tree use rights limited to: collecting dead wood and straw; harvesting fruits, leaves, roots, bark, gums, resins and honey for food and medicinal purposes; grazing livestock and pruning forage species; cutting of wood for construction and repair of dwellings, and use of sacred woods for worship (Art. 29 Forest Code). Management of protected forests is by district and commune authorities: these include community nature reserves, communal woods, communal nature reserves and communal forests, sites of local interest (Art. 2.16). Communities may only enter conventions (agreements) with forestry departments to execute management (Art. 2.10).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource and cannot be owned (Art. 2 Water Code 1981).  Allocation of water places priority on the supply of water to the population (Art. 75). "When human water needs have been met, priority is given to the needs of livestock farming, agriculture, forestry, fish farming and reforestation projects"(Art. 76).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, 1981. 4 March 1981.
indicators.additional_info: Note that Senegal's rural population was recorded in 2022 as 9 million people; with only 385 local governments (Communes, or now called Municipal Councils), averages  23,000 persons, suggesting a large number of villages within each Commune/Municipal Council domain.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Unclassified Protected Areas are those delegated to Municipalities to manage. Originate in villages wish to set aside local commons as  communal nature reserves, communal woods, communal forests, sites of local interest (Art. 2.16). By Agreements, the village/s may manage under rules approved by Forest Ministry. Hundreds exist, many donor-funded for charcoal & other income projects.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, 2018 Law No. 2018-25 of 02 November 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Classified Protected Areas are owned by the State. Within the unregistered rural land sector domain, villages may set aside areas for protection or production (Art. 2.16). However, it is the Municipality, not village, which is charged with management.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law is explicit that Malays are the indigenous people of Singapore. Beyond that, however, little legal protection is specifically given to land-rights. In addition, the indigenous fishing communities of the Seletar (also know an the Orang Asli Laut) are not given formal legal recognition or protection.
indicators.law_and_provision: Article 152(2) of Singapore's Constitution.
indicators.additional_info: Article 152(2) reads "The Government shall exercise its functions in such manner as to recognize the special position of the Malays, who are the indigenous people of Singapore." While there are many laws that protect the ethnic and religious heritage of Singapore's Malay population, there is no land-specific protections. The Seletar, or Orang Asli Laut, are traditional fishing communities. Rapid development has polluted their communities, and in turn, endangered their livelihood.

SLE.name: Sierra Leone

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: History since 1927 of recognizing customary tenure. 2022 land law removes trustee ownership by Chiefs/Councils. Other new legal strengths: a. recognition of customary rights as absolute property rights including over communal lands; b. obligation to apply FPIC in state taking of family or community lands; c. strong provisions for gender equity; d. certification of existing rights is voluntary.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 1991 (2008) Art. 170-171). Local Courts Act, 2011 Art. 27, 38, 120). Customary Land Rights Act, No. 20 of 2022 (Arts 13-14, . The National Land Commission Act, No. 19 of 2022. SI No. 64 of October 2023 on the National Land Commission (Para-Surveyors and Paralegals) Operational Regulations and The Customary Land Rights Regulation No 12 of 2023, on rules of  investment on customary lands.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution (1991) recognizes customary law in force within all 149 Chiefdoms, and to guide disputes in 149 Local Courts (2011). The Customary Land Right Act 2022  & National Land Commission Act 2022 clarify ownership under customary tenure, require gender equality, and aims to regulate external takings for investment with FPIC. Land directly vested in families (farms, house plots etc), and in community for communal lands. Governance is by the family or village/town land committee under oversight of Chiefdom Councils (sec. 9).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights have same legal force & effect as non-customary rights, even if not registered (voluntary)  Titles available at District Land  Commissions (NLCA, 2022 s. 34 (2b). FPIC required for public takings (CLRA 2022 s. 28, 43, Regs 2023 s. 12). Limits on plantations, housing etc in designated old growth or other sensitive areas of family & community properties (CLRA 2022 s. 21).
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Rights Act (CLRA), 2022 & Regulations, 2023 (No 65/2023). National Land Commission Act (NLCA, 2022), and Regulations No 64/2023.
indicators.additional_info: The National Land Commission Act 2022 establishes powers and composition  of Chiefdom Land Committees (sec. 42-48), Town and Village Area Land Committees (sec.49-56). Mass customary land titling envisaged as indicated by Regulation No. 11 of 2023 of CLRA, providing for para-surveyors and paralegals to be accredited to the National Land Commission, to advance formalization of family and communal  ownership.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: While cheap, simple and accessible titling intended, not yet developed under Regulations. Positive moves through devolving registration to District Land Commissions (CLRA 2022, s. 34 (2c) and cutting costs & speed by training para-surveyors and para-legals (Reg. 64/2023 under NLCA 2022).
indicators.law_and_provision: Customary Land Rights Act (CLRA), 2022 & Regulations, 2023 (No 65/2023). National Land Commission Act (NLCA, 2022), and Regulations No 64/2023.
indicators.additional_info: National Land Policy 2015 (Part.7.10) aims to establish a single cadastral based title deed system inclusive of customary rights, recording group, family and individual ownership, and those authorised to act on behalf of groups of persons.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The CLRA accepts families and communities as legal persons; neither required to form corporate entities to hold land on their behalf; recognition as existing &titles to be vested directly in members in undivided shares.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1996, revised 2008, available as of 2013. Community Land Rights Act (CLRA) No 20 of 2022 & Regulation No 65 of 2023. National Land Commission Act (NLCA), No. 19 of 2022, &  Regulation No.64 of 2023.
indicators.additional_info: Most land is family, lineage, clan or community land in Sierra Leone. Long-standing Constitutional support for customary tenure as lawful property; customary law, written or not written, is defined as part of common law, to be upheld, failures to respect these laws justiciable (1996 Art. 170). This also states that 'customary law' means the rules of law which by custom are applicable to particular communities in Sierra Leone (Art. 170 (3).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Inclusive, localized decision-making an aim of the 2022 laws, via elected village/town land committees and modified Chiefdom Land Committees (NLCA 2022 s. 49) now including reps from each section (s. 43). Chiefdom Co. has final authority over communal lands (s. 44) only 'until the town or village establishes its land committee' (s. 18). Chiefdom by- laws apply to all villages and towns (s. 19).
indicators.law_and_provision: Chieftaincy Act No. 10 of 2009, s. 2, 29 .Customary Land Rights Act (CLRA), 2022 & Regulations, 2023 (No 65/2023). National Land Commission Act (NLCA, 2022), and Regulations No 64/2023.
indicators.additional_info: Town or village land committees are elected by majority vote of 2/3 of the adult residents (s. 50 (2)). Paramount Chiefs and their councillors are 'men of note' (Provinces Land Act Cap 122 d. 2), elected by councillors (by customary norms), election supervised by Electoral Commission (Chieftaincy Act, 2009 s. 5 & 28). May be removed by President as result of inquiry (s. 19). Functions include preservation of customs & traditions (s. 29). Chiefdomship is constitutionally protected (Art. 72 (1)). In some areas, land rights have been plagued by chief capture & disposal of communal lands, exacerbated by surge in foreign investments.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Lawful to hold rights in perpetuity for so long as customary law upholds this. Non-natives to chiefdom may hold only leasehold. Family land  vested in the family as a unit, administered by a family head. Subject to consent of 60% of adult members, may grant tenancies up to 50 yrs and seasonal access rights (CLRA,2022, s. 11) & 15).
indicators.law_and_provision: Chieftaincy Act, 2009 (last amended in 2022 by CLRA, 2022, sec. 18). Customary Land Rights Act (CLRA), 2022 & Regulations, 2023 (No 65/2023). National Land Commission Act (NLCA, 2022), and Regulations No 64/2023
indicators.additional_info: The holding of rights in perpetuity is dependent upon customary norms. Customary law is constitutionally recognized as part of the country's legal system applicable outside the small urbanized Western Province or State Lands. All benefits from communal land and its resources belong to the community (CLRA 2022, sec. 17). The Chiefdom Committee manages this land only 'until the town or village establishes its land committee' (sec. 18). Chiefdom by-laws apply to all villages and towns (sec. 19).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The CLRA 2022 requires FPIC for all transactions affecting family or community land, and imposing significant duties on investors (CLRA 2022 s. 10, 11, 18-19, 28, 32, 38, 43). Quorum for FPIC is 2/3 adult members of family or community. Must be in writing for family land. NOTE: no FPIC is required for comp. acq. for public purpose, only investors.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution Art. 21.1. Customary Land Rights Act (CLRA), 2022 & Regulations, 2023 (No 65/2023). National Land Commission Act (NLCA, 2022), and Regulations No 64/2023
indicators.additional_info: The CLRA 2022 establishes that investors are legally bound to provide equivalent or better alternative sources of communal resources where to be affected by an investment (s. 36). Nor may the investor interfere with occupation and use, without paying prompt and adequate compensation (s. 38). No investment induced displacement and resettlement unless there is compelling need, and FPIC obtained for resettlement with full costs borne by investor (s. 43 (6)). Displacement can only take place following payment of adequate compensation (s. 43 (12), & when required structures are constructed in the new location and certified as fit for habitation by Government and independent assessment (s. 43 (14)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No legal indication that a family or community do not own indigenous and planted trees on their lands. However, Authorized Officers bound to ensure that wetlands, wildlife habitats, steep slopes, virgin forests etc are protected from degradation (CLRA 2022 s. 20).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Act, 1988 (as last amended in February 2022). Forestry Regulations, 1989 (Notice No. 17 of 1990).
indicators.additional_info: Authorized Officers are to ensure that no mining, plantations, farming, housing or other development activities take place in or next to sensitive family or community lands such as old growth forests, steep slopes (CLRA 2022 s.21). These 'sensitive' areas to be co-managed by the community, Chiefdom Council and the 'responsible government agency' (sec. 22 (3)).  Traditional use is permitted (sec. 23). The Town/Village is to adopt and enforce rules for sustainable use (sec. 23 (4)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water is attached to the land and owned by the customary or registered owner. Land includes ' land covered by water, any house, building or structure whatsoever and estate, interest or right in, to or over land or water' (NLCA 2022 s.1).  Note that 'public land' is defined as 'land reserved, held or used by the government, local councils or communities for public purposes ..."  (NLCA 2022,s. 1).
indicators.law_and_provision: National Land Commission Act, 2022, sec. 1, 17. Public Lands Ordinance Cap 116 1808, last amended 1959 referring to the former Colony, now Western Area.
indicators.additional_info: Chiefdom Councils and Town/Village Land Councils are obliged  to identify and protect wetlands, and other ecologically sensitive areas (CLRA 2022 s. 20).  Access and use rights to rivers and swamps are guaranteed (sec. 23 (1)) and rules are to be devised and enforced by Town or Village Area Committees (23 (4)).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Ownership of forests on customary land and rights to access wildlife recognizes  by CLRA 2022. Rights to national forest reserves to be sustained or compensated for if extinguished. Community Forests may be created, classified as Protected Areas, and managed by Village Forest Associations (Reg 42 of Regs 1989). Less community empowerment in the wildlife sector pending promised new law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife Policy, 2010. Wildlife Conservation Act No. 27 of 1972, amended in 1990 and 2022). Forestry Act, 1988 (2022) and Forest Regulations, 1989.
indicators.additional_info: Community Forests provided for, and common since the 1990s under the Forestry Act, 1988 (Part V). Act provides for compensation via share of annual rent to those who lose rights to trees when establishing a National Forest (s.10.2.b) and also creates Community Forests on chiefdom lands by agreements, with compensation for lost rights be paid and those confirmed as allowed to continue (s. 18.2.c, d. & e). Any protection developments for forests or wildlife are bound by the entrenched tenure of families and communities in customary land domains, as per the CLRA 2022. From 1988, the Forestry Act provided for sustaining use rights where possible (s. 10 (2) (a) or leasing land from Chiefdoms  for rent to create new National Forest Reserves or Parks . Wildlife Act 1972 (2022) requires consent of Chiefdom Council to declare a Strict Nature Reserve (s. 3). Chiefdoms may create Game Sanctuaries (s. 21). While rights extinguished by Minister this is only by agreement of the community and for negotiated compensation under the CLRA, 2022. Investors may not execute projects in land or marine protected areas (CLRA 2022 s. 25).

indicators.comment: Water is attached to the land and owned by the customary or registered owner. Land includes ' land covered by water, any house, building or structure whatsoever and estate, interest or right in, to or over land or water' (NLCA 2022 s.1).  Note that 'public land' is defined as 'land reserved, held or used by the government, local councils or communities for public purposes ..."  (NLCA 2022,s. 1).
indicators.law_and_provision: National Land Commission Act, 2022, sec. 1, 17. Public Lands Ordinance Cap 116 1808, last amended 1959 referring to the former Colony, now Western Area.
indicators.additional_info: Chiefdom Councils and Town/Village Land Councils are obliged  to identify and protect wetlands, and other ecologically sensitive areas (CLRA 2022 s. 20).  Access and use rights to rivers and swamps are guaranteed (sec. 23 (1)) and rules are to be devised and enforced by Town or Village Area Committees (23 (4)).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Ownership of forests on customary land and rights to access wildlife recognizes  by CLRA 2022. Rights to national forest reserves to be sustained or compensated for if extinguished. Community Forests may be created, classified as Protected Areas, and managed by Village Forest Associations (Reg 42 of Regs 1989). Less community empowerment in the wildlife sector pending promised new law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Wildlife Policy, 2010. Wildlife Conservation Act No. 27 of 1972, amended in 1990 and 2022). Forestry Act, 1988 (2022) and Forest Regulations, 1989.
indicators.additional_info: Community Forests provided for, and common since the 1990s under the Forestry Act, 1988 (Part V). Act provides for compensation via share of annual rent to those who lose rights to trees when establishing a National Forest (s.10.2.b) and also creates Community Forests on chiefdom lands by agreements, with compensation for lost rights be paid and those confirmed as allowed to continue (s. 18.2.c, d. & e). Any protection developments for forests or wildlife are bound by the entrenched tenure of families and communities in customary land domains, as per the CLRA 2022. From 1988, the Forestry Act provided for sustaining use rights where possible (s. 10 (2) (a) or leasing land from Chiefdoms  for rent to create new National Forest Reserves or Parks . Wildlife Act 1972 (2022) requires consent of Chiefdom Council to declare a Strict Nature Reserve (s. 3). Chiefdoms may create Game Sanctuaries (s. 21). While rights extinguished by Minister this is only by agreement of the community and for negotiated compensation under the CLRA, 2022. Investors may not execute projects in land or marine protected areas (CLRA 2022 s. 25).

SOM.name: Somalia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.language: English - available for two federal laws & two state laws
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Constitution 2012 fails to clarify what constitutes 'property' or even if customary law applies. Nat. Land Policy still lacking. Article 43 offers no guidance on the status of unrepealed 1970s land laws. Focus since 2012 with continuing conflict is on shelter for 3.9 million IDP mainly from rural to urban 'safety'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Provision Constitution, 2012. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, 1999 (2001). Urban land laws in Puntland (2020),  Southwest State  (2022), Galmudug (2022), Somaliland (2008, 2014).
indicators.additional_info: Civil war rooted in the struggle for land rights continues, including Al-Shabaab insurgency (esp. Jubaland State). Inter-clan conflicts persist over whole country. Recourse to customary inter-clan Xeer Agreements in disarray & norms disputed. 1970s privatization delivered in <1% country. Constitution 2012 (Art. 3b) guarantees registration; contested. Failed attempts to delivery the promised National Land Policy. No Federal Member State has finalized a State Land Policy(Const. Art 43.3.g.). Key common problem is how to address contested rangelands & clan overlaps from pre and post civil war. Somaliland, the breakaway State, is most advanced including repeal of the 1970s laws & a Draft Policy in 2016..

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unable to assess equality of customary & statutory land rights & regimes as no statement/law on the former; but remains the major regime, along with Sharia for land inheritance. Civil Code 1973 reactivated by Somaliland State supports localized rule Art. 18 & includes communal rights Arts 698-702. Somaliland also only State to develop rural land law but limited to arable lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999. Draft Somaliland National Land Policy, 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Somaliland State repealed laws between 1969 and 1991, including the 1970 law abolishing clans and the 1975 agricultural law which abolished customary tenure. Its State Constitution 2001 makes land the public property of the Somaliland nation, regulated & managed by the State (Art. 12). Assures the right to own private property (Art. 31) but fails to mention pastoral or customary rights. Its Agricultural Law 1999 Art 17 focuses on irrigated land, limits enclosure of rangelands for farming. Its  Draft National Land Policy 2016 provides for public, private and community land, vests natural resources in the State, and recognizes customary tenure as lawful in rural areas (Policy Statement 3) BUT unclear if adopted since 2016.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The breakaway Somaliland is most advanced in legal address of land rights, but limited to urban & arable lands; despite 55% pop being pastoralists. 3000 titles issued in Hargeisa under urban law, unknown no. for 8ha rainfed and/or 4 ha irrigated lands under agricultural law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Urban Land Law 2001. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Somaliland Constitution pledges to establish regional & district councils in consultation "with prominent members of village communities, propose village committees whose appointment shall be subject to approval of the district council" (Art. 111). No  village level land administration. Despite Art 17 of Urban law disallowing any rainfed land taken out of common land, reported as occurring at scale.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No federal or state legal provision recognizing communities or clans as legal persons but this is de facto customary practice; clan rights over pasturelands may be broadly assumed to be operational if  highly contested among clans and militias.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Draft Land Policy 2016

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No evidence of legal empowerment of village or clan land committees in limited federal and state laws. The one rural land law in force in Somaliland (1999 (2001) intends consultation with village notables for district administration, focused on issue of private titles for farming. The Draft Somaliland Land Policy 2016 provides for community land but final unseen.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Draft Land Policy 2016. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Note: No development of pastoral codes in Somalia at federal or state levels.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: There is no federal or state laws indicating whether rights in rural land may be owned in perpetuity although in local customary rules inheritance assumed, and likely to be upheld under widely active Sharia rules.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Land is nationalized in the Somaliland Constitution, rendering property to mean owning rights to the land, not ownership of the land itself.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No evidence found in federal Constitution 2012 or state laws requiring consent of registered or majority de facto land owners prior to taking of their lands for public purposes. In practice sustained takings, evictions and flight due to violent inter-clan & inter-militia, and federal-al Shabaab  conflicts.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal Constitution 2012 vests authority over natural resources in the Federal Government (Art. 44) and while declaring the power of self-governance begins and ends with the people, does not empower communities on ownership of land - or resources such as trees. The Environmental Protection and Management Act, 2024 provides no indication of tree ownership. No federal forest law enacted.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Federal Environmental Protection and Management Act, April 2024 (English).  Somaliland State Forestry and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015 (not available in English).
indicators.additional_info: Tree ownership is not covered in Somaliland's Forest and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No Federal Water Law. Somaliland & Puntland States have enacted water laws. Puntland Water Act 2018 makes water public property of Puntland nation, controlled by government, to be used equitably (Art. 9).  No licences needed for domestic needs (Art. 15). Rural water points for livestock & domestic use by pastoral communities to be by customary norms (Art. 50).
indicators.law_and_provision: Puntland Water Resources Act, 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Puntland Water Act 2018: Groundwater, lakes springs, streams cannot be privatized, and all water rights including traditional rights must be registered (Art. 11). Community juries must mediate disputes. "This Act recognizes. legitimizes, authorizes, and approves the traditional rural water rules of use". Art. 50 (3)

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No federal forest law enacted.  Somaliland's Forest and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015 (not available in English) proposes creation and management of private and community forests, and to establish of village  environmental protection committees. This law also addresses conservation of grazing lands, bans hunting, privatization of wildlife.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland State Forestry and Wildlife Act, No 69 of 2015

Article 43 offers no guidance on the status of unrepealed 1970s land laws. Focus since 2012 with continuing conflict is on shelter for 3.9 million IDP mainly from rural to urban 'safety'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Federal Provision Constitution, 2012. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, 1999 (2001). Urban land laws in Puntland (2020),  Southwest State  (2022), Galmudug (2022), Somaliland (2008, 2014).
indicators.additional_info: Civil war rooted in the struggle for land rights continues, including Al-Shabaab insurgency (esp. Jubaland State). Inter-clan conflicts persist over whole country. Recourse to customary inter-clan Xeer Agreements in disarray & norms disputed. 1970s privatization delivered in <1% country. Constitution 2012 (Art. 3b) guarantees registration; contested. Failed attempts to delivery the promised National Land Policy. No Federal Member State has finalized a State Land Policy(Const. Art 43.3.g.). Key common problem is how to address contested rangelands & clan overlaps from pre and post civil war. Somaliland, the breakaway State, is most advanced including repeal of the 1970s laws & a Draft Policy in 2016..

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Unable to assess equality of customary & statutory land rights & regimes as no statement/law on the former; but remains the major regime, along with Sharia for land inheritance. Civil Code 1973 reactivated by Somaliland State supports localized rule Art. 18 & includes communal rights Arts 698-702. Somaliland also only State to develop rural land law but limited to arable lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999. Draft Somaliland National Land Policy, 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Somaliland State repealed laws between 1969 and 1991, including the 1970 law abolishing clans and the 1975 agricultural law which abolished customary tenure. Its State Constitution 2001 makes land the public property of the Somaliland nation, regulated & managed by the State (Art. 12). Assures the right to own private property (Art. 31) but fails to mention pastoral or customary rights. Its Agricultural Law 1999 Art 17 focuses on irrigated land, limits enclosure of rangelands for farming. Its  Draft National Land Policy 2016 provides for public, private and community land, vests natural resources in the State, and recognizes customary tenure as lawful in rural areas (Policy Statement 3) BUT unclear if adopted since 2016.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The breakaway Somaliland is most advanced in legal address of land rights, but limited to urban & arable lands; despite 55% pop being pastoralists. 3000 titles issued in Hargeisa under urban law, unknown no. for 8ha rainfed and/or 4 ha irrigated lands under agricultural law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Urban Land Law 2001. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Somaliland Constitution pledges to establish regional & district councils in consultation "with prominent members of village communities, propose village committees whose appointment shall be subject to approval of the district council" (Art. 111). No  village level land administration. Despite Art 17 of Urban law disallowing any rainfed land taken out of common land, reported as occurring at scale.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No federal or state legal provision recognizing communities or clans as legal persons but this is de facto customary practice; clan rights over pasturelands may be broadly assumed to be operational if  highly contested among clans and militias.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Draft Land Policy 2016

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No evidence of legal empowerment of village or clan land committees in limited federal and state laws. The one rural land law in force in Somaliland (1999 (2001) intends consultation with village notables for district administration, focused on issue of private titles for farming. The Draft Somaliland Land Policy 2016 provides for community land but final unseen.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Draft Land Policy 2016. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Note: No development of pastoral codes in Somalia at federal or state levels.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: There is no federal or state laws indicating whether rights in rural land may be owned in perpetuity although in local customary rules inheritance assumed, and likely to be upheld under widely active Sharia rules.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).
indicators.additional_info: Land is nationalized in the Somaliland Constitution, rendering property to mean owning rights to the land, not ownership of the land itself.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No evidence found in federal Constitution 2012 or state laws requiring consent of registered or majority de facto land owners prior to taking of their lands for public purposes. In practice sustained takings, evictions and flight due to violent inter-clan & inter-militia, and federal-al Shabaab  conflicts.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Somaliland State Constitution, 2001. Somali Civil Code, 1973. Somaliland Agricultural Land Ownership Law, No. 8 of 1999 (amended by No 17 of 2001).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal Constitution 2012 vests authority over natural resources in the Federal Government (Art. 44) and while declaring the power of self-governance begins and ends with the people, does not empower communities on ownership of land - or resources such as trees. The Environmental Protection and Management Act, 2024 provides no indication of tree ownership. No federal forest law enacted.
indicators.law_and_provision: Provisional Federal Constitution, 2012. Federal Environmental Protection and Management Act, April 2024 (English).  Somaliland State Forestry and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015 (not available in English).
indicators.additional_info: Tree ownership is not covered in Somaliland's Forest and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No Federal Water Law. Somaliland & Puntland States have enacted water laws. Puntland Water Act 2018 makes water public property of Puntland nation, controlled by government, to be used equitably (Art. 9).  No licences needed for domestic needs (Art. 15). Rural water points for livestock & domestic use by pastoral communities to be by customary norms (Art. 50).
indicators.law_and_provision: Puntland Water Resources Act, 2018.
indicators.additional_info: Puntland Water Act 2018: Groundwater, lakes springs, streams cannot be privatized, and all water rights including traditional rights must be registered (Art. 11). Community juries must mediate disputes. "This Act recognizes. legitimizes, authorizes, and approves the traditional rural water rules of use". Art. 50 (3)

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No federal forest law enacted.  Somaliland's Forest and Wildlife Conservation Law, No. 69/2015 (not available in English) proposes creation and management of private and community forests, and to establish of village  environmental protection committees. This law also addresses conservation of grazing lands, bans hunting, privatization of wildlife.
indicators.law_and_provision: Somaliland State Forestry and Wildlife Act, No 69 of 2015

SSD.name: South Sudan

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution 2011 provides for community, private & public land. Land Act 2009 stipulates customary rights have same force as freehold or leasehold rights. Recognition of community lands is a key principle. Public land is a governance rather than tenure class. public lands definable from village to federal state levels. Still no regulations to implement Land Act 2009 as of Mar 2025.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011, Art. 171 Land Act, 2009, s. 5, 6, 8 (6). National Land Policy, October 2023 still in draft as of Mar 2025.
indicators.additional_info: Rights in land under customary tenure 'shall be an assured security of occupancy whether or not held individually or in association with others' (Land Act sec. 8 (3)).  Special provision for protecting pastoral lands and communal grazing rights (Land Act, 2009 s. 66-67). Restitution is  provided for via claims to Southern Sudan Land Commission (s. 78-83). However, due to civil conflict, mass displacement due to flooding, influx of North Sudan refugees, and armed political conflict, many laws remain bills and many enacted laws lack regulations in 2024. Efforts to approve National Land Policy since 2006 still struggling as of March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights including those held in common shall have equal force and effect in law with freehold or leasehold rights acquired through allocation, registration or transaction' Land Act s. 8(6). Legal title not required to prove ownership. 8(3). 'Community land' includes communal grazing, forest, marshes, settlements & farmed lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011, Art. 170-171; Land Act, 2009, s.9 -10, s. 39 (3).
indicators.additional_info: Compensation to be paid to community where access & rights terminated for public purposes. Land Act 2009 s. 65. Ownership may be customary or statutory title s. 84 (2). Strong provisions for customary tenure system, protection of customary rights, customary law lawful source of law. Land Act  protects communities from eviction if on land since 1983 (start of civil war).s. 82.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Clear intentions for devolved, simple and cheap  registration of every community's domain, issue of individual & family titles. Not undertaken as no implementing law or supporting administration at Sub-County (payam) and Ward (Boma) levels. Registration is not compulsory and protection of unregistered customary lands continues, likely to remain the reality for many years.
indicators.additional_info: In legal words, protection is strong, but zero application, and contradictory laws and manner of allocations to investors suggest a different reality.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community, clan, and family are legal persons for purposes of registering rights. Community land may optionally be registered "in the name of community, clan, family, association, or traditional leader as trustee with consent of community" (s. 53, 58). Individual right also registrable. However,  as no Regulation, no uptake or testing of viability, or reliability.
indicators.additional_info: No requirement for community to create a legal entity (Land Act, 2009, s. 58).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Devolved land administration intended but no regulatory details. Traditional Authorities may allocate lands, subject to notification to Sub-County (Payam) & County Land Authority. Land Act, s. 15. Boma Land Council also instituted for village clusters (s. 48-50) including duty 'to protect customary land rights of communities, communal grazing land, forest wetlands and water resources' (s. 50).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011. Art. 5,  Land Act 2009, s. 15
indicators.additional_info: Below Counties are c. 530 Payam (sub-countries) and c. 2,500 Bomas (wards, or village clusters). Appointed chiefs are also recognized as part of governance regime. Courts to apply customary law. Unclear how far members of villages can control decisions affecting their lands. Regulations awaited.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights held in perpetuity principally through inheritance. Precise terms depend upon local customs ('customary law'). Land Act awards ownership to communities, prior to and after registration of their community domains, and ownership is defined as the right to possess, occupy and use in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2009, s. 4
indicators.additional_info: Definitions in Land Act 2009  s. 4 include: 'Customary land rights means rights conferred by or derived from customs or customary law and practices'; 'customary law' means the conventions and rules which a particular community observed, develops over time and unusually uncodified'. 'Ownership means the right provided by law to possess, occupy and use land in perpetuity' (Land Act, 2009, s. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: FPIC is not found in land law. Obligatory consultation for public purpose acquisitions but failure to consent may be overridden. Traditional Authority needs consensus before agreeing lease to an outsider. 'Public purpose' includes commercial enterprises. Contradiction under Investment Act 2009 yet to be resolved.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2009, s. 27, 73-76. Investment Promotion Act, 2009
indicators.additional_info: If area sought is more than 250 feddan) (acres) Investment Authority must approve lease (Land Act, 2009 s. 27 (3)). Lease contract is between community & grantee, not the Government (Land Act, 2009, s. 27 (6)).Consultation & benefit-sharing required including from subterranean assets, with 'states, localities and communities' (Const.  Art. 168). indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No legal provision but as land includes above surface assets in customary regimes may be assumed that communities own trees on customary lands, unless these fall within Protected Areas.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land Act declares rivers, lakes, canals, haffirs, wetlands and other areas of water to be public land (owned collectively by nation) except for pools, streams, swamps or secondary rivers traditionally owned and managed by a community. Water Policy in 2007 does not define community rights. A Water Bill 2013 has never been enacted.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2009, s. 10 (f). Water Policy 2007.
indicators.additional_info: Water Policy, 2007 not instructive on community land rights to water. No Water law enacted. indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution 2011 provides for community, private & public land. Land Act 2009 stipulates customary rights have same force as freehold or leasehold rights. Recognition of community lands is a key principle. Public land is a governance rather than tenure class. public lands definable from village to federal state levels. Still no regulations to implement Land Act 2009 as of Mar 2025.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011, Art. 171 Land Act, 2009, s. 5, 6, 8 (6). National Land Policy, October 2023 still in draft as of Mar 2025.
indicators.additional_info: Rights in land under customary tenure 'shall be an assured security of occupancy whether or not held individually or in association with others' (Land Act sec. 8 (3)).  Special provision for protecting pastoral lands and communal grazing rights (Land Act, 2009 s. 66-67). Restitution is  provided for via claims to Southern Sudan Land Commission (s. 78-83). However, due to civil conflict, mass displacement due to flooding, influx of North Sudan refugees, and armed political conflict, many laws remain bills and many enacted laws lack regulations in 2024. Efforts to approve National Land Policy since 2006 still struggling as of March 2025.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights including those held in common shall have equal force and effect in law with freehold or leasehold rights acquired through allocation, registration or transaction' Land Act s. 8(6). Legal title not required to prove ownership. 8(3). 'Community land' includes communal grazing, forest, marshes, settlements & farmed lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011, Art. 170-171; Land Act, 2009, s.9 -10, s. 39 (3).
indicators.additional_info: Compensation to be paid to community where access & rights terminated for public purposes. Land Act 2009 s. 65. Ownership may be customary or statutory title s. 84 (2). Strong provisions for customary tenure system, protection of customary rights, customary law lawful source of law. Land Act  protects communities from eviction if on land since 1983 (start of civil war).s. 82.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Clear intentions for devolved, simple and cheap  registration of every community's domain, issue of individual & family titles. Not undertaken as no implementing law or supporting administration at Sub-County (payam) and Ward (Boma) levels. Registration is not compulsory and protection of unregistered customary lands continues, likely to remain the reality for many years.
indicators.additional_info: In legal words, protection is strong, but zero application, and contradictory laws and manner of allocations to investors suggest a different reality.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community, clan, and family are legal persons for purposes of registering rights. Community land may optionally be registered "in the name of community, clan, family, association, or traditional leader as trustee with consent of community" (s. 53, 58). Individual right also registrable. However,  as no Regulation, no uptake or testing of viability, or reliability.
indicators.additional_info: No requirement for community to create a legal entity (Land Act, 2009, s. 58).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Devolved land administration intended but no regulatory details. Traditional Authorities may allocate lands, subject to notification to Sub-County (Payam) & County Land Authority. Land Act, s. 15. Boma Land Council also instituted for village clusters (s. 48-50) including duty 'to protect customary land rights of communities, communal grazing land, forest wetlands and water resources' (s. 50).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2011. Art. 5,  Land Act 2009, s. 15
indicators.additional_info: Below Counties are c. 530 Payam (sub-countries) and c. 2,500 Bomas (wards, or village clusters). Appointed chiefs are also recognized as part of governance regime. Courts to apply customary law. Unclear how far members of villages can control decisions affecting their lands. Regulations awaited.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights held in perpetuity principally through inheritance. Precise terms depend upon local customs ('customary law'). Land Act awards ownership to communities, prior to and after registration of their community domains, and ownership is defined as the right to possess, occupy and use in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 2009, s. 4
indicators.additional_info: Definitions in Land Act 2009  s. 4 include: 'Customary land rights means rights conferred by or derived from customs or customary law and practices'; 'customary law' means the conventions and rules which a particular community observed, develops over time and unusually uncodified'. 'Ownership means the right provided by law to possess, occupy and use land in perpetuity' (Land Act, 2009, s. 4).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
