STP.name: Sao Tome and Principe

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land is State, Private  or Reserved. 90% farmland is under absolute private title or usufructs issued for > 2 ha to former workers on 19 nationalized slave-run colonial plantations. Land owner for usufructs is the State. 'Culture' respected in allocating relatives adjacent plots.  Art 42/1991. No provision for spousal, family or communal titles or communal usufructs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2003. Decree-Law No. 32/1988 Establishing State Land Use. Decree Law No. 51/1991 Regulating Distribution of State Agricultural Lands. Law No. 03/1991 on Land Tenure amended 1999.
indicators.additional_info: Sao Tome & Principe were not occupied prior to Portuguese establishment of  sugar (& later, cocoa and coffee) plantations from c. 1500, dependent on slave labour (Gabon, Congo, Angola). Despite 70%  pop. mixed European-African Creole, African origins dominate; eg. Fang from Gabon (10%), others from Angola,  Mozambique, latterly Cabo Verde. Law  4 /1991 limits State Public Land to river banks, unchartered waters, islets, lands reserved for military defence, roads, airports etc. The rest under State as private property and registered usufructs. Const. recognizes public, corporate/private land ownership, & usufructs on public land Art. 9.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No equality between rural usufructs and absolute titles 1991 Art. 12. No legal requirement that usufructs are even registrable (Art. 39).  No provision for communal lands, yet high farmer dependence on forest use (33%) including for grazing. Forests cover 50+ % of the two islands, all state property. Forest Law No 5/2001.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No 03/1991 (1999) on Land Tenure. Regulations by Decree 30/1992 for Distributing Agricultural Lands. Forestry Law No. 5/2001.
indicators.additional_info: Note that cultural origin rather than customary tenure enables family members & relatives to be allocated adjacent farm parcels in rural settlements. "The sale, division or sharing of land acquired under this Statute will always observe correspondence to the unit of culture due to it location and dominant culture..." Art. 42 No. 03/1991.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Usufructs are free and fully accessible to former workers on plantations  (Art. 43 No. 4/1991). The law is opaque as to recordation. No evidence that plots must be mapped. Investors secure lands as concessions (contracts) from the State and, as for titled lands, must be mapped and registered (Art. 39 No. 03/1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 46 and Article 13 of Expropriation Code, No. 32/1978. Decree-Law on Distribution of Agricultural Land No. 51 of 1991. Decree No 30 of 1992.
indicators.additional_info: Allocation of usufructary rights to farm plots on State is free of charge for the benefit of plantation workers (Art. 43 No. 03/1991). Accessible and affordable. Issue of private absolute title for rural lands via mapping & registration is handled by ministries, unlikely to be affordable to majority.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for family, communal or village allocations in usufruct to be made, most evident in issue of rural parcels to individuals only (Art.30 No. 03/1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991 (1999). Decree No. 51 of 1991 Distribution of State Agricultural Land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for local village administration of landholdings. Possible that cultural units in a rural settlement manage land administration but no direction on this in the land law 1991 (1999).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991 (1999).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Private parcels mapped, title and registered are owned in perpetuity. Majority of rural parcels are usufructs rights on state property with uncertain recordation. Indirect guidance that may be inherited (potentially in perpetuity) in reference to culture of those holding allocated plots. Art 31 No. 03/1991 (1999).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law, No. 03 of 1991. Distribution of the State's Agricultural Lands,  No 51 of 1991 and Decree No. 30 of 1992
indicators.additional_info: The term customary is nowhere used in Sao Tome & Principe laws. Cultural identity (country & tribal origin of forebears) is respected in allocation of plots by implication as to whom plots are transferred.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for consent of holder of a usufructary right to a farm parcel. No provision for either family or community tenure or authority over communal lands in the settlement.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991. Distribution of agricultural lands of the State, No. 51 of 1991 and Decree No 30. of 1992.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Planted trees belong to the planter; these are usually shade trees planted by cocoa or coffee farmers. Strong intention in Forest law 2001 to fund and apply farmer reforestation schemes Art.6g, 13k. Forest use permitted eg. forest grazing Art. 73.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law No  05/2001.
indicators.additional_info: All forests are state property. Some areas brought under protection as reserves, such as Decree 08/2023 creating Special Reserves on Sao Tome Island.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource and the Government is obliged to supply good quality water, and ensure the equal and fair distribution of charges and benefits. The law does not state that domestic water is free. Law aims at managed and protecting inland waters, whether superficial, transitional, coastal or groundwater to limit degradation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Framework Law No 07 of 2018.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: All forest belongs to Government No. 05/2001. Agencies to educate communities including need to respect the 15 new Reserves created on Sao Tome Island. Directive to fund & support community reforestation. Art 6 & 13 but no provision for community ownership. Each rural property must set aside 10% land for ecosystem protection Art. 24.2.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law, No 05/2001. Law No. 11/1999 on Flora and Fauna Conservation and Protected Areas. Decree-Law No. 08/2023 Creating Special Reserves on the Island of Sao Tome.
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Law 2001 & Law No. 11/ 1999 on Flora and Fauna Conservation and Protected Areas, and Decree Law No 08/2023 do not enable communities or groups to create Community Forests or manage Protected Areas. All forest belongs to the state. Every rural property to set aside 10% of land as compulsory reserve Art. 24 No. 5/2001. Agencies bound to  educate local communities, including those living next to the 15 Reserves created in 2023 (No. 08/2023).

indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Land is State, Private  or Reserved. 90% farmland is under absolute private title or usufructs issued for > 2 ha to former workers on 19 nationalized slave-run colonial plantations. Land owner for usufructs is the State. 'Culture' respected in allocating relatives adjacent plots.  Art 42/1991. No provision for spousal, family or communal titles or communal usufructs.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2003. Decree-Law No. 32/1988 Establishing State Land Use. Decree Law No. 51/1991 Regulating Distribution of State Agricultural Lands. Law No. 03/1991 on Land Tenure amended 1999.
indicators.additional_info: Sao Tome & Principe were not occupied prior to Portuguese establishment of  sugar (& later, cocoa and coffee) plantations from c. 1500, dependent on slave labour (Gabon, Congo, Angola). Despite 70%  pop. mixed European-African Creole, African origins dominate; eg. Fang from Gabon (10%), others from Angola,  Mozambique, latterly Cabo Verde. Law  4 /1991 limits State Public Land to river banks, unchartered waters, islets, lands reserved for military defence, roads, airports etc. The rest under State as private property and registered usufructs. Const. recognizes public, corporate/private land ownership, & usufructs on public land Art. 9.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No equality between rural usufructs and absolute titles 1991 Art. 12. No legal requirement that usufructs are even registrable (Art. 39).  No provision for communal lands, yet high farmer dependence on forest use (33%) including for grazing. Forests cover 50+ % of the two islands, all state property. Forest Law No 5/2001.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No 03/1991 (1999) on Land Tenure. Regulations by Decree 30/1992 for Distributing Agricultural Lands. Forestry Law No. 5/2001.
indicators.additional_info: Note that cultural origin rather than customary tenure enables family members & relatives to be allocated adjacent farm parcels in rural settlements. "The sale, division or sharing of land acquired under this Statute will always observe correspondence to the unit of culture due to it location and dominant culture..." Art. 42 No. 03/1991.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Usufructs are free and fully accessible to former workers on plantations  (Art. 43 No. 4/1991). The law is opaque as to recordation. No evidence that plots must be mapped. Investors secure lands as concessions (contracts) from the State and, as for titled lands, must be mapped and registered (Art. 39 No. 03/1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 46 and Article 13 of Expropriation Code, No. 32/1978. Decree-Law on Distribution of Agricultural Land No. 51 of 1991. Decree No 30 of 1992.
indicators.additional_info: Allocation of usufructary rights to farm plots on State is free of charge for the benefit of plantation workers (Art. 43 No. 03/1991). Accessible and affordable. Issue of private absolute title for rural lands via mapping & registration is handled by ministries, unlikely to be affordable to majority.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for family, communal or village allocations in usufruct to be made, most evident in issue of rural parcels to individuals only (Art.30 No. 03/1991).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991 (1999). Decree No. 51 of 1991 Distribution of State Agricultural Land.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for local village administration of landholdings. Possible that cultural units in a rural settlement manage land administration but no direction on this in the land law 1991 (1999).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991 (1999).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Private parcels mapped, title and registered are owned in perpetuity. Majority of rural parcels are usufructs rights on state property with uncertain recordation. Indirect guidance that may be inherited (potentially in perpetuity) in reference to culture of those holding allocated plots. Art 31 No. 03/1991 (1999).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law, No. 03 of 1991. Distribution of the State's Agricultural Lands,  No 51 of 1991 and Decree No. 30 of 1992
indicators.additional_info: The term customary is nowhere used in Sao Tome & Principe laws. Cultural identity (country & tribal origin of forebears) is respected in allocation of plots by implication as to whom plots are transferred.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No provision for consent of holder of a usufructary right to a farm parcel. No provision for either family or community tenure or authority over communal lands in the settlement.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Tenure Law No. 03 of 1991. Distribution of agricultural lands of the State, No. 51 of 1991 and Decree No 30. of 1992.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Planted trees belong to the planter; these are usually shade trees planted by cocoa or coffee farmers. Strong intention in Forest law 2001 to fund and apply farmer reforestation schemes Art.6g, 13k. Forest use permitted eg. forest grazing Art. 73.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law No  05/2001.
indicators.additional_info: All forests are state property. Some areas brought under protection as reserves, such as Decree 08/2023 creating Special Reserves on Sao Tome Island.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource and the Government is obliged to supply good quality water, and ensure the equal and fair distribution of charges and benefits. The law does not state that domestic water is free. Law aims at managed and protecting inland waters, whether superficial, transitional, coastal or groundwater to limit degradation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Framework Law No 07 of 2018.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: All forest belongs to Government No. 05/2001. Agencies to educate communities including need to respect the 15 new Reserves created on Sao Tome Island. Directive to fund & support community reforestation. Art 6 & 13 but no provision for community ownership. Each rural property must set aside 10% land for ecosystem protection Art. 24.2.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law, No 05/2001. Law No. 11/1999 on Flora and Fauna Conservation and Protected Areas. Decree-Law No. 08/2023 Creating Special Reserves on the Island of Sao Tome.
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Law 2001 & Law No. 11/ 1999 on Flora and Fauna Conservation and Protected Areas, and Decree Law No 08/2023 do not enable communities or groups to create Community Forests or manage Protected Areas. All forest belongs to the state. Every rural property to set aside 10% of land as compulsory reserve Art. 24 No. 5/2001. Agencies bound to  educate local communities, including those living next to the 15 Reserves created in 2023 (No. 08/2023).

SUR.name: Suriname

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (indigenous peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Suriname does not have a statutory or regulatory framework that recognizes the land rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Suriname; Act relative to land for agricultural use 1936
indicators.additional_info: NOTE: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights recognized the rights of communities in Suriname, but there is no national legislation in place recognizing such rights. Inter-American Court of Human Rights. 2007. Case of Saramaka People v. Suriname. Judgment of November 28. http://www.corteidh.or.cr/docs/casos/articulos/seriec_172_ing.pdf

local_communities_entries.framework: Community forests
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law grants communities rights to "community forests" which are defined as property belonging to many owners that cannot be divided because the forests are supposed to be managed as a whole. However, there are no explicit community rights to other commons aside from forest lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.
indicators.additional_info: Reviewer could not locate a copy of the relevant laws on community forests online, but used the following secondary source: Abrusova, L. et al. (2015). Forest Land Ownership Change in Slovakia. COST Action FACESMAP Country Reports, European Forest Institute Central-East and South-East European Regional Office: Vienna. Available at: https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=1&ved=0ahUKEwiNjZqbuuTNAhXDaz4KHRqFAIcQFggeMAA&url=http%3A%2F%2Ffacesmap.boku.ac.at%2Findex.php%2Flibrary2%2Fdoc_download%2F449-fp1201-country-report-slovakia&usg=AFQjCNHtjRUS-VJhKVXOqltCw5AHQ7hAIQ&sig2=-R8e6KpdVmCvOYJzYFFgOw

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community forests may be expropriated and the legal restrictions on buying or selling forest land do not apply to community forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: In Slovakia, there are two legal main ways in which communities may form community forests: 1) by forming a land association with legal entity and 2) by forming land association without "corporate entity" status. However, it is unclear whether there are provisions on affordability and accessibility.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.
indicators.additional_info: According to Abrusova, L. et al. (2015), "land associations with legal entity are based on the contractual association of physical persons who are the owners of shares of common. These associations are typical corporations with special management bodies established in accordance with the provisions of the Act on Land Associations".

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Owners of community forests are granted legal personality through land associations.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Land associations have are corporate bodies with management bodies that have legal authority over the management of community forests. Land associations without legal personality are based on the free association of physical persons who are owners of shares of common property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.
indicators.additional_info: According to Abrusova, L. et al. (2015), "the central management body of such land association is the plenary assembly of all shareholders. The main executive body of the land association with legal personality is the executive committee lead by the elected chairman as a legal representative of the land association. The supervisory board is the central control body of the land associations which consist of all three bodies...the owners themselves undertake forest management activities. They use the timber either for their own consumption or sell it to the different business entities. The main way by which small private forest owners can be involved in forest management is through participation in joint meeting at which collective decisions are made regarding the exploitation of the timber resources of their forest".

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: There no durational limits on community forest rights established by law, which indicates that rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant community forest owners the right to give consent prior to acquisition by the government or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Community members are the owners of the timber resources located within community forests.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights to water located within community forest areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act, 2004; Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Slovakia; Act on rental of agricultural lands, agricultural enterprises and forest lands; Act No. 180/1995 Coll. on Certain Measures for the Settlement of Ownership Rights to Land; Law on Community Land; Act on Land Associations.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Sami have a recognized right to co-manage land within the Laponia Tjuottjudus (Laponia World Heritage Site). However, Sami land rights are not statutorily recognized outside of the Laponia World Heritage Site.
indicators.law_and_provision: Government of Sweden. 2011. The Laponia Ordinance (Svensk forfattningssamling 2011:840); Management plan for Laponia Tjuottjudus. Available at: http://laponia.nu/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/Laponia-forvaltningsplan-eng-web-150327_2.pdf;Consitution of Sweden; Land Code (SFS 1970:994) 2006
indicators.additional_info: Laponiatjuottjudus is the organization with the  overall management responsibility for the Laponia World Heritage Site which is recognised for both its cultural and natural values (which includes for example four large national parks and four nature reserves). The organisation has been characterised as a co-management regime consisting of members from Sami reindeer herding communities (Swedish: samebyar), municipalities, county administrative boards and the Swedish EPA. Decision-making in Laponiatjuottjudus is based on consensus. NOTE: Article 20 of the Constitution recognizes reindeer husbandry rights of the Sami populations in Sweden. According to a secondary source, "the Swedish State has never acknowledged that Sami own land. The Sami have only, at best, generally customary rights to traditionally use some areas of and (all of the mountain area and some of the winter grazing areas) Borchert, N. Land is Life: Traditional Sami Reindeer Grazing Threatened in Northern Sweden. Available at: https://www.sametinget.se/6816 NOTE ALSO: The Swedish Reindeer Husbandry Act of 1971 and Draft Nordic Sami Convention grant the Sami populations of Sweden year round rights to reindeer herding, grazing, and seasonal usufruct. (The Reindeer Husbandry Act (SFS 1971:437), SOU 2006:14, NJA 2011 s.109; Draft Nordic Sami Convention,)

Decision-making in Laponiatjuottjudus is based on consensus. NOTE: Article 20 of the Constitution recognizes reindeer husbandry rights of the Sami populations in Sweden. According to a secondary source, "the Swedish State has never acknowledged that Sami own land. The Sami have only, at best, generally customary rights to traditionally use some areas of and (all of the mountain area and some of the winter grazing areas) Borchert, N. Land is Life: Traditional Sami Reindeer Grazing Threatened in Northern Sweden. Available at: https://www.sametinget.se/6816 NOTE ALSO: The Swedish Reindeer Husbandry Act of 1971  and Draft Nordic Sami Convention grant the Sami populations of Sweden year round rights to reindeer herding, grazing, and seasonal usufruct. (The Reindeer Husbandry Act (SFS 1971:437), SOU 2006:14, NJA 2011 s.109; Draft Nordic Sami Convention,)

SWZ.name: Swaziland

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary tenure produces lawful property interests over family parcels and commons in 54% of country ('Swazi National Land' (SNL). Absolute titles over rest of country (46%) governed by Roman-Dutch Law. Key limitation is that SNL is vested in the King in trust for the Swazi Nation & his active authority limits local-level decisions and adaptivity of norms.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Arts 39, 59 (6), 115 210-217. Swazi Administration Order 1998. Swazi Courts Act, No. 80 of 1950, The Marriage Act, No. 17 of 1964, The Administration of Estates Act, 1902. The Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act, 1910. The Definition of Swazi Areas Act, 1916.
indicators.additional_info: Constitution, 2005 provides that 'all land including existing concessions, save privately held title deed land ... vests in the King in trust for the Swazi Nation' (Art. 211 (1). These lands (Swazi National Land, SNL) are regulated by custom through  hierarchy of actors from King to hereditary village headmen and area chiefs (Tikhulu), appointed and easily removed by King who enjoys right to issue Orders (Constitution Cht XIV, Art. 10-11 & The Swazi Administration Order, 1998, s. 5, 7, (4), 27 (esp. 27 (bb), 32, and over which the Courts have limited jurisdiction (s. 24). Chief Courts constituted in accordance with customary law hear customary disputes (s. 15 & 20). Written and unwritten customary law is protected by the Constitution (2005, Art. 252 (2), 268); applies so long as consistent with the 'Constitution, natural justice and morality or general principles of humanity' (Art. 252 (3),

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: In theory customary rights in SNL and common law titles ('Title Land')have equal legal force, eg. both referred to as 'property' rights, and individuals paid same compensation as individual titleholders at compulsory acquisition. Equity undermined by lack of provision for customary titling in SNL & right of the King's Land Board to alienate SNL into Title Land including to foreigners.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Art 19 read with art. 39.  Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act, No. 39 of 1910.Definition of Swazi Areas Act, 1916.  Swazi Administrative Order 1998.
indicators.additional_info: Title Land relies on Concession Acts (1904, 1907, Subdivision of Land Act 1957, Survey Act,1961). SNL (customary land) relies on Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act 1910, Definition of Swazi Areas Act 1916, Swazil Administration Order 1998. Within SNL the local chief is bound to ensure every member has enough land for house and farm (Constitution 2005 Art. 211 (2)). Interpretation of 'property' includes customary rights (Art 19, 39). Yet Land Board appointed by and accountable to King and may order takings; SNL area has declined from 63% to 54% since Independence through allocations of private titles as permitted by Const. Art. 212.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary transactions localized, cheap and upheld. No provision for certification of customary rights. No statute governing customary tenure and customary law remains unwritten. National Land Policy 1997-2010 never adopted; proposed hereditary private title (usufruct) and leaseholds,  community lands to be demarcated and gazetted requiring community consent to alienation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act, No. 39 of 1910. Swazi Administrative Order 1998.
indicators.additional_info: Land administration and dispute resolution are executed by headmen and sub-chiefs in the 38 Swazi Land Areas, who do the bidding of the royal hierarchy and government - not as independent as many community members would wish. Striking absence of a statute related to customary norms or their governance in Swazi National Land (SNL), compared to detailed retained colonial legislation providing for the issue of titles, and newer urban law (2004).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: In customary law the community is a de facto legal person in that it can hold land right in common, but such lands are not registrable any more than family/individual homestead parcels are registrable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Acts, 1910,  Definition of Swazi Areas Act, 1916.
indicators.additional_info: 38 discreet Swazi Areas defined in 1917,v sustained, each under a chief, sub-chiefs and hamlet/village headmen. The rest of the country is under leasehold titles ('concessions'), paying rent to the King.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary law is indisputably the source of land tenure and land use rules. But no provision for a community to lease out its land, or to elect a land administration body. This is the prerogative of headmen &  chiefs reporting to the King. Elders advice and community consensus is sought under unwritten customary law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005. Natural Resources Act, No. 71 of 1950, which defines  land, minerals and water as national resources.
indicators.additional_info: Swazi customary law has full legal support and provides for a community-based regime of decision-making except where the King-in-State intervenes directly or through his hierarchy. Assessor has been unable to ascertain how far local custom is fully inclusive of community members or accountable, although by tradition and necessity, consensus is needed to uphold rules. Chief's Courts provide route of appeal.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary law provides for heritable usufructs of male household head, now female household heads included. Assumed that customary rights to the King's land are rights held in perpetuity, transmissible to next generation, but this does not appear in written statute.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Art. 28.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for consent outside of customary law when compulsory acquisition affects customary land (although consultation and consensus normally preferred in customary regimes)  Although the King is  trustee for Swazi Nation, not outright owner, his  prerogative is tangible, most seen in steady alienation of SNL to Title Land for mainly private & commercial purposes, rent paid to King.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005. Acquisition of Property Act, No. 10 of 1961.Natural Resources Act No 71 of 1951.
indicators.additional_info: Note that the Natural Resources Act 1951 does not permit any Swazi lands to be set aside for conservation. The Acquisition of Property Act 1961 refers only to Title Land outside Swazi National Land. Owner may negotiate, (s. 3), public purpose is narrowly defined (s. 2), and increase in value due to purpose to which the property will be put must be considered in calculating compensation (Arts. 15 (1) (b) and 14 (2) (e)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: By customary law trees are attached to the land. The Forest Preservation Act, 1901 defined 'indigenous timber' as any naturally growing trees on Government land or Swazi National Land (customary lands). No cutting without permit.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Swazi Administration Order, 1998, s. 28 (f). Forest Preservation Act, 1910.
indicators.additional_info: King may issue orders prohibiting, restricting or regulating the cutting or destruction of trees (The Swazi Administration Order, No. 6 of 1998, s. 28 ((f)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water is owned by the nation. Free access for domestic purposes. S. 34 of Water Act declares all water found naturally to be a national resource. It is not necessary for any person or community to obtain a permit for the use of water for primary (domestic) purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act, No. 7 of 2003, s. 34.
indicators.additional_info: No private rights of property in any natural water. Primary purposes defined as including water for domestic requirements, sanitation, watering of up to 30 head of cattle, irrigation up to 1/4 ha (s. 2).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Other than provision for sanctuaries to be declared, protection is mainly of species of trees, birds, game (Royal Game), but land owners have strong rights. No Protected Areas on Swazi National Land (customary lands); all on Title Land (under renewable leasseholds or concessions to private busineesses or persons).
indicators.law_and_provision: The Forests Preservation Act, No. 14 of 1910, s. 3 (b). Natural Resources Act, No. 71 of 1951, s. 28. The Game Act 1953 with Amendment Act No 4 of 1991, s. 8, 9, 15 & 21.
indicators.additional_info: Constitutional pledge to protect land, mineral and water resources, flora and fauna (Art. 210) . Game law, natural resources law, national trust law, forest protection law, private forest law & flora law all give landowners privileges such as hunting common game without licences, but directions fall back on The Swazi Administration Order, No. 6 of 1998, s. 28 empowering the King to issue orders on natural resource among many other matters in respect of customarily held land (Swazi National Land).

indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Art 19 read with art. 39.  Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act, No. 39 of 1910.Definition of Swazi Areas Act, 1916.  Swazi Administrative Order 1998.
indicators.additional_info: Title Land relies on Concession Acts (1904, 1907, Subdivision of Land Act 1957, Survey Act,1961). SNL (customary land) relies on Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act 1910, Definition of Swazi Areas Act 1916, Swazil Administration Order 1998. Within SNL the local chief is bound to ensure every member has enough land for house and farm (Constitution 2005 Art. 211 (2)). Interpretation of 'property' includes customary rights (Art 19, 39). Yet Land Board appointed by and accountable to King and may order takings; SNL area has declined from 63% to 54% since Independence through allocations of private titles as permitted by Const. Art. 212.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Customary transactions localized, cheap and upheld. No provision for certification of customary rights. No statute governing customary tenure and customary law remains unwritten. National Land Policy 1997-2010 never adopted; proposed hereditary private title (usufruct) and leaseholds,  community lands to be demarcated and gazetted requiring community consent to alienation.
indicators.law_and_provision: Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Act, No. 39 of 1910. Swazi Administrative Order 1998.
indicators.additional_info: Land administration and dispute resolution are executed by headmen and sub-chiefs in the 38 Swazi Land Areas, who do the bidding of the royal hierarchy and government - not as independent as many community members would wish. Striking absence of a statute related to customary norms or their governance in Swazi National Land (SNL), compared to detailed retained colonial legislation providing for the issue of titles, and newer urban law (2004).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: In customary law the community is a de facto legal person in that it can hold land right in common, but such lands are not registrable any more than family/individual homestead parcels are registrable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Safeguarding of Swazi Areas Acts, 1910,  Definition of Swazi Areas Act, 1916.
indicators.additional_info: 38 discreet Swazi Areas defined in 1917,v sustained, each under a chief, sub-chiefs and hamlet/village headmen. The rest of the country is under leasehold titles ('concessions'), paying rent to the King.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Customary law is indisputably the source of land tenure and land use rules. But no provision for a community to lease out its land, or to elect a land administration body. This is the prerogative of headmen &  chiefs reporting to the King. Elders advice and community consensus is sought under unwritten customary law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005. Natural Resources Act, No. 71 of 1950, which defines  land, minerals and water as national resources.
indicators.additional_info: Swazi customary law has full legal support and provides for a community-based regime of decision-making except where the King-in-State intervenes directly or through his hierarchy. Assessor has been unable to ascertain how far local custom is fully inclusive of community members or accountable, although by tradition and necessity, consensus is needed to uphold rules. Chief's Courts provide route of appeal.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary law provides for heritable usufructs of male household head, now female household heads included. Assumed that customary rights to the King's land are rights held in perpetuity, transmissible to next generation, but this does not appear in written statute.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005, Art. 28.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision for consent outside of customary law when compulsory acquisition affects customary land (although consultation and consensus normally preferred in customary regimes)  Although the King is  trustee for Swazi Nation, not outright owner, his  prerogative is tangible, most seen in steady alienation of SNL to Title Land for mainly private & commercial purposes, rent paid to King.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 2005. Acquisition of Property Act, No. 10 of 1961.Natural Resources Act No 71 of 1951.
indicators.additional_info: Note that the Natural Resources Act 1951 does not permit any Swazi lands to be set aside for conservation. The Acquisition of Property Act 1961 refers only to Title Land outside Swazi National Land. Owner may negotiate, (s. 3), public purpose is narrowly defined (s. 2), and increase in value due to purpose to which the property will be put must be considered in calculating compensation (Arts. 15 (1) (b) and 14 (2) (e)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: By customary law trees are attached to the land. The Forest Preservation Act, 1901 defined 'indigenous timber' as any naturally growing trees on Government land or Swazi National Land (customary lands). No cutting without permit.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Swazi Administration Order, 1998, s. 28 (f). Forest Preservation Act, 1910.
indicators.additional_info: King may issue orders prohibiting, restricting or regulating the cutting or destruction of trees (The Swazi Administration Order, No. 6 of 1998, s. 28 ((f)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water is owned by the nation. Free access for domestic purposes. S. 34 of Water Act declares all water found naturally to be a national resource. It is not necessary for any person or community to obtain a permit for the use of water for primary (domestic) purposes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Act, No. 7 of 2003, s. 34.
indicators.additional_info: No private rights of property in any natural water. Primary purposes defined as including water for domestic requirements, sanitation, watering of up to 30 head of cattle, irrigation up to 1/4 ha (s. 2).

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Other than provision for sanctuaries to be declared, protection is mainly of species of trees, birds, game (Royal Game), but land owners have strong rights. No Protected Areas on Swazi National Land (customary lands); all on Title Land (under renewable leasseholds or concessions to private busineesses or persons).
indicators.law_and_provision: The Forests Preservation Act, No. 14 of 1910, s. 3 (b). Natural Resources Act, No. 71 of 1951, s. 28. The Game Act 1953 with Amendment Act No 4 of 1991, s. 8, 9, 15 & 21.
indicators.additional_info: Constitutional pledge to protect land, mineral and water resources, flora and fauna (Art. 210) . Game law, natural resources law, national trust law, forest protection law, private forest law & flora law all give landowners privileges such as hunting common game without licences, but directions fall back on The Swazi Administration Order, No. 6 of 1998, s. 28 empowering the King to issue orders on natural resource among many other matters in respect of customarily held land (Swazi National Land).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory legal framework does not recognize land rights held by indigenous or local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Syria Nationality law 1969
indicators.additional_info: The nationality of the Syrian Arab Republic shall be considered confirmed for every person enjoying it in accordance with Legislative Decree 67 dated 31 October 1961. The majority of the population in Syria are sunni Muslims, and the minority groups are- Alawis, Druze, Isma'ilis, Christians, Kurds, Circassians, Mandeans, Shiites, Salafis, and Yazidis. They are all citizens but not defined as indigenous communities by law.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory legal framework does not recognize land rights held by indigenous or local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: civil code, law 161/1958
indicators.additional_info: In terms of property and tenure, it is estimated that out of the total Syrian land area (18.5 mill ha) 62 percent (11.5 mill ha) comes under the general term of state land. The remaining 38 percent of the territory, or about 7 million hectares, are privately owned and operated.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory legal framework does not recognize land rights held by indigenous or local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: civil code, law 56/2004
indicators.additional_info: The law regulates investments in farmland by both landowners and farmers. It Reduces the level of protection that the peasantry had hitherto enjoyed in order to encourage private investments, Lays down rules governing the contractual process, And Outlines contractual structures for share-cropping.

indicators.additional_info: The law regulates investments in farmland by both landowners and farmers. indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue

indicators.additional_info: The law regulates investments in farmland by both landowners and farmers. It Reduces the level of protection that the peasantry had hitherto enjoyed in order to encourage private investments, Lays down rules governing the contractual process, And Outlines contractual structures for share-cropping.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory legal framework does not recognize land rights held by indigenous or local communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: civil code law 161/1958
indicators.additional_info: The land reform program was preceded, before the Union, by the Agricultural Relations Law which regulated working conditions between landowners and sharecroppers and agricultural laborers. It stipulated the limits of the landlord’s share of the crop according to the nature of the land. It further prohibited life contracts and required written leases and curtailed the landlord’s right to cancellation. The goal of the reform is to deal with the phenomena that the possession of a large amount of agricultural land by a few people, on the one hand, and the sharing of a small, fragmented farm area by a large number of peasants on the other. This is the reason why the reform prohibit life time contracts.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Maintains more or less the favourable provisions towards landlords.
indicators.additional_info: The law seeks to put an end to manipulations of rents and other problems that have arisen between landlords and tenants.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communal pastures and forests are mainly state controlled
indicators.law_and_provision: Research needs to find the exact law in the civil code
indicators.additional_info: The use of forests is managed by the state with limited rights of use by certain  groups.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Syrian water law does not acknowledge communal ownership and management of water resources.
indicators.law_and_provision: Syrian Water Law
indicators.additional_info: The Syrian water sector is both highly centralized and fragmented between sector institutions that have overlapping functions and responsibilities. A Council of General Commission for Water Resource Management is in charge of integrating water policies between various Ministries.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Syria’s laws do not explicitly uphold community land rights in formally protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: civil code law 12/2012
indicators.additional_info: The law Sets rules for protecting and developing the state of the environment in Syria and entrusts the Ministry of State for Environmental Affairs with these tasks.

TCD.name: Chad

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; an agro-pastoral & fishing code for pastoralists 2018
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: While new land law is on the horizon, 1967 laws remain in force. These sustain colonial rules that property exists only if proven by statutory title and removing the parcel from customary sector which is only occupancy & use on State lands. National Land Policy validated in 2024 is preface to new land law, repeatedly delayed since 2011.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 24/1967 On the Property Regime and Customary Rights. Art. 1, 9, 13, 15. Law 43/2018 Concerning Agro-Pastoral and Fisheries Development. Constitution 2018, Arts 161-166.
indicators.additional_info: Lois 24/1967 state that property and its protection exists only in the form a land title (Art. 1), that unregistered land is 'vacant and without master' (terres sans maîtres). Loi No. 25/1967  sur les limitations des droits fonciers et son décret d’application No. 187/PR du 1er août 1967 confirms that lands subject to customary rights will not be considered owned but may see compensation when needed for public purpose (Art. 24). Law No. 43 of 2018 promises secure tenure for farmers & pastoralists but needs the backing of new land law. Inter-pastoral-farm antagonism complicates content of land law drafts, compounded by changing administrations and civil conflict.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Unequal legal effect of customary and statutory rights in land. The former remains permissive occupancy on State lands, the latter endows maximum security for individual/corporate persons holding titles. Law No 43/ 2018 provides for groups to establish legal entities capable of holding title, but no implementing decree as of 2024.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 24 du 22 juillet 1967 sur le régime de la propriété foncière et des droits coutumiers, Art. 1, 9, 13, 15. Constitution, 2018. Art. 162. Loi No 43 of 2018 art. 61-63.
indicators.additional_info: Plan to recognize customary tenure as per Law No. 43/2018 have no legal backing, but validation of new National Land Policy in 2024 suggests new land bill may appear in 2025. 1967 land laws still in force. Constitution 2018 made no reference to customary rights as property interests.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Individual or communal titling is not available to the customary sector, although those with means may secure private titles, removing the parcel from community land & jurisdiction. Constitution 2018 devolves authority to communes but no law enabling commune or its parts to be mapped & titled. Law No. 24/1967 still in force.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 24 du 22 juillet 1967 sur le régime de la propriété foncière et des droits coutumiers, Art. 1, 13, 20. Constitution 2018, Art. 201.
indicators.additional_info: Art 19 of Loi No. 24 due 22 juillet 1967 provides that collectively used land may be registered when the collective has acquired legal personality. No approved policy or legal commitment yet to collective entitlement.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No group, clan or community is endowed with legal personality. May form and register an association, cooperative or company to hold land on its behalf, not normal practice nor specifically envisaged under National Land Policy 2024. However existing law does permit statutory  entitlement for registered collectives. Law No 24/1967.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 24 du 22 juillet 1967 sur le régime de la propriété foncière et des droits coutumiers, Art. 1, 19.
indicators.additional_info: Art 19 of Loi No. 24 due 22 juillet 1967 provides that collectively used land may be registered when the collective has acquired legal personality.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: In practice all rural communities govern lands under customary norms. Legal support is scant but forthcoming: Constitution 2018 supports customary law & Traditional Authorities & promises law. Law 43/2018 states that cultural rights (sic) may be exercised in communal resource domains, but lacks implementing decrees until present (Mar 2025).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution 2018, Law 43 of 2018 agricultural, pastoral, forest and fisheries management
indicators.additional_info: Law 43/2018: 'Cultural rights may be exercised on cultivable land reserves, fallows, pasture land, rangelands, water areas, community forests and protected areas used regularly by the local community' (Art 62). Constitution 2018 Art. 217-220 states that the Traditional and Customary Authorities are the guarantors of use and custom, and that a law will determine their status and roles (yet to be enacted).Unless codified, customary law cannot apply outside the communities where recognised (Constitution 2018 Art. 161).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Customary use rights owned in perpetuity through transmission to heirs but with limited legal force or protection for as long as classed as occupancy and use rights on state land, able to be cancelled at any time. Law No. 24 and 25 of 1967.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 24 du 22 juillet 1967 sur le régime de la propriété foncière et des droits coutumiers, Art. 1, 9, 13, 15,, 16. Loi portant Limitation aux droits fonciers No. 67-25 du 22 juillet 1967, Art. 16, 24. Ordinance No. 043/PR/2018 of August 31, 2018 on agro-sylvo-pastoral and fisheries orientation.
indicators.additional_info: Although promise of land law change since 2011, progress sullied by contestation as to competing pastoral & farmer rights. Law No. 43/2018 law is vague in its prescriptions and lacks implemented decrees. Nor has potential of individual Communes to map & register lands in autonomous manner, seen implementing decrees.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The right to give or withhold consent is nowhere found in any Chadian laws except for matrimonial and inheritance matters (Constitution Art. 162). Communities vulnerable to losing lands as occupants on State land. Consultation at takings is limited. However, compensation for developments is required and occupants may not be evicted prior to payment. Land Law No. 25/1967.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi 67-25 du 22 juillet 1967, Art. 24. Law on Forestry Wildlife and Fisheries Resources, No. 08-014 of 10 June 2008, Art. 17, 26, 32.
indicators.additional_info: Local participation is favoured in respect of managing forests and wildlife (Law 43/2018 Art. 119), the result of earlier forest policy and law (No. 14 of 2008 and Decree No. 579 2015).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Under customary tenure planted trees are the property of the owner, echoed in forest & wildlife law 2008.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry Wildlife and Fisheries Resources, No. 08-014 of 10 June 2008, Art. 17, 26, 32.
indicators.additional_info: Chad actively supported participatory forest management between 1989-1997 including creating village forest management associations & restocking forests in pilot areas. Did not last. Sacred forests may be managed in accordance with custom (Law, No. 08-014 of 2008, Art. 32). Outside classified forests, traditional use rights incl. domestic logging permitted (Art. 72).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All land and water is state property with free use by lawful occupants and private owners assured for non-commercial use.
indicators.law_and_provision: Loi No. 016/PR/99 Portant Code de l'Eau, Art. 1 & 5.
indicators.additional_info: Water Law of Chad, Loi 016/PR/99 of 2 juillet 1999;  'All resources within the boundaries of the national territory are a public good, inalienable and imprescriptible' (Art. 1). Existing rights of occupation on public domain includes water use rights in accordance with the area occupied, but does not imply ownership (Art. 5). Collection and use of rainwater on property is free (Art. 6). Water from canals, wells, boreholes is subject to regulation (Art. 6). Water security may be jeopardised by absence of clear provision for communal rights.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities cannot own classified areas but these may be classified for their benefit. Traditional use rights for subsistence free of charge and without permits. May also establish Community Forests and Wildlife Management Areas for co-management outside Reserves - even, in theory, be granted title following reforestation and regeneration (Art. 89-90) if form a legal association for this purpose.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Forestry Wildlife and Fisheries Resources, No. 08-014 of 10 June 2008, Art.14, 26 -27, 31-32, 72-77, 89-90.
indicators.additional_info: Provision for communities to secure ownership of forests up to 100 ha if they are reforested - requires registration of legal entity (Art. 89-90, Loi No. 08-014 of 10 June 2008 on Forests, Wildlife and Fisheries). Communities guaranteed free access without permits to protected areas for domestic uses only (Art. 76). State can dedicate a forest to local use, but not ownership. Law makes provision for community forests and wildlife management areas for co-management with communities (no implication of ownership) (Art. 26-28). Only Sacred Forests are 'inviolable and inalienable community property' governed by custom (No. 14-2008, Art. 14, 31-32). No provision for restitution of any other lands to communities.

TGO.name: Togo

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Land & Property Code, 2018 enables individuals, families and groups to secure customary titles over houses & farms as legal ownership. Communal land is vested in communes as land which 'belongs to no one' (Art. 9.16, 9.37). Minimal changes since 1926 colonial law; eg still no provision for villages to own communal forest, pastures, undeveloped lands within its customary domain.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, No. 2018-005 of 14 June 2018.
indicators.additional_info: The 2018 Code brings all aspect of tenure since 1974 under one document with  few changes. All land belongs to the State (Art. 6, 2018). Within this, the National Land Estate comprises "land that cannot be classified either as land held by customary communities and individuals on the basis of a land title or under customary land law, nor of land constituting the public and private domains of the State and local authorities'"(Art. 9.52). Ownership is not lost through non-use, and exists as 'the exclusive and perpetual right to use, enjoy and dispose of things and rights' (Art. 136). Families and lineage groups may register ownership in their name (Art. 252) without forming legal entities.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Registration is either through survey, adjudication &  issue of a Land Title, or registration as owned under customary law. Encouraged but not compulsory (Art. 55). Once registered the customary right "has the value of a private deed ... and valid for as long as the beneficiary or his successors are actually occupying the land" (Art. 633). Not equivalent; Title land may be sold.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1992 (2019). Land and Property Code, No. 2018-005.
indicators.additional_info: A customary land right may be used as security for the granting of land loans (Art. 627). However, commons/communal lands still cannot be directly owned by the village/hamlet community, but by the local government authority (Commune).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The procedure for securing customary rights is straightforward and cost-effective. However, these rights are limited to homesteads and farmlands. Land registration by farmers remains reputedly low. Land governance is in practice by local headmen.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, 2018.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: A family or lineage may secure customary deed of ownership in its own name. However, no legal provision for a village or a group of villages to secure title over communal lands. May register a  Land Associations as a syndicate of private parcels seeking to pool their lands, such as for restoring the land,  developing roads or other works (2018, Art. 98-100).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code 2018, Sub-title 7: Land Associations, Art. 96 ff.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Each village may govern its local land relations under customary law, as led by chief/headman. The Constitution recognizes the traditional chiefdom as guardian of use and customs (Art. 143). The 2018 law aims to institute a consultative Commission in each commune, with branches called Village Land Management Sections (Art. 29-31) not yet established.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code 2018 Art. 29-31
indicators.additional_info: A custom is defined as a rule resulting from prolonged usage and the belief in the existence of sanction for failure to observe this usage (2018 Code, Art. 9.45).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary law establishes occupancy and use rights as inheritable, and thus held in perpetuity. This is sustained in the 2018 law for voluntary registration of family homes & farms. Art. 627-628, Art. 640. "The title thus obtained ... is valid for as long as the beneficiary or his successors are actually  occupying the land" (2018, Art. 633).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code Law No. 2018-005, Title 8; Articles 624-663.
indicators.additional_info: Provisions for customary land tenure are addressed in the Land and Property Code under Title 8. The notion of 'vacant land' still appears  does not refer to unregistered land but to communal lands. The difference between registered & unregistered customary lands clear in Art 644 and 645. Art. 644: "Owners of rural land under customary tenure exercise all the prerogatives attached to their ownership rights over their land". Art. 645: "Holders of a right to use rural land under customary land tenure exercise all the prerogatives attached to their rights over this land, so long as their rights are not contested ...". Deeds endow ownership; lack of deeds endow use rights.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No provision found requiring the consent of an individual, family or group at compulsory acquisition of their land. However, improved process including 'amicable transfers' referring to right to negotiate compensation (Art. 370-372) and equivalent compensation by area for lands under customary and title deeds (Art 646-647). .
indicators.law_and_provision: Land and Property Code, 2018, Arts. 370-389
indicators.additional_info: "No one must be forced to surrender customary land tenure, except for the implementation of development policies or in the public interest, and in all cases subject to fair and prior compensation" Art. 646. "For an equal surface area, the compensation due in accordance with the previous  article is equal to that due in the event of expropriation of a property registered in the land register, except where the registration costs are deducted" Art. 647.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Forest Code defines rights of access and use of trees and products as the same for individuals and 'natural' or 'grassroot groupings' (villages) (2008, Art. 25). This does not explicitly indicate if the customary holder owns both planted and natural trees on the land, although this will be almost always assumed to be the case under customary law.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forestry Code, Law No. 2008-09 .

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public asset (Water Code, 2010, Art. 5). A Free Use Regime is applied for all domestic uses, without need for its use to be exercised by declaration, authorization of concession regimes (Art. 12). The Code aims for water management to be as localized to villages and communes.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code No. 2010-004 of 14 June 2010.
indicators.additional_info: The Free Use Regime applies to use of water for domestic purposes, limited to needs of individuals and the family within dwellings, and for persons and for domestic animals, the watering of gardens, and provided extracted water does not exceed thresholds.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: All National Protected Areas  (PA) belong to the State. Communities may own forests outside PA.  As forest belongs to the state, the forest is 'allocated' to the community even though it is within its communal domain. Order of 13 June 2016 defines procedure for declaring & managing Community Forests on customary lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Code, No 9 of 2008. Order Defining the Procedure for Allocating and Managing Community Forests in Togo, 13 June 2016.
indicators.additional_info: To secure a Community Forest, the community or other group must establish a management entity, such as a Village Association or Village Development Committee (2008, Art. 6). A map & management charter (plan) is agreed for preliminary period, renewable for 15 years (Arts. 10-12). The plan details traditional use rights of forest dwellers, the management regime, distribution of income from forestry operations (Art. 20). Rules of access & use approved by all members of the community for managing the resource. Ownership can result: "Reforested land or land with natural afforestation, recognized as the property of individuals, community organizations and cooperatives, comes under the private estate of these individuals, community organizations and cooperatives" (2018 Land Code, Art. 581).
