However, these rights are limited to homesteads and farmlands. Land registration by farmers remains reputedly low. Land governance is in practice by local headmen. (Land and Property Code, 2018.)
TGO.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: Partial, limited progress — A family or lineage may secure customary deed of ownership in its own name. However, no legal provision for a village or a group of villages to secure title over communal lands. May register a  Land Associations as a syndicate of private parcels seeking to pool their lands, such as for restoring the land,  developing roads or other works (2018, Art. 98-100). (Land and Property Code 2018, Sub-title 7: Land Associations, Art. 96 ff.  )
TGO.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Each village may govern its local land relations under customary law, as led by chief/headman. The Constitution recognizes the traditional chiefdom as guardian of use and customs (Art. 143). The 2018 law aims to institute a consultative Commission in each commune, with branches called Village Land Management Sections (Art. 29-31) not yet established.  (Land and Property Code 2018 Art. 29-31)
TGO.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — Customary law establishes occupancy and use rights as inheritable, and thus held in perpetuity. This is sustained in the 2018 law for voluntary registration of family homes & farms. Art. 627-628, Art. 640. "The title thus obtained ... is valid for as long as the beneficiary or his successors are actually  occupying the land" (2018, Art. 633).  (Land and Property Code Law No. 2018-005, Title 8; Articles 624-663. )
TGO.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: Partial, limited progress — No provision found requiring the consent of an individual, family or group at compulsory acquisition of their land. However, improved process including 'amicable transfers' referring to right to negotiate compensation (Art. 370-372) and equivalent compensation by area for lands under customary and title deeds (Art 646-647). . (Land and Property Code, 2018, Arts. 370-389)
TGO.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — The Forest Code defines rights of access and use of trees and products as the same for individuals and 'natural' or 'grassroot groupings' (villages) (2008, Art. 25). This does not explicitly indicate if the customary holder owns both planted and natural trees on the land, although this will be almost always assumed to be the case under customary law.  (Forestry Code, Law No. 2008-09 . )
TGO.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water is a public asset (Water Code, 2010, Art. 5). A Free Use Regime is applied for all domestic uses, without need for its use to be exercised by declaration, authorization of concession regimes (Art. 12). The Code aims for water management to be as localized to villages and communes.  (Water Code No. 2010-004 of 14 June 2010. )
TGO.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress —  All National Protected Areas  (PA) belong to the State. Communities may own forests outside PA.  As forest belongs to the state, the forest is 'allocated' to the community even though it is within its communal domain. Order of 13 June 2016 defines procedure for declaring & managing Community Forests on customary lands.  (Forest Code, No 9 of 2008. Order Defining the Procedure for Allocating and Managing Community Forests in Togo, 13 June 2016. )

THA.name: Thailand

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities (indigenous and non-indigenous)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution establishes that communities shall have the right to participate in the management, maintenance and exploitation of natural resources. Community Land Use Permits granted since 2011, but no community ownership rights are granted.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 67, Constitution of Thailand (2007); Regulation of the Prime Minister's Office on the Issuance of Community Land Title Deeds, 2010; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf
indicators.additional_info: Thailand has not enacted legislation that implements Article 67 of the Constitution and recognizes indigenous community rights, but not ownership rights to land. The Office of the Prime Minister passed a regulation in 2011, which grants indigenous communities the rights the right to manage and use state-owned land for their living.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Since communities can only manage and use state-owned land under a "Community Land Use Permit", community land rights do not receive the same level of protection as rights acquired under freehold tenure.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Use Permit Regulation; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf
indicators.additional_info: Communities cannot alienate their land rights under a community land use permit. There are also durational limits on permits which are decided by the Government on a case-by-case basis.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Regulation allows for communities to formally register their customary land use permits, but it is unclear whether a detailed and georeferenced map of communal property is provided. Also unclear if procedures are affordable or accessible.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Use Permit Regulation; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Regulation grants indigenous communities temporary use rights, similar to leaseholds. However, the law does not establish the indigenous communities as legal persons for the purposes of ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Use Permit Regulation; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Indigenous communities with community land use permits can only collectively manage and use state-owned land. The government retains legal authority over the land permitted to communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Use Permit Regulation; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The indigenous community has to renew its Community Land Use Permit periodically within a time decided on a case-by-case basis by the government.
indicators.law_and_provision: Community Land Use Permit Regulation; http://www.rightsandresources.org/documents/files/doc_4693.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Immovable Property Expropriation Act does not require the government to consult or obtain consent from indigenous groups/communities prior to acquiring land in a compulsory manner.
indicators.law_and_provision: Immovable Property Expropriation Act (1987)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Constitution grants all citizens the rights to use natural resources (Art. 25, Constitution). The National Reserved Forests Act; the Forest Act;  the National Parks Act do not grant communities rights to trees.
indicators.law_and_provision: The National Reserved Forest Act, B.E. 2507 (1964); Forest Act 1941; The National Parks Act 1961

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Constitution of Thailand grants all citizens the rights to use natural resources (Art. 25).   Therefore, communities, as citizens have a rights to use water. Since communities are only granted Community Land Use Permits to forest areas, it can be implied that community water rights are limited to such areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 25, Constitution of Thailand; Art. 1339 of the Civil and Commercial Code
indicators.additional_info: Article 1139 of the Civil and Commercial Code provides that "the owner of a piece of land is bound to take the water that flows naturally on to it from higher land. Water that flows naturally on to lower land and is necessary to such land may be retained by the owner of the higher land only to such extent as is indispensable to his land." However, communities are not granted land ownership rights in Thailand. The Constitution establishes that communities shall have the right to participate in the management, maintenance and exploitation of natural resources. Community Land Use Permits granted since 2011, but no community ownership rights are granted

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The National Reserved Forests Act and the National Parks Act do not explicitly grant indigenous communities rights in Protected Areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: The National Reserved Forest Act, B.E. 2507 (1964); The National Parks Act 1961

local_communities_entries.framework: Pasture User Unions
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Pastures are state property in Tajikistan. However, local communities can obtain rights to use pastures under short-term leases if the community obtains a certificate signifying the Pasture User Union is registered.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 14 of the Law on Pasture Unions provides " 1. The right to use pastures occurs if the certificate for the right to use land or lease. 2. Certificate of land use right shall be issued on the pastures natural and legal persons, taking into account the type of livestock and livestock at their disposal, and further development of the industry, in the manner prescribed by the Land Code of the Republic of Tajikistan." Article 3 of the Law on Pasture Unions defines "Pasture users" as "individuals and legal entities having the right to use the pastures" and "User community pastures" as a body of public initiative created by users pasture for joint use of pastures in accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Tajikistan. Article 8 of the Law establishes the following types of pastures: "1. Pastures, depending on the purpose, are divided into the following types: Pasture area cities, districts and towns; Areas provided for the roads of livestock; Reserve pasture areas. 2. Depending on the application season, pastures are divided into the following types: Winter pastures; Summer pastures.3. Depending on the location, pastures are divided into the following types Pastures located in the valleys; Foothill grassland areas; Mountain pasture zones; Alpine pasture areas."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Community use rights to pastures are not as protected as full ownership rights. The government retains broad authority may terminate the leases granted to Pasture User Unions early.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 20 provides that the "Grounds for termination of the right to use pasture: 1 the right to use pasture terminated at the expiry of the contract or a certificate for the right to land. 2. The grounds for early termination or suspension of the right to use the pastures are: voluntary renunciation of the right to use pasture pastures; regular non-observance of the established rules pasture  use; emergencies on the basis of the opinion of the commission for emergency situations; non-use of pastures in the specified term of the contract

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The procedures for establishing Pastures User Unions and obtaining a certificate are vague. There are no clear provisions ensuring registration is accessible and affordable.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: After local communities apply for a certificate to use pasture land as a Pasture User Union, the government develops medium-term and annual plans for the use of pastures. Article 17 states "In the medium-term and annual plans for the use of pastures included: Maps that defined the boundaries of pastures, derived from the use and protected areas, grazing lands of the forest fund land fund of the state reserve, underpasses roads, watering and other infrastructure pasture condition and quality of all areas of pasture; Requirements for the optimal loading of pastures; Development plans and restoration of pastures; Requirements for the use of pastures, including the seasonal use of pastures and rotation measures to improve grazing conditions, the conservation of biological diversity and to prevent the degradation of vegetation, soil erosion and damage to watersheds; Plan for pasture use for other purposes". The lease granted to Pasture User Unions contains - Conditions for the use of pastures; land area, location, borders and infrastructure facilities pastures; Term use of pastures; Payment of the sum for the use of pastures; The rights and obligations of the parties and other information (Art. 18).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Law on Pastures recognizes the legal personality of Pasture User Unions, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 20(4) provides "In case of disagreement with the decision of pasture on early termination of its right to use the pasture, it can in the legislation of the Republic of Tajikistan apply to the relevant authority or court."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Local government authorities retain broad authority over pastures, including developing management and use plans which local communities (Pasture User Unions) must follow.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 11 of the Law on Pastures provides that the powers of local governments include: Approval of the medium-term management plan for pasture and their use, and control of its implementation; - The establishment in the prescribed manner fund the development of local public authority pastures and establish procedures for its use;- Control of land and water areas provided for the pastures, in order to ensure environmental safety, protection of historical monuments and objects of cultural heritage; - Consideration of requests and proposals of the towns and villages self-management and use of pastures; - The establishment of commissions for the regulation of the use of pastures; Ensuring compliance with state standards and procedures of monitoring and evaluation of the state of pasture quality; - Consideration of other issues pasture use within its powers in accordance with the normative legal acts of the Republic of Tajikistan". Article 12 of the Law on Pastures provides "the powers of self-government of settlements and villages in the area of pasture management and use. The powers of self-government bodies of settlements and villages in the area of pasture management and use includes: acceptance of direct involvement in the regulation of relations connected with the use of pastures; making the list of livestock and pasture their livestock by type of farming in the book; representation in the Commission on regulation of use of pastures; The submission of requests to the appropriate authorities on the allocation of grazing land; Promote the establishment of community pasture; Participation in the management of pastures within its powers; Consideration of other issues related to the use of pasture, within their powers".

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Pastures establishes that the use rights granted to Pasture User Unions have durational limits.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Tajikistan; Law on Pastures, 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 17 states ""the use of pastures is carried out on the basis of medium-term and annual plans for the use of pastures"". Article 20 states ""The right to use pasture terminated at the expiration of the contract or a certificate for the right to land"".

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant local communities the right to give consent prior to acquisition by the government and outsiders.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Turkmenistan's statutory laws are silent on whether communities have legal rights to land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Turkmenistan; Land Code, 2004; Law "On state registration of rights to immovable property and transactions related thereto" 2014; Law on Peasant Associations 1995
indicators.additional_info: Article 9 of the Constitution provides "The property is inviolable. Turkmenistan approves the right to private ownership of the means of production, land and other material and intellectual values. They can also belong to the associations of citizens and the state. The law establishes objects that are exclusive property of the state. The state guarantees equal protection and creation of equal conditions for development of all forms of ownership." Article 1 of the Land Code, 2004 provides that Land in Turkmenistan is the property of the Turkmen people, it is under the protection of the state. Article 16 of the Land Code provides that individuals can own and use property, but there is no explicit mention of community land rights. NOTE: In practice, peasant associations allocate rights to shepherds to use pastures. Thus, some communities have de facto property rights in Turkmenistan (Behnke, R., A. Jabbar, A. Budanov, and G. Davidson 2005. The administration and practice of leasehold pastoralism in Turkmenistan. Nomadic Peoples, 9, 147-169)

indicators.comment: Article 3 of the Water Code provides that all water bodies, including rivers, reservoirs, lakes, inter-farm canals and drainage collectors, ground water, as well as surface waters and water courses are property of the State. Article 4 indicates that ownership of water in Turkmenistan are exclusively held by the State. Individuals are granted rights to use water for drinking and household needs (Arts. 16-17, and 21 of the Water Code). Thus, communities, as citizens, can use water for domestic purposes.

indicators.additional_info:

They can also belong to the associations of citizens and the state. The law establishes objects that are exclusive property of the state. The state guarantees equal protection and creation of equal conditions for development of all forms of ownership." Article 1 of the Land Code, 2004 provides that Land in Turkmenistan is the property of the Turkmen people, it is under the protection of the state. Article 16 of the Land Code provides that individuals can own and use property, but there is no explicit mention of community land rights. indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 3 of the Water Code provides that all water bodies, including rivers, reservoirs, lakes, inter-farm canals and drainage collectors, ground water, as well as surface waters and water courses are property of the State. Article 4 indicates that ownership of water in Turkmenistan are exclusively held by the State. Individuals are granted rights to use water for drinking and household needs (Arts. 16-17, and 21 of the Water Code). Thus, communities, as citizens, can use water for domestic purposes.

TLS.name: East Timor

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (indigenous peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Bernardo Almeida, PhD Candidate, Leiden University, The Netherlands

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law establishes that 'community property is the land that it is used in common by a community, according to their customary practices'. There is no restriction to the type of property that can be owned by a community.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code)
indicators.additional_info: Despite recognizing community property, the details of this type of property are not regulated in any legislation. The Constitution of 2002 recognizes customary practices, if not contrary to its provisions (art. 2.4). There is no other regulation regarding customary practices.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law does not  regulate how community property is acquired and which protection is given to this type of land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code)
indicators.additional_info: The lack of any detailed regulation regarding community land leaves communities in a very fragile position. It is not clear whether communities can simply invoke their land rights or if any kind of registration is needed. The lack of regulation regarding the legal personality of communities further complicates their position. Practice reflects the lack of guidance in the law (e.g., in land acquisition processes by the state sometimes compensation includes the value of the land, other times only the value of crops).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law allows land registration, but only for individuals or groups of determined individuals. Families, groups, or communities can claim land, but there is no mechanism for registration of land in the name of that family, group or community.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 2 (a) and 8 of Decree-Law 27/2011 that allows the registration of undisputed parcels. Art. 1 (b) of Ministerial Decree 23/2011.
indicators.additional_info: Groups, families and communities are not recognized as legal entities.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no provision recognizing families, groups and communities as legal persons, and no mechanisms to form legal entities.
indicators.law_and_provision: N/A
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution establishes that '[o]nly national citizens can own land in Timor-Leste'. If literally interpreted, this provision excludes legal persons of owning land, because such entities are not per se citizens (e.g., communities, companies, associations). Such debate remains unclear in the Timorese legal system.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: There is no specific provision regarding the authority of communities over their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: N/A
indicators.additional_info: It can be argued that once considered the owner, the community has full authority over the land, as any other owner (cf. Art. 1225 of the Civil Code). However, the lack of a mechanism to give a legal status to communities makes their right over property in practice inapplicable.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The legislation does not specify the duration of the community rights, but it is implicit in the Civil Code.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code). Art. 1227 of the Civil Code a contrario.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not provide any ruling regarding consultation or consent of a community in case of a land acquisition process. The law does not stipulate consultation, consent or procedure for appeal in case of compulsory acquisition.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code)
indicators.additional_info: Article 54.3 of the Timorese Constitution establishes the limits of expropriation: (1) public purpose; (2) fair compensation; and (3) following the procedure established in law. However, an expropriation law has yet not been approved, leaving a gap in the land acquisition process.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law makes no reference about the property of the trees in community land. According to the Civil Code, the trees attached to the ground are considered part of the land. The Civil Code establishes the right of the owner of the land to plant trees, if not contrary to any other legislation (e.g., land use and environmental legislation).
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 195.1 (c) of the Civil Code. Art. 1286.1 of the Civil Code.
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution establishes that all natural resources vital to the economy are property of the state (Art. 139.1). This vague provision is at times used by state officials to claim ownership of natural resource, such as trees. Customary practices in several areas of the country separate the ownership of trees from the ownership of land, contradicting the ruling of the Civil Code.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law creates the category of 'community water', but gives no definition. The law leaves the regulation of community water to customary practices.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 1305 of the Civil Code.
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution establishes that all natural resources vital to the economy are property of the state (Art. 139.1). This vague provision is at times used by state officials to claim ownership of natural resources, such as water. The Civil Code divides water into three categories: (1) Public, (2) community, (3) private. Only private water is further regulated by the Civil Code, the types of water remain unregulated.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law explicitly allows for communal ownership of protected areas that are not considered part of the public domain of the state. However, the national legislation still misses a clear definition of public domain of the state. Furthermore, the classification as protected area gives the state the right to expropriate the areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 2.3 and 2.4 of UNTAET Regulation 2000/19. Art. 1(c) of Decree-Law 26/2012 establishing the Bases for the Environmental Legal framework. Government Regulation 8/2007 creates the Nino Konis Santana National Park. Government Resolution 38/2015 creates the Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão National Park.
indicators.additional_info: The UNTAET Regulation 2000/19 regarding protected areas was repealed by Decree-Law 5/2016. Currently there are two national parks: (1) the Nino Konis Santana National Park (Government Regulation 8/2007); (2) the Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão National Park (Government Resolution 38/2015).

TLS.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — The law allows land registration, but only for individuals or groups of determined individuals. Families, groups, or communities can claim land, but there is no mechanism for registration of land in the name of that family, group or community.  (Art. 2 (a) and 8 of Decree-Law 27/2011 that allows the registration of undisputed parcels. Art. 1 (b) of Ministerial Decree 23/2011.)
TLS.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — There is no provision recognizing families, groups and communities as legal persons, and no mechanisms to form legal entities. (N/A)
TLS.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: No, the law does not address the issue — There is no specific provision regarding the authority of communities over their land. (N/A)
TLS.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Partial, significant progress — The legislation does not specify the duration of the community rights, but it is implicit in the Civil Code. (Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code). Art. 1227 of the Civil Code a contrario.)
TLS.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — The law does not provide any ruling regarding consultation or consent of a community in case of a land acquisition process. The law does not stipulate consultation, consent or procedure for appeal in case of compulsory acquisition. (Art. 4 of Law 10/2011 (which approves the Civil Code))
TLS.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — The law makes no reference about the property of the trees in community land. According to the Civil Code, the trees attached to the ground are considered part of the land. The Civil Code establishes the right of the owner of the land to plant trees, if not contrary to any other legislation (e.g., land use and environmental legislation).  (Art. 195.1 (c) of the Civil Code. Art. 1286.1 of the Civil Code.)
TLS.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — The law creates the category of 'community water', but gives no definition. The law leaves the regulation of community water to customary practices. (Art. 1305 of the Civil Code.)
TLS.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress — The law explicitly allows for communal ownership of protected areas that are not considered part of the public domain of the state. However, the national legislation still misses a clear definition of public domain of the state. Furthermore, the classification as protected area gives the state the right to expropriate the areas.  (Arts. 2.3 and 2.4 of UNTAET Regulation 2000/19. Art. 1(c) of Decree-Law 26/2012 establishing the Bases for the Environmental Legal framework. Government Regulation 8/2007 creates the Nino Konis Santana National Park. Government Resolution 38/2015 creates the Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão National Park.)

TUN.name: Tunisia

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.language: English translation of Arabic and French
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Tunisia has recognized collective tribal or community lands since 1901 under French law. These remain lawful property. Decline in area due to promoted privatization since 1956 & increase in settled agro-pastoralism by nomads 4.0 Mha in 1964 to 1.35Mha in 2024. Possession Certificates issued to families & cooperatives also often remain under community jurisdiction.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2021 modifying and supplementing Law No. 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Governing Collective Landholdings.
indicators.additional_info: The community is a legal person for purposes of property holding & 1964 law recognizes community ownership.  Law No. 59-83 of 1959 enabled title for cultivated lands and houses instead customary usufructs on community's land. Members still share grazing lands. Law of 2016 sustains pressure to privatize holdings except for grazing lands. Art.1 of 2016 law rejects applications for new collective lands.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Inequality of collective & private ownership although in principle equally protected as lawful properties (Const. 2022 Art 29). 1964 law placed community lands under state control for first time. Privatization of homesteads & farms favoured & compulsory under 2016 law. Grazing lands remain collective, recorded, but no collective title issued.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Governing Collective Landholdings. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2021 modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28 above. National Constitution, 2022.
indicators.additional_info: The 2016 amendments to the 1964 law on collective lands includes coercion to subdivide all but grazing commons within the community domain. The new Art. 15 also excludes from community's lands: (i) state owned land; (ii) land for which title deeds have been duly established; (iii)  land developed by occupants over last decade, except unlawfully encroached grazing lands; (iv) declared cadastral (titling) zones; and (v) land under public irrigation schemes.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No information as to costs of survey-based titling but likely to  subsidized given priority objective to bring all farmed land within collective domains under private title. Grazing lands are delimited and recorded in the process as communal, but without title.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 16 of 32 November 1957. Law No. 59-83 of 21 July 1959. Law No. 71-1 of 14 January 1971. Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 85-5 of 8 February 1988. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2016.
indicators.additional_info: Laws since 1957 have been focused on privatization of homesteads and farmed lands within collective properties, sped up by 1988 and 2016 laws.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The tribe or community is a legal person; routinely registered in its own name where community lands were delimited over last century, progressively shrunk to communal grazing reserves as subdivision and titling of collective farmed lands is undertaken. Records maintained by Regional Trusteeship Council, copy sent to Local Management Council (2016, Art. 15).
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964, Law 2016-69 Modifying and Supplementing Law 64-28 Governing Collective Landholdings
indicators.additional_info: Strong trend, coerced or voluntary, of sedentized agro-pastoralism in central & south Tunisia. "In the case of lands reserved for grazing, communal enjoyment will be exercises by members of the community" (2016, Art 16c).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Local Management Councils are elected & empowered as local land administrators.  However, strong supervisory and final authority by Regional Trusteeship Councils.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Law 2016-69 Modifying and Supplementing Law 64-28 Governing Collective Landholdings

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: No indication that customary rights within the tribal/community domain are not rights held in perpetuity, as are rights under cadastral titles and rights under deeds of transfer increasing being converted into title deeds.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August  modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: No evidence of consent required, although consultation with communities/tribes clearly exists via duties of Local and Regional Trusteeship Councils.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: No provision found as to tree ownership in the forest law 1988 (2005). Law authorizes forest use for domestic purposes free of charge (Art.36). Includes access & use of State Forests for citizens living within  5 km radius, provided they have prior authorization (Art. 38). Public is free to pick mushrooms, moss, wildlife flowers, capers, myrtle, berries etc (Art. 39).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law No. 88-20 of 13 April 1988. Law No. 2005-13 of 26 January 2005 amending and supplementing the Forestry Code. Law No. 2009-59 of 20 July 2009 Simplifying Administrative Procedures in the Agricultural and Fisheries sector. Decree No. 2010-1970  Relating to the Organization of the Hunting Season 2010/2011.
indicators.additional_info: Grazing rights are treated under the Forest Law 1988 & Law 2009. Stock may be grazed in State Forests in times of drought and fire, on payment of fees  set by Decree (Art. 63). Hunting of wildlife is regulated by Forest Law 1988,  Decrees issued annually on hunting season for each major species of wild animal and birds, with procedures for securing licences. A Pastoral Code in draft for a decade, aims to fill gaps in other laws.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is a public resource controlled by Government (Art 1 Water Code 1975). While inalienable and imprescriptible (Art. 3), rights to water may be acquired, including by communities. For this they must form Water User Associations granted status  legal persons (Art.154.4).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code, No. 75-16 of March 31 1975, as amended.
indicators.additional_info: Water from all sources is a public resource regulated and controlled by Government (Art. 1  Water Code 1975). The Ministry of Agriculture administered water (Art. 4).  Private rights may be acquired (Art.2). Existing water property rights, particular in the Southern Oases are converted into water use rights covering the same volume of water (Art. 21). All owner have the right to use and dispose of rainwater that falls on their land (Art. 33). Communities and other interest groups may form Water User Associations for irrigation, operating drinking water systems (Art. 154). These shall be for collective interest.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Private & community forests may exist on private & collective lands, not in State Protected Areas, but within which grazing areas opened for communities during droughts (Art 35-38). Communities may register Forestry Associations  to protect forest, wildlife rich areas, dunes, or wetlands on their lands, the Association treated as a legal person  (Art. 43).
indicators.law_and_provision: Forest Law No. 88-20 of 13 April 1988. Law No. 2005-13 of 26 January 2005 amending and supplementing the Forestry Code.  Law No. 2009-59 of 20 July 2009 Simplifying Administrative Procedures in the Agricultural and Fisheries sector.
indicators.additional_info: The 'legitimate interest' of citizens are to be taken into account in State land, including provision for grazing areas (Art. 16). Use rights including collecting brush, dead trees, water, and grazing rights are free of charge (but not for camels) (Art. 36). Communities within 5 km of a forest may use all resource lands in the state domain excepting  in National Parks, Nature Reserves and Recreational Forests. These cover 8% of Tunisia (2023) as 148 Terrestrial Protected Areas including 40 Ramsar wetlands. Tunisia's forest law is explicit that land ownership does not define rights of use, determined by the regulations in each Governorate; may differ for state, private and collective lands.

Possession Certificates issued to families & cooperatives also often remain under community jurisdiction. (Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2021 modifying and supplementing Law No. 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Governing Collective Landholdings.)
TUN.Communities Q2: Does the law give indige: Partial, significant progress — Inequality of collective & private ownership although in principle equally protected as lawful properties (Const. 2022 Art 29). 1964 law placed community lands under state control for first time. Privatization of homesteads & farms favoured & compulsory under 2016 law. Grazing lands remain collective, recorded, but no collective title issued. (Law No. 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Governing Collective Landholdings. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2021 modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28 above. National Constitution, 2022.)
TUN.Communities Q3: Does the law require the: Partial, significant progress — No information as to costs of survey-based titling but likely to  subsidized given priority objective to bring all farmed land within collective domains under private title. Grazing lands are delimited and recorded in the process as communal, but without title. (Law No. 16 of 32 November 1957. Law No. 59-83 of 21 July 1959. Law No. 71-1 of 14 January 1971. Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 85-5 of 8 February 1988. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August 2016.)
TUN.Communities Q4: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — The tribe or community is a legal person; routinely registered in its own name where community lands were delimited over last century, progressively shrunk to communal grazing reserves as subdivision and titling of collective farmed lands is undertaken. Records maintained by Regional Trusteeship Council, copy sent to Local Management Council (2016, Art. 15).  (Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964, Law 2016-69 Modifying and Supplementing Law 64-28 Governing Collective Landholdings )
TUN.Communities Q5: Does the law recognize t: Partial, significant progress — Local Management Councils are elected & empowered as local land administrators.  However, strong supervisory and final authority by Regional Trusteeship Councils.  (Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964 Law 2016-69 Modifying and Supplementing Law 64-28 Governing Collective Landholdings )
TUN.Communities Q6: Do the law and formal ti: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully — No indication that customary rights within the tribal/community domain are not rights held in perpetuity, as are rights under cadastral titles and rights under deeds of transfer increasing being converted into title deeds. (Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August  modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28. )
TUN.Communities Q7: Does the law require the: No, the law does not address the issue — No evidence of consent required, although consultation with communities/tribes clearly exists via duties of Local and Regional Trusteeship Councils.  (Law 64-28 of 4 June 1964. Law No. 2016-69 of 10 August modifying and supplementing Law No 64-28.)
TUN.Communities Q8: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — No provision found as to tree ownership in the forest law 1988 (2005). Law authorizes forest use for domestic purposes free of charge (Art.36). Includes access & use of State Forests for citizens living within  5 km radius, provided they have prior authorization (Art. 38). Public is free to pick mushrooms, moss, wildlife flowers, capers, myrtle, berries etc (Art. 39). (Forest Law No. 88-20 of 13 April 1988. Law No. 2005-13 of 26 January 2005 amending and supplementing the Forestry Code. Law No. 2009-59 of 20 July 2009 Simplifying Administrative Procedures in the Agricultural and Fisheries sector. Decree No. 2010-1970  Relating to the Organization of the Hunting Season 2010/2011. )
TUN.Communities Q9: Does the law explicitly: Partial, significant progress — Water is a public resource controlled by Government (Art 1 Water Code 1975). While inalienable and imprescriptible (Art. 3), rights to water may be acquired, including by communities. For this they must form Water User Associations granted status  legal persons (Art.154.4).  (Water Code, No. 75-16 of March 31 1975, as amended. )
TUN.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: Partial, significant progress — Private & community forests may exist on private & collective lands, not in State Protected Areas, but within which grazing areas opened for communities during droughts (Art 35-38). Communities may register Forestry Associations  to protect forest, wildlife rich areas, dunes, or wetlands on their lands, the Association treated as a legal person  (Art. 43). (Forest Law No. 88-20 of 13 April 1988. Law No. 2005-13 of 26 January 2005 amending and supplementing the Forestry Code.  Law No. 2009-59 of 20 July 2009 Simplifying Administrative Procedures in the Agricultural and Fisheries sector.)

TUR.name: Turkey

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities (indigenous and non-indigenous)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 4 of the Law on Pastures, 1998 provides that villages have right to use rangelands, pastures and winter pastrues.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4, Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: While villages are granted the right to use pastures and rangelands, the state retains underlying authority over the pastures and has discretion dispose of rights to these areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 4, Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)
indicators.additional_info: Art. 12 provides that the Commission has discretion to make allocation decisions regarding pasture lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Law on Pastures establishes a Commission to administer and manage pastures, and the Commission is tasked with  administering, surveying and registering pastures and rangelands. However, the law does not ensure that the registration process will be accessible and affordable for villages.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)
indicators.additional_info: Article 9-10 and 17 of the Law on pastures establishes procedures by which the Comission must demarcate pasture land and establish a registry.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Villages are granted legal personality under the Law on Pastures, but not for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)
indicators.additional_info: Article 13 indicates that villages can object to decisions made by the Commission regarding pastureland allocation.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law indicates that villages can use pastures and rangelands for grazing and subsistence prupose. Villages can also utilize forest resources located on pasturelands. However, the Commission retains authority to allocate land areas and set limitations on grazing and other uses.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Law on pastures suggest that the grazing and use rights to pastures and rangelands are temporary in nature, though there are no clear durational limits set.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not establish that villages have a right to give consent in an inclusive manner prior to acquisition by outsiders and others.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Article 28 of the Law on pastures provides that villages may use forest areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998);

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities, as citizens of Turkey, are granted rights to drink and use water for domestic purposes. Use rights to pastures and rangeland are granted to municipalities and villages. Thus, it can be implied that communities have rights to use water located on pastures and rangelands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law No. 831 on water (1926); Law No. 7478 on potable water for villages (1960);. Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998);
indicators.additional_info: Law No. 7478 on potable water provides drink water for villages.. NOTE: Reviewer had difficulty translating Law NO. 831 on wate/r Article 4 of the Law on Pastures provides that rights to use rangeland, pastures and winter pastures are granted to villages and municipalities."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly establish that communites have rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on pastures No. 4342. (1998)

TZA.name: Tanzania

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights & community-based governance fully lawful in Village Lands (60% of country area), governed by  c. 12,500 elected Village Councils. Titling voluntary by CCRO (Certificate of Customary Right of Occupany), no fixed term & may also be issued to spouses, families, groups, communities. Communal lands must be identified and set aside prior to issue of  CCRO.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s.4 (3). Village Land Act, 1999, s. 18 (1). NOTE: Zanzibar has own land laws not covered here.
indicators.additional_info: All land in Tanzania is owned by citizens in common, vested in President as trustee (Land Act 1999 s. 3 (1a). Therefore property rights constitute rights to the land, not ownership of the land itself. Hence termed Rights of Occupancy. Elected Village Council is the lawful Manager, not owner of the community's domain, owned in undivided shares.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Equal legal force and effect between state Granted Right of Occupancy and Customary Right of Occupancy. Registration of the latter is voluntary, right protected whether registered or not. Compensation is equitable for granted & customary rights at compulsory acquisition and the community may reject State claims of less than 250 ha, but due to poor drafting not for larger areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s. 4. Village Land Act, 1999, s. 12 (1) (b), s. 13, s. 18, 20; Village Land Regulations, 2001, Part III. Land Acquisition Act, 1967. s. 12
indicators.additional_info: Authority devolved to elected village government which conducts adjudication should individual/family seek Certificate. Compensation procedure for extinction of customary rights at compulsory acquisition or transfer into General or Reserved Land are precise & generous in Village Land Regulations (2002) s. 8-25, but still limited  to 'unexhausted improvements', deleterious for common properties other than pastures (exempt).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Formalization (Certificates of Customary Right of Occupancy, CCRO) is voluntary, cheap, inclusive & Register kept in both Village and District Office. Allocations subject to approval of Village Assembly (all adults). Off-farm lands may be registered as the collective property of all members, more commonly recorded as communal property in Village Land Register.
indicators.additional_info: Perimeter boundary of each community area (Village Land Area) may be based on formal survey or agreements with neighbours (Village Land Act s. 7). Certificate of Village Land (CVL) following formal survey is issued to authorize the Village Council as the Land Manager. Rights within the Village Land Area formalized voluntarily to individuals, spouses, families, groups, but only after community has identified & recorded its common property. Two or more villages may decide to share certain resources  eg. forest or grazing land (Village Land Act, s.11).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Any person, family unit, group of persons including a community is  a recognized land right holder and may receive a formal Certificate of Customary Right of Occupancy, without creating a legal entity to hold the land of their behalf.
indicators.law_and_provision: Village Land Act, 1999, s. 22. Village Land Use Planning Act, 2007.
indicators.additional_info: Special application required by a person or group not ordinarily resident in the village, also a Non-Village Organization, but must be citizens, Commissioner of Lands to be consulted, and special conditions may be imposed by village government (Village Land Act, 1999, s. 23).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Elected village government (Village Council) is legally responsible for zoning, management and administration of all land within the village area, including allocations for private, family or group parcels, & maintaining Village Land Register.
indicators.law_and_provision: Village Land Act, 1999, s. 8. Land Use Planning Act, No. 10/2007
indicators.additional_info: Obligatory for Village Council to secure approval of community (Village Assembly) for allocations of rights ((s. 8 (5)). usbject to oversight by district officials (s. 9). Any villager has legal standing to sue the Village Council in respect of management (s. 8 (12).  100 villagers or the Village Assembly   may complain to District Council, obliged to act on the matter (s. 8 (8)). Non-villagers may obtain a lease directly from the Village Council on conditions, subject to approval of Village Assembly (s. 32-33).  Application difficulties include:  (a) state interference especially re forest and wildlife assets of villages areas (b) onerous land use planning law introduced in 2007 now requiring villages to set aside land for investment; (c) application of zoning as specified in a 2007 law which is so complex that usually to hire District officials to assist.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law accepts customary rights as held in perpetuity; 'A customary right of occupancy shall be presumed to be granted for an indefinite term, unless a grant of a customary right of occupancy specifies otherwise' Village Land Act, 1999 s. 27
indicators.law_and_provision: Village Land Act, 1999, s. 27
indicators.additional_info: Note that urban Rights of Occupancy have limited term, usually 30, 60 or maximum of 99 years, unrenwable. Land Act, 1999.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: No consent requirement although there may be no transfers from Village Land to General or Reserved Land until the type, amount, method & timing of compensation agreed by Village Council (Village Land Act, s. 4 (8)). Government may remove hazard land (mangroves, reefs, foreshores, etc) from village jurisdiction (s. 6).
indicators.additional_info: Contradiction on scope of General Land: Land Act states this includes 'unoccupied and unused village land' cf. Village Land Act which excludes such definition; unremedied as of Mar 2025. Community approval (Assembly) obligatory for internal transfers of lands including issue of lease to non-village organizations (Village Land Act, s. 12 (1) (c) (2), s. 32).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Concerning tree ownership, individuals, families or communities own all trees on customary land. Legal definition of land includes 'natural things growing on the land'.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s. 2 Village Land Act, 1999, s. 2.
indicators.additional_info: The Forest Act, 2002 restricts declaration of protected trees or plants to General Land (s 65), enabling each village to  determine protected species.  Forest Act 2002 commits to subsidiarity; no new Protected Areas vested in Government may be approved unless shown that there is no adjacent community is available to include the area within its domain. Community Forests fully provided for under Forest Act, 2002.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Water belongs to the nation, vested in the President as trustee. Customary water rights are upheld as of equal status and effect to a granted water use rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Resources Management Act, 2009, s. 10 -12, 52.
indicators.additional_info: As with land, water is owned by the national community in common, vested in the President as its trustee. Lawful occupants of lands may collect water, dig wells, collect rainwater etc. for domestic uses without permits. Customary water rights are explicitly recognized and declared to be 'in every respect of equal status and effect to a granted water right' (s. 52). Domestic uses included stock watering and irrigation in the non-commercial (subsistence) economy.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Reserved Land comprises lands subject to conservation laws, may be owned by communities. More than 1,000 Community Forests (Village Land Forest Reserves) declared on village lands covering 2+ Mha. Unlike Forest Act,  Wildlife Act fails to adopt subsidiarity principle so takings for new Wildlife Parks and Reserves persist, evicting villages, generating court cases.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s. 2; Village Land Act, 1999, s. 2, Forest Act, 2002, Wildlife Act, 2013, s. 4 (1), s. 22-24; National Parks Act (CAP 282) (1959, last amended 2003) s.6-7; Tanzania Wildlife Authority Act (TANAPA), 2013, s. 54.
indicators.additional_info: Forests Act does not refer to ownership, classifying forests as governed by national, local authority, village or private persons/entities (s. 4). Delgates responsibility to the most local level possible (s. 3 (d)), encourages Minister to establish village land or community forest reserves in preference to a national reserves where customary rights affected (s. 24 (3)). Communities may be given a national forest to manage (s. 27). Wildlife Act 2013 enables interest groups in villages to create Wildlife Management Areas including right to negotiate & sign agreements with investors (s.22-24). Negative trends: declaration of new national parks,  game reserves, wetland reserves affecting pastoralist commiunities. Expansion of Ruaha National Park is also dispossessing villages. Forestry sector has engineered legal interpretation of unfarmed lands in Village Land Act  to enable district and state foresters to issue licences to use village lands which are outside the community's Community Forests; also contested.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights & community-based governance fully lawful in Village Lands (60% of country area), governed by  c. 12,500 elected Village Councils. Titling voluntary by CCRO (Certificate of Customary Right of Occupany), no fixed term & may also be issued to spouses, families, groups, communities. Communal lands must be identified and set aside prior to issue of  CCRO.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s.4 (3). Village Land Act, 1999, s. 18 (1). NOTE: Zanzibar has own land laws not covered here.
indicators.additional_info: All land in Tanzania is owned by citizens in common, vested in President as trustee (Land Act 1999 s. 3 (1a). Therefore property rights constitute rights to the land, not ownership of the land itself. Hence termed Rights of Occupancy. Elected Village Council is the lawful Manager, not owner of the community's domain, owned in undivided shares.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Equal legal force and effect between state Granted Right of Occupancy and Customary Right of Occupancy. Registration of the latter is voluntary, right protected whether registered or not. Compensation is equitable for granted & customary rights at compulsory acquisition and the community may reject State claims of less than 250 ha, but due to poor drafting not for larger areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1999, s. 4. Village Land Act, 1999, s. 12 (1) (b), s. 13, s. 18, 20; Village Land Regulations, 2001, Part III. Land Acquisition Act, 1967. s. 12
indicators.additional_info: Authority devolved to elected village government which conducts adjudication should individual/family seek Certificate. Compensation procedure for extinction of customary rights at compulsory acquisition or transfer into General or Reserved Land are precise & generous in Village Land Regulations (2002) s. 8-25, but still limited  to 'unexhausted improvements', deleterious for common properties other than pastures (exempt).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Formalization (Certificates of Customary Right of Occupancy, CCRO) is voluntary, cheap, inclusive & Register kept in both Village and District Office. Allocations subject to approval of Village Assembly (all adults). Off-farm lands may be registered as the collective property of all members, more commonly recorded as communal property in Village Land Register.
indicators.additional_info: Perimeter boundary of each community area (Village Land Area) may be based on formal survey or agreements with neighbours (Village Land Act s. 7). Certificate of Village Land (CVL) following formal survey is issued to authorize the Village Council as the Land Manager. Rights within the Village Land Area formalized voluntarily to individuals, spouses, families, groups, but only after community has identified & recorded its common property. Two or more villages may decide to share certain resources  eg. forest or grazing land (Village Land Act, s.11).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Any person, family unit, group of persons including a community is  a recognized land right holder and may receive a formal Certificate of Customary Right of Occupancy, without creating a legal entity to hold the land of their behalf.
indicators.law_and_provision: Village Land Act, 1999, s. 22. Village Land Use Planning Act, 2007.
indicators.additional_info: Special application required by a person or group not ordinarily resident in the village, also a Non-Village Organization, but must be citizens, Commissioner of Lands to be consulted, and special conditions may be imposed by village government (Village Land Act, 1999, s. 23).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Elected village government (Village Council) is legally responsible for zoning, management and administration of all land within the village area, including allocations for private, family or group parcels, & maintaining Village Land Register.
indicators.law_and_provision: Village Land Act, 1999, s. 8. Land Use Planning Act, No. 10/2007
indicators.additional_info: Obligatory for Village Council to secure approval of community (Village Assembly) for allocations of rights ((s. 8 (5)). usbject to oversight by district officials (s. 9). Any villager has legal standing to sue the Village Council in respect of management (s. 8 (12).  100 villagers or the Village Assembly   may complain to District Council, obliged to act on the matter (s. 8 (8)). Non-villagers may obtain a lease directly from the Village Council on conditions, subject to approval of Village Assembly (s. 32-33).  Application difficulties include:  (a) state interference especially re forest and wildlife assets of villages areas (b) onerous land use planning law introduced in 2007 now requiring villages to set aside land for investment; (c) application of zoning as specified in a 2007 law which is so complex that usually to hire District officials to assist.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law accepts customary rights as held in perpetuity; 'A customary right of occupancy shall be presumed to be granted for an indefinite term, unless a grant of a customary right of occupancy specifies otherwise' Village Land Act, 1999 s. 27
