UGA.name: Uganda

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land vested in citizens. Customary tenure accorded equivalent legal force & affects  freehold, leasehold & mailo systems. Rights issued to individuals, families, groups & communities (eg. grazing land).Nat Land Policy 2015 commits to titling & attention to women & pastoral rights. IP include  forest peoples & pastoralists; collective title actively sought by all IP.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995 Art. 237, Land Act, 1998 (2001, 2004, 2010) s.3 & 4. National Land Policy Implementation Plan, 2015-2019.
indicators.additional_info: Mailo is a colonial-introduced tenancy of chiefs unique to Uganda. Constitution excludes forest & wildlife reserves, lakes & rivers, vests these in Government or Local Governments in trust for citizens (Art. 237 (2) (b)). Titling is voluntary. Includes two routes for collective titles: i) customary certificates available to 'any person, family or community' (Art. 4) or ii)  forming a Communal Land Association to own the parcel under customary or freehold title (Arts. 15-23).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary, freehold/leasehold and mailo rights have equivalent legal force and effect. The law upholds customary rights without formalization. Family & collective property included. Constitutionally, equitable compensation at compulsory acquisition is obligatory, but only needs be prompt, not prior to eviction (Art. 26 (2)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995 (2017), Art. 26 & 237; Land Act, 1998, s. 4, 5. Land Acquisition Act
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution recognizes customary,  freehold, mailo and leasehold as lawful forms of owning land (Art. 237 (3)). It refers to "protection of property or any interest or right over property of any description", implying equitable compensation (Art.26). However the Land Acquisition Act, 1965, allows discretion by the assessment officer, s. 5 (1) (b).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Families, communities & individuals may acquire certificates of customary ownership &/or create Communal Land Associations. Process is simple, cheap, accessible but everywhere handicapped by weak admin. at mandated County & Sub-County Offices, & corruption.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5 -9; Regulations, 2000, Reg. 3-82; Registration of Titles Act (CAP 230) (1924).
indicators.additional_info: Limitations in practice include reliance of  District Land Boards (s. 8), not all in place, use of Sub-County Chiefs as Recorders, rather than the national registry (s. 69) implying inequity with freehold, mailo, leasehold registration (rather than accessibility as the presumed intent). Also tendency of Recorder to issue Certificates of Customary Ownership in name of head of household  rather than all family members. Out-dated Registration of Titles Act (1924) does not provide easily for registration of family, community or communal land association titles. Law directed District Registrar of Titles to open register of Communal Land Associations (s. 16) for collective land ownership under mailo, freehold or leasehold or customary tenure. Incomplete implementation after 25 years.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law recognizes customary rights held by families and communities without forming legal entity & may secure Certificates of Customary Ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5, Land Regulations 2000, Reg.3 & 73.
indicators.additional_info: Law also provides option of groups & communities forming Communal Land Associations in which to vest & manage collective ownership; Land Act, 1998, s. 16-27, Land Regulations 2000, Regs. 73-82. Unclear why Sub-County Chief is Recorder of customary rights while Associations must be registered by District Registrar.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Devolution to communities strong by institution of Parish Land Committees (village cluster level). However, the members are not elected by villages but appointed & paid by District Council. Customary regulation & management to apply.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5 & 28, Constitution, 1995, Art. 33, 34 & 35.
indicators.additional_info: Customary institutions, custom, tradition and practices of the concerned community to apply, except if contradict constitutional human rights or deny women or children or persons with disability access to ownership, occupation or use of any land (Land Act, 1998, s. 28). Communities may also create Communal Land Associations as registered entities with the District Registrar of Titles (Land Act s. 16-27). Additional requirement for the elected Officers of the Managing Committee to be incorporated (s. 18)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights stated in law as owned in perpetuity along with other incidents of ownership, s. 4 (2), including the right to lease, mortgage, subdivide, sell, transfer, or dispose of land by will (section 4 (2)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 4 (h).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Constitution and Land Acquisition Act do not require consent to land acquired for public purpose; may hear and consider objections. Compensation must be paid promptly, not necessarily prior to taking. Right of appeal exists.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995, Art. 26, 237 (2). Land Acquisition Act, 1965, s.5
indicators.additional_info: Public purpose is not defined in The Land Acquisition Act, 1965. Constitution defines broadly as 'in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health' (Art. 26). While investments/economic demands are not included, it is these which most impose upon communities in practice.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Trees are owned by landowner, and customary rights are recognized as  ownership of the land, whether this ownership is formally titled or not. Minister or District Council may protect tree species.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Forestry and Tree Planting Act, 2003, s. 27, 31.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Water is vested in Government in trust for the people, who have a right of use for domestic, fire fighting and garden irrigation, and may obtain additional specific rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Statute, 1995, s. 4, 7.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities may declare Community Forests and/or Wildlife Management Areas (WMA) on customary lands, active in Karamojong pastoral lands. Communities may not  own any Park or Reserve but provision for use rights. Restitution claims by two Forest Peoples in process but constrained by absence of prescription enabling claims for restitution.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, Art. 237 (2) (b); National Forestry and Tree Planting Act, 2003,s.4-12, s. 17-21; Uganda Wildlife Act, 2019.
indicators.additional_info: Communities liaison committees established for Wildlife Reserves (sec. 20). Note that IP are only guaranteed access and use; sec. 32 "The Uganda Wildlife Authority may establish guidelines for sustainable access of communities neighbouring conservation areas to resources which are historically crucial to the survival of those communities", and sec. 32 (2) "... may study, identify and protect historical cultural interests of any community resident around a wildlife conservation area" (eg. park, reserve).

local_communities_entries.framework: All communities; no law specific to Indigenous Peoples
local_communities_entries.source: Liz Alden Wily, Independent Land Tenure Specialist

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Land vested in citizens. Customary tenure accorded equivalent legal force & affects  freehold, leasehold & mailo systems. Rights issued to individuals, families, groups & communities (eg. grazing land).Nat Land Policy 2015 commits to titling & attention to women & pastoral rights. IP include  forest peoples & pastoralists; collective title actively sought by all IP.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995 Art. 237, Land Act, 1998 (2001, 2004, 2010) s.3 & 4. National Land Policy Implementation Plan, 2015-2019.
indicators.additional_info: Mailo is a colonial-introduced tenancy of chiefs unique to Uganda. Constitution excludes forest & wildlife reserves, lakes & rivers, vests these in Government or Local Governments in trust for citizens (Art. 237 (2) (b)). Titling is voluntary. Includes two routes for collective titles: i) customary certificates available to 'any person, family or community' (Art. 4) or ii)  forming a Communal Land Association to own the parcel under customary or freehold title (Arts. 15-23).

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary, freehold/leasehold and mailo rights have equivalent legal force and effect. The law upholds customary rights without formalization. Family & collective property included. Constitutionally, equitable compensation at compulsory acquisition is obligatory, but only needs be prompt, not prior to eviction (Art. 26 (2)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995 (2017), Art. 26 & 237; Land Act, 1998, s. 4, 5. Land Acquisition Act
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution recognizes customary,  freehold, mailo and leasehold as lawful forms of owning land (Art. 237 (3)). It refers to "protection of property or any interest or right over property of any description", implying equitable compensation (Art.26). However the Land Acquisition Act, 1965, allows discretion by the assessment officer, s. 5 (1) (b).

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Families, communities & individuals may acquire certificates of customary ownership &/or create Communal Land Associations. Process is simple, cheap, accessible but everywhere handicapped by weak admin. at mandated County & Sub-County Offices, & corruption.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5 -9; Regulations, 2000, Reg. 3-82; Registration of Titles Act (CAP 230) (1924).
indicators.additional_info: Limitations in practice include reliance of  District Land Boards (s. 8), not all in place, use of Sub-County Chiefs as Recorders, rather than the national registry (s. 69) implying inequity with freehold, mailo, leasehold registration (rather than accessibility as the presumed intent). Also tendency of Recorder to issue Certificates of Customary Ownership in name of head of household  rather than all family members. Out-dated Registration of Titles Act (1924) does not provide easily for registration of family, community or communal land association titles. Law directed District Registrar of Titles to open register of Communal Land Associations (s. 16) for collective land ownership under mailo, freehold or leasehold or customary tenure. Incomplete implementation after 25 years.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Law recognizes customary rights held by families and communities without forming legal entity & may secure Certificates of Customary Ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5, Land Regulations 2000, Reg.3 & 73.
indicators.additional_info: Law also provides option of groups & communities forming Communal Land Associations in which to vest & manage collective ownership; Land Act, 1998, s. 16-27, Land Regulations 2000, Regs. 73-82. Unclear why Sub-County Chief is Recorder of customary rights while Associations must be registered by District Registrar.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Devolution to communities strong by institution of Parish Land Committees (village cluster level). However, the members are not elected by villages but appointed & paid by District Council. Customary regulation & management to apply.
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 5 & 28, Constitution, 1995, Art. 33, 34 & 35.
indicators.additional_info: Customary institutions, custom, tradition and practices of the concerned community to apply, except if contradict constitutional human rights or deny women or children or persons with disability access to ownership, occupation or use of any land (Land Act, 1998, s. 28). Communities may also create Communal Land Associations as registered entities with the District Registrar of Titles (Land Act s. 16-27). Additional requirement for the elected Officers of the Managing Committee to be incorporated (s. 18)

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Customary rights stated in law as owned in perpetuity along with other incidents of ownership, s. 4 (2), including the right to lease, mortgage, subdivide, sell, transfer, or dispose of land by will (section 4 (2)).
indicators.law_and_provision: Land Act, 1998, s. 4 (h).

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Constitution and Land Acquisition Act do not require consent to land acquired for public purpose; may hear and consider objections. Compensation must be paid promptly, not necessarily prior to taking. Right of appeal exists.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution, 1995, Art. 26, 237 (2). Land Acquisition Act, 1965, s.5
indicators.additional_info: Public purpose is not defined in The Land Acquisition Act, 1965. Constitution defines broadly as 'in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health' (Art. 26). While investments/economic demands are not included, it is these which most impose upon communities in practice.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Trees are owned by landowner, and customary rights are recognized as  ownership of the land, whether this ownership is formally titled or not. Minister or District Council may protect tree species.
indicators.law_and_provision: National Forestry and Tree Planting Act, 2003, s. 27, 31.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.comment: Water is vested in Government in trust for the people, who have a right of use for domestic, fire fighting and garden irrigation, and may obtain additional specific rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Statute, 1995, s. 4, 7.

local_communities_entries.framework: Non-indigenous communities
local_communities_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Articles 142-143 of the Constitution recognize community property rights. Article 83 of the 2001 Land Code and Article 9 of the 1994 Forest Code recognize communal ownership rights to land and forests in Ukraine. Article 56 of 2009 the Land Code provides that  forest lands are held in state, communal and private property.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004
indicators.additional_info:
Article 5 of the 2001 Land Code provides "ensuring equality of land ownership rights of citizens, legal entities, local communities and the state." Article 54 states " Lands of historical and cultural significance may be in state, communal and private property."  Article 83 of the 2001 Land Code provides that "Land ownership rights of local communities are: 1. Lands belonging by right of ownership of territorial communities of villages, towns, cities, municipal ownership. 2. In the municipal property are all lands within settlements, except land to private and public property, and the land beyond, which are objects of communal property. 3. communally-owned lands that can not be transferred to private ownership:
a) public land settlements (squares, streets, driveways, roads, embankments, beaches, parks, gardens, parkways, cemeteries, places of disposal and waste management, etc.); b) the land under the railways, roads, objects of air and pipeline transport; c) lands under nature conservation, historical, cultural and recreational purposes, having special ecological, recreational, scientific, aesthetic, historical and cultural value, unless According to a secondary source, forest ownership in Ukraine has change very little since the Soviet era; more than 99% of the forest is state owned. A small amount of privatisation occurred between the passing of the Land Code in 1992 and the enactment of the 1994 Forest Code which stated that all forests shall be the exclusive property of the state. The Land, Civil and Commercial Codes mention private and communal forest ownership but no legal framework exists to transfer ownership from the state. Forests are ascribed to  organisations or institutions for ‘permanent use’ allowing them to manage the forest but ownership remains with the state. PROFOR. 2006: Ukraine. Forestry Sector Note: Status and Opportunities for Development. Available at: http://www.profor.info/Documents/pdf/UkraineForestSectorNote2006.pdf

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The state retains broad authority transfer, purchase, withdraw, expropriate, confiscate, and terminate land  and forest rights held by communities (Articles 9-12, 143-149, Land Code).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The Land Code establishes the registration of all property within Ukraine is compulsory (Section X, Transitional Provisions).  Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land establishes vague procedures for registering communal property (Art. 7, 12). Under the Forest Code (Art. 11), communities can acquire ownership rights to communal forests through registration, but there are no explicit legal protections ensuring the registration process is affordable or accessible.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004
indicators.additional_info: Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land (Art. 7) states " the demarcation of state and municipal property to land of communal property of territorial communities of villages, Cities passed: All land within settlements, in addition to private land property and lands assigned to the state  land outside the settlements, which objects of communal property; reserve lands that were previously transferred to territorial communities of villages, towns according to the laws of Ukraine; land plots on which the immovable property which is jointly owned by the local community and the state. Article 8. Powers of executive power on separation of state and municipal property. Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine shall determine the boundaries of land plots on which the immovable property."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2001 Land Code and the Forest Code recognize the legal personality of communities for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law suggests the communities have limited authority over their lands and forests. Governments authorities at federal, state, municipal, and town levels are granted broad authority to dispose, transfer, withdraw, purchase land held by local communities (Arts. 9-12, 2001 Land Code). The government also retains authority to monitor community use and compliance with environmental legislation under the Land Code (Art. 12(f))
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004
indicators.additional_info:
Articles 9- 12 provide government bodies with authority over a) disposal of lands of the territorial community; b) transfer of communal land ownership in the property of citizens and legal entities in accordance with this Code; c) the provision of land for the use of communal ownership of land in accordance with this Code; d) withdrawal of land plots of communal property in the manner prescribed by this Code; e) purchase of land for public needs of the city; f) termination of land use in the cases provided by this Code; g) decision to release illegally occupied land; h) preparing recommendations on withdrawal (redemption) of land and provision of state-owned land held by the executive; i) establishing and altering the boundaries of villages, districts in cities; j) organization of land;
k) coordination of activities of local land resources; i) monitor the use and protection of lands of communal property, land and compliance with environmental legislation; l) restrictions, temporary prohibition (suspension) or stopping use of land by citizens and legal entities for violations of land legislation requirements; m) inform the public about the provision, withdrawal (redemption) of land; n) submission to the established order proposals to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine to establish and change the boundaries of cities; o) the resolution of land disputes; p) other issues in the sphere of land relations pursuant to law. Article 103 of the Forest Code states "local authorities decide disputes relating to the security, protection, use and reproduction of forests that are communal property."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The 2001 Land Code and 1994 Forest Code do not establish durational limits on the ownership rights held by communities, which suggests that such rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities the right to give consent prior to acquisition by the government or outsiders.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Forest Code recognizes community ownership rights to forests (Art. 9).
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Article 59 of the Land Code recognizes that water rights may be granted to communities, but Article 6 of the Water Code of Ukraine that water is only available for use (not ownership).
indicators.law_and_provision: Water Code (No.213/95-VR of 1995); Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Ukraine; Forest Code (No.3852-XII of 1994); Land Code (No. 2768-III of 2001); Civil Code; Law No. 1457-IV regarding demarcation of public and municipal land, 2004

UKR.Communities Q10: Does the law uphold ind: No, the law does not address the issue — The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas. indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The state owns all water in the public domain (Art. 16, Water Code, 1978).  All citizens are granted rights to use water in the public domain if they register, so communities, as citizens, have a right to use public waters. (Art. 8, Water Code). The Water Code also recognizes that private property owners have rights to rain water and riverbeds located on their property. However, since national level statutory and regulatory laws do not grant communities land ownership rights, communities are also not granted the water rights granted that apply to privately owned land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley Nº 14.859 - Código de Aguas (1978); Constitution of Uruguay; Law No. 18638 (2009) - Amend the end of the period established by art. 1 of Law 18.461, on the ownership of rural properties or farms through corporations or other legal entities; Law No. 18.461 (2009) Interprétanse rules on the ownership of rural properties and farms through corporations or other legal entities; Law No. 18,308 (2008)- rules on land use planning and sustainable development; Law No. 18,187 (2007) - Standards for land settlement. 2 November 2007; Law No. 18,092 (2007)- Declares general interest holders the right to ownership of rural properties and farms are those that are determined; Uruguay: Law No. 17930; Law No. 15,239 (1981) - Declares of national interest the use and conservation of soil and surface water intended for agricultural purposes; Law No. 13,968 (1971) - Delivery of land for farms conducting cooperatively; Law No. 13,667 (1968)- Declares of national interest the conservation of soil and surface and groundwater; Law No. 10,051 (1941) - Regime fractionation of land for expropriation and exploitation.
indicators.additional_info: According to Article 8 Of the Water Code Ley Nº 14.859), individuals can obtain rights to use water by registering. Article 11 further specifies that "the rights to water use and river beds owned by individuals, constituted before entry into force of this Code may only be opposed to the administration and bona fide third parties if they are registered in the register referred to the Article 8 and within the period specified therein. Rights to water use and privately owned riverbeds, which were established in the future, will only be opposable to the administration and to third parties in good faith from the moment in which they are registered. Article 19 recognizes that property owners havea right to own rainwater falling on their property.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The state owns all water in the public domain (Art. 16, Water Code, 1978).  All citizens are granted rights to use water in the public domain if they register, so communities, as citizens, have a right to use public waters. (Art. 8, Water Code). The Water Code also recognizes that private property owners have rights to rain water and riverbeds located on their property. However, since national level statutory and regulatory laws do not grant communities land ownership rights, communities are also not granted the water rights granted that apply to privately owned land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Ley Nº 14.859 - Código de Aguas (1978); Constitution of Uruguay; Law No. 18638 (2009) - Amend the end of the period established by art. 1 of Law 18.461, on the ownership of rural properties or farms through corporations or other legal entities; Law No. 18.461 (2009) Interprétanse rules on the ownership of rural properties and farms through corporations or other legal entities; Law No. 18,308 (2008)- rules on land use planning and sustainable development; Law No. 18,187 (2007) - Standards for land settlement. 2 November 2007; Law No. 18,092 (2007)- Declares general interest holders the right to ownership of rural properties and farms are those that are determined; Uruguay: Law No. 17930; Law No. 15,239 (1981) - Declares of national interest the use and conservation of soil and surface water intended for agricultural purposes; Law No. 13,968 (1971) - Delivery of land for farms conducting cooperatively; Law No. 13,667 (1968)- Declares of national interest the conservation of soil and surface and groundwater; Law No. 10,051 (1941) - Regime fractionation of land for expropriation and exploitation.
indicators.additional_info:
According to Article 8 Of the Water Code Ley Nº 14.859), individuals can obtain rights to use water by registering. Article 11 further specifies that "the rights to water use and river beds owned by individuals, constituted before entry into force of this Code may only be opposed to the administration and bona fide third parties if they are registered in the register referred to the Article 8 and within the period specified therein.
Rights to water use and privately owned riverbeds, which were established in the future, will only be opposable to the administration and to third parties in good faith from the moment in which they are registered. Article 19 recognizes that property owners havea right to own rainwater falling on their property.

USA.name: United States

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Native American legal rights to land may be established by aboriginal possession, by treaty, by act of Congress, by executive action, by purchase, or by action of states. But the gov't retains broad power to expropriate.
indicators.law_and_provision: 25 U.S. Code Section 81, 3501; United States v. Shoshone Tribes 304 U.S. 111 (1937). Tee-Hit Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955); Indian Reorganization Act, 1994; Land Consolidation Act (2000)
indicators.additional_info: 25 U.S. Code Section 81 provides that "Indian lands" means "lands the title to which is held by the United States in trust for an Indian tribe or lands the title to which is held by an Indian subject to a restriction by the United States against alienation." Federal statutes establish native reserves, which is technically government owned land used for Indian use. Native Americans can also establish aboriginal title or obtain reserves through executive orders, but are generally granted only use and occupancy rights to their land. Compensation for expropriation is only payable when aboriginal title is recognized through treaties and statutes enacted by US Congress. Indians holding lands under "permissive occupancy"---without Congressional authorization through statute or treaty---may be removed from their lands by Congress at its own discretion without compensation under the 5th Amendment (Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States 348 U.S. 272 (1955)). There must be a "definite intention by congressional action to accord legal rights", not merely permit occupation (337 US 86 (1949)). Native American reserves can also be established through executive order and purchase. NOTE: this assessment does not account for state-recognized Indian reservations.

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The degree of protection varies depending on source (statute, treaty, etc.) which defines those rights. In general, Native Americans are often granted use/ occupancy rights to reserve land held by the government. But occupancy is considered "as sacred as the fee" by SC.
indicators.law_and_provision: Indian Claims Commission Act (1946); United States v. Sante Fe Pac. R. Co., 324 U.S. 339 (1942); United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); United States v. Shoshone Tribes 304 U.S. 111 (1937)
indicators.additional_info: When treaties or statutes recognize Native American lands, Native Americans are entitled to just compensation for expropriation (United States v. Sioux Nation 1980; Indian Claims Commission Act, 1946). However, Native Americans are not entitled to compensation under the 5th amendment of the Constitution if aboriginal title is not recognized by Congress (Tee-Hit Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)). The Supreme Court also ruled that US Congress has a federal Indian trust responsibility, which is a legally enforceable fiduciary obligation on the part of the US to protect tribal treaty rights, lands, assets, and resources (United States v. Kagama, 118 U.S. 375, 384 (1886)). In United States v. Shoshone Tribes, the Court held that the right of occupancy "is as sacred as the fee...the right of perpetual and exclusively occupancy of the land is not less valuable than full title in fee."

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Native American groups can be formally recognized by an act of Congress, administrative procedures established in 25 C.F.R.  Part 83, or by US court decision, but there are no clear procedures for assistance and mapping of lands.
indicators.law_and_provision: Tee-Hit Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955); 25 Code of Federal Regulations Part 83- Procedures for Establishing that an American Indian Group Exists in an Indian Tribes; Indian Claims Commission Act, 1946
indicators.additional_info: Aboriginal title can be established by showing a actual, exclusive and continuous use and occupancy for a long time prior to the loss of the property (Tee-Hi-Ton Indians v. United States). 25 Code of Federal Regulations Part 83 provides procedures for establishing "American Indian Groups", but these procedures do not contain provisions for formally documenting/mapping Native American lands and providing petitioners with financial and other forms of assistance. The Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act requires the Secretary of the Interior to publish annually a list of the federally recognized tribes. Otherwise, Congress must enact a statute which officially recognizes a tract of land as a Native American Reserve for rights to formalize. 25 CFR 83.5 establishes "Duties of [the Department of the Interior]"and states that the Department must, upon request, provide petitioners with suggestions and advice regarding preparation of the documented petition.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Native Americans are recognized as legal persons by the Supreme Court, but not necessarily for purposes of private property ownership
indicators.law_and_provision: Indian Reorganization Act, 1994; Land Consolidation Act (2000); United States v. Sante Fe Pac. R. Co., 324 U.S. 339 (1942); Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903); United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980).

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Native Americans are granted the power to regulate their internal and social relations and enforce civil/criminal laws against tribal members, but the government retains broad authority over Native American Reserves.
indicators.law_and_provision: United States v. Kagama, 118 U.S., 375, 381-382; Duro v. Rein, 495 U.S. 676 (1990); Tribal Self-Governance Act of 1994; Mitchel v. United States 34 U.S. 711 (1835)).
indicators.additional_info: One policy objective of the Tribal Self-Governance Act is to provide Indian tribes with meaningful authority to plan, conduct, redesign, and administer programs, services, functions, and activities that meet the needs of individual tribal communities (Sec. 458aa, Tribal Self-Governance Act of 1994). The Supreme Court held that Native American rights to exclusive enjoyment in their own way and for their own purposes were as much respected..." (Mitchel v. United States 34 U.S. 711 (1835)). In Duro v. Reina,  the Supreme Court held that Native American tribes are limited sovereigns, necessarily subject to the overriding authority of the United States, yet they retain the sovereignty needed to control their own internal relations and preserve their own unique customs and social order (495 U.S. 676, 677).

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court held that Aboriginal title may be held until land is abandoned or alienated/extinguished through a federal statute, treaty, or executive order.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 465, Indian Reorganization Act 1994; Mitchel v. United States 34 U.S. 711 (1835)
indicators.additional_info: In Mitchel v. United States, the Supreme Court held that Native American rights to enjoy their lands terminates upon by the Native American tribe or cessation to the Government.

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation permits the Secretary of the Interior to acquire lands, water rights, or surface rights to lands within existing Native American Reservations without obtaining consent or consulting Native Americans.
indicators.law_and_provision: Sec. 465, Indian Reorganization Act 1994; Indian Claims Commission Act, 1946
indicators.additional_info: In United States v. Sante Fe P.R. Co., 314 U.S. 339 (1941), the Supreme Court held that the power of Congress to extinguish Indian title and the manner, method, and time of such extinguishment is not justiciable. Native Americans holding aboriginal title are not entitled to compensation, unless recognized by statute or treaty, when their land is expropriated for a public purpose (Tee-Hit Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)).

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court held that tribal rights to land on Reservation, included the rights to timber resources located on the Reservation.
indicators.law_and_provision: United States v. Shoshone Tribe, 304 U.S. 111, 118 (1938)
indicators.additional_info: In United States. v Shoshone Tribes, the Court held that, unless a treaty provides otherwise, the Court ruled the Shoshones had the right to compensation for taking of natural resources.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The Supreme Court held that water rights are defined by Congress, but when American Indian reservations are established by treaty, statute or executive order, implied reservation of water rights is included.
indicators.law_and_provision: Winters v. United States, 207 U.S. 564 (1908); Arizona v. California, 531 U.S. 1 (2000)
indicators.additional_info: The implied right to water resources on reservations applies to water sources that are within the reservation or on the border. In Winters v. United States, the Supreme Court held that reserve water rights should be equal to the amount needed to sufficiently irrigate the land within the reservation.

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Federal legislation is silent on whether Native Americans have land rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: The Organic Act 1916; Federal Land Policy and Management Act, 1976

UZB.name: Uzbekistan

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (indigenous peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The statutory and regulatory legal framework does not explicitly recognize the rights of indigenous and local communities in Uzbekistan
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Uzbekistan; Land Code, 1998; Civil Code; Law on Peasant Farms, 1998
indicators.additional_info: Article 16 of the Land Code, 1998 provides "land ownership in the Republic of Uzbekistan land is the property of state and the basis for national wealth, it ought to be used rationally, protected by the state and it is not liable to sale, exchange, give as a present, mortgage with the exception of cases established by the legislative acts of the Republic of Uzbekistan." Article 17 provides "rights of juridical and real persons to land parcels. Juridical persons can possess land parcels according to the right to permanent possession, permanent use, temporary use, lease and property according to this Law and other legislative acts. Real persons can have land parcels according to the right to life-long inheritable possession, permanent use, temporary (urgent) use, lease and property according to this Law and other legislative acts. "The Civil Code provides that land may be held in ownership (Article 169). Both private and state ownership are allowed (Article 167) and the right of ownership in plots of land “shall arise in instances, in the procedure and upon the conditions provided for by legislation” (Article 188). For additional information on land tenure in Uzbekistan, see 2005 USAID report: http://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/Pnadc874.pdf

VEN.name: Venezuela

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Indigenous Peoples (Amerindian groups)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Harvard Law and International Development Society (LIDS)

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution recognizes collective ownership of lands of native peoples, which are inalienable, nontransferable, indefeasible, and imprescriptible
indicators.law_and_provision: The 1999 Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, Art. 119
indicators.additional_info: Note: ILO Convention 169 (Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention) was ratified May 22, 2002. According to Article 119 of the Constitution, "the state recognizes the existence of native peoples and communities.. as well as their habitat and original rights to the lands they ancestrally and traditionally occupy… It shall be the responsibility of the National Executive, with the participation of the native peoples, to demarcate and guarantee the right to collective ownership of their lands, which shall be inalienable, not subject to the law of limitations..., and nontransferable, in accordance with this Constitution and the law".

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Community land receives the same protections as other types of property. It is unclear whether the land must be registered to receive these protections.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Título II, Capítulo III
indicators.additional_info: The law grants rights that are applicable to registered indigenous lands, but does not state whether those rights are unavailable to indigenous groups that have not yet demarcated and titled their lands.

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law establishes clear procedures and guarantees that the government will assist with the human/economic/technological resources necessary for mapping/applying.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Título II, Capítulo IV
indicators.additional_info: The law explains the process of formalizing indigenous land rights in Art. 38, and explains in Art. 34-37 the types of assistance that will be provided by the National Commission of Demarcation of the Habitat and Lands of Indigenous Peoples and Communities. Art. 35 provides that the commission will provide the human, economic, scientific, and techonological resources necessary, and the Geographic Institute of Venezuela will lend support for the demarcation.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law explicitly recognizes the legal personhood of indigenous peoples and communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Art. 7
indicators.additional_info: The law recognizes the legal personhood of indigenous peoples and communities for the purposes of exercising collective rights under the Constitution, treaties, etc. It allows the indigenous communities to determine their own representation according to their traditions and customs.

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Law states that the community can govern itself and choose its own governance systems.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2001 Ley de Demarcación y Garantía de Hábitat y Tierras de los Pueblos Indígenas, Arts. 15-16; 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Arts. 5-6
indicators.additional_info: The 2001 law states that the demarcation of the land will be achieved according to the indigenous customs/uses, in consultation with the  community and participation with the traditional authority structure. In executing the project, the communities can define their own boundaries according to traditional or ancestral use. The 2005 law provides that indigenous communities have autonomous control of the "use, protection, and defense of their habitat and lands," and that government authorities cannot undermine the legitimate authority of indigenous peoples and communities.

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: There is no durational limit in the 2005 Constitution, which indicates that indigenous land rights may be held in perpetuity.
indicators.law_and_provision: The 1999 Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, Art. 119

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: Consent is required and the community must hold an inclusive assembly meeting to gather consent.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Título I, Capítulo II
indicators.additional_info: The 2005 Law states that all activities such as resource extraction or development projects that will take place on community lands is subject to a process of preliminary consultation with the indigenous community. Those pursing the project must submit a proposal to community 90 days in advance, and the community must hold an assembly to discuss it. Then they will work together to reach an agreement. No project can start without the approval of the community

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law includes flora and fauna as part of the "indigenous habitat," but Art. 54 mentions natural resources owned by the State located in indigenous communities
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Arts. 3(5), 53-54
indicators.additional_info: The law defines indigenous habitat as including "the ground, the water, the air, the flora, the fauna, and generally all the material and immaterial resources." Art. 53 provides that the community have the right to use resources on their land and to manage, conserve, and preserve the environment. Art. 54 recognizes use rights to state owned natural resources located on indigenous lands, and establishes that the use of such resources depends on the consultation.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law includes water as part of the "indigenous habitat," but Art. 54 mentions natural resources owned by the State located in indigenous communities
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Arts. 3(5), 53-54

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The law establishes that protected natural areas should be included in the titling of indigenous lands, but the procedures for implementing this provision are not entirely clear.
indicators.law_and_provision: 2005 Ley Orgánica de Pueblos y Comunidades Indígenas, Art. 32
indicators.additional_info: Art. 32 of the 2005 Law states "The habitat and lands of indigenous peoples and communities on which protected natural areas have been established, should be included in the demarcation and titling of the habitat and lands in accordance with this Act and other laws governing the matter."

VNM.name: Vietnam

indigenous_peoples_entries.framework: Communities in general (Indigenous Peoples may use this framework but they do not have specific laws)
indigenous_peoples_entries.source: Nicholas K. Tagliarino, WRI

indicators.question: Does the law recognize all rights that Indigenous Peoples or communities exercise over their lands as lawful forms of ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities may only be allocated land use rights through certificates. The State retains broad authority to recover land use rights granted to communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Constitution of Vietnam, 1992; Art. 4,5, 61-66, 131 Law on Land 2013;
indicators.additional_info: The Constitution vests all land- including forests, rivers, lakes, water resources in the populations, but the state is empowered to manage land and allocate land use rights to communities -Article 4 of the Law on Land 2013). The State shall hand over land use rights to land users in accordance with this Law." Article 5 includes "communities" as a category of land users and defines communities as "Communities, including Vietnamese communities residing in the same village, street quarter or similar residential area sharing the same customs and practices or the same family line." Article 131(3) of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "Communities are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State to preserve national identities associated with the traditions and customs of the people; b) Communities which are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State shall protect the allocated land and may use land for combined purposes of agriculture and aquaculture, but may not use such land for other purposes."

indicators.question: Does the law give indigenous or community land rights the same level of protection as the rights under other tenure systems?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: Communities must be allocated land use rights by the state and granted land use certificates, but the State retains broad authority to take back land allocated to communities.
indicators.additional_info: Art. 26 of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "State protects the lawful rights to use land and land-attached assets of land users." However, the State has broad authority to take back the land from communities for public purposes, violations of land use rights, etc. Article 75(2) grants compensation from expropriation to communities without allocated land that are eligible for a land use certificate, but have not yet been granted that certificate. NOTE: According to USAID article, communities without land use rights are especially vulnerable to encroachment by outsiders (Vietnam Land Tenure Profile: http://www.usaidlandtenure.net/sites/default/files/country-profiles/full-reports/USAID_Land_Tenure_Vietnam_Profile.pdf)

indicators.question: Does the law require the government to provide Indigenous Peoples or communities with a formal title and map to their land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, significant progress
indicators.comment: The law on land provides clear procedures for registering land use rights, and requires the government to obtain detailed information on land parcels. However, there is no legal provision addressing the issue of affordability or accessibility.
indicators.law_and_provision: Arts. 95, 96, Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 95 of the Law on Land provides that "land registration is compulsory for land users and people who are allocated land for management. Registration of ownership of houses and other land-attached assets is conducted at the request of the owner." "Registration of land, houses and other land-attached assets includes the first registration...conducted at the registration organization...in the form of paper or electronic registration." Article 96 of the Law on Land 2013 provides that ". Cadastral records include paper or digital documents which show detailed information on each land parcel, people assigned to manage the land, the land user, the owner of any land-attached asset, land use rights and changes of land use rights, and the ownership of land-attached assets."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are granted legal personality as land users, but they are not legal persons for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 169, Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 169 provides that "communities…may acquire land use rights through the successful conciliation of land disputes which is certified by a competent People's Committee, the decision of a competent state agency or settlement of land disputes, complaints or denunciations, the decision or judgement of a People's Court, or the judgement enforcement decision of the judgement enforcement agency which has been executed."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Authority over community land is vested in representatives or heads of communities. The use rights granted to communities through state-issued certificates entitles holders to sell, rent, exchange, mortgage and exclude others from their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 14, 26 ,131, Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 131(3) of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "communities are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State to preserve national identities associated with the traditions and customs of the people; b) Communities which are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State shall protect the allocated land and may use land for combined purposes of agriculture and aquaculture, but may not use such land for other purposes." Article 26 of the Law on Land 2013 establishes that the state is responsible for adopting policies on...land for community activities for ethnic minorities in conformity with their customs, practices and cultural identities and the practical conditions of each region." Article 14 of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "The State shall decide on land use purposes through master plans and plans on land use, and permit the change of land use purposes."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communities may use agricultural land for a "long and stable term", but community land use rights are not granted for an unlimited duration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 126, Law on Land 2013

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Land 2013 provides communities whose land is recovered or public purposes the right to be consulted on compensation, resettlement, and support. However, the government does not need to obtain the community's consent in order acquire community land use rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 69(2)(a), Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Art. 69(2)(a) provides that "the making and appraisal on plans for compensation, support and resettlement are prescribed as follows: a) The organization in charge of compensation and ground clearance shall make the plan for compensation, support and resettlement and coordinate with the commune-level People’s Committee in the locality to conduct consultations on the plans for compensation, support and resettlement in the forms of meetings with land users living in the recovered area, posting up the plan for compensation, support and resettlement at offices of the commune-level People’s Committee and at common public places of the residential areas of which land is recovered...The consultation results must be recorded in minutes which are certified by representatives of the commune-level People’s Committee and Vietnam Fatherland Front, and land users whose land is recovered."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law establishes that forests can be assigned to village population communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land 2013; Law on Forest Protection and Development 2004
indicators.additional_info: Article 30 of the Law on Forest Protection and Development provides that communities have the right "to have the forest use rights recognized by competent State bodies for stable and long term corresponding to the forest assignment term: to exploit and use forest products and other forest yields for public purposes and domestic use for community members" and other rights. Article 30 further provides that communities that are assigned forests are obligated to formulate forest protection and development rules (to be approved by the People's Committees, to organize forest protection and development, and to fulfill financial and other obligations under the law." Article 29 states that the assignment of forests to village population communities must be in line with approved protection and development plans, and that villages can be assigned forests which are managing efficiently, which lie in areas adjoining villages, communes, etc.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution vests all land- including forests, rivers, lakes, water resources in the populations, but the state is empowered to manage land and allocate land use rights to communities -Article 4 of the Law on Land 2013). The State shall hand over land use rights to land users in accordance with this Law." Article 5 includes "communities" as a category of land users and defines communities as "Communities, including Vietnamese communities residing in the same village, street quarter or similar residential area sharing the same customs and practices or the same family line." Article 131(3) of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "Communities are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State to preserve national identities associated with the traditions and customs of the people..." Under Article 1 of the 1998 Water Resources Act, communities, as citizens of Vietnam, are also granted rights to use water "for life and production"
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Water Resources 1998; Law on Land 2013; Constituon of Vietnam
indicators.additional_info: Article 1 of the 1998 Water Resources Act provides that "1. The water resource comes under the ownership of the entire people under the unified management of the State. 2.Organizations and individuals are entitled to exploit and use the water resource for life and production. At the same time they have the responsibility to protect the water resource, prevent, combat and overcome the harmful effect caused by water as prescribed by law. The State protects the legitimate interests of organizations and individuals in the exploitation and use of the water resource."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land 2013; Law on Forest Protection and Development 2004

Article 96 of the Law on Land 2013 provides that ". Cadastral records include paper or digital documents which show detailed information on each land parcel, people assigned to manage the land, the land user, the owner of any land-attached asset, land use rights and changes of land use rights, and the ownership of land-attached assets."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as a legal person for the purposes of land ownership?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Communities are granted legal personality as land users, but they are not legal persons for purposes of land ownership.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 169, Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 169 provides that "communities…may acquire land use rights through the successful conciliation of land disputes which is certified by a competent People's Committee, the decision of a competent state agency or settlement of land disputes, complaints or denunciations, the decision or judgement of a People's Court, or the judgement enforcement decision of the judgement enforcement agency which has been executed."

indicators.question: Does the law recognize the Indigenous Peoples or community as the legal authority over the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: Authority over community land is vested in representatives or heads of communities. The use rights granted to communities through state-issued certificates entitles holders to sell, rent, exchange, mortgage and exclude others from their land.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 14, 26 ,131, Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Article 131(3) of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "communities are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State to preserve national identities associated with the traditions and customs of the people; b) Communities which are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State shall protect the allocated land and may use land for combined purposes of agriculture and aquaculture, but may not use such land for other purposes." Article 26 of the Law on Land 2013 establishes that the state is responsible for adopting policies on...land for community activities for ethnic minorities in conformity with their customs, practices and cultural identities and the practical conditions of each region." Article 14 of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "The State shall decide on land use purposes through master plans and plans on land use, and permit the change of land use purposes."

indicators.question: Do the law and formal title recognize that indigenous or community land rights may be held in perpetuity?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: Communities may use agricultural land for a "long and stable term", but community land use rights are not granted for an unlimited duration.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 126, Law on Land 2013

indicators.question: Does the law require the consent of Indigenous Peoples or communities before government or an outsider may acquire their land?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The Law on Land 2013 provides communities whose land is recovered or public purposes the right to be consulted on compensation, resettlement, and support. However, the government does not need to obtain the community's consent in order acquire community land use rights.
indicators.law_and_provision: Art. 69(2)(a), Law on Land 2013
indicators.additional_info: Art. 69(2)(a) provides that "the making and appraisal on plans for compensation, support and resettlement are prescribed as follows: a) The organization in charge of compensation and ground clearance shall make the plan for compensation, support and resettlement and coordinate with the commune-level People’s Committee in the locality to conduct consultations on the plans for compensation, support and resettlement in the forms of meetings with land users living in the recovered area, posting up the plan for compensation, support and resettlement at offices of the commune-level People’s Committee and at common public places of the residential areas of which land is recovered...The consultation results must be recorded in minutes which are certified by representatives of the commune-level People’s Committee and Vietnam Fatherland Front, and land users whose land is recovered."

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to all trees on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Partial, limited progress
indicators.comment: The law establishes that forests can be assigned to village population communities.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land 2013; Law on Forest Protection and Development 2004
indicators.additional_info: Article 30 of the Law on Forest Protection and Development provides that communities have the right "to have the forest use rights recognized by competent State bodies for stable and long term corresponding to the forest assignment term: to exploit and use forest products and other forest yields for public purposes and domestic use for community members" and other rights. Article 30 further provides that communities that are assigned forests are obligated to formulate forest protection and development rules (to be approved by the People's Committees, to organize forest protection and development, and to fulfill financial and other obligations under the law." Article 29 states that the assignment of forests to village population communities must be in line with approved protection and development plans, and that villages can be assigned forests which are managing efficiently, which lie in areas adjoining villages, communes, etc.

indicators.question: Does the law explicitly recognize that indigenous or community land rights include the rights to local water sources on the land?
indicators.score_meaning: Yes, the law addresses the issue fully
indicators.comment: The Constitution vests all land- including forests, rivers, lakes, water resources in the populations, but the state is empowered to manage land and allocate land use rights to communities -Article 4 of the Law on Land 2013). The State shall hand over land use rights to land users in accordance with this Law." Article 5 includes "communities" as a category of land users and defines communities as "Communities, including Vietnamese communities residing in the same village, street quarter or similar residential area sharing the same customs and practices or the same family line." Article 131(3) of the Law on Land 2013 provides that "Communities are allocated land or recognized land use rights by the State to preserve national identities associated with the traditions and customs of the people..." Under Article 1 of the 1998 Water Resources Act, communities, as citizens of Vietnam, are also granted rights to use water "for life and production"
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Water Resources 1998; Law on Land 2013; Constituon of Vietnam
indicators.additional_info:
Article 1 of the 1998 Water Resources Act provides that "1. The water resource comes under the ownership of the entire people under the unified management of the State. 
2. Organizations and individuals are entitled to exploit and use the water resource for life 
and production. At the same time they have the responsibility to protect the water 
resource, prevent, combat and overcome the harmful effect caused by water as prescribed 
by law. The State protects the legitimate interests of organizations and individuals in the exploitation and use of the water resource."

indicators.question: Does the law uphold indigenous or community land rights in the ownership and governance of national parks and other protected areas?
indicators.score_meaning: No, the law does not address the issue
indicators.comment: The law does not explicitly grant communities rights in protected areas.
indicators.law_and_provision: Law on Land 2013; Law on Forest Protection and Development 2004
